News.title: Lucy Letby inquiry - latest: Nurse's 'boyfriend' doctor 'put her before patients'
News.content:
Serial killer Letby, now 36, was convicted of killing seven babies and attempting to murder seven more - now a scathing report has criticised the hospital where she worked

An inquiry into the crimes of Lucy Letby - who was convicted of killing seven babies and attempting to murder seven more - has found two of the deaths could have been avoided if hospital staff had acted differently and criticised her doctor "boyfriend".

A scathing report has found there was a "complete failure to protect babies" at the Countess of Chester Hospital where Letby, now 36, worked between 2015 and 2016. It found that, if action had been taken, with Letby moved off the ward, then the deaths of babies referred to as O and P would not have occurred, and neither would attacks on babies J, K, L, M and N.

The inquiry also found that Letby's doctor "boyfriend" consultant paediatrician Dr Mark Deakin, and a colleague of the nurse at the hospital, had blurred boundaries and put his desire to help her above his duties to his patients.

Lady Justice Thirlwall, who chaired the inquiry, said no-one at the hospital seems to have understood "that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt". She added that the "lack of consideration shown to parents" by hospital management was "reprehensible".

The report found that senior nurses never accepted concerns from consultants about Letby were - or might be - justified and that there was a delay in senior management calling the police.

Letby was found to have killed and harmed babies by injecting air into their blood, poisoning them with insulin, and overfeeding them with milk.

News.title: Boy, 14, rushed to hospital with 'serious knife injuries' as two teens arrested
News.content:
Boy, 14, rushed to hospital with 'serious knife injuries' as two teens arrested

A 14-year-old boy was left with "serious" knife injuries in Orton Goldhay, Peterborough. Two other teenagers, also 14, have been arrested

View Image A police cordon was set up in Orton Goldhay

A 14-year-old boy has suffered "serious" knife injuries and has been rushed to hospital with two people arrested.

Emergency services were called to Bushfield in Orton Goldhay, Peterborough at around 4pm on Monday following reports that a teenager had suffered a wound from a knife and he was taken to Peterborough City Hospital.

Cambridgeshire Police described the boy's condition as "serious" but not life threatening.

A cordon was set up on a field at the back of Ormiston Bushfield Academy with an investigation underway into the incident and police have said that there will be additional officers in the area.

Two 14-year-old boys from Peterborough have been arrested with one on suspicion of grievous bodily harm, possession of a knife and theft, and he is being held in custody.

The other was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm and assisting an offender, and he has been bailed until December 14, reported CambridgeshireLive.

A statement from Cambridgeshire Police reads: "We were called at about 4pm yesterday (14 September) with reports of a 14-year-old boy with a knife injury at Bushfield, Orton Goldhay.

"Officers and ambulance attended and the victim was taken to Peterborough City Hospital for treatment for serious, but not life-threatening injuries.

"Two 14-year-old boys from Peterborough have been arrested in connection - one on suspicion of grievous bodily harm, possession of a knife and theft. He remains in custody.

"The other was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm and assisting an offender. He has been released on bail to return 14 December. There will be an additional policing presence in the area today."

News.title: UK mountain rescue teams 'on course for their busiest year on record'
News.content:
UK mountain rescue teams 'on course for their busiest year on record'

Keswick Mountain Rescue Team said August was its busiest month ever with 30 rescues, and Eryri mountain rescue urged walkers to take "personal responsibility" after their highest rescue figures to date in Snowdonia

Injured dog and walker saved from cliff by Derby Mountain Rescue

Mountain rescue teams across the UK are on track for their busiest year on record as they warn they are stretched to the limit.

‌



Keswick Mountain Rescue Team (KMRT) said August was its busiest month ever with 30 rescues. Their volunteers have conducted 136 rescues so far in 2026.

‌



They backed Eryri mountain rescuers who urged walkers to take "personal responsibility" after their highest rescue figures to date in Snowdonia, Wales. Many callouts could have been easily prevented with 'extra planning, reliable navigation backup and the right gear' for changing conditions.

‌



KMRT volunteers are "experiencing the exact same trend" in the Lake District, with 129 callouts in 2025. Other UK teams in England and Wales have said that the rescue levels 'are not sustainable'.

View 2 Images A mountain rescue vehicle in Snowdonia (Image: Daily Post Wales)

"The sheer volume of callouts means our volunteers are being stretched further than ever before," KMRT said in the Facebook post. In 2025, both the Keswick and Coniston teams in Cumbria said they had their busiest year ever, responding to more than 200 incidents between them.

‌



Teams in Llanberis, Wales warned social media images and videos could make difficult and technical routes such as Crib Goch "look like just another route to the summit".

View 2 Images Mountain rescuers in the Lake District (Image: Emma Charvet / SWNS)

Similarly in the Lake District, KMRT said one of its notorious accident black spots was a gully off Blencathra Sharp Edge, a graded technical scramble. Earlier in September, volunteers were called to help two 18-year-olds who "took a tumble" when they decided not to continue with the scramble and descended down the gully.

Article continues below

"Every callout takes our team members away from their jobs, comfort, and families... as the days get shorter and autumn weather sets in, we want to make sure everyone gets home safely," KMRT said.

In January, the Mirror told how two walkers rescued from England's highest peak left a hotel bill unpaid and took head torches belonging to mountain rescuers who had saved their lives. The owner of the Wasdale Head Inn by the 978m (3209ft) high Scafell Pike in the Lake District told how the ungrateful pair, brought down after a seven-hour rescue in freezing temperatures, failed to pay their £130 bill. The Inn helped the men, aged 18-22 and "from the London area", after they were rescued by the Wasdale Mountain Rescue team. Despite promising to settle their bill for a room, they gave the inn false contact details and left without paying a penny.

Well wishers paid the £130 bill, and donated thousands of pounds to the mountain rescue team. One member with 40 years experience said it was the first time anyone rescued had left without paying "in living memory".

News.title: Major hotel chain to open 10 new venues across the UK - full list
News.content:
Major hotel chain to open 10 new venues across the UK - full list

The hotels will open close to stations, motorways, attractions and stadiums

View 3 Images The expansion will create nearly 700 additional rooms, with the hotels expected to begin welcoming guests between late 2026 and 2028

A popular hotel chain has announced plans to open 10 new locations across the UK. The expansion will create nearly 700 additional rooms, with the hotels expected to begin welcoming guests between late 2026 and 2028.

‌



The properties will be positioned near major railway stations, motorways, stadiums, business centres and visitor attractions. Hilton confirmed the hotels will operate under Spark by Hilton, its value-focused “premium economy” brand.

‌



The company says Spark offers reliable and comfortable accommodation at an accessible price, although room rates and individual opening dates have not yet been announced. A total of 672 rooms will be added across nine locations in England and one in Wales.

‌



View 3 Images Hilton confirmed the hotels will operate under Spark by Hilton, its value-focused premium economy brand

The new hotels will open in Cardiff, Coventry, Derby, Doncaster, Hull, Peterborough, Runcorn, Sunderland, Wakefield and Washington. The 10 properties have been signed through an agreement between Hilton and UK hotel owner and operator AG Hotels Group.

‌



Paul Blackmore, vice-president of development for the UK and Ireland at Hilton, said: “With nearly 700 rooms in the pipeline, including the brand’s first hotel in Wales, Spark continues to gain momentum.”

View 3 Images The properties will be positioned near major railway stations, motorways, stadiums, business centres and visitor attractions

News.title: State pension triple lock explained with payments set to rise nearly £500 a year
News.content:
State pension triple lock explained with payments set to rise nearly £500 a year

The triple lock guarantees how much the state pension will go up by every April - but the pledge has become controversial over its affordability

View 2 Images The triple lock is set to push more state pensioners into paying tax (Image: Getty)

The exact amount the state pension is set to rise by under the triple lock has been revealed today.

‌



The state pension is on course to rise by just under £500 a year next year for millions of retirees - but it also means the state pension will be pushed over the tax-free threshold for the first time.

‌



But what exactly is the triple lock and what does it mean for your state pension?

‌



What is the triple lock?

The triple lock ensures that the state pension rises every April by whichever is higher out of inflation (using the previous September inflation figure), wages (average growth between May and July) or 2.5%.

New figures published today show average wage growth, including bonuses, was 3.9% in the three months to July.

In comparison, inflation is currently at 2.9%. This means unless inflation rises sharply, wage growth will likely be used to determine the state pension next April.

‌



We will not know the September inflation figure until it is published in October. The Government will also not officially announce the state pension increase for next year until the Budget.

View 2 Images The state pension rises every year in line with the triple lock (Image: Getty)

So how much will my state pension actually go up by?

The new state pension is currently worth £241.30 a week, so an increase of 3.9% would add £9.40 a week to this figure, taking it to £250.70 a week. This is a cash boost of around £489 a year.

‌



It is worth noting that this is the full amount of state pension you can get. You may receive less state pension depending on your National Insurance contributions. You normally need 35 years of National Insurance years to get the full state pension.

The new state pension applies to men born on or after April 6, 1951, or women born on or after April 6, 1953. Those born before these dates are on the old state pension.

The full basic pension is worth £184.90 a week and if it goes up by 3.9%, this would rise to £192.10 - an increase of around £374 a year.

‌



Get the best deals and tips from Mirror Money WHATSAPP GROUP: Get money news and top deals straight to your phone by joining our Money WhatsApp group here. We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

Will I need to pay tax on my state pension?

The state pension is set to rise above the £12,570 tax-free allowance for the first time next year. The new state pension is currently worth £12,547.60 a year but an increase of 3.9% would see it increase to £13,036.40.

The Treasury has said that people whose only income is the state pension "without any increments" will not have to pay income tax next year. However, it has not specifically set out how this will work.

‌



Pension experts have speculated that this could mean those who deferred their state pension, or receive additional top-ups, may be subject to paying tax.

You get an extra 5.8% added to your state pension for each year you defer receiving your payments. While those on the basic state pension get a bigger boost of 10.4% for every year they defer, or a lump sum plus interest.

They may also receive SERPS or the State Second Pension, which is extra money on top of the basic state pension.

‌



Those who have extra income, such as from a workplace or private pension, will find more of their income is subject to tax.

Why is the triple lock controversial?

The triple lock was introduced in 2011 but has face intense political debate in recent years over questions of its long-term cost.

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that the state pension triple lock will cost around £15.5billion a year by 2030, three times more expensive than originally expected when it was introduced.

‌



The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has previously recommended scrapping the state pension triple lock because it estimates it could add up to £40billion a year to the welfare bill by 2050.

But on the flip side, we are a nation that does not save enough for our retirement - and those in favour of the triple lock say it is vital in preventing older Brits from falling into poverty.

Only 9% of the UK working population is currently on track to achieve a comfortable retirement, according to Pensions UK.

Article continues below

Labour has made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029.

News.title: Kevin Sinfield reveals secret MND charity run weapons include ice baths and special pants
News.content:
Kevin Sinfield reveals secret MND charity run weapons include ice baths and special pants

Ice baths, 'pressure pants' and detailed training plans are among the key aids to Sir Kevin Sinfield's success. But the enduring love from the public and the generosity of his donors are what really keep him going

Kevin Sinfield on his last MND challenge

Sir Kevin Sinfield will use a series of 'secret weapons' in his superhuman fundraising feats for MND research.

‌



Ice baths, 'pressure pants' and detailed training plans are among the key aids to his success. But the enduring love from the public and the generosity of his donors are what really keep him going.

‌



The modest hero revealed yesterday that he thinks of winning the EuroMillions when times get really tough during his ultramarathons. He has seven lined up in seven days for the last of his epic fundraisers in memory of his former teammate Rob Burrow, who died from Motor Neurone Disease in 2024, four-and-a-half years after his devastating diagnosis.

‌



View 2 Images Kevin Sinfield sporting bin bags to cover his footwear as he runs through flood water in Cattal on day seven of the 7 in 7: Together 2025 Challenge in Leeds (Image: PA)

Two dead and four injured after car slams into crowd of people in Doncaster READ MORE :

Sir Kev uses ice baths at the end of every run to aid his recovery. His 'pressure pants' look like a sleeping bag on each leg. They are designed to reduce the lactic acid buildup that causes cramps during such feats of endurance. And his training and recovery plans have extraordinary attention to detail.

"During his playing career, Kevin was renowned for his comebacks from injury," said a team insider. "He would set his alarm through the night if he needed to ice an injury and get up and do it. He would do anything to get on the pitch. He has brought that same attention to detail to his fundraising runs."

‌



Sir Kevin, who admits that he 'does not like running', only started to cover long distances thanks to his training partner Chris Stephenson. Chris persuaded Sir Kev to try a 10k in Brisbane, Australia. And the rest, as they say, is fundraising history.

View 2 Images Sir Kevin Sinfield admitted his gruelling ultra marathon challenges are a "different type of pain" to his rugby league days. (Image: Richard Sellers/PA Wire)

The rugby league legend has raised more than £11million for Motor Neurone Disease research in honour of his old Leeds Rhinos team mate Rob. His 'compression' pants cut down on lactic acid build up and stiffness after his 30-mile daily runs.

‌



But the support from the crowds of well-wishers, MND patients and their families is what really keeps him going.

"The support from the volunteers and people coming out to see us, the team, has been incredible," he said. "And all the experiences in rugby, getting dropped, getting injured. I don't talk about it but those values, support and training have helped me a lot.

"There is so much work that goes into it before you arrive on the start line for Day One, anyone who has trained for a marathon will tell you that."

Article continues below

You can find out full details of this year’s challenge at https://www.therhinos.co.uk/the-club/sinfield-grand-finale

News.title: Crypto billionaires hand Reform more than 10 times what Labour gets from unions
News.content:
Crypto billionaires hand Reform more than 10 times what Labour gets from unions

Donations from crypto billionaires to Reform UK amount to more than 10 times the funding Labour has received from unions, analysis of official data shows

View 2 Images More than half of all political donations since the last election have been made to Reform UK (Image: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Donations from crypto billionaires to Reform UK amount to more than 10 times the funding Labour has received from unions, analysis of official data shows.

‌



More than half of all political donations since the last election have been made to Reform UK. The party made headlines this weekend when it was revealed that they had received two record-breaking donations from their biggest donors.

‌



Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo have each given the party £36million, making them the joint single largest donations in British political history. They eclipsed the previous record of £10million made by Lord John Sainsbury to the Conservative Party in September 2023.

‌



But the latest donations may fall foul of incoming changes to the law that would restrict donations from expats to £100,000. Mr Delo and Mr Harborne's gifts are likely to be affected by the new rules, as they came into effect on March 25, when they were announced.

You can see the donations received by each party since the last general election by using our interactive chart:

‌



If Reform has to hand back the cash, Nigel Farage has threatened to cut off Labour's union funding if his right-wing outfit ever wins power. In an article for The Telegraph, he said: "I would just warn the Labour Party here and now: if you try and ban our donors, we in government would certainly ban funding from the trade unions. I don't want to go down that route. But it is something we would be prepared to do."

Labour’s largest donations since the election have tended to be from the unions. A total of £9million has been received by the party from a variety of different unions.

Reform has received more than 10-times that amount from crypto billionaires, with the latest donations pushing the total to £95million from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo.

‌



Unite the Union has given £2.7million since July 2024. GMB, meanwhile, has donated £1.8million, Union of Shop Distributive and Allied Workers (USDAW) has given £1.8million, UNISON has given £1.6million, while Gary Lubner has given just under £1.4million.

Since the last general election, Reform UK has now received almost £107million. That’s more than half (55%) of all money given to parties in that time, including public funds.

Data from the Electoral Commission shows every donation received by political parties up to the end of June this year.

‌



View 2 Images More than half of all political donations since the last election have been made to Reform UK

Reform UK had received almost a third (28%) of all donations up to that point. The newly announced £72million takes Reform' total to over £107m which dwarfs the amount received by their rivals and is far more than The Conservatives (£37million), Labour (£21million), Lib Dems (£17million), SNP (£2million) and Green (£2million) combined. The Conservative Party have received their largest contribution from public funds.

The House of Commons has given the party almost £9.1million in central funding since the last election. Games software magnate, Jeremy Elliott San, has given the party £3.0million. The National Conservative Draws Society £1.4million, the House of Lords £1.3 million, the House of Commons Fees Office £1.3million, and Mary V Doran £1.1million.

Article continues below

Broaden the timeframe, however, and we see the traditional parties receiving more money. In the whole of 2024, Labour received £42million. The bulk of that (£32million) was in the months leading up to the general election.

The Conservatives received £32million that year, and £48million in 2023.

Reform UK have now received almost £110million since the start of 2021. The Conservatives have received £150million in that time, Labour have received £129million, the Lib Dems £45million, and the Greens £5million.

News.title: Lucy Letby's lawyer issues fiery statement after two top experts quit hours before inquiry verdict
News.content:
Lucy Letby's lawyer issues fiery statement after two top experts quit hours before inquiry verdict

As two experts quit Lucy Letby's defence team over "fundamental unresolvable problems", a bombshell public inquiry has concluded that vulnerable babies could have been saved if hospital bosses hadn't failed to act on warnings

View 3 Images Serial killer nurse Lucy Letby is serving 15 whole-life terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to kill seven others (Image: Countess of Chester Hospital)

Lucy Letby's lawyer has insisted her campaign for freedom has not been undermined after two key experts quit her defence team, warning that some of her legal arguments have "fundamental, unresolvable problems”.

Engineering expert Helen Shannon and bioengineering professor Geoff Chase withdrew from the team on Monday, raising concerns about legal arguments put forward by Letby’s team, adding that it was placing the killer's nurse chances of freedom at "serious, unnecessary, and unacceptable risk."

The former neonatal nurse, who maintains her innocence, is serving 15 whole-life terms for murdering seven babies and the attempted murders of seven others at the Countess of Chester hospital between June 2015 and June 2016.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is currently considering evidence presented on her behalf by an international panel of medics, who claim the infants died of natural causes or poor medical care.

View 3 Images Lead barrister Mark McDonald (second from left) insists Letby's CCRC bid remains strong despite two experts walking away from the defence team (Image: PA Archive/PA Images)

In a joint letter to the CCRC and reported by The Guardian, the two departing experts maintained their belief that two alleged insulin poisonings were "very unlikely."

However, they criticised the wider legal strategy, writing: "Whilst it is entirely legitimate for the defence to advance multiple arguments, some of the other arguments now being put forward we cannot support as scientifically credible and which have, in our view, fundamental unresolvable problems.”

Asked by BBC Newsnight whether their withdrawal undermined Letby’s case, lawyer Mark McDonald said he “fundamentally” disagreed.

“They don’t know what I put into the CCRC because I haven’t told them. So how on earth could they make that conclusion?” he said. “But really, it comes back to this. Both sets of experts say that Lucy Letby is innocent.

“One set of experts remains in the CCRC. One set of experts have withdrawn. But they both are of the same position that whatever happened at the trial, what took place at the trial, was wrong, that the jury was misled.”

McDonald, Letby’s barrister, told the Guardian: "We now have evidence from a number of leading international experts in insulin, endocrinology and laboratory medicine which fundamentally undermines the scientific evidence relied upon at trial. Importantly, the case does not stand or fall on any one expert.

"The strength of the new evidence lies in its breadth and convergence, with independent experts from different disciplines and jurisdictions identifying fundamental problems with the scientific basis upon which the jury were invited to conclude that babies [6] and [12] had been deliberately poisoned.”

The defence split comes as a bombshell public inquiry concluded today that some of Letby's victims could have been saved if hospital managers had acted earlier.

View 3 Images A public inquiry found a "complete failure" of safeguarding leadership at the Countess of Chester Hospital neonatal unit (Image: Cheshire Police)

"There was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital," said Lady Justice Thirlwall.

“This was because no-one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt.

“My report describes dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding.”

Addressing the heart-wrenching legacy of the hospital's inaction, the senior judge added: "How many lives could have been saved had the hospital acted differently? This is something we will never know for sure.

“It is clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier.”

Lady Justice Thirlwall said had neonatal cot video monitors been in place at the time, attacks on four babies would “probably have been detected”. She recommended that all cots and incubators in all neonatal units should be fitted with the monitors.

She said: “This will deter someone who wants to harm a baby and, irrespective of harm, parents will be reassured and may be delighted to see their babies when they cannot be with them.”

‌



She also recommended installing CCTV cameras directed on fridges and other units storing insulin.

Following the findings, Lucy Letby’s barrister said it is "particularly regrettable” that his client could not take part in the inquiry.

In a statement, Mark McDonald said: "This inquiry has proceeded on the wrong premise, and it follows that this has inevitably affected the report as a whole. Errors made at trial have in important respects been repeated in the inquiry’s conclusions, and the alternative narrative identified by nearly 30 internationally renowned experts has not been properly considered.

"I do however wholeheartedly agree with the introduction of CCTV in all neonatal units and cots – this would have significantly impacted the outcome at trial and we would not be where we are today with an innocent woman in prison for crimes she did not commit.

"It is particularly regrettable that Lucy’s application to participate in the Inquiry was rejected. Had she been represented, the inquiry would have been able to hear an alternative account – one that said that insulin results were unreliable, one that said the deaths did not stop when Lucy left the unit and one which, in the view of international experts, provides a fundamentally different and more accurate understanding of what happened.”

News.title: Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry
News.content:
The first three deaths in June 2015 (babies A, C and D) were not viewed as a cluster of deaths, even though this was the annual number of deaths, concentrated into two weeks.

The fourth death, (baby E) in August 2015, was unexpected and therefore reviewed at a serious incident panel meeting attended by the medical director and director of nursing - but it was treated as a formality.

"What is surprising is that no connection was made by any of the people involved to the earlier deaths," Thirlwall noted.

By August of that year, the total of four deaths was the highest since 2008, and was to double by the end of the year.

Thirlwall found that if a doctor â named in the report as Dr ZA - had not disregarded the insulin test result for baby F in August 2015 then there should have been safeguarding action.

The report also found:

The safeguarding action would have prevented the attacks on babies G and H, J, K, L, M and N and the deaths of baby I, O and P

If safeguarding action had been taken by October 2015 - after the death of baby I - by moving Letby off the ward, the deaths of babies O and P would have been prevented, as would the attacks on babies J, K, L, M and N

In, February 2016 Dr Ravi Jayaram should have reported what he had seen with regard to baby K

In May 2016, no-one raised safeguarding at meeting with execs - if they had done it would have prevented the deaths of babies O and P

Thirlwall said it would never be possible to know for sure how many lives could have been saved.

But she found there was a "complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit" at the Countess of Chester Hospital, where Letby, now 36, murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others - one of them twice.

Thirlwall described a system of "dysfunctional management and governance".

She said: "If all the babies whom [Letby] was convicted of murdering were removed from the annual number of deaths in the neonatal unit, the mortality figures would have been three in 2015 and three in 2016 - broadly consistent with previous years," she wrote.

"Since July 2016 there has been one death on the unit, in Sept 2019."

News.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
News.content:
The state pension is expected to top Â£13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by Â£488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

News.title: Five things you may not know about Emmy history-maker Matthew Rhys
News.content:
Rhys' first language is Welsh and regularly speaks it at home in New York.

The passionate Welshman dedicated his second award "to the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurture as anyone else".

"We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible," he said, adding, "diolch yn fawr iawn" which means "thank you very much" in Welsh.

Rhys has also been revealed as the voice of Han Solo in a new Welsh language adaptation of Star Wars.

Star Wars will be dubbed in Welsh for the first time ahead of the sci-fi classic's 50th anniversary next year.

Rhys told New York Times podcast The Interview that the Welsh language project brought up some unexpected feelings.

"What was weird is obviously, they'd had to translate all these things that we'd grown up with, knowing Star Wars," Rhys said.

"I was saying in Welsh things like, 'pelydr cyrchu' - it's kind of like, 'tractor beam'."

He's keen to remain connected to all things Welsh, and in 2025, Rhys took on the role of Welsh icon Richard Burton in the one-man show, Playing Burton, raising funds for the Welsh National Theatre.

Rhys said he first saw the play as a student in London more than 30 years ago and dreamed of portraying Burton ever since.

News.title: Political donors could face tougher residency rules
News.content:
It also wants to introduce a minimum residency period of at least 12 months in which the cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Under the current rules, foreign donations are illegal in the UK, but British voters living abroad can give as much as they want to political parties.

MPs have supported the government's proposals by approving amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. The bill is currently being scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Speaking as the bill was debated by peers, Communities Minister Baroness Taylor of Stevenage said: "We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy."

Baroness Taylor said this was "in addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures that donors contributing above the Â£100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection" to the UK.

Tax is one area that already has residency requirements. The criteria includes someone being declared resident for tax purposes if they have lived in the UK for at least 183 days in the tax year.

Challenged on whether the government was targeting Reform donors, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said policy on donations is "never about one political party or one particular set of issues".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Fundamentally we need to make sure that people who want to influence British politics, who want a say in British politics have a stake in Britain.

"That should apply to everyone and will apply to everyone, so I wouldn't make it about any particular donations or anything that's been in the public domain."

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart accused the government of "playing whack-a-mole", as she said Labour's residency requirements "aren't good enough".

She said: "We must urgently go further and introduce a universal donation cap to stop Trump's America becoming Farage's Britain."

On Monday, Farage criticised the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal.

He told the BBC: "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost Â£43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

News.title: Supreme Court blocks Trump's plan to restrict mail-in ballots
News.content:
About 30% of voters, mostly Democrats, cast postal ballots in the general election two years ago. However, several states like Oregon, Washington, and Colorado rely heavily or entirely on mail ballots for their elections, requiring Republicans to use the system as well.

Seven Republican state election officials warned the justices, external that allowing significant changes to mail ballot rules so close to the midterm elections would "lead to mistakes, delays, and confusion".

Local election officials told the BBC this week they were proceeding as normal but had begun drafting contingency plans in case the court upended existing mail ballot procedures.

The rule changes would have resulted in "thousands of people disenfranchised" in Cherokee County, Georgia, its election director Anne Dover told the BBC. The heavily Republican county voted 69% for Trump in the 2024 election, in which about 10,000 of its residents voted by mail, according to Dover.

Monday's decision earned praise from legal groups who have challenged other aspects of the Trump agenda.

"Today's Supreme Court decision prevents the US Postal Service from sowing chaos in our elections," Trevor Potter, president of Campaign Legal Center, said in a statement.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has sought to restrict voting by mail. While he himself has voted by post, he has long claimed this method allows non-citizens to cast ballots and is prone to fraud.

In March's executive order, the president directed USPS to introduce unique barcodes on postal ballot envelopes.

State and local election officials would also be required to supply information to an online portal about voters who receive mail ballots.

Twenty-three states and Washington DC sued to stop Trump's order.

The postal workers' union also said clerks could not be trained in time for the election.

In court filings, the Trump administration maintained the new USPS rules were constitutional.

It said states "cannot choose to use the federal mails to carry out their elections but then insist that their election-related mail is somehow exempt from the Postal Service's rule-making authority, conferred by Congress".

Boston-based Judge Indira Talwani imposed an injunction on 4 September blocking Trump's order. She ruled that implementing the measures close to November's elections could disenfranchise voters.

Last week, a US appeals court refused to put Judge Talwani's order on hold.

On Sunday, another federal judge, Judge Carl Nichols, ruled against Trump's order.

Some states have already begun distributing mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.

Some states that had not yet sent ballots had already printed their election materials, and changing their voting materials would have required starting the process anew.

"Hypothetically, if we did have to implement, it would have a huge impact, and it would be very costly. At this point, we already have our envelopes printed," Josh Zygielbaum, the Adams County, Colorado clerk and recorder, told the BBC the day before the Supreme Court ruled.

Colorado conducts its elections by mail, and Zygielbaum had been creating contingency plans in the event its voting system had been disrupted.

The Supreme Court decision is not the first setback on postal ballots for Trump.

In June, the justices ruled that states may count ballots postmarked by election day, rejecting the Trump administration's push to block votes being tallied when they are received after polls close.

Trump has previously made false claims that he lost the 2020 election owing to widespread electoral fraud.

News.title: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling admits dangerous driving after M3 crash
News.content:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving after he crashed his Lamborghini into motorway barriers in May.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing on the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May.

Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

Hampshire Police previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision on the M3 southbound, near the Minley interchange.

The force said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

News.title: Two dead after car hits group of pedestrians
News.content:
Two people have died and four have been seriously injured after a car crashed into a group of people in Doncaster.

South Yorkshire Police said officers were called to White Rose Way when a black Mitsubishi L200 hit a group of pedestrians at 11:00 BST on Sunday, before hitting a black Audi and silver BMW on the opposite carriageway.

The force said two of the pedestrians had died at the scene while four other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

The driver of the Mitsubishi, a 30-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and driving while unfit and later released on bail.

News.title: Fall in small boat Channel crossings down to law enforcement, agency says
News.content:
Law enforcement activity has been a "key factor" in reducing the number of small boat Channel crossings, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says.

The number of people arriving in the UK in the first half of 2026 was down 41% on the year before, government figures show.

The NCA said the drop followed a "significant increase in arrests and seizures", although added "fluctuating demand" for crossings, and the French authorities preventing boat launches had also played a role.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, says it is "impossible" to disentangle the effects of government policy and other factors on small boat arrivals.

While recent policy changes appear to have led smugglers and migrants to alter their behaviour, Cuibus says fewer unauthorised arrivals into the EU and developments in key origin countries - such as improved security in Syria - may be partially behind the decline.

"It is hard to know how much restrictive measures contributed to reducing [arrivals] in 2026," he continues.

He said limitations on refugee family reunion and a reduction in the asylum grant rate could also have had an impact.

The Conservatives have previously said the weather played a huge role in the fluctuating numbers of crossings from France and Belgium.

NCA director general of operations Rob Jones said the agency was "devoting more resources to tackling organised immigration crime than ever before".

"That is bringing results.

"However, we are not complacent, and the job is by no means done," he continued.

"We must continue to keep up the pressure on these criminal gangs, as they continue to put lives at risk in the Channel."

News.title: Harry and Meghan change children's school over security concerns due to traffic
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have changed their children's school only days after they first started over security concerns about traffic during the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

It's understood that the security for the children meant travelling with another car, and that driving in convoy proved difficult in the busy school run traffic.

The checks on the route are believed to have initially taken place before term time, but with the school traffic it was deemed not safe enough.

A source close to the couple said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements."

They added: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It has also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

News.title: We must heed warnings of AI tech developers, says UK minister
News.content:
The UK government must "heed the warnings" of "those who are at the forefront" of developing artificial intelligence (AI) technology, a senior minister will say later.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh will address the growing anxiety over AI safety when she speaks at the TUC congress on Tuesday.

She is expected to say the government is "ready to work with international partners" to prioritise public safety and national security.

Fears about the potential dangers of AI have ramped up in recent days after executives and current and former staff in the field warned the tech could endanger humanity.

On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the recent discussion of the risks, with his spokesperson saying: "It's a good thing that the companies developing the most advanced AI systems are now talking openly about the risks as well as the opportunities."

Speaking at the TUC congress later on Tuesday, Haigh is also expected to acknowledge the benefits, saying: "AI has enormous potential to transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs."

In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said people should "never be complacent" about the impact AI might have but "we've got to be careful not to get hyperbolic about this either".

"Of course there are risks but, let's be frank, there are some tremendous upsides, whether it's public services, healthcare, the contribution to the economy," he added.

News.title: Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high
News.content:
The number of people claiming Personal Independence Payments (Pip) in England and Wales has hit a record high, according to new government figures.

As of July, just over four million people were entitled to claim the benefit, compared to 3.83 million the previous year, an increase of 7%, data from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) showed.

Pip is designed to support people with the extra costs of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions, and eligibility is not affected by a person's income or savings.

In July, Sir Stephen Timms, who is leading a review on Pip, said in his interim report that the system was "not fit for purpose".

Of the 4.1 million claimants, those aged 50 and above accounted for more than half.

Just under three in ten were aged 30 to 49, while 17% of claimants were aged 16 to 29.

Pip seeks to offset the extra costs that can occur for those living with certain long-term health conditions.

According to the charity Scope, the extra cost of being disabled â known as the disability price tag â has reached more than Â£1,100 a month.

Pip has been in the spotlight since the summer of 2025 when the government, led by former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, proposed reforming and tightening eligibility criteria for the benefit as the cost of running the system increased.

Spending on Pip stood at Â£16.3bn in 2019-20, when adjusted for inflation to today's prices, and had increased to Â£27.3bn by 2024-25, government figures showed.

It is currently forecast to rise to Â£41.5bn by 2030-31.

News.title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules
News.content:
Trade unions are putting pressure on the government to soften proposed changes to immigration rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.

If the plans are approved, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for permanent residence, rather than five years, while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.

The proposals were announced last year by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, who has kept the same role under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Delegates at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) backed a motion calling for any changes affecting workers already in the UK to be withdrawn.

A government spokesperson said ministers had received 200,000 responses to a consultation on the proposals, which was launched under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, and they were carefully considering them.

Mahmood has previously defended the plans, saying the "unprecedented" number of people arriving in the UK demands an answer from the government.

Under the government's proposals the standard wait to qualify for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, would increase to 10 years.

People who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years.

Indefinite leave to remain gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

The changes would not apply to people who have already obtained settlement but would cover people already living in the UK, including those who had been expecting to get permanent residence in the coming months.

Some Labour MPs have also criticised plans for the changes to apply to migrants already in the UK.

Earlier this year, when she was a backbench MP and not a government minister, Angela Rayner, herself a former care worker, labelled the proposals "un-British".

Rayner, who has since been appointed housing secretary by Burnham, warned that "moving the goalposts undermines our sense of fair play".

At the time, Burnham, who was still Greater Manchester mayor, said he understood where Rayner was "coming from" and that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

News.title: Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language
News.content:
Ecology and wildlife experts hope to use the discoveries to help rebuild oyster populations in suitable coastal locations.

The recent findings marked the culmination of several years worth of hard work, titled Project Eisirean.

It is a collaboration between ecology and environment researchers, Gaelic and education experts at the University of Glasgow and local community organisations on the west coast of Scotland.

Dr Anna McGregor, an expert in coastal ecology and a lecturer at the University of Glasgow , had the original idea of locating oysters through traditional place-names, then applying scientific techniques to confirm oyster presence within them.

She explained: "This is a really exciting outcome, for a project that started off looking for the historic distribution of oysters along the West Coast.

"We thought that as native oysters are now really rare throughout Europe, is there a way to look where they used to be, using people's memory and understanding - that can come through place names.

"We found two areas with oyster in the name, both on Mull, and after about two years we found another one on Lewis. Then we broadened the search to look for habitat related names, like sand banks."

The group then examined those locations for factors like the sea bed and the level of the water flow.

News.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
News.content:
Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

News.title: US drinks giant completes purchase of viral Au Vodka brand for £300m
News.content:
US drinks giant Sazerac said it has "big plans" for Au Vodka after completing a takeover reported to value the Welsh business at about Â£300m.

The Swansea-based vodka brand, known for its gold packaging and viral social media campaigns, was founded by friends Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn in 2015.

With investment from DJ Charlie Sloth it enjoyed rapid growth before being formally acquired by one of the world's largest spirits companies.

Financial terms have not been disclosed, but the Reuters news agency reported the deal values Au Vodka at about Â£300m ($405m).

Sazerac chief executive Jake Wenz said Au had enjoyed a "phenomenal growth trajectory" since it was founded in Swansea.

"Au Vodka is a brand we've long admired," he said.

"What Charlie, Jackson, and Charlie have achieved in just over a decade is spectacular and rare, and we have big plans for Au as we welcome the brand into the Sazerac family."

News.title: Balaclava ban aims to address 'substantial' problems
News.content:
Offenders wearing balaclavas to hide their identity cause "substantial" problems in Nottingham, a police chief has said as a new ban came into force in the city.

Nottingham has become one of the first cities in the UK to introduce restrictions on balaclavas, allowing police and community protection officers to ask people to remove them if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or anti-social behaviour.

Anyone who refuses to comply could face a Â£70 fixed penalty notice or be prosecuted, with courts able to impose a maximum fine of Â£1,000.

Supt Chris Pearson said an "awful lot of people" described being intimidated by balaclavas.

The enforcement will not apply to face coverings worn for legitimate reasons, including religious, cultural, health, work, weather or personal safety reasons.

It will be up to officers to determine whether or not coverings are being worn legitimately.

Pearson, who is the city commander for Nottinghamshire Police, said: "We've seen ourselves, CCTV and video footage of people wearing balaclavas, throwing fireworks, chucking things off the roofs of buildings.

"[The problem] is substantial. They are predominantly very young people, normally young males wearing balaclavas, and sadly, in a lot of circumstances, they are involved in drug dealing, carrying weapons."

President Donald Trump dismissed warnings Monday that the rise of AI could lead to robots marching on U.S. cities — just a week after sharing an AI-generated image depicting exactly that.

The 80-year-old’s robot remarks came hours after he posted a series of comments on Truth Social, dismissing concerns about AI and data centers as a “hoax,” and comparing them to past warnings about climate change. He also accused those raising such concerns of being “revolutionaries” working against American interests.

“I am the Hoax Buster, and I’m right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!” Trump wrote around 4:30 p.m. Monday.

“This is even wilder than the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX, or the Global Warming Scam. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” he added.

The post appears to contradict an image Trump shared last week depicting him walking through a dystopian Washington, D.C., surrounded by armed humanoid robots and spider-like machines with glowing red eyes. The U.S. Capitol looms in the background and a caption below reads: “THEY WILL NEVER SLEEP AGAIN.”

open image in gallery Trump posted an AI-generated photo of him marching with robots to Truth Social September 6 ( Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump )

Debate over the risks of rapidly advancing AI have intensified following warnings from researchers and some of the industry’s most prominent executives.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for AI companies to deliberately “slow the pace” of increasingly powerful models, warning that progress could soon outpace efforts to make the technology safe. Amodei said AI agents could potentially cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage within months if they were able to operate across the internet.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI CEO Elon Musk and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis have also backed the need to pace AI development.

Trump, however, rejected calls for new guardrails, saying the U.S. already has “tremendous” criminal and regulatory powers over AI companies and that the only guardrail the technology needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump dismissed AI fears as a ‘hoax’ Monday, including warnings that robots could eventually march into U.S. cities, just days after sharing an AI-generated image depicting that scenario ( AP )

"The Trump Administration has stopped AI 'people' from doing bad, or potentially bad, 'things,' like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel' — and we will continue to do so!" Trump wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!"

He also argued that slowing AI development could allow China to overtake the U.S. in the technology race.

Trump’s posts also targeted concerns over the growing number of AI data centers, calling opposition to both the technology and its infrastructure part of a “SICK conspiracy” and arguing that AI and data centers could become the greatest economic development engine in history.

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Kelly Osbourne has revealed that she became “a shell of” herself after her father Ozzy’s death and lost “a lot of friends” while grieving.

The Prince of Darkness and Black Sabbath frontman died aged 76 in July last year. His cause of death was a heart attack, after suffering a number of health problems over the years, including complications from Parkinson’s disease, sepsis, blood clots, pneumonia and a back injury.

His daughter Kelly, 41, has now shared that she no longer speaks to certain people who expected her to “be over” her father’s death, having struggled in the aftermath.

Speaking on Paul C Brunson’s podcast We Need to Talk, Kelly said: “I was a shell of myself. I couldn’t speak. I couldn’t eat. I couldn’t do anything. I was just empty.

open image in gallery Osbourne spoke to Paul C. Brunson about struggling to cope after father Ozzys's death ( YouTube: We Need to Talk )

“Broken in every way a human being could possibly be broken and completely unable to even take care of myself. I was at ground zero. I started drinking again. I lost my mind. I couldn’t handle it.”

The reality TV star has previously spoken about her addiction issues, having been a heroin user as a teenager and also struggling with alcohol. In 2021, she said she had relapsed after four years of sobriety.

Adding that she has now been sober for eight months, Kelly said that she has “the most incredible people” around her but that she “lost a lot of friends” while grieving. “I closed my circle because I lost a lot of friends because people don’t like sadness and they expected me to be over it,” she said. “I will never be over it. I will never, ever be over it.”

The former Fashion Police presenter, who recently split from her partner Sid Wilson, also revealed that she’s “not close” to her older sister Aimée – the eldest of Ozzy’s children with wife Sharon, who has always stayed out of the limelight.

open image in gallery Sharon and Ozzy Osbourne with Kelly, Jack and Aimee as children ( PA )

“If I’m honest, my older sister didn’t really ever acknowledge me and my brother,” Kelly said, referring to her younger brother, Jack. “She was just in her own world doing her own thing. I do to a certain extent, if I’m honest, feel as though she was embarrassed of us. The whole family.

“We’re very different. I never got a big sister and I had to learn how to do certain things that a big sister should have taught you on my own. I do have a resentment there. I’ll have that forever.”

When asked whether there was hope for a reconciliation, she said “No. I respect her and I accept her but we’re different.”

Earlier this month, Kelly addressed concerns surrounding her weight loss after Ozzy’s death, revealing that she had “no idea” how thin she had become.

In an interview with The Mail on Sunday, she said that she “couldn’t see what other people saw” because she was in so much pain. “All I saw was a broken person,” she added.

If you have been affected by this article, you can contact the following organisations for support: actiononaddiction.org.uk, mind.org.uk, nhs.uk/livewell/mentalhealth, mentalhealth.org.uk.

If you or someone you know is suffering from alcohol addiction, you can confidentially call the national alcohol helpline Drinkline on 0300 123 1110 or visit the NHS website here for information about the programmes available to you.

News.title: Rob Reiner’s son in court today as prosecutors weigh death penalty for parents’ murder
News.content:

Nick Reiner, the 33-year-old son of famed filmmaker Rob Reiner and photographer Michele Reiner, is set to appear in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom today for a high-stakes pretrial hearing following his grand jury indictment for the brutal murders of his parents inside their Brentwood home.

The grand jury unsealed a multi-count indictment charging Nick Reiner with two counts of murder with special circumstances, alleging he personally used a knife to slaughter his 78-year-old father and 70-year-old mother. Prosecutors allege the killings involved lying in wait, extreme violence, and "a high degree of cruelty, viciousness, or callousness" against particularly vulnerable victims. The indictment bypasses a preliminary hearing and moves the case straight to trial.

Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Sam Ohta conditionally sealed the grand jury transcripts following defense motions aimed at preserving trial fairness. Prosecutors noted that the victims' surviving children, Jake and Romy Reiner, requested the transcripts remain private to avoid additional trauma. District Attorney Nathan Hochman called the slayings "a profound betrayal," confirming his office is evaluating whether to seek the death penalty.

open image in gallery The grand jury unsealed a multi-count indictment charging Nick Reiner with two counts of murder with special circumstances, alleging he personally used a knife to slaughter his 78-year-old father and 70-year-old mother ( Reuters )

Autopsy records show the couple died from "multiple sharp force injuries." LAPD officers arrested Nick Reiner near USC less than six hours after his sister discovered the bloody scene on Dec. 14. He remains held without bail.

Meanwhile, a bitter legal fight brews over Nick Reiner's access to a $1.5 million trust fund his parents established in 1993. Defense attorneys argue the mandatory inheritance is needed to retain private counsel after prominent lawyer Alan Jackson left the case for nonpayment. However, access to the funds faces hurdles under California’s "slayer statute," which bars killers from profiting from their victims' estates.

open image in gallery Rob Reiner and wife, Michelle, arrive at "Turn Up the Heat- Fight Global Warming", a benefit to help the Natural Resources Defense Council in 2003 ( Getty )

Reports reveal tension boiled over the night before the murders at a holiday party hosted by Conan O'Brien, where Rob Reiner reportedly argued with his son over erratic behavior. Sources indicate Nick Reiner, who has a documented history of severe drug addiction, homeless spells, and a schizophrenia diagnosis, checked into a Santa Monica hotel hours later, where police subsequently discovered blood.

Rob Reiner, the iconic star of All in the Family and legendary director of The Princess Bride and When Harry Met Sally, married Michele Singer in 1989. The double homicide has devastated Hollywood and left the surviving family pleading for privacy.

Michael Carrick hopes Manchester United can harness the frustration from Sunday's costly derby defeat to reignite their stuttering campaign when they host Brighton in the Carabao Cup.

After restoring optimism and securing Champions League football last term, the atmosphere around Old Trafford has soured following a sluggish start that has yielded only four points from four Premier League fixtures.

United delivered a subdued performance in Sunday’s 1-0 home loss to Manchester City, failing to take advantage of Phil Foden’s early red card before Erling Haaland scored a contentious winning goal.

Pro Ref later contacted United to acknowledge an "error of judgment", having allowed the goal to stand despite an offside interference by Enzo Fernandez in the build-up going unchecked.

"We’ve got to move on," Carrick said regarding the defeat. "We’ve still got to look at it for ourselves and we’ve got to win games. We have done, we’ve won a lot of games and we need to continue to do that.

open image in gallery Erling Haaland scored a controversial winner against United on Sunday ( PA Wire )

"I understand it’s a new season, it’s a fresh season and the points tally right now is not what we want it to be, so I’m not hiding from that.

"But it’s more of getting winning games, getting that feeling, getting the habit. It’s easier said than done, of course it is, but we’re capable of it."

United defender Lisandro Martinez branded the derby decision "unacceptable" and an "injustice" – a sense of grievance Carrick wants his side to use as motivation on Wednesday.

"The players have got an edge," he said. "I think they’ve shown that to me since I’ve been here. We’ve had setbacks and they’ve bounced back particularly well and had some really good performances and good results, so they’ve got an edge.

"It does give you something when something like that happens (on Sunday) to use moving forward."

They will require that resolve against a Brighton side who head to Old Trafford following a 5-0 win at Coventry on Sunday. The Seagulls have won four of their past five visits to the stadium across all competitions.

The most recent of those victories came in the FA Cup in January, just prior to Carrick taking over, compounding a miserable domestic cup run that included an early Carabao Cup exit at Grimsby.

Avoidable errors aside, the necessity of silver success remains paramount for Carrick.

open image in gallery Brighton have a strong record at Old Trafford in recent times ( PA Wire )

"For me, trophies is the beauty and the feeling of winning is what we’re in football for, what we’re in sport for, and certainly what I’m at this club for is to try and win," the former United midfielder said. It’s not straightforward and you decide you want to win and you go and win. Of course not.

"But it’s important and I think trophies and achieving things and giving supporters that feeling of the emotion of that is important, definitely."

Carrick indicated Luke Shaw "could possibly be fit" to feature against the Seagulls, though it remains "not clear-cut". Meanwhile, £70 million summer recruit Carlos Baleba will not face his former side as he recovers from an ankle injury.

The United boss added: "He’ll be back in and around the group at some point over the next week or so, so that means after international (break) he should be in good shape."

News.title: Trump interrupts live event to claim AI concerns are ‘hoax’
News.content:
Donald Trump called Nvidia's CEO during a summit, claiming that concerns over artificial intelligence are a "hoax."

The US president made a surprise call to Jensen Huang as he spoke at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday (14 September).

After being put on speakerphone, Trump downplayed concerns about AI and the data centers that run it.

Trump said: “The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax.”

He added that data centers are "great" and make people and states "wealthy."

News.title: Lucy Letby: The hospital bosses sorry for ‘significant delay’ in alerting police
News.content:
For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Former senior managers at the hospital where Lucy Letby murdered seven babies and attempted to kill a further seven gave evidence at the Thirwall Inquiry, which investigated how they handled the case.

Among them were former chief executive Tony Chambers, former medical director Ian Harvey and former director of nursing Alison Kelly - who were all in post at the Countess of Chester Hospital when Letby committed her crimes.

At the beginning of the inquiry, held at Liverpool Town Hall, the trio issued an apology for not alerting Cheshire Police sooner to concerns over Letby. Reading parts of a statement on their behalf, Kate Blackwell KC said they felt they had needed to first investigate concerns to gain potential evidence of wrongdoing before contacting police.

Ms Blackwell said: “This was a cause of a significant delay in contacting the police and for this, they [the managers] are truly sorry.

“But the reviews were commissioned in good faith, not to conceal the truth but to uncover it... on the issue of when such matters should be properly brought to the police in a hospital setting, guidance is overdue and such recommendations as the inquiry sees fit will be well appreciated.”

Concerns were first voiced over Letby at the end of June 2016 - before almost a year later, in May 2017, police were formally called in to investigate.

Here we look at the roles of key management members at the hospital:

Tony Chambers

open image in gallery Tony Chambers ( Supplied )

Tony Chambers was chief executive at the Coutness of Chester Hospital at the time Letby murdered seven babies in 2015 and 2016. He resigned in September 2018.

He began his evidence at the inquiry by apologising to the families of Letby’s victims. “Right at the outset I just want to offer my heartfelt condolences to the families whose babies are at the heart of this inquiry,” he said.

“I can’t imagine the impact this has had on your lives and I am truly sorry for the pain that may have been prolonged by any decisions or actions I took in good faith.”

He said he first knew of concerns from consultant paediatricians over Letby harming babies in late June 2016.

Letby was redeployed to an administrative role when she returned from annual leave in July.

However, she was due to go back to the unit weeks before the police were finally called in by the hospital in May 2017 after bosses had instead opted to commission a series of reviews to look at the increased mortality.

When detectives began investigating, Mr Chambers told them the executives “felt that the explanations for what had happened do not lie in a single place or cause and are certainly not criminal”, the inquiry heard.

Mr Chambers said: “I think it’s fair to say that we were very much taking the independent experts’ view that there were no unnatural causes of deaths identified, there were two cases that were unascertained.”

He told the inquiry his biggest personal failing was the communications with families which “could and should have been better”. He also accepted that the trust’s systems failed and “there were opportunities missed to take earlier steps to identify what was happening”.

Ian Harvey

open image in gallery Ian Harvey ( Thirwall Inquiry )

Ian Harvey was the hospital’s medical director. He left his post to retire in August 2018.

He had held other managerial roles within the trust and was medical director for six years.

Concerns over Letby were raised with Mr Harvey by neonatal clinical lead Dr Stephen Brearey in May 2016, the inquiry heard, with Dr Brearey saying the number of deaths in 2015 and early 2016 was “exceptional”. He also highlighted the only common theme was the association with Letby being on duty

But giving evidence, Mr Harvey said that “did not accord with my recollection of that meeting” and he did not remember Dr Brearey being “that detailed or that assertive”.

He added: “At no stage during this meeting did I feel that it was being reported because there was worry that Letby was responsible for the deaths.”

Mr Harvey went on to commission the series of reviews into the increased mortality as Cheshire Constabulary was not called in to investigate the matter until almost a year later. Consultants pressed on with expressing their concerns amid dropped plans in early 2017 to return Letby to the neonatal unit, the inquiry has heard.

Mr Harvey said: “One of the greatest regrets of my career is the breakdown in communication between the executives and paediatricians, and with me in particular.

“I recognise how intense and difficult a situation that was.”

Alison Kelly

open image in gallery Alison Kelly ( Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust/YouTube )

Alison Kelly was director of nursing at the hospital before resigning in 2021.

She went work as director of nursing at the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Salford Royal Hospital and Royal Oldham Hospital. The trust said Ms Kelly no longer worked for them when asked this week.

The inquiry heard how Letby was moved off the unit in July 2016 to an administrative role after consultant paediatricians told Ms Kelly and other senior managers at the end of June that they were concerned she may be deliberately harming infants.

Police were not formally called in to investigate until May 2017 after the hospital bosses opted to commission the series of reviews.

Ms Kelly, who as part of her role was the executive lead for safeguarding children, told the inquiry she never regarded the increase in deaths as a safeguarding matter which could have led to contact with the police earlier.

When asked if she failed to take appropriate steps and trigger the safeguarding process while presented with concerns, she said: “Yes, that is one of the things that I have spent a lot of time reflecting on but at the time it didn’t feel obvious.

“There were lots of things going on and now I know so much more information it seems obvious to me that that should have happened.”

When consultants told Ms Kelly and senior managers of a pattern of six out of nine deaths occurring at night, and that the pattern stopped when Letby was moved to days, she told the inquiry that “we needed to get more facts” to gain a fuller picture.

She said: “I think we needed to look at everything in the round in terms of clinical outcomes as well as looking at one individual. I didn’t take the hearsay of consultants as evidence at the time.”

News.title: Man who approached young girls and asked to sniff their feet named and pictured
News.content:
