Sports.title: Hunt reiterates need for 'role models' after Sweeney advert backlash
Sports.content:
Amy Hunt at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship

Amy Hunt fears Sydney Sweeney's controversial betting advert could become a "barrier" to young girls wanting to play sport.

Sweeney's new advert for American betting company Novig, which features the Euphoria star wearing little to no clothing and covering herself with sports equipment, has received a significant backlash from the female sporting community.

Hunt had already hit back by telling the Hollywood actress that "this is what women in sport look like" after finishing fourth in the 200m at the the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest at the weekend.

"When we're trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it's about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like," Hunt said on Good Morning Britain.

"When we see the the stats of 64 per cent of young girls drop out of exercise and sport before they reach the age of 16, we don't need to place any kind of barrier whatsoever in their way in terms of providing the opportunity and the empowerment for them to still exercise, whatever that looks like, professional or kind of just going to do a ParkRun with your friends.

"It's about empowering young girls and young women and young people to show that you really can just get out there and you don't have to worry what you look like, you don't have to worry about what you're wearing.

Hunt won four golds at the European Championships last month

"Sport, it's not pretty, and that's the thing to get to the level that we're at. It's shown to people that being aspirational and trying to be elite is something amazing, and you should really want to be the best version of yourself you can be.

"And that doesn't always look attractive, and that doesn't always look nice. Sometimes it looks like throwing up in the corner of the track, or I've had sessions this year where I've been crying afterwards."

Hunt was not alone in voicing her criticism of the advert.

Former US Olympic gymnast Gracie Kramer posted a video of her competing with the caption: "Idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing but this is what a woman in sport looks like."

Australian boxer Skye Nicolson also wrote on Instagram: "There's a big difference between looking 'sexy' because you do sport compared to using sex to sell 'sport'."

Sweeney, in a possible response to the criticism, posted a series of images from ESPN Magazine's BODY Issue which included nude images of the likes of Serena Williams and Megan Rapinoe to her Instagram stories.

Hunt is one of Britain's biggest stars in athletics

Hunt believes the positivity of women in sport speaking out against the advert has already overtaken any negative impact.

"The reaction has almost outweighed the moment because the first thing I saw was all of the positive compilations of women in sport," she added.

"It's actually kind of moved. It's separated itself from from the moment entirely, and it's not anything personal against that actress.

"It's more the the kind of intention, and it's just moved into a completely different spin now, where we're able to kind of have all these different things celebrating women's sport."

Sports.title: Craig Bellamy says he rejected Burnley manager’s job to stay in ‘right place’ with Wales
Sports.content:
Craig Bellamy said he rejected the chance to take charge of Burnley in the summer after deciding the Wales job is “the right place for me”. The 47-year-old was among the managers targeted by the Championship club, who appointed Nicky Hayen.

Bellamy is preparing to lead Wales in the Nations League, with next Thursday’s trip to Portugal the first of four matches across the extended international break. Bellamy spent two years on the staff at Burnley, working as an assistant to Vincent Kompany and taking caretaker charge after Kompany left for Bayern Munich. Burnley were granted permission to hold talks with him after a triggering release clause in his Wales contract.

“This is the first time I’m talking about it and I made the decision to stay because this is the right place for me,” Bellamy said. “There’s only one person you have to prove [something] to, and that’s to yourself, your morals, what you live by. I’ve never moved for money, I’ve never done anything for money and I ain’t going to change now.

“I’m comfortable with myself, I’m comfortable with the decision I’ve made and I have always been committed in everything I do, that hasn’t changed. I said: ‘No, it’s not for me.’ There was no walking away from discussions. It wasn’t for me. It was that simple.”

Bellamy revealed, when addressing a question about his decision to remain silent in recent months, that he spent a week in intensive care last summer after rupturing his appendix before Wales won in Kazakhstan last September.

“I try to stay quiet, mostly,” he said. “I feel like I’ve got nothing worth saying when I’m not working … l lead a very boring life. I’m sorry if it looks that way [that I have been quiet]. I’ve really enjoyed this summer and got a hang of it. I’ve enjoyed my time with the family and my time working as well.”

Sports.title: How Promise David emerged from Maltese shadows into the Premier League
Sports.content:
Promise David had a five-year plan. He would score bags of goals, earn a transfer to a top European league and play for Canada at the 2026 World Cup. There was just one problem: apart from his parents, teammates and coaches, no one in soccer seemed to know his name.

It was 2023, and the striker was scrapping for minutes in Estonia’s Meistriliiga – a league small enough that streaming services didn’t bother with its matches. He was 22 and already a football nomad. He had been cut from his home town club’s academy. Passed over by NCAA college programs. Relegated to the reserve squad of almost every club he played for.

Even to an optimist, the prospect of playing at a World Cup – let alone a move to the Premier League – was about as distant as Brighton’s shores from David’s home town of Brampton, Ontario. But then, David has never minded the road less travelled.

“He’s worked a lot to get where he is,” says Kaido Koppel, David’s former head coach at Estonia’s Nomme Kalju. “It’s not by accident.”

That perseverance has paid off: David’s loan from Royale Union Saint-Gilloise to Brighton, if made permanent, may yet become the second-most expensive Canadian soccer player transfer in history, after the $34m move of Jonathan David (no relation) from Gent to Lille in 2020. This past summer, Promise David became the fifth Canadian ever to score at a men’s World Cup. Another appearance in 2030 seems likely.

Even to those who have known the wandering striker since the beginning, his rapid ascent has defied expectations. And now the biggest question is what comes next.

View image in fullscreen Promise David turned heads with impressive performances for Royale Union Saint-Gilloise in Belgium. Photograph: Luc Claessen/BELGA/AFP/Getty Images

‘He’s not missing’

David, born Promise Oluwatobi Emmanuel David Akinpelu, is used to being overlooked. He was cut from Toronto FC’s academy at age 15. He was a riddle for coaches: smart and preternaturally gifted, but – like many a teenager – unfocused.

He was “never on time for anything”, laughs Jorden Feliciano, who coached a teenaged David at Vaughan SC, where he played after getting cut by Toronto FC.

Still, Feliciano says, “the kid could turn it on when he wanted”.

Vaughan, a semi-pro soccer club north of Toronto, has a reputation as one of Canada’s best incubators for men’s and women’s talent, having produced the likes of Celtic’s Alistair Johnston and Chelsea’s Kadeisha Buchanan.

“On the field, you never really knew what you were getting from him,” says Stefan Copetti, David’s teammate at Vaughan. “Either he was going to come off the bench and score two goals, or kind of just coast around.”

Still, Copetti says, “When he’s in front of goal, he’s not missing.”

View image in fullscreen Promise David, back row, center, pictured with Vaughan SC in 2019. Photograph: Courtesy Jorden Feliciano

Most of David’s teammates at Vaughan earned full-ride scholarships to US college soccer programs. He received one offer: a partial scholarship to Appalachian State University. At the suggestion of a trainer, he took a shot at a Toronto-area talent showcase hosted by NK Hrvatski Dragovoljac, a second-tier Croatian club. He impressed the scouts and club president Niko Tokic Kartelo enough to earn an invite to their youth academy in Zagreb. But as soon as David landed in Croatia, Kartelo was ousted from his role. The club offer fell through. The ex-president took David into his home.

“I could not simply abandon [him] in a foreign country,” Kartelo says. He tried to find David another playing opportunity in Croatia, but met closed doors.

“No club wanted him,” he says.

David landed in Croatia’s third division, but left after getting little playing time. His journey continued, first to FC Tulsa in the USL Championship, and then, in 2022, to Valletta in the Maltese Premier League. He arrived as a 21-year-old with dwindling hopes of a pro career, and wasted no time making an impression. He scored a 90th-minute equalizer in his third match for the club, then followed up with another goal in his next match. In 14 appearances, he notched four goals and assists apiece, including the goal that sent Valletta to the Maltese FA Trophy final.

“Lots of clubs try to get these tall, physical strikers,” says Valletta forward Andrea Zammit, a former teammate, “but how ‘Tobi’ was built – 6 ft 5in, physical, a good finisher – it’s quite rare to find someone like that.”

View image in fullscreen Promise David scored Canada’s goal against Switzerland at the 2026 World Cup. Photograph: Sarah Stier/FIFA/Getty Images

From Estonia to the World Cup

David parlayed his scoring burst with Valletta into a two-year deal with fellow Maltese club Sirens FC. He left after seven months, six goalless appearances, and just 135 minutes total before moving to Estonia.

He arrived at Nomme Kalju with “some things to work on”, Koppel says. David could outmuscle most defenders, but his defensive effort lapsed. Koppel played Promise with the reserves, a team of mostly high schoolers.

“It was like he got pissed off,” Koppel says, “and decided to make his mark.”

David netted 22 goals in 19 matches with the reserves, then added seven more with the first team. He wrote “2026” on his locker and went on a scoring tear that hasn’t ended. In 2024, he notched 14 goals and three assists in just 16 appearances. It earned him a move to Belgium’s Royale Union Saint-Gilloise, where he earned the nickname “Baby Lukaku” for his head-turning finishes. He bagged a brace against Gent to earn Union their first Belgian Pro League title since 1935. He scored at PSV Eindhoven in his Champions League debut. He scored again at Galatasaray, ending a 33-match home unbeaten run for the reigning Turkish champions. He scored with defenders tearing off his shirt.

David’s nose for goal – and his off-the-cuff interviews – made him a fast favorite among Union supporters. In recent years, that same joie de vivre has turned him into one of the emerging faces of Canada’s national team.

“It’s his personality that gets you,” says Feliciano. “He’s funny, he’s goofy, he’s always in a good mood.”

David earned his first call-up from Jesse Marsch in 2025. He scored against Ukraine in his debut for Canada and managed to earn a World Cup roster spot despite rupturing a hip tendon mere months before the tournament. There, he dispelled any lingering doubts about his abilities. In their opener against Bosnia and Herzegovina, he assisted Cyle Larin on Canada’s lone goal a mere 17 minutes after subbing on for Jonathan David. Two matches later against Switzerland, he scored on his first touch of the match, an outside-of-the-boot volley that sent Vancouver’s BC Place into hysterics.

David had achieved one part of his goal. The other was soon to come.

New league, new expectations

Now, David faces his biggest challenge: can he keep bagging goals while playing at the likes of Anfield instead of Anderlecht?

In announcing David’s signing on loan from Union for the 2026-27 season, Brighton sporting director Mike Cave called the 25-year-old an “out-and-out striker” and a player the club had “been watching for some time”. Brighton’s brass hope David’s scoring touch will help fill the void left by Danny Welbeck, who departed for Chelsea in August.

David made his Premier League debut against Welbeck’s Chelsea on 30 August, playing 10 minutes in a 4-3 loss at Stamford Bridge. He saw another short stint against Leeds in a 1-1 draw. A first start, and a first goal, awaits. So, too, does the spotlight of the sport’s most demanding league, which forgives little and asks plenty.

Feliciano, for one, believes his former charge is up to the task.

“He’s only ever had to endure adversity. He’s never had it easy.”

Sports.title: Are Manchester United as poor as the early Premier League table suggests?
Sports.content:
Manchester United are 13th in the Premier League, having taken four points from their first four games: a 2-0 defeat at Hull, 5-2 win against Ipswich, 2-2 draw at Everton and the 1-0 defeat by Manchester City on Sunday. Mitigation regarding the City reverse can be found in the derby coming three days after the Champions League win against Sabah on Thursday, with Enzo Maresca’s side having 48 hours more rest after winning at Porto. So are United, who host Brighton in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday before visiting Fulham in the league on Sunday, as poor as the table suggests?

Is Carrick becoming the new Solskjær?

After Ole Gunnar Solskjær was appointed as temporary manager in December 2018 as a result of José Mourinho’s tempestuous tenure, he won 14 of 19 games and took over permanently in March 2019. What followed was a nosedive of two victories from 10 matches and United ended in sixth – the position when Solskjær arrived. Carrick revived the club’s fortunes as the interim coach last season after Ruben Amorim’s meltdown and sacking, and guided United to third. Yet after assuming the permanent role results have worsened. Just because Solskjær had an unstable team and was never secure in the job (being sacked in November 2021) does not mean his former teammate and assistant will have a similar experience. But how many more poor results is Carrick away from Jason Wilcox being accused of hastily appointing another popular former United player? A clue that the director of football may have had reservations regarding Carrick may lie in the brevity of the contract given to him: it runs to 2028.

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick guided Manchester United to third last season but results have worsened since his position became permanent. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

A troubling passiveness

When Phil Foden was sent off after 23 minutes at Old Trafford on Sunday, United had a man advantage over City. But Carrick’s men remained becalmed, the Kobbie Mainoo-Youri Tielemans central axis unable to exert control and create chances for the front four of Bruno Fernandes, Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha and Marcus Rashford. For the first time in 12 home Premier League games under Carrick, United generated less than 1.0 xG (0.95), which should be more of a concern for Carrick than the quasi-farcical video assistant referee decision that allowed Erling Haaland’s winner (Enzo Fernández was, as Pro Ref later admitted, interfering with play). The same issue was evident in the opening defeat at Hull, where Andrey Santos partnered Tielemans, there was close to zero goal threat and Carrick’s side were a portrait of passiveness.

No new left-back starting to bite

You have to wonder why a summer window-long interest in a left-back that included Newcastle’s Lewis Hall (the No 1 target), Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly and RB Leipzig’s David Raum drew a blank. Identifying that a position needs strengthening, then failing to do so, seems amateurish and cannot have delighted Carrick. Instead, three midfielders were bought: Tielemans, Santos and Carlos Baleba. With Mainoo and Manuel Ugarte (who has a long-term injury) in the squad, a case can be made that this was one too many recruits for the engine room. Instead, the finance for, say, Santos (£48m + £2m) could have been invested at left-back. Four games into the season the potential folly of this was underlined. Luke Shaw, the first-choice left-back, whose career is injury-plagued, was unavailable for City’s visit owing to a knock and Carrick was forced to field a stopgap in Patrick Dorgu. In last season’s corresponding fixture the Dane played as the wide-left forward – and scored. On Sunday, when Josko Gvardiol crossed from United’s right for Haaland to net at the far post, Dorgu was the player challenging the Croat, instead of being in his left-sided defensive zone to mark City’s centre-forward. It was also Dorgu’s errant header that handed City the ball to allow the attack to be launched.

View image in fullscreen Patrick Dorgu has been a stopgap for the injured Luke Shaw at left-back but has not been effective in the role. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters

United’s summer signings need to start working

For a £148m investment United acquired Santos, Tielemans (£35m) and Carlos Baleba (£65m). The net result so far? A single start for Santos (the Hull loss) and anonymity from Tielemans, who has been in the XI for all four league matches. Then you come to Baleba, the headline acquisition, who is yet to kick a ball owing to injury, the Cameroonian not expected back until after the international break. In this early season phase none of this would matter if results were rosier. During an interview at United’s County Kildare pre-season training camp in August Tielemans admitted no other clubs were interested in triggering his £35m release clause at Aston Villa. As United attempt to jump-start their campaign, Belgium’s captain needs to offer more – as a player and leader.

Time for Sesko to start?

View image in fullscreen Benjamin Sesko scores in the Champions League match against Sabah. Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP

Benjamin Sesko returned from injury as the season started and has made substitute appearances in all United’s league matches, plus a start at home to Sabah, against whom he scored. The Slovenian also got a goal in the 2-2 draw at Everton, making him United’s joint-third-highest scorer in the league, behind Bruno Fernandes (three) and Bryan Mbeumo (two). Matheus Cunha and Marcus Rashford have zero strikes in the league from four and three starts respectively, and Sesko’s directness as a natural No 9 may be an option worth exploring from kick-off at Fulham.

Sports.title: De Zerbi backs ‘sensitive guy’ Solanke to find form before tricky Anfield trip
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi has no doubt Dominic Solanke will rediscover his best levels as the head coach made clear he had left no stone unturned in the mission to solve Tottenham’s goalscoring problem.

Spurs go to Liverpool in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday after the 0-0 home draw with Everton in the Premier League on Saturday; they have not found the net in their four matches in the competition. Tottenham did beat Charlton 5-1 at home in the second round of the Carabao Cup.

Solanke is the only forward in De Zerbi’s squad to have enjoyed a prolific season in England’s top division; he scored 19 times for Bournemouth in 2023-24, which convinced Tottenham to pay £55m for him. The 29-year-old has 22 additional goals in the Premier League, 12 of them for Spurs. De Zerbi has Omar Marmoush, who scored seven times in the league for Manchester City in the second half of 2024-25 after joining from Eintracht Frankfurt in January. That apart, the pickings for De Zerbi’s attacking players have been slim in the competition.

Solanke, whose pre-season was undermined by an injury sustained on the club’s tour of New Zealand and Australia, was ineffective against Everton and a target for criticism is some quarters. De Zerbi will keep the faith. He remembers being amazed at how well Solanke played for Bournemouth against his Brighton team in September 2023. Brighton won 3-1 but Solanke scored. De Zerbi knows that when Solanke is fully fit the goals and performances will follow. He intends to involve the former Liverpool striker at Anfield, whether from the start or as a substitute.

“Dom is a sensitive guy,” De Zerbi said. “He needs to feel full confidence – and from myself, he has big, big confidence. I believe he can score 10-15 goals, for sure. He’s already scored in Bournemouth so why not he can score in Tottenham? It’s the same sport.

“[He is] sensitive because he’s a smart guy. Sensitive guys are smart. Maybe [he has had] many injuries, maybe he doesn’t feel in the best physical condition, maybe he would like to do something different on the pitch. But now he’s not fit yet. He has to play. It can be important for him [at Anfield]. And then I think he comes back to the player who was in Bournemouth. I remember Brighton v Bournemouth in the Amex Stadium; he was incredible. I said to my assistant: ‘Who is this striker?’”

View image in fullscreen Dominic Solanke scores Tottenham’s second goal in their 5-1 Carabao Cup second round victory over Charlton. Photograph: John Walton/PA

De Zerbi continues to try to bond his players away from the pitch. He said he had again taken them for dinner in Mayfair last week and paid the bill. “As long as I keep some money for my cigarettes, then no problem,” he said with a smile.

De Zerbi is leaning heavily into video analysis, going through clips from matches in team meetings and giving the players individual ones to study. There has been an emphasis in training on attacking crosses in the right way and regaining possession in the final third. The players have also stayed behind for extra shooting practice of their own volition, De Zerbi said.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“If we want to change from the last two or three seasons we have to be stronger here,” he said, pointing to his head. “We have to believe in the quality of the players and the decisions we made one month ago. Or we change. You can change players or change coaches … change, change, change and nothing changes. Or you stay with the head, stay humble and with the right spirit to work. I believe in my players. I hope they believe in themselves like I believe in them.”

De Zerbi reported that Sandro Tonali would miss the Liverpool game with a knock, and Richarlison will not be involved despite being eligible for the Carabao Cup; the Brazilian forward was omitted from Spurs’ Premier League squad.

Pedro Porro is still out but Destiny Udogie is back, and Mohammed Kudus is ready to start. James Maddison, though, is still unavailable. De Zerbi will make changes and he mentioned Marcos Senesi, Tosin Adarabioyo, Ben Davies, Lucas Bergvall and Mathys Tel as being in contention to come into the XI. Spurs have not won at Anfield in 17 matches.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola tells Liverpool forwards they must do more to make his system work
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola has shifted the focus on to Liverpool’s forwards for the team’s uninspiring display against Fulham, insisting they need to give more to make his system work.

The head coach admitted his team took “a step backwards” with their goalless draw on Saturday. His central midfield pairing of Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai struggled to contain their Fulham counterparts, winning two of five duels and one of nine duels respectively. But Iraola believes the problems started further forward with the pressing of Liverpool’s expensively assembled attack.

“It’s not a matter of just the midfielders,” he said. “When we have been good collectively the mid­fielders have looked a lot better and recovered more balls. It’s not because they are winning duels that they play better, it’s because we are helping them more to win the duels.

“If the ones up front do their job very well then the defenders and midfielders look good. If we are allowing them to defend one v one all the time and we are not aggressive, then our defenders will also struggle. If the players ahead of you are doing their job then you look a better midfielder or defender because you win more easier duels, you have more chance of winning one. It is more collective.

“It isn’t about changing this player for that player. That’s the help we have to give to our defenders and midfielders so everyone looks better, looks smarter and are in better positions.”

Iraola is unlikely to field the same frontline of Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Víctor Muñoz when Tottenham visit Anfield in the Carabao Cup third round on Tuesday. Trey Nyoni is pressing for a start in midfield and Iraola confirmed that Giorgi Mamardashvili, whom he tried to sign for Bournemouth, would replace ­Alisson in goal.

View image in fullscreen The Liverpool goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili will make his first appearance of the season in the Carabao Cup tie against Tottenham. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

On the issues of Saturday, which contributed to a third draw in four Premier League games, he also said: “Compared to previous games, we won the ball a lot lower in the pitch. We don’t concede a lot, and the only big chance we conceded was our goal‑kick that we messed up. But we were recovering the ball always very low and when that happens you have to attack against 11 players and that makes it more difficult to make the difference.

“In previous games we could win it a lot higher and use our quick transitions to attack against less players and use the space better. That is key to our system. We need to recover the ball as high as possible because it makes the offensive side a lot easier, and we have more situations to attack in one v one.”

Sports.title: Calvert-Lewin shows the way as Leeds thrash limp Newcastle and rise to third
Sports.content:
At what stage does a good start become something more significant? Perhaps we are not quite there yet; maybe we are. But as the goals flew in on a chaotic night at Elland Road, it was difficult not to think the boundaries of expectation for Leeds were potentially being redrawn.

Ask those close to the action over the summer at Leeds and the feeling was that there was a possibility of something special materialising this season. Having found their feet in the Premier League in the last campaign, the platform had been set and a very good summer transfer window seemed like the catalyst for even brighter days to return to West Yorkshire.

But even with that optimism in mind, this night felt significant. Leeds did not just beat a Newcastle side who themselves have started brightly under Matthias Jaissle, they dismantled them. And with the manner of this victory, Daniel Farke’s side sit third in the table.

Perhaps, in this world of demanding success overnight, there is a lesson here in patience for both clubs too. As Elland Road’s patrons likely pinched themselves when the outstanding Dominic Calvert-Lewin made it 3-0 before half-time it was easy to forget that, under a year ago, large swathes of supporter were suggesting time was up for Farke.

His decision to change to a back three against Manchester City last November saved his job and sparked an upturn in form that saw Leeds secure safety before starting this campaign in magnificent fashion. If this start continues with another win over Crystal Palace on Sunday, perhaps this side can do greater things than many first thought.

As for Jaissle, this was his first large bump in the road as Newcastle manager and there will possibly be more over the coming months as he imprints his vision on this team. But the decision-making of the Leeds side who vanquished them is evidence enough that patience can often pay off and Jaissle and his team could have no complaints about the scoreline.

Leeds were magnificent from start to finish. The opening goal was perhaps a touch fortuitous as Ao Tanaka’s shot bounced off the substitute Sean Steur and Lewis Miley to wrongfoot Lukas Hornicek, but it was the least Leeds deserved. Two minutes later, the lead was doubled when Jayden Bogle headed home a James Justin cross.

View image in fullscreen Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s header for Leeds’ second was deflected in off Jayden Bogle. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

Bogle has quietly been one of Leeds’ standout performers for some time and he is one of a few Leeds players who Thomas Tuchel may find difficult to ignore before naming his latest England squad later this week. The man who slotted home Leeds’ third in first-half stoppage time has perhaps even greater a claim for a call-up.

Calvert-Lewin’s latest goal was brilliantly taken; a measured finish that made it 3-0 at half-time.

With James Trafford between the sticks, Leeds have a clutch of players who may be fancy their chances of international recognition if they keep this up; a surefire sign of a club trending upwards.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They may have a manager in that bracket as well. “There’s never a perfect performance in football but that was top class for more or less the whole game,” Farke said. “We know we have to stay humble; we might not have the best individual quality but we can be an outstanding team.”

The prospect of a grand Newcastle comeback appeared unlikely from the moment Sven Botman carelessly gave away possession to Anton Stach shortly after half-time and Stach spurned a glorious chance to make it 4-0. But Leeds did not have to wait long for their fourth goal, as Noah Okafor struck through a crowded penalty box to put the result beyond doubt.

Jaissle’s demeanour became more and more exasperated as the evening wore on and unsurprisingly he cut a frustrated figure afterwards. “We couldn’t match the intensity of Leeds and you see how difficult it can be to win a game in the Premier League,” he said. “We’ll have some ups and downs and this was a big down. A tough night.”

There was at least a consolation in the final moments as Bazoumana Touré, a bright spark after coming on, capitalised on a rare Leeds error to make it 4-1.

But the damage had long since been done – and the party among the home support by this time was already well under way.

Sports.title: European football: Inter roar back to beat Udinese 5-3 and join Roma at top
Sports.content:
Inter fought back ⁠from two goals down ​to beat Udinese 5-3 on Monday, maintaining their perfect Serie A start alongside Roma, who won 2-0 at Torino before Saturday’s match between ⁠the joint leaders. Both sides have 12 points from four matches and share top spot before their encounter at the Stadio Olimpico, while Como are third on 10 points ⁠after beating Parma 2-1.

Udinese stunned Inter with two goals in the opening 16 minutes, as James Abankwah headed home ​unmarked after nine minutes before Jurgen Ekkelenkamp doubled ‌the visitors’ lead with a ‌close-range finish seven minutes later. Inter hit back through Carlos Augusto, whose long-range effort flew into the bottom corner, ‌before Nicolò Barella levelled 10 minutes before half-time.

The champions completed the turnaround in the 59th minute when Marcus Thuram netted from inside the box after Andy Diouf’s cutback from the byline. Francesco Esposito added a fourth and Ange-Yoan Bonny made it 5-2 with 11 minutes remaining. Udinese pulled one back in stoppage time through Idrissa Gueye, but it proved no more than a consolation.

There was an injury concern for Inter as John Stones limped off with an apparent hamstring injury just after the hour mark. The England centre-back was making his first start after joining on a free transfer this summer.

The Inter manager, Cristian Chivu, confirmed Stones would have to be fully assessed to determine the extent of the issue. “I don’t know, I haven’t had a chance to talk to him,” Chivu told Dazn. “I think he felt something on his flexor [muscle], and he will probably need to get some tests done.”

Roma made it four ‌wins from four thanks to goals from Donyell Malen and Niccolò Pisilli at Torino. Malen broke the deadlock five minutes before the interval after ​pouncing on a misplaced pass from goalkeeper Lucas Perri that had been intercepted by Paulo Dybala. Pisilli wrapped up the win in stoppage time, firing home from an angle after Gianluca Mancini kept the ball in play near the byline.

View image in fullscreen Roma scorers Niccolò Pisilli and Donyell Malen celebrate at the final whistle. Photograph: Alessandro Di Marco/EPA

The Roma coach, Gian Piero Gasperini ,praised the understanding between Malen and Dybala. “Clearly, these are two players who are very talented ⁠individually, but they also complete each other as a pair. They combine beautifully ​to create goals in many games,” ​he told Dazn Italia.

Como followed up their winning Champions League debut against RB Leipzig with a 2-1 home win over Parma, with Jacobo Ramón and Kaiki Bruno scoring for Cesc Fàbregas’s side. “This is an important victory for me as a coach, because I am starting to realise what team we could become,” Fàbregas said.

Meanwhile in Spain, Real Betis secured a 2-1 win at Villarreal to move third in La Liga and leave their opponents in the relegation zone. Goals from Cucho Hernández and Natan helped Betis claim three points and pull level with Real Madrid, after Gerard Moreno opened the scoring for the home side.

View image in fullscreen Natan (centre) and his Real Betis teammates fought back from 1-0 down to beat Villarreal 2-1. Photograph: José Jordan/AFP/Getty Images

“Right now everything’s going against us, teams are punishing us,” Moreno told Movistar. “We have to stick together and demand more of ourselves … maybe when we go behind, anxiety kicks in and it’s more difficult. It’s hard to explain [how few] points we have... we have to be a team now more than ever.”

Sports.title: WSL talking points: Olid must weather United storm, Arsenal wasteful again
Sports.content:
Is Olid under pressure?

The frustration among Manchester United fans at full-time was evident at Leigh Sports Village after they had watched their team being thrashed 5-0 by a rampant Chelsea. There are certainly things to be worried about, but perhaps judging United’s new manager, Eva Olid, on the basis of how they performed against Sonia Bompastor’s established side is a little premature. The likelihood of United taking three points was always slim, despite the false hope after Chelsea’s 1-1 draw with Aston Villa last weekend. Chelsea have not been an easy opponent for the Red Devils, who have lost three WSL games by more than three goals, all against Chelsea. Having had three weeks with her side, Olid had a harsh WSL baptism with losses to London City Lionesses and Chelsea. United face Arsenal next. “These are difficult games to build the confidence in attack, but I’m here to build an identity and I have to be faithful to that,” said the Spaniard. Suzanne Wrack

Arsenal lack finishing touch again

There was a strong sense of deja vu at the Emirates Stadium as Arsenal’s annual early season woes continued with goalless draw at home to Crystal Palace. For much of the game, it felt like they were re-winding the tape from seasons gone by, frustrated by resolute defensive visitors and their own lack of clinical finishing. Arsenal dominated every attacking metric – they had 79% possession, created 30 shots (nine on target) and recorded 70 touches in the Eagles’ area. The Gunners hit the woodwork twice, wasted golden opportunities and were denied by a standout performance from Pauline Peyraud-Magnin, who made eight saves. “Yes, there were good things, but it’s about scoring,” the head coach, Renée Slegers, said. Arsenal’s title tilt last season was ended by six draws and they will have to improve on that if they are to challenge this season. Sophie Downey

View image in fullscreen Chloe Kelly and Leah Williamson were part of a dominant, but goalless, Arsenal display against Crystal Palace. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/WSL/Getty Images

West Ham expose London City

After beating Manchester United last time out, London City Lionesses were brought back down to earth by an inspired West Ham to suffer their first defeat of the campaign. West Ham put in a performance that caught the eye for their own qualities as well as highlighting the early frailties of Eder Maestre’s team. If you were to just glance at the stats, you would think the visitors dominated, but it felt anything like that at Dagenham: Rita Guarino, the Hammers manager, set up her team perfectly. The burgeoning midfield relationship between Katie Zelem and Saki Kumagai nullified the threat of Alexia Putellas and Rosa Kafaji, Riko Ueki swept everything up in front of them, while the combined transitional threat of Viviane Asseyi and Kelly Gago had London City’s right side teetering. West Ham’s French duo found their touch in front of goal after precise counterattacking moves to secure a first win of the new season. SD

Flexibility helps Liverpool close the gap

Two games, four points and frustration that it is not all six: Liverpool have come a long way in a year. Last season, it took them until 25 January to earn a win and that win came against their opponents on Sunday, Tottenham, a similarly resurgent side who are possibly a few steps further ahead in their project. It was tactical flexibility that helped Gareth Taylor’s side earn a draw, with Liverpool responding well after Signe Gaupset’s effort took a heavy deflection off Sam Kerr to give Spurs a lead, somewhat against the run of play. The half-time introduction of Aurélie Csillag, who joined in January and grabbed the goal that gave them a point, was key. “They’re not going to give up the spaces easily,” said Taylor. “At times the spaces changed. Aurélie coming on to the pitch is a different type of proposition for back-fours as she’s physically very good.” SW

Champions flex their muscle

The only team with a perfect record after two games, Manchester City, the reigning WSL champions, showed they can be ruthless, with a comprehensive 4-1 defeat of Aston Villa. Yes, City have played a promoted side, Birmingham, and an unconvincing Aston Villa. Yes, we are yet to see how City fare when they add Champions League football into the mix, but the firepower at Andrée Jeglertz’s disposal is enviable. Khadija Shaw has three goals from two games and City had 55 touches in the opposition area to Villa’s 15 and 23 shots to Villa’s five. Chelsea’s profligacy cost them last weekend and Arsenal’s cost them this weekend, but City are scoring for fun. SW

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Khadija Shaw scored her third goal of the season at Aston Villa. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

Hills’ regret after red card

The Charlton manager, Karen Hills, said she was disappointed after the second-half red card for Ashleigh Neville against Everton led to a 1-0 defeat. Neville was sent off in the 58th minute for a high boot on Ruby Mace. While Hills suggested there was more hip-to-hip contact than anything else, she did not outright criticise the officials. “I don’t think the referee made the decision, it’s the fourth [official] and I guess they have to work together. Yes, her foot is a little bit high, but disappointed because that changes the game.” Charlton went down to nine players after Hawa Cissoko received two yellow cards in quick succession. Emillia Hawkins

View image in fullscreen Ashleigh Neville was sent off in the 58th minute for a high challenge. Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/Getty Images

Birmingham’s lack of WSL experience shows

On paper, Birmingham’s 2-2 draw against Brighton is an impressive feat for a promoted side, but the head coach, Amy Merricks, did not look too happy at the final whistle. Her team led the match by two goals with 15 minutes left to play, but Olivia Garcia got one back for Brighton in the 77th minute before Kiko Seike snatched a point with a last-gasp equaliser. The difference in experience between the two sides probably played a part in the later stages, with Birmingham in the WSL for the first time since 2022. “We’ll take a massive lesson today from those dying moments and how we see that out a bit better,” said Merricks. “What we can’t question is this group’s application and intent. They were on the front foot, they were tenacious. We look improved from last week, which, for me, is brilliant. We’re going to go up a notch because I know this team, they won’t settle, they’re very hungry.” EH

Sports.title: Hyrox announces rule change after Australian athlete won event despite soiling herself - with bosses apologising for allowing her to continue
Sports.content:
Hyrox organisers have confirmed immediate rule changes after a female athlete was allowed to continue while covered in her own faeces to win an event in Beijing.

Australian fitness star Joanna Wietrzyk, 24, powered to victory in China on the weekend despite suffering a bowel incontinence during the event.

Images showed the athlete running, performing burpees and carrying heavy bags with her own excrement dripping down her leg.

Wietrzyk, from Melbourne, posted an image to Instagram from her hospital bed after the race, reading: 'Go hard or go home they say... a win is a win. In all seriousness, thank you all for the support. I'll be back soon.'

But the athlete's gruelling triumph sparked backlash, with organisers accused of causing a biohazard by allowing Wietrzyk to continue after her accident.

On Tuesday, Hyrox bosses apologised for allowing the Melbourne athlete to finish the race, and pledged immediate rule changes.

Hyrox have apologised and announced immediate rule changes after an athlete soiled herself and was allowed to continue in Beijing

Melbourne-based athlete Joanna Wietrzyk won her event despite soiling herself

Prior to the weekend's incident, official event rules punished athletes for minor infringements such as littering on the course, or clearing their nose on the floor. There were no rules relating to faecal matter.

In a statement posted to Instagram, Hyrox co-founder Moritz Furste apologised to everybody affected 'directly or indirectly' by Wietrzyk's victory.

'Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not,' Furste said.

He clarified that Hyrox has made 'rulebook changes immediately'.

'As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again.'

Hyrox China and Hyrox World confirmed that affected areas of the course were isolated for deep cleaning overnight, contaminated equipment was removed and the venue carpet was replaced before the resumption of the competition the following day.

Hyrox is an increasingly popular fitness event whereby participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at high-intensity stations. These include burpee jumps, medicine ball throws, sled pushes, lunges and the rowing machine.

Ms Wietrzyk, from Melbourne, posted an image to Instagram from her hospital bed after the race - but her victory has sparked backlash

The competition was launched in Germany in 2017 and events are held in locations across the world.

Male competitor Joe Ho said: 'For people who were exposed to that situation, there could be genuine physical and psychological consequences.

'I paid Hyrox to provide a professionally organised and safe event. So while I understand the athlete perspective, ultimately my contract and expectation is with Hyrox.

'If the organisation accepts that something went wrong, why not offer affected participants refunds, credits or some meaningful form of accreditation?'

A US-based nurse meanwhile argued that the competition's winner should have been stopped 'immediately'.

Erica Dodge said on Instagram: 'From a basic health and sanitation standpoint, the athlete should have been stopped immediately, and any contaminated areas should have been closed off and properly cleaned before other athletes were allowed through.'

A podcast host questioned whether other athletes may have touched faeces left behind by Ms Wietrzyk on apparatus.

'Because of the nature of this sport, you go to different stations,' the host explained. 'So you do running, you do burpees, you do row machine... you do stuff like this with the medicine ball,' the host said.

'If you are doing burpees and this person in front of you has stuff on their legs, you don't know what you're putting your hands on.

'But at the same time, it's like, you're in the middle of a race, how thorough can they be if they want to keep the race going at the pace it's supposed to be going?'

In a statement released on Monday, Hyrox admitted it will 'examine what happened' and 'take responsibility for continuing to improve'.

The company added: 'In this instance, an unforeseen situation arose in which protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood.

'We recognise that this can understandably lead to frustration, questions and strong views within our community.

'Those concerns are legitimate and, as organisers, we must be prepared to hear them, examine what happened and take responsibility for continuing to improve. And we will.'

The Hyrox format sees competitors alternate between a 1km (one mile) run and a functional workout station, repeated eight times.

The eight workout stations are 1,000m SkiErg (simulating Nordic skiing), 50m Sled Push, 50m Sled Pull, 80m Burpee Broad Jumps, 1,000m row, 200m Farmer’s Carry (walking while holding heavy kettlebells or weights), 100m Sandbag Lunges, 100 Wall Balls (squatting and throwing a medicine ball to a target).

Hyrox has surged in popularity in recent years, especially among ageing millennials and office workers, and now stages events around the world.

Sports.title: Raheem Sterling arrives at court to hear fate after being charged with dangerous driving and possessing 'hippy crack' after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini
Sports.content:
Raheem Sterling arrives at court to hear fate after being charged with dangerous driving and possessing 'hippy crack' after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former England and Premier League footballer Raheem Sterling has arrived at court to face charges of dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas following a car crash in May.

Police were called to the M3 in Hampshire on May 28 to reports of a £270,000 Lamborghini swerving around the road just before 9am.

Footage obtained by the Daily Mail appeared to show the black luxury 4x4 veering across the three lanes as other vehicles dodged out of the way.

The driver appeared to be inhaling from a balloon - which is how people ingest laughing gas, also known as 'hippy crack'.

Minutes later, Sterling allegedly crashed the vehicle into the motorway barriers and was cuffed by Hampshire Police.

The force said he would not give a sample after his arrest - leading to a third charge of failing to supply a specimen.

More to follow.

Sports.title: Philippe Coutinho, 34, reunites with Neymar as he signs for Santos six months after dramatically quitting his boyhood club for 'health' reasons
Sports.content:
Philippe Coutinho has signed for Santos and will be reunited with former international team-mate Neymar Jr.

The 34-year-old has joined the Brazilian side for the rest of the season after leaving boyhood club Vasco da Gama back in February.

Coutinho marked the transfer by posing for a picture with Neymar, as the pair recreated an old photograph from their days in the Brazil youth set-up, with a digital camera.

And when speaking for the first time as a Santos player, the former Liverpool and Barcelona midfielder confirmed that Neymar had a major part to play in his decision to make the move.

'Neymar certainly played a very important role in my coming here,' Coutinho said on Monday. 'He's a player who needs no introduction, a friend I've had since childhood, and I think he was the first person in football to send me a message when I left Vasco.

'The next day he had already sent me a message, but at that moment I said: "Look Ney, it would be a pleasure to play with you, but I'm not feeling well right now, it's not possible" and it really didn't make sense to me.

Philippe Coutinho has joined Santos for the remainder of the season in the Brazilian league

'Months later he contacted me again, but my answer was the same. Then two weeks ago he sent me another message... Then I stopped, reconsidered... I wanted to go back to playing football and I thought: "Why not?"

'I'm going to a big club, in another city. It would be unfair to me not being able to go back to work and not being able to go back to playing football.

'I wanted to thank the president, Mattos and Ney. I'm happy to accept this challenge.'

Coutinho confirmed his departure from Vasco earlier this year, saying that he is 'mentally exhausted' in an emotional statement on social media.

Coutinho re-joined the Brazilian side on a permanent deal last year, following a short loan spell during his stint at Aston Villa, and seemed likely to extend his stay at the club.

However, after being repeatedly booed by his own fans in his final weeks at the club that, he realised that it was a good time for him 'step back' from playing for a period, which is now over.

In a statement at the time, he said: 'The truth is, I'm very mentally exhausted,' he continued. 'I've always been very reserved, so saying this here isn't easy, but I need to be honest.

'My relationship with Vasco is one of love. And it will continue to be forever. With a heavy heart, I understand that now is the time to take a step back and end this chapter at Vasco.

'I am grateful for everything I experienced here. I will carry Vasco with me forever. In my heart. In my history. In my life. From the bottom of my heart… Thank you for everything.'

The midfielder came through Vasco's youth academy before being scouted by Serie A giants Inter Milan in 2008, returning on loan for a brief spell as a teenager.

He impressed at the San Siro as a youngster ahead of signing for Liverpool in 2013, where he spent another five years before moving to Barcelona in still one of the most expensive transfers of all time.

During his time at Anfield, Coutinho made 152 appearances for the Reds and netted 41 goals.

His sale fee enabled Liverpool to sign a handful of important players under Jurgen Klopp, including Virgil van Dijk and Alisson Becker.

Sports.title: Nick Woltemade is ripped apart by Italian press weeks after loan move to Juventus - as £69m Newcastle flop is accused of 'doing everything WRONG'
Sports.content:
The Italian media have ripped into Newcastle flop Nick Woltemade despite the German striker having only just moved to Juventus. Woltemade, 24, joined the Italian giants on a season-long loan on Deadline Day, and he has made two substitute appearances over the past few weeks. However, after Sunday's 3-2 defeat by Sassuolo - a game in which Woltemade missed two clear-cut chances - Italian outlet Gazzetta dello Sport were heavily critical of his display. 'Woltemade is clearly having major problems integrating himself into the team's dynamic,' they wrote. 'He tried his best. But in the decisive moments, he lacks clarity in his actions, which is particularly noticeable in these games where every action can be crucial.' They added: 'Woltemade squanders: The German lacks precision and does everything wrong.' The Italian media have ripped into Newcastle flop and Juventus loanee Nick Woltemade Woltemade has struggled in his two substitute appearances since joining the Italian giants Woltemade and fellow attacker Randal Kolo Muani, who struggled on loan at Tottenham last season, have come under particularly heavy criticism after being two of the club's statement summer signings. Writing about the pair - who are yet to 'make a difference' since joining - the same outlet said: 'Four games and not a single goal, plus several scenes that quickly circulated as mocking social media clips among rival fans. 'Clumsy ball control, botched back heel flicks that landed at the feet of the opposition, and – what is particularly troubling – hardly any dangerous scoring opportunities. No, this cannot continue. Juventus' attack is not working.' That view was echoed elsewhere, with Corriere dello Sport similarly brutal in their assessment of the two strikers. 'How annoying is it when the very new signings you chased for months (and paid far too much for) turn out to be the biggest disappointments of the team?,' they wrote. The latest criticism for Woltemade comes after Juventus boss Luciano Spalletti bizarrely compared him to 'a horse that likes to be petted and ridden' after his debut. The German striker had come off the bench in the 75th minute of a clash against AC Milan, with Juventus trailing 1-0. Woltemade nearly made an immediate impact when the ball fell kindly for him in the penalty area and he swung a boot at it, but was ultimately unable to keep his shot down as the chance went begging. Woltemade did manage to win a free-kick in stoppage time, however, and the Turin side capitalised, with Federico Gatti heading home a dramatic equaliser to secure a valuable point against Ruben Amorim's side. After the match, Spalletti compared his new player to a Friesian horse, the breed known for its long, flowing mane and tail. Juventus boss Luciano Spalletti previously bizarrely compared Woltemade to a Friesian horse Spalletti told Tuttosport: 'What type of horse is he? I have a Friesian, he seems very similar to me. 'He is statuesque, he inspires a bit of fear from a physical point of view and then he is very sweet and lets himself be stroked and ridden. 'He becomes very good also in relations with his teammates. He’s good at holding his own physically, and ever since I met him, he’s been smiling constantly. He’s so happy to be here, and that’s already a big thing.' Juventus have seven points from four Serie A games so far this season, and are back in action on Thursday when they take on NEC Nijmegen in the Europa League.

Sports.title: Shocking moment Millwall fan tells West Ham star 'I'll cut your f***ing face off' in violent threat ahead of London derby this weekend
Sports.content:
Shocking moment Millwall fan tells West Ham star 'I'll cut your f***ing face off' in violent threat ahead of London derby this weekend

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

West Ham star Tomas Soucek received a violent threat from a Millwall fan ahead of the London rivals' hotly-anticipated clash this weekend.

The Hammers travel to The Den on Saturday where they will meet for the first time in 14 years, in what is widely-regarded as one of the fiercest rivalries in English football.

Czech international Soucek, 31, is nursing an ankle injury and has not featured for the Hammers this season, but has cheered Nuno Espirito Santo's team on from the sidelines.

However, the midfielder has been warned to stay away from The Den by a Millwall supporter during a chance encounter in public.

In a video clip that has been shared on social media, Soucek was warned: 'If I see you at the Den next Saturday I'm going to cut your f***ing face off, you ****.'

Just a Millwall fan telling Tomás Soucek that he’s “going to cut his f*cking face off next Saturday at the den”



Soucek just laughing back at him😂😂😂



Embarrassing Millwall fan… pic.twitter.com/Kg0CEburtB — Now Football (@Nowfootball) September 14, 2026

Tomas Soucek received a violent threat from a Millwall fan ahead of Saturday's derby

West Ham travel to Millwall on Saturday, in one of English football's fiercest rivalries. Pictured: West Ham fans at Green Street, Upton Park during a League Cup clash with Millwall in 2009

Previous contests between Millwall and West Ham have been marred by racism aimed at players from both sets of fans, while a 44-year-old fan was stabbed in the chest when the two teams met in the League Cup in August 2009.

That particular contest saw three pitch invasions unfold, while hundreds of Hammers fans congregated outside the club's former stadium, Upton Park, at full time, where police were bombarded with flying crates and bottles.

The Met deployed 200 riot officers, at least 20 mounted officers and a helicopter for the game, which one Millwall fan described as feeling like a 'war zone'.

The Millwall fan told the BBC: 'It was like a war zone outside the stadium. There was fighting all round.

'I brought my kids with me tonight and they've seen some violence that is indescribable.'

A local kebab shop owner added: 'All hell broke loose - it was very frightening.

'Bottles and bricks were being thrown from the back and some were hitting West Ham fans at the front.

'There were loads of people with bloodied faces.'

Sports.title: Britain's golden girl Amy Hunt doubles down on Sydney Sweeney row after accusing Hollywood star of 'sexualising women's sport' in naked betting advert
Sports.content:
Amy Hunt has doubled down on her criticism of Sydney Sweeney after she posed naked in a betting advert.

Hunt had accused the actress of sexualising women's sport after she featured in a promotional video for bookmaker Novig in which she used various pieces of sports equipment to cover herself up.

The advert has drawn widespread condemnation from across the world of women’s sport, in particular from female Olympians.

This included British sprinter Hunt, who used her post-race interview at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship on Sunday to rip into the promo.

On Tuesday, Hunt then appeared on GMB where she doubled down on her views and highlighted the potential dangers of Sweeney's actions.

'When we're trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it's about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like,' she said.

Amy Hunt has doubled down on her criticism of Sydney Sweeney after the actress posed naked in a betting advert

Sweeney was accused of sexualising women’s sport in the hugely controversial promo

'When we see the stats that 64 per cent of young girls drop out of exercise and sport before they reach the age of 16, we don't need to place any kind of barrier whatsoever in their way in terms of providing the opportunity and the empowerment for them to still exercise, whatever that looks like, whether it's professional or just going to do a park run with your friends.

'So it's about empowering young girls and young women and young people to show that you really can just get out there and you don't have to worry what you look like. You don't have to worry about what you're wearing.'

When pressed on whether the advert could impact how men view female athletes, Hunt agreed and added: 'That was a big thing this year for us with the introduction of new broadcasting regulations, in showing the correct or the more appropriate angles of women competing.

'And it being an empowering thing, because I want to race and I want to enjoy it and I want to run as fast as possible. So it's really important to me that I feel comfortable and I show other people that you can feel comfortable.

'But also we get a choice of what to wear. Like, we're not kind of forced into wearing the briefs.

'It's important to show young people that it's OK to be whoever you want to be, to wear whatever you want to wear, to look however you want to look, and you can achieve your dreams.'

Hunt has received significant praise for speaking out since Sunday and the athlete added that Sweeney may have inadvertently helped her cause.

'The reaction has almost outweighed the moment,' she said. 'Because the first thing I saw was all of the positive compilations of women in sport. And that's also what my sister said.

'She said she'd had so many friends reach out to her and say: “thank you so much for saying something”, because it's been more positive. It separated itself from the moment entirely.

'And it's not anything personal against that actress. It's more the intention. It's just moved into a completely different sphere now where we're able to have all these different things celebrating women in sport.'

Sweeney used various pieces of sports equipment to cover herself up in the advert

During her initial interview on Sunday, which came after Hunt finished fourth in her 200m race, she fired back at Sweeney.

The 24-year-old, who became the first athlete to win four gold medals at a single European Championships earlier this year, said: 'It was incredible to be part of such an incredible race.

'Sydney Sweeney, this is what women is sport look like. 21.4 [seconds, the winning time of Melissa Jefferson-Wooden], muscles, hard work, sweat, blood, tears. This is a beautiful evening.'

The sprinter – who has previously called herself 'sexy and aggressive' – added that the reality of being a female athlete is rather different than Sweeney's advert suggests.

Hunt continued: 'Obviously we've seen in the last 24 hours everything about the Sydney Sweeney ad, you know, and when you're a woman in sport, it's not pretty. It's not glamorous. It's not sexy all the time, definitely.

'There's some low moments. Even turning up to this championship, my period started yesterday, so that's not really ideal, and that's not ever what you try to really plan for.'

Sports.title: Wembley snubbed as UEFA name Champions League and Europa League final hosts for 2028 and 2029 at committee meeting in Greece - and new Nations League format with promotion and relegation is confirmed
Sports.content:
Wembley's bid to host either the 2028 or 2029 Champions League final has been rejected in favour of both the Allianz Arena and the Nou Camp.

UEFA hosted an executive committee meeting in Thessaloniki, Greece on Tuesday, in order to decide the hosts for European football's most prestigious football match, among others.

London was hoping to host a fourth Champions League final in less than 20 years but UEFA bosses opted to snub the national stadium.

European football's governing body has instead awarded the 2028 final to Bayern Munich's Allianz Arena, which hosted the match as recently as 2025, and Barcelona's newly renovated Nou Camp.

It will be the first time the Spanish ground, which will become Europe's biggest stadium once the long-awaited refurbishment is complete, has hosted the final since Manchester United's famous stoppage-time comeback victory over Bayern.

Borussia Dortmund's Signal Iduna Park also put in a bid alongside Wembley but missed out.

Wembley has been snubbed by UEFA in its bid to host the Champions League final in 2028 or 2029

The national stadium last hosted the final in 2024 when Jude Bellingham's real Madrid won a 15th title

The Nou Camp will host the final in 2029 for the first time since Manchester United's miracle stoppage time comeback over Bayern Munich

Wembley last hosted the final in 2024, with Real Madrid lifting their 15th title following a 2-0 victory over Dortmund.

However, the final was shrouded in controversy after a Daily Mail Sport investigation showcased how ticketless fans were able to breach security to gain entry into the stadium. A reporter managed to gain entry without a ticket by handing a steward £100 in cash.

UEFA also decided the hosts of the Women’s Champions League finals, Europa League finals and the Conference League finals across the same two years.

The Parc Olympique Lyonnais in Lyon and Cardiff's Principality Stadium have been selected as hosts for the 2028 and 2029 finals in the women's game.

Meanwhile, Bucharest and Belgrade will play host to the Europa League finals in those years, while the Juventus Stadium and the Puskas Arena in Budapest, which hosted the latest Champions League final, have been selected as the venues for the Conference League showpieces.

During the meeting in Greece, UEFA bosses also discussed the format of the upcoming Nations League, which begins in the upcoming international break.

The committee approved adjustments to the promotion and relegation system, which will allow the competition to transition from four leagues down to three in the 2028-29 edition.

Sports.title: Paolo Maldini's son 'has driving licence suspended after he was tested at almost twice Italy's legal alcohol limit' - as his Serie A club deny drug accusations
Sports.content:
Paolo Maldini's son 'has driving licence suspended after he was tested at almost twice Italy's legal alcohol limit' - as his Serie A club deny drug accusations

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Daniel Maldini, son of Italian legend Paolo, has reportedly had his driving licence suspended after allegedly failing a breathalyser test following a car crash in Milan.

Maldini, 24, was involved in the incident just hours after he scored the winning goal for Cagliari on Saturday night as they beat Atalanta 2-1.

The attacking midfielder collided with another vehicle while driving his Porsche Carrera at around 5:15am on Sunday morning.

Maldini was among six people to suffer minor injuries and he was taken to Milan's Fatebenefratelli Hospital for precautionary tests before being released.

Milan City Police confirmed to BBC Sport that Maldini was involved in a road traffic accident and revealed the news about the breathalyser.

In a statement, they said: 'Mr Maldini was administered a breathalyser test at the scene' and his 'driving licence was confiscated following a positive result.'

Daniel Maldini, son of Italian legend Paolo, has reportedly had his driving licence suspended after allegedly failing a breathalyser test following a car crash in Milan

That incident came just hours after he scored the winning goal as Cagliari beat Atalanta

Reports in Italy said Maldini's initial test at the scene recorded a blood alcohol level of 0.91 grams per litre, before a second reading came in at 0.89 grams per litre.

Those figures are both higher than Italy's legal limit of 0.5 grams per litre.

Italian outlet La Gazzetta dello Sport also reported that Maldini failed a preliminary drugs test following the accident, although they added that those results needed to be confirmed through further toxicological tests in hospital.

However, Maldini and Cagliari vehemently denied this, with the Serie A side releasing a statement on Monday defending their player in relation to the drug accusations.

They said: 'Cagliari Calcio announces that, following reports that emerged in the Italian media in recent hours, Daniel Maldini underwent toxicology tests.

'All tests carried out returned negative results. The player will regularly join the squad this afternoon as the team resumes training ahead of their upcoming fixture.'

Maldini also took to Instagram to share the results of the toxicology tests conducted after the accident.

He posted a screenshot demonstrating that he tested negative for several substances in an attempt to publicly clarify the situation.

Maldini posted an Instagram story sharing the results of the toxicology tests conducted after the accident as he denied Italian reports that he failed a drugs test

The incident came soon after Maldini, who has previously represented multiple clubs including AC Milan, Monza and Lazio, enjoyed a memorable evening on Saturday.

Not only did he score the winner from the spot, but ironically the attacking midfielder is on loan from Atalanta after being deemed surplus to requirements by his parent club.

It was Maldini's second goal in just four league games this season, with Cagliari currently in fourth place in Serie A following an extremely positive start.

Maldini's father Paolo is widely regarded as one of Italy's greatest footballers of all-time during a career where he represented just AC Milan and Italy.

His late grandfather Cesare also earned legendary status at the San Siro before enjoying a managerial career that included stints with his former club and his country.

Meanwhile, the 24-year-old previously came through the ranks at AC Milan during a period when his dad served as the club's technical director.

Maldini left in 2024 in search of more regular first team football, spending a year with Monza before he moved to Atalanta.

He has also won six caps for Italy, and could be back in action on Saturday when Cagliari travel to Udinese.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
