Linda Mwananchi leaders during a rally in Western Kenya. [Linda Mwananchi, X]

The Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) has said it will not disrupt the planned Linda Mwananchi rally scheduled for Sunday at Jacaranda Grounds.

In a statement on Friday, September 11, ODM Nairobi Chairman George Aladwa said the party had no business interfering with the rally, noting that Linda Mwananchi had a right to speak to Nairobi residents.

“I want to make it clear that nobody in ODM has any intention of disrupting or interfering with the Linda Mwananchi rally,” Aladwa stated.

He added: “We believe that political competition should be about ideas, policies and the ability to convince Kenyans, rather than confrontations between supporters of different political formations.”

Aladwa said ODM’s opponents had a right to tell Nairobi residents what they stood for and what they intended to offer Kenyans.

“The people are intelligent enough to listen to different political messages and make their own decisions,” Aladwa said.

At the same time, Aladwa said ODM was engaged in an extensive programme to market and strengthen the party across Nairobi as it prepared for activities to commemorate the anniversary of the death of its former party leader, the late Raila Amolo Odinga.

The chairman lauded Odinga for his contribution to Kenya’s democracy, the struggle for constitutional reforms and the political transformation of the country, saying his contribution could not be erased.

“His legacy remains an important part of ODM and Kenya’s political history. As we approach the 2027 General Election, our responsibility is to ensure that ODM remains strong, organised and firmly rooted across Nairobi,” the chairman stated.

“We will continue engaging residents in all constituencies and wards and explaining the party’s agenda to the people. I appeal to ODM supporters to remain calm and focused. Do not allow yourselves to be provoked into unnecessary political confrontations,” he added.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro tells Ruto to keep off Tata Chemicals
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

PPK leader Ndindi Nyoro addresses a rally at Nambale market in Busia on August 30, 2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro has cautioned President William Ruto against meddling in the affairs of Tata Chemicals, Africa’s largest soda ash plant in Lake Magadi, Kajiado County.

Nyoro, who is the Peoples’ Party of Kenya leader, has accused President Ruto of an alleged plot to take control of Tata Chemicals through a shareholding scheme.

He said Ruto’s directive on Tata Chemicals closure raises concerns over the future of multinational firms and their operations in the country.

Speaking during a tour of Wote, Makueni County, on Thursday, Nyoro termed the Head of State’s move selfish, saying even if he had since softened his stance on the firm, it remains wanting for investors.

“His utterances were and remain wanting for external and internal investors. We don’t want investors to work in a bad political environment. Even if he seems to have made a U-turn on the matter, we are aware he has been pushing to be a shareholder in the company. We don’t want investors to be interfered with politically because we must create an environment where our people have access to job opportunities. It is almost reaching a catastrophic level in terms of lack of jobs for our people,” he said

The PPK leader warned that the country is in a bad economic state with a Sh13.5 trillion debt that is projected to grow further by next year.

“When Ruto exits next year the debt will be more than Sh15 trillion. The next president, who will be coming from the opposition, will have hard times in running this country. For every Sh100 that will be collected as tax from 2028, Sh91 will be used to repay government debts. We should not have time now to fight as opposition and also as Kenyans. We must hold hands and send the president back home because of his failures,” Nyoro said.

The MP urged opposition leaders to put aside their political differences and unite behind a single presidential candidate ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying that a united opposition would have a better chance of defeating President Ruto.

“If the opposition wants to defeat President Ruto, they must come together and present one presidential candidate. I am ready to talk to all the opposition principals,” Nyoro said.

Nyoro also outlined a raft of proposals he says could help revive Kenya’s economy and ease the financial burden on ordinary citizens.

Among his proposals is the use of the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) to strengthen the health sector. He argued that Kenyans should be able to access quality healthcare without being forced to bear the full cost of medical services.

Nyoro further proposed changes to the way education is financed, suggesting that bursaries currently administered through the National Government Constituencies Development Fund (NG-CDF) and county governments be channelled towards financing free primary and secondary education.

He said such an approach would create a more uniform education financing system and ensure that children from poor households are not disadvantaged because of their parents' inability to meet school-related expenses.

Nyoro's proposals come amid growing debate over the country's economic direction, the cost of living, access to healthcare and the financing of education.

World.title: Mama Tutam acquitted of Sh25m fraud, says Nigerian tycoon cost her marriage
World.content:
Nairobi Woman Representative aspirant Faith Mwikali Ndiwa, alias Faith Nguthu addresses journalists at the Milimani Law Courts in Nairobi on September 9, 2026. [David Gichuru, Standard]

A Nairobi Woman Representative aspirant has confessed the frustrations and embarrassment that befell her after befriending a wealthy Nigerian businessman who later accused her of defrauding him of Sh25 million.

Faith Mwikali Ndiwa, alias Faith Nguthu, popularly known as Mama Tutam, said she was kicked out of her marriage after the father of her three children discovered reports linking her to an alleged love affair with Nigerian investor Jude Olabayo Veracruz.

World.title: Three ways the Iran war changed the global economy
World.content:
The effects of the Iran war are obvious to most Americans: Gas prices have been hovering above $4 for weeks, mortgage rates are rising toward seven percent and companies are adding shipping surcharges to make up for record diesel costs.

Those cost-of-living increases have lasted longer than the Trump administration had claimed they would, although they should eventually reverse themselves if and when the United States and Iran reach a ceasefire agreement.

But other economic changes won’t be so easily reversed. The war has altered the global economy in lasting ways that have reshaped the way the world does business.

Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz

Before the war, ships under any country’s banner could freely transit the Strait of Hormuz to collect and deliver goods to and from the Middle East. A fifth of the world’s oil traveled through the narrow passage every day.

The idea of who controls the strait permanently changed after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Iran declared the strait its own to control, and it attacked vessels that tried to enter or exit the Persian Gulf. The effective closure of the strait gave Iran economic leverage over the United States and its Gulf state allies, closing off 13 million barrels of oil supply to the global economy.

Iran changed its strait tactic in May. Rather than attempting to close the strait, it started regulating the channel’s use. It formed the Persian Gulf Strait Authority and began requiring transiting ships to register with the group, follow an authorized navigation path and pay a toll to cross. After signing a Memorandum of Understanding with the United States in June, Iran agreed to stop charging tolls for 60 days, but it continued to attack transiting ships that failed to register with the authority.

People spend time at a beach as commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on August 5, 2026. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/AP

After effectively tearing up the memorandum of understanding, the US military began coordinating and escorting “dark,” nighttime transits across the strait to increase Persian Gulf oil exports and avoid Iranian drone attacks. The effort has been working, but the need for such a massive, taxing and expensive operation proves how much influence Iran has gained over the Strait of Hormuz.

“It seems likely that Iran will emerge from the war with a stronger position over control of the strait, and that will force countries reliant on Middle Eastern crude to adapt,” said Ross Mayfield, investment Strategist at Baird. “Hormuz closure went from a hypothetical tail risk to a demonstrated and effective tactic.”

Oil analysts believe the conflict’s eventual resolution could ultimately involve some kind of agreement to allow Iran to charge tolls for safe passage through the strait. Some critics fear that would set a precedent for other countries to charge ships to pass through international waterways.

But such precedent already exists, noted Natasha Kaneva, head of commodities analysis at JPMorgan. The United Nations allows countries to charge service fees – not to transit waterways but for navigational safety, traffic management, security escorts, emergency response and environmental protection. Turkey, Denmark, Sweden, Russia and Indonesia all charge service fees for transiting various straits, Kaneva pointed out.

The change could add $1 or so to the price of oil if Iran adopts a fee structure similar to what Turkey charges for the Turkish Straits, Kaneva said. A very large crude carrier could pay around $260,000 for a round-trip transit.

China cements its role as an oil market power

It doesn’t produce much oil, but China proved it is the most powerful force in the oil market during the Iran war.

That’s because China demonstrated a unique ability to modulate its demand, said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist for RSM US.

China’s heavy reliance on the massive oil stockpiles it built up before the war dramatically reduced the country’s crude imports by around 5 million barrels per day. At some point, it will need to refill its stockpiles and demand will pick up again.

But some changes in Chinese consumer behavior will become permanent.

A mobile charging robot works at a charging and swapping station on August 3, 2026 in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province of China. Wang Luxian/VCG/AP

For example, during the five-day May Day holiday, EV charging on China’s highways surged 55.6% over the previous year, according to China’s Ministry of Transport. Over the course of the holiday, just under a quarter of cars traveling on China’s highways were EVs — up 33% from a year earlier.

China was also able to quickly switch from oil- and gas-burning electricity plants to coal, demonstrating unparalleled resilience in the face of an unprecedented oil shock.

Demand for oil plunged during the war — much more than oil industry analysts had expected — proving that the world is much more flexible about its oil usage than previously believed.

Of the 1.9 billion barrels of Middle Eastern crude that the market lost during the course of the war, 800 million barrels — just under half — were absorbed by people and businesses consuming less oil, according to JPMorgan.

It’s not clear how much of that flexibility is permanent and how much is temporary. But permanent declines in oil usage, even just from China, could dent demand enough that it never fully recovers. We may have reached peak oil.

“History suggests that past oil shocks often left lasting declines in gasoline demand, and this episode may prove no different,” said Kaneva.

Production outside the Middle East ramped up

Another significant adjustment during the Iran war was the ramp-up in oil production from unexpected sources.

Exploration and alternative energy development outside the Middle East is ramping up, noted Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. And existing oil projects are dialing up their drilling: Brazil added 800,000 barrels per day to its crude output. Guyana added 300,000, Canada 200,000 and Norway 150,000, according to JPMorgan.

And the United States, which initially resisted increasing its output out of fear of getting burned by a temporary oil price spike, now produces 900,000 barrels a day more than it did at this point last year.

Most of America’s increased production came from privately operated rigs shipping to refineries to produce jet fuel and natural gas for the European market, which is running low on supplies. US production could dip a bit once the Strait of Hormuz is fully opened, but JPMorgan expects America’s output to remain close to today’s levels.

An oil refinery operates 24 hours a day in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on March 25, 2026. Fabio Teixeira/Anadolu/Getty Images

Brazil surprised oil analysts by producing far more than thought capable of at this point, but strong execution in its oil projects will probably lead the country to ramp up production even more. And a new offshore production vessel arriving off the coast of Guyana this month will help the country up the pace of its production from its gigantic well.

To compensate, Middle Eastern producers are changing the way they transport crude, developing alternate routes. Saudi Arabia hired massive truck convoys to ship goods across the country to the Red Sea and maxed out its East-West pipeline to bypass the strait. Iraq is in conversations with Chevron to build a pipeline to the Mediterranean Sea.

Meanwhile, OPEC is in a fight for its own survival after the United Arab Emirates, one of the consortium’s most significant members, announced it would leave the group in April.

Iraq, the bloc’s second-largest oil producer, is reportedly the next shoe to drop — the country’s oil minister told Bloomberg that Iraq would have to decide whether or not to remain with OPEC if production targets don’t dramatically increase. Iraq wants permission to produce a record 5 million barrels a day coming out of the war, with a long-term aim of up to 7 million barrels a day, Bloomberg reported.

That could force Saudi Arabia to allow other countries to produce more oil than the world demands. That could be good for consumer prices, driving them lower. But it could also create a permanent oil glut that could dramatically reduce oil profits.

World.title: Russia’s drone strike near Ukraine-Poland border puts NATO neighbors on edge
World.content:
It doesn’t really matter if they meant to do it.

The Russian drone strike that hit a train near Ukraine’s border with Poland as a group of former Western officials travelled out of the country is a clear escalation by Moscow. Ukraine’s railway network said it believes former CIA chief David Petraeus, former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and other dignitaries who were all nearby, either at the local railway station or on trains, were likely targeted.

Intent is hard to prove in conflict. The proof, to some degree, is an afterthought in the rubble – the damage is by then clear, as is the need for retaliation. Killing a former CIA chief on a railway platform would have provided some element of deniability for Russia; how could they know for sure he was there? But it would fulfil the warnings of Western intelligence, circulating for some time now, that Moscow will seek some form of escalation with Ukraine’s NATO allies in the near future.

A full-on military conflict with NATO seemed an unlikely goal for a Russian state struggling to suppress and occupy its relatively tiny neighbor. Instead, a lateral move, in the deniable hybrid space, seemed more likely, and Ukraine and others warned its borders with NATO states might come under attack.

The immediate impact of Ukraine’s diplomatic commuter link being under attack is profound. The railway is the best method for heads of state or senior officials from Ukraine’s allies to get in and out of Kyiv, to show vital support, share the most sensitive intelligence, or discuss vital matters. Trains, and the civilians on them, now routinely come under attack from Russian drones. The latest versions use other airborne Russian drones to transmit signals and even video feeds, in real time, back to their pilots inside Russia. These “mesh” networks extend their range and lessen the risk electronic warfare can disrupt them, a remarkable development that helped Moscow hit trains so close to Poland.

Ukraine’s Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha, left, greets Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham upon his arrival by train in Kyiv on August 24. Henry Nicholls/Getty Images

The net result is Western officials and their security details, whose job it is to minimize risk, must now either rethink how they get in and out of Ukraine or widen the envelope of acceptable risk. In a wartorn country where air travel is too perilous to even consider, the roads are the obvious option, but are jammed, precarious, and cursed with long, torturous border queues. New ideas are needed to maintain the flow of high-profile visitors to Kyiv at a time when shows of support, real aid, and proper partnership are essential. It is likely that without the option of a swift and safe railway, Western officials facing a longer trip time than about 10 hours each way will reconsider whether a remote video call isn’t just better.

This is likely part of Russia’s aim – to deny Ukraine the easy and free use of its border crossings and rail network to move goods and important visitors, and to leave its Western neighbors on edge. Moscow’s drip-drip escalation has been palpable for years now, as sabotage incidents become more frequent, and recklessness in the form of stray drones or ballistic missiles cross into and test NATO’s outer defenses.

The latest example came early Tuesday, when Lithuania said NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered its airspace. “With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region,” said Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda.

None of this sustained probing is accidental. It all fits inside Russia’s grey-zone doctrine of conflict, in which heightening confrontation happens in gradual, tiny steps, none of which, in themselves, appear worth starting a war over.

Passengers wait outside their sleeper train during an air alert of Russian missiles and drones near the city of Smila, Ukraine, on August 20. Reuters

But the picture is increasingly bleak for NATO and, of course, Ukraine. Moscow correctly calculates that NATO – fractured between the Trump administration and Europe and partially distracted with Iran – does not have the bandwidth or budget for proper conflict with a Kremlin that believes winning – or even sustaining – this war in some way is a matter of survival.

Similarly, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin lacks the resources to risk a full-on war with NATO. But his military-industrial base is slowly edging into a new era of cheaper, longer-range, more accurate and deadly drones and missiles. The new Russian jet-powered Geran 4 and 5 drones travel at 600 kilometers (373 miles) an hour over 1,000 kilometers. Ukraine struggles to stop them, and its engineers are working on the issue 24/7 as a matter of life and death. For NATO, they represent a future horror that European member states hope never comes their way, given that their military spending on the technology they would need to defend themselves is, to be polite, uselessly behind the curve.

Ukrainians already face a winter blighted by heightened attacks on heating and food supplies. That is guaranteed, especially as the West has failed to supply them with more Patriot interceptors. The fresh struggle of the coming months will be for NATO to tackle Moscow’s growing reach, daring and persistence, when it comes to threatening their borders, former prime ministers on railways, and probably border crossing points too.

The warnings of escalation have amplified for months. With Sunday’s railway attack, the moment of their realization is upon a poorly-equipped Western alliance.

World.title: Trump won’t put the brakes on AI because he wants to beat China. How big a threat is Beijing?
World.content:
Hong Kong —

Last weekend, as the world worried about the possibility of unconstrained artificial intelligence wiping out humanity, the leaders of the United States and China articulated their visions for the era-defining technology.

They came from almost opposite sides of the spectrum.

Brushing aside the calls from AI scientists and executives from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to slow the development, US President Donald Trump said what was most important was keeping the US in the lead against China in the intensifying AI superpower race.

“We’re leading China in AI…and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins,” he said on Saturday.

On Sunday, China’s leader Xi Jinping made his own call for more international cooperation. Countries should “encourage open source, openness, collaboration and sharing,” he said in a speech in India to Global South leaders, in which he reiterated a proposal for a global AI governance pact – although he did not give details on what that framework would look like.

The juxtaposition of Trump and Xi’s messages underscores the lack of consensus and a deep trust deficit between the two superpowers in the high-stakes race to dominate AI.

The US appears to be increasingly weaponizing its dominance in the sector, seeing it as a strategic asset to be protected, and exported to friendly countries, while China, lagging in the race, is proposing a more open model.

AI will loom large at the highly anticipated Trump-Xi summit in two weeks in Washington. At their May meeting in Beijing, the two discussed AI guardrails but produced limited results, and last week the Chinese Ministry of Commerce said the two leaders had agreed to set up an intergovernmental dialogue on AI. But with their broader geopolitical rivalry, experts have low expectations for any meaningful breakthrough.

How big of a threat is China?

Chinese AI has trailed its American competitors for years. That’s partly thanks to US technology controls that limit Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI processors — essential for training increasingly complex AI models.

But last year Chinese AI startup DeepSeek shocked the global industry with a model that approached the performance of leading American systems using what it said were far fewer computing resources.

Since then, Chinese AI labs have iterated faster, with Alibaba, Z.AI, Minimax and most recently Moonshot unveiling similarly capable models that challenge the dominance of American frontier companies like Anthropic and OpenAI.

Alongside the advances of Chinese models, however, came ever louder US accusations of cheating. Washington, as well as OpenAI and Anthropic, have alleged that Chinese companies stole American intellectual property by training their models on the outputs of frontier US models, a process known as distillation in the industry.

Last week, US federal agencies, including the FBI, National Security Agency, and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, claimed Chinese AI firms are committing “industrial-scale” theft of their American counterparts.

US President Donald Trump listens to members of the media aboard Air Force One, en route to Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, following a two-day visit to Ireland, September 13, 2026. Kylie Cooper/Reuters

In a lengthy report last week, Anthropic also detailed attempts by bad actors, including alleged Chinese government-affiliated operators, misusing its systems to develop weapons and conduct surveillance on minorities like Uyghurs in Xinjiang.

In one example, Anthropic uncovered sensitive information about Chinese surveillance attempts because queries from a user – believed to be linked with the Chinese military – sent to Moonshot’s Kimi model were rerouted to Claude, exposing Moonshot’s secret attempt to divert user requests to Claude, the report said. Other Chinese firms like DeepSeek also engaged in such a practice, it added.

Beijing has rejected the allegations, while Chinese AI labs have largely stayed silent. Moonshot declined to comment on the report to CNN last week, while DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.

“Spreading various threatening narratives, pursuing confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt efforts toward global AI governance and serve the interests of none,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun on Monday.

“All parties should work together to promote AI that is open, inclusive, accessible and beneficial to humanity,” he added.

What’s China proposing?

Just as the US feels increasingly threatened by China’s rapidly advancing models, Beijing is also alarmed by the cyber capabilities of systems developed by American companies – capabilities on display this summer when agents from OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue and launched unauthorized hacks of other systems.

Beijing also sees AI safety risks differently, beyond the US understanding of existential risks, like AI agents going rogue. Besides prioritizing political control and maintaining social stability, it sees the US as a “hegemonic threat” to its own development of the technology.

In an article on Sunday, State Security Minister Chen Yixin highlighted the risks of “hegemonic practices” in a veiled jab at the US for “establishing entity lists, imposing technology controls, monopolizing industry standards, and creating closed-source ecosystems” under the name of safeguarding national security.

“These actions fragment global AI industry and supply chains, worsening the development imbalance in the global AI industry,” he wrote.

An editorial in state-backed tabloid Global Times over the weekend also dismissed the recent essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

“On the surface, this appears to be a ‘rational statement’ focused on global AI security,” the editorial read. “A close reading, however, reveals its hidden agenda: The article is packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.”

Are people in China worried about AI?

While prominent executives and researchers in the US have gone public with their fears about the technology’s risks, raising similar concerns in China, where the ruling Communist Party tightly controls the media and surveils its population, is far more difficult and comes with much higher risks.

China’s technology sector also operates within a far more top-down regulatory environment, with the government setting extensive rules governing what AI systems can produce and how they are deployed. China’s national AI safety standards, for example, set requirements covering training data, privacy, security and prohibited content.

The 2026 Bund Conference concludes at the Huangpu Expo Park in Shanghai, China, on September 12, 2026. VCG/AP

There is also greater public optimism about AI in China. A 2025 Edelman survey found that 72% of respondents in China said they trusted AI, compared with just 32% in the US.

And while Chinese AI labs have rapidly narrowed the gap with their American counterparts, they still trail the most advanced US systems. That may give Chinese companies and researchers less incentive to voluntarily constrain the development and deployment of increasingly capable AI systems as they seek to catch up.

Can the two powers come together on AI?

There appears to be little reason for optimism. Despite a trade truce reached between the two countries in October last year, tensions have continued to flare.

The central obstacle is trust. Washington fears that cooperation could give China access to technology that strengthens its military and economic power, while Beijing sees “national security” as a US excuse to constrain China’s technological rise.

A post last month by Yuyuantantian, a social media account affiliated with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, laid out the conditions for the US-China AI dialogue, saying Washington must guarantee its AI companies would follow any agreed-upon rules and regulations before any negotiations can take place.

“A clear distinction must be made between genuine safety threats and mere technological competition,” it said. “The real question is not ‘whether to govern,’ but who should define the safety boundaries of these frontier models.”

World.title: Canada is pursuing a ‘unique alliance’ with the EU as US ties remain fraught. Here’s what we know
World.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is pursuing a “unique alliance” with the European Union, a further signal of Ottawa’s efforts to pivot away from the Washington amid a deepening trade war.

The notion of Canada joining the 27-member bloc — or at least pursuing closer ties with it — has gained traction within the country in the past two years as Canada has sought to reduce its economic dependence on the US.

A Wall Street Journal report published Saturday detailed how, in the wake of Trump’s tariffs, Carney pushed to bolster ties with the trading bloc, instructing a special envoy to Europe to scope out possibilities “short of full membership in the EU or its common market,” citing people familiar with the matter.

Speaking to reporters Sunday, Carney said Canada is not “looking to become a member of the European Union,” but rather beginning discussions on forming a “unique alliance” with the bloc, with which it already has a far-reaching trade agreement.

“We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths,” said Carney, who is set to deliver a speech to the European Parliament this week.

Here’s what we know about Canada and the EU’s growing ties.

Could Canada feasibly join the EU?

The short answer is no, at least not as a full member.

Canada, a former British colony, shares deep cultural and historical ties to Europe and resembles European models when it comes to its parliamentary democracy, universal health care and social welfare, among other things.

Canada even shares a small land border with Europe, through Denmark on Hans Island, a small landmass off northwest Greenland.

But while Canada would likely satisfy the political, economic and legal standards for joining the bloc, there is one obvious barrier: it is not geographically in Europe.

To get into the EU, a country must follow a strict, multi-stage process called accession, and its candidacy must be unanimously approved by all 27 member states.

There is a lineup of countries waiting to get in, with nine countries currently recognized as candidates for EU membership.

Other European countries, such as Norway and Switzerland, are not formal EU members but partner with the bloc on trade and open borders.

Mark Carney, Canada’s Prime Minister, during a Bloomberg Television interview in Toronto on September 14. Cole Burston/Bloomberg/Getty Images

What would a ‘unique alliance’ look like?

According to the Journal, Carney has suggested to European leaders that Canada take on a tailored, highly integrated role as a so-called “associate member” — an idea that at least some leaders in the bloc seem open to, according to officials from both sides.

Among the things European and Canadian officials have discussed, according to the Journal: reducing trade barriers; laying underwater cables linking Europe and Canada; redirecting pipelines to grant Europe access to Canadian gas; building new AI and tech infrastructure; and even granting Canadians the right to live and work in Europe visa-free.

Under these terms, Canada would have a relationship with the EU that is unprecedented for a country outside of Europe. The EU’s ambassador to Canada told the Canadian Press last week the partnership would be unlike anything that currently exists, without giving specifics.

Details about what a potential alliance could look like have yet to be announced publicly. But there are signs that Canada and the EU are growing closer.

Ahead of Carney’s speech Thursday in Strasbourg, France, the European Parliament announced it will open a new antenna office in Ottawa, underlining its commitment to “deepening political dialogue and cooperation with Canada,” according to a news release.

The allies already share a sizable trading relationship, which has grown steadily since large parts of the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement came into force in 2017.

Bilateral trade in goods and services reached €130.8 billion ($151 billion) last year, according to the European Commission, up more than 80% over the past decade. Major EU exports to Canada include cars, machinery and pharmaceuticals. Canadian exports to Europe include crude oil, fertilizer, critical minerals and base metals.

What have European leaders said?

Carney, a former governor of the Bank of England, has strong ties in Europe from his banking days, and has cultivated his relationships with like-minded European leaders since becoming prime minister in March 2025.

In Paris last year, during his first official foreign trip as leader — which was notably not to the US in a break from modern tradition — Carney described Canada as “the most European of non-European countries.”

Since then, several European Union countries have floated the idea of Canada joining the bloc, including Finland’s President Alexander Stubb, who once called the possibility “a marriage made in heaven.”

Stubb and Carney reportedly text each other daily and are known for squeezing in a jog or a game of ice hockey between meetings on official trips.

In an April interview with CNN newsgathering partner CBC News, Stubb said he can “envisage a much larger EU, whether Canada is a part of it or not is up to Canada to decide,” and said with the two countries’ close values they could “forge a really close strategic partnership.”

“Wouldn’t it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?” asked Stubb, according to the Journal.

France’s President Emmanuel Macron (R) gestures as he greets Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney during the G7 summit, in Evian, France, on June 15. Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

Carney has also leaned into Canada’s long-standing relationship with France, traveling to the country several times during his tenure, to warm reception from French President Emmanuel Macron. The two leaders are set to meet Sunday in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon — a tiny French island just 25 kilometers (15 miles) off the coast of Newfoundland.

In March, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot raised the idea of Ottawa joining the EU, telling a conference that “maybe Canada at some point” will sign up, according to the Canadian Press.

That’s not to say all EU leaders would support Canada’s bid. Ten member states have yet to ratify the trade agreement Canada and the EU signed in 2016, eliminating nearly all preexisting tariffs.

What’s the reception been in Canada?

Canadians are largely in favor of strengthening relations with the EU, though support for full membership remains split, according to recent data.

A survey conducted earlier this month by Canadian polling firm Abacus Data found about 80% of Canadians said Canada should deepen cooperation with the EU on foreign policy, defense, and economic priorities — a 6-point increase from when the question was last asked in February.

A further 56% of those surveyed said Canada has more in common with EU countries than with the US, according to the survey. Nearly half (49%) said they would support Canada joining the EU, with support higher among center and left-leaning voters.

However, some in Canada are skeptical of cozying up to the EU, fearing it could further isolate Canada from its southern neighbor and largest trading partner, while others are concerned about a loss of sovereignty.

Pierre Poilievre, the leader of Canada’s opposition Conservative Party, called Carney’s effort to deepen ties with the EU “out of touch,” in a post to X following the report.

“We will NEVER be the 51st U.S. state. And we will NEVER be the 28th EU state.”

World.title: Content creator arrested in Cairo over ‘offensive videos’
World.content:
Security authorities in Cairo on Monday apprehended a content creator for posting videos on her social media pages showing her dancing in indecent attire.

The General Administration for the Protection of Public Morals, part of the Specialized Police Sector, spotted the content creator’s activities.

Following the necessary legal procedures, she was arrested in Nasr City, eastern Cairo.

Two mobile phones were found in her possession; upon examination, they were found to contain evidence confirming her criminal activity.

When confronted, she admitted to posting the aforementioned videos on her social media pages to increase viewership and generate financial profit.

World.title: More hot weather ahead in Egypt for Wednesday and Thursday
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) forecasts a continued temporary rise in temperatures across most parts of the country on Tuesday.

Temperatures are expected to peak in the south, with felt temperatures reaching 46C on Wednesday—a day when September’s weather merges with the heat typical of August.

The weather will be hot during the day and tend towards mildness at night, with a chance of mist appearing on some roads.

The EMA said that weather conditions on Wednesday and Thursday will see a continued slight and temporary rise in temperatures across most regions.

Hot conditions will prevail during the day, while the night will be humid and mild—leaning towards hot—with persistent high humidity levels intensifying the perceived temperature.

According to weather forecasts, maximum temperatures along the northern coast will range between 30C and 33C, while Cairo and the Lower Egypt will see highs of around 35-36C.

Temperatures in northern Upper Egypt will range from 38-40C, reaching 44-45C in southern Upper Egypt.

The weather will rise by approximately two degrees due to high humidity levels.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egypt, Singapore explore means to expand cooperation
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty held talks with Singaporean Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Home Affairs Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim on ways to further advance bilateral relations and broaden the scope of cooperation between the two countries.

The two sides also exchanged views on a number of regional and international issues of mutual interest.

Minister Abdelatty expressed appreciation for the positive trajectory of Egyptian-Singaporean relations and the momentum they have gained in recent months, particularly following the visit of the President of Singapore to Egypt in September 2025.

He underscored the importance of following up on the outcomes of the presidential visit, including the implementation of the agreements and memoranda of understanding concluded during the visit.

He also highlighted the need to explore proposals for further developing bilateral ties across various fields, particularly as Egypt and Singapore prepare to celebrate next year the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations.

Minister Abdelatty also outlined promising opportunities for the localization of priority industries in Egypt, calling on Singaporean companies to expand their investments and capitalize on the competitive advantages offered by the Egyptian economy, particularly the incentives and facilities available in the Suez Canal Economic Zone.

The minister stressed the importance of further strengthening institutional relations between Egypt and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), in light of Egypt’s close ties with the bloc’s member states.

He noted that Egypt was among the first Arab and African countries to sign the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation with ASEAN in 2016.

He expressed Egypt’s desire to upgrade its relationship with the association to the status of Sectoral Dialogue Partner, which would create broader opportunities for cooperation with ASEAN member states across a wide range of areas.

The talks also covered a number of regional and international issues of mutual interest, particularly developments concerning the Palestinian Cause.

Minister Abdelatty stressed the need to move forward with the second phase of US President Donald Trump’s peace plan, secure Israel’s withdrawal from the Gaza Strip, ensure the full and sustained delivery of humanitarian assistance, support early recovery and reconstruction efforts, and empower the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, paving the way for the Palestinian Authority to resume the full exercise of its responsibilities in both the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.

For his part, the Singaporean minister expressed his country’s appreciation for Egypt’s tireless efforts to consolidate the ceasefire, implement the understandings reached under the Sharm El-Sheikh agreement, and complete the roadmap.

He also commended Egypt’s pivotal role in ensuring the delivery of humanitarian and relief assistance to the Gaza Strip.

World.title: President al-Sisi to receive Saudi crown prince Tuesday
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is expected to receive Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia in Cairo on Tuesday for extensive talks on bilateral relations and regional developments.

The two leaders will hold a bilateral meeting, followed by an extensive round of talks involving delegations from both countries, and a banquet hosted by President Sisi in honor of the crown prince, according to the presidential spokesman.

Discussions will focus on ways to bolster bilateral relations at various levels, and on sharing views on regional and international developments of mutual concern.

World.title: Breach Or Betrayal? Liberia Grapples With Fallout From Child Data Leak
World.content:
Monrovia — A controversy that began with a single Facebook post has widened into a pointed question for the Liberian government: how did confidential records on some of the country’s most vulnerable children end up in the public domain?

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh | [email protected]

The post, published by Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, was meant to showcase results from the government’s Save the Future Project. Instead, it disclosed names, ages, schools, home addresses, and family details of children enrolled in the program. Ali deleted the post soon after — but child-protection advocates say that response missed the point entirely.

“If he put it down, Mark Zuckerberg got it,” said Alex Destiny Newon, an executive member of the Child Protection Network, at a meeting with Ministry of Gender officials. Once information is posted online, he said, it can be copied and redistributed regardless of whether the original is removed.

What the Ministry Has Confirmed

In a statement issued September 13, the Ministry of Gender confirmed the records were authentic and belonged to the Save the Future Project. It clarified they were not a list of survivors of sexual or gender-based violence, but records of children removed from street begging or vending and enrolled in support services.

That clarification answered one question — but not the one advocates say matters most: how the records left government custody.

The Unanswered Question: Who Had Access?

The Ministry acknowledged sharing collated statistics and supporting data with funding partners for monitoring and accountability purposes. But advocates note a critical distinction: authorization to share aggregated data for program oversight is not the same as authorization to publish identifiable personal information.

That distinction is now central to calls for an investigation. Key unresolved questions include:

• Who collected, entered, and maintained the records, and who had access to the electronic files?

• Were copies shared with external partners, and under what safeguards?

• Was the information transmitted electronically, printed, or shared through messaging platforms?

• Could aggregated, non-identifying data have served the same purpose?

One advocate, who said he spent 10 months on child-protection work and had previously sought Save the Future data through official channels, said he was denied the same information now circulating publicly. “I couldn’t get it,” he said — a detail that raises its own questions about who could.

The Stakes for the Children Involved

Keifala Kromah, Chairperson of the Child Rights Advocacy Alliance and the Child Protection Network, warned the fallout could be “far-reaching,” particularly for children with disabilities, and for minors who may now feel unable to return to schools or communities where their circumstances have become public knowledge.

The National Association of Social Workers of Liberia (NASOWL) went further, framing the disclosure as a political act. In a statement issued Monday, the association said personal information obtained through government office “should not be treated as information that can be publicly disclosed to advance a political argument,” adding: “Children must never become political ammunition or pawns.”

NASOWL cited Liberia’s Children’s Law of 2011, which guarantees children’s rights to privacy, and called for comprehensive data-protection safeguards covering health, education, disability, and case-management records.

A Test for Liberia’s New Data Laws

The timing is notable: President Joseph Boakai recently signed the Cybercrime and Data Protection Acts into law, aimed at strengthening safeguards around personal information. Advocates argue this incident is an early test of whether that legislation translates into practice — through staff training, access controls, and clear disclosure procedures — or remains largely symbolic.

What Comes Next

The Ministry says it is investigating. But advocates are watching for two things beyond the inquiry itself: whether it identifies a breach of law or professional responsibility, and whether anyone is held accountable if it does.

The bigger risk, advocates say, is one of trust. If families believe information they share with government programs could later surface online, they may grow reluctant to seek help at all — undermining the very interventions meant to protect them.

As one advocate put it, the authenticity of the leaked records is no longer in question. What remains is simpler, and harder to answer: how did the data get out?

World.title: Liberia: Saudi Rice Trial Goes to Court, But Victims Say They Still Want the Help They Were Promised
World.content:
Former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and other defendants leave court after an August appearance in the Saudi rice trial. Credit: Willie Togbah

Summary

The long-delayed trial over Saudi-donated rice intended for vulnerable and disaster-affected Liberians but was allegedly diverted to line officials’ pockets has begun in Monrovia.

Some flood victims in River Cess said they know little about the case and are receiving few updates as the trial moves forward.

Victims said justice should mean more than prosecution. They want missing public assets recovered and affected communities to benefit.

By Joyclyn Wea, gender correspondent with New Narratives

INTERNATIONAL TIMBER INDUSTRY VILLAGE, River Cess County — When Eric Kollor learned that former government officials were finally on trial over thousands of bags of Saudi-donated rice meant for vulnerable and disaster-affected Liberians, he was surprised. The case had been moving through the courts in Monrovia, but Kollor, one of the flood victims the assistance was supposed to help, did not know the trial had begun.

Kollor still remembers the 2024 flood that swept through International Timber Industry Village, widely known as ITI Village, damaging homes, the bridge, the police station and leaving families struggling. Residents were told government relief, including food and blankets, was coming. Kollor said none of it reached him.

Homes overtaken by floodwaters in ITI Village. Credit: Eric Doue

“I want justice to be served well,” Kollor said.

Advocates said the trial is testing more than whether former officials illegally handled thousands of bags of Saudi-donated rice. It is also testing whether Liberia’s accountability system can deliver something meaningful for disaster victims who said promised assistance never reached them.

Saudi Arabia donated 29,000 bags of 25-kilogram rice to Liberia in 2023 for vulnerable and disaster-affected people in Margibi and River Cess counties. Prosecutors allege that 25,054 bags of rice, worth about US$425,918, were stolen, misapplied, or improperly distributed. For families in flood-hit communities such as ITI Village and nearby Glanyah Town, the bigger question is whether prosecution and recovery of public assets will ever translate into help for the people the rice was intended to serve.

More than a year after senior former officials were arrested over the handling of that donation, their trial is now underway in Criminal Court “C” in Monrovia. The defendants have pleaded not guilty and are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. The trial began August 17 after months of delays.

In Glanyah Town, Veronica Wesseh had heard about the case. But for her, putting former officials on trial is not enough. She wants the missing assistance recovered and affected families to benefit.

“Let them bring our food. We are waiting for it,” Wesseh said.

Keita lives now in squalid conditions, lacking basic shelter and furniture, including the mattress he once used: Photo by Eric Opa Doue

For residents of ITI Village and Glanyah, the case has reopened painful memories of a disaster that destroyed homes and left many families waiting for assistance. A previous New Narratives investigation found that the 2024 floods swallowed 27 homes in the two communities and left at least one person dead. Six months later, residents said much of the government assistance they had been promised had still not arrived.

Across Liberia, floods affected about 100,000 people in 2024, according to Liberia’s disaster authorities. River Cess, Bong and Grand Cape Mount were among the hardest-hit counties. Wesseh remembers days of heavy rain before floodwater entered Glanyah.

She said soldiers later brought small quantities of rice, gari, salt and other supplies to the community. But she said many residents did not receive the larger assistance they had been told was coming.

The disaster reflects a growing national challenge.

The World Bank has warned that worsening climate impacts could shrink Liberia’s economy by 15 percent and push another 1.3 million people into poverty by 2050 if the country does not strengthen its ability to adapt. That makes the handling of disaster relief especially important for communities likely to face more flooding in the years ahead.

The Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce, which investigated the Saudi rice case, said affected communities were involved in parts of the investigation.

Joseph F. Daniels, public relations officer of the Taskforce, said investigators visited communities in River Cess, Margibi, Bomi and Sinoe and spoke with residents and community leaders. He said some residents remain in contact with investigators and may testify for the state as the trial unfolds.

But Daniels acknowledged that this does not mean every affected resident is receiving individual updates about what is happening in court. Before the trial began, he said, the Taskforce issued public statements and appeared on radio programs, mostly in Monrovia, to explain developments in the case. It also relies on journalists to help keep the wider public informed.

A court gag order now limits what the Taskforce can publicly say while the case is underway, Daniels said. He said broader public updates are expected after the trial ends. For now, that communication has not reached everyone.

Anthony Ben Jones, a former stipendiary magistrate and elder with relatives in Glanyah, said some residents are only now beginning to understand the details of the case. In ITI Village, Kollor learned that the trial had begun only during his interview with New Narratives.

For victims, that information gap adds another layer to a case already centered on whether public assistance reached the people for whom it was intended.

The Task Force said its goal goes beyond securing convictions. Daniels said its responsibility is to investigate the alleged misuse of public assets and recover anything that can be retrieved.

But recovery does not automatically mean flood victims such as Kollor and Wesseh would receive the recovered rice, money or other assets. Daniels said decisions about who receives disaster assistance would fall to the National Disaster Management Agency, the government institution responsible for identifying disaster victims and distributing relief.

That leaves an important unanswered question for residents. There is no guarantee that prosecutors will recover the missing rice or its value. Even if assets are recovered, there is no guarantee they will be returned directly to the communities and families who say they went without assistance.

For victims far from the Monrovia courtroom, justice may be measured differently: by whether accountability eventually delivers something tangible to the people who were supposed to benefit in the first place.

This story was produced by New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. The funder had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Whispers of a Handshake: Inside the Rumor Mill Surrounding Kolubah and Pres. Boakai
World.content:
MONROVIA — Rumors move fast in Liberian politics, but few in recent memory have traveled as quickly, or generated as much chatter, as the reports now circulating about a possible reconciliation between expelled lawmaker Yekeh Kolubah and President Joseph Boakai.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

No press conference has been called. No joint statement has been issued. Yet across party circles, radio call-in shows, and political WhatsApp groups, the same question is being asked is it actually happening?

Where the Rumor Started

The reports trace to a single, semi-official source from Samson Moseray, Kolubah’s Public Relations Officer, who has told inquirers that a reconciliation meeting between his boss and the president is in the works. Moseray has framed the move in patriotic terms, saying Kolubah has decided to “mend fences and put Liberia first.”

Beyond that comment, however, the picture thins out considerably. There has been no confirmation from the Executive Mansion, no statement from Kolubah in his own voice, and no disclosed date, venue, or agenda for any such meeting. What exists, in other words, is a claim from one side of the story — enough to set tongues wagging, but not enough to call it fact.

A Silence That Speaks Loudly

Perhaps the most telling detail in this entire episode is what Kolubah himself has not said. Despite the swirl of speculation, he has offered no public explanation of whether he intends to soften his opposition posture, under what conditions he might do so, or whether “reconciliation” means anything beyond a symbolic sit-down.

FrontPage Africa editor seeking his direct comment has come up empty so far. In the absence of his voice, the rumor has been left to grow largely on its own momentum, shaped by Moseray’s brief remarks and by the political imagination of observers filling in the blanks.

Why the Rumor Is So Combustible

Ordinarily, a report that two politicians might meet would barely register as news. What makes this one different is the sheer distance the rumor asks people to travel. Kolubah has spent recent years as one of the most unrelenting critics of the Boakai administration, and he did so, by his own reported words, in absolute terms — declaring on more than one occasion that reconciliation with the president was something he could never accept.

His strongest version of that vow reportedly invoked the memory of his late mother, framing any future reconciliation as an act he equated with betraying her. Whether or not the meeting materializes, the rumor’s power comes precisely from how far it would require Kolubah to walk back his own past declarations.

The Political Backstory Fueling Speculation

To understand why so many are willing to entertain the rumor, it helps to remember that Kolubah and Boakai were once on the same side. During the 2023 election, Kolubah was among the opposition figures who campaigned for the Unity Party’s ticket, part of the coalition that ultimately unseated then-President George Weah. That alliance frayed after Boakai took office, as Kolubah accused the new administration of failing to deliver on its campaign promises and became one of its most vocal detractors.

Observers point to that earlier alliance as evidence that a political relationship, however damaged, is not necessarily beyond repair — which is part of why the current rumor has found an audience willing to believe it, rather than dismiss it outright.

The Legal Shadow Hanging Over the Rumor

Adding another layer to the speculation is the unresolved status of Kolubah’s own seat. He was expelled from the House of Representatives after remarks he made during the Liberia-Guinea border dispute, in which he suggested the disputed territory belonged to Guinea — comments that lawmakers treated as a breach of his duty to defend Liberia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, serious enough in their view to warrant expulsion.

Kolubah has challenged that decision, and the matter remains before the Supreme Court more than four months later, with the District 10 seat still vacant. Against that backdrop, some of the speculation has taken on a transactional flavor that could reconciliation with President Boakai be less about sentiment and more about strategy, timed to a moment when Kolubah’s legal fate is still undecided?

That theory remains unproven, but it is precisely the kind of question rumors like this one tend to invite.

Reading the Opposition’s Reaction — Or Lack of One

So far, there has been little public reaction from within the opposition, a silence that is itself part of the story. Kolubah’s own camp has reportedly voiced frustration with what it calls the “disintegration and unseriousness” of opposition politics generally, a comment that has been read by some as a justification, in advance, for any reconciliation that might follow. Without a formal opposition response, however, it is difficult to say whether that framing will hold up once — or if — an actual meeting takes place.

What Would Confirm the Rumor

For a story built almost entirely on secondhand accounts and a single spokesperson’s comments, the natural next question is what it would take to move this from rumor to reality. A joint appearance, a statement from Kolubah himself, or confirmation from the Executive Mansion would each mark a meaningful shift from speculation to substance.

Until one of those happens, the reconciliation remains exactly what it has been since the story first surfaced about a widely discussed possibility, resting on limited confirmation, in a political environment primed to believe almost anything.

A Story Still Being Written

Rumors of this kind rarely stay static for long in Liberian politics — they either collapse under the weight of denial or harden into fact once the parties involved step forward. For now, the Kolubah-Boakai reconciliation sits in that in-between space that is too persistent to ignore, too unconfirmed to accept at face value. Whether it becomes a defining political moment or simply another rumor that faded once scrutinized will depend on what Kolubah and the president each choose to say next — and, unlike the rumor itself, that part of the story has not yet been written.

World.title: The Long Wait for Fistula Surgery in Liberia
World.content:
‘Lorpu’ suffered the loss of her baby as well as the debilitating effects of obstetric fistula. The condition afflicts almost half a million women and girls a year, with half of those in Sub-Saharan Africa. Copyright: Tina S. Mehnpaine / Daily Observer

For more than three years, Lorpu has lived with the constant leakage of urine and feces caused by obstetric fistula, a debilitating childbirth injury.

By: Tina S. Mehnpaine

The condition where a hole forms between the birth canal and the bladder or rectum. can result from prolonged, obstructed labour, often when timely medical care is unavailable.

It afflicts almost 500,000 women and girls a year worldwide, with half of those in Sub-Saharan Africa, according to the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).

Lorpu developed obstetric fistula after a lengthy labour in Sinoe County, southeastern Liberia, in June 2020, aged 17. She endured hours of painful contractions with the baby trapped in her birth canal.

“I kept hearing the midwife say, ‘Push, push!’ until I couldn’t breathe,” Lorpu told the Daily Observer, struggling to hold back her tears.

“The midwife kept telling me to wait, that the baby was coming. But the baby never came. The pain was like fire, and then everything turned dark.”

Eventually, the baby was delivered stillborn.

Three days later, Lorpu was discharged with no explanation that she had developed an obstetric fistula.

Struggling with incontinence, as well as the pain of losing her baby, Lorpu began to suffer from postnatal depression and insomnia. At one point, she could not even recognize her mother or boyfriend.

Costly ‘cures’

Three weeks later, Lorpu and her mother began searching for answers. They visited a local herbalist, who told them that the leakage was caused by a bruise on Lorpu’s womb. They paid 3,000 Liberian dollars (US$17), along with three kilograms of rice, three chickens and a gallon of red palm oil, for a month’s treatment. It did not work.

Another herbalist was recommended, but again, there was no cure. Lorpu’s aunt then gave her US$300 to travel to Monrovia for further treatment. There, she visited two hospitals in Paynesville, outside the Liberian capital.

“Some doctors said it was an infection that was around my womb,” Lorpu said.

She eventually found help through a family friend in Monrovia, who told her about a free fistula treatment campaign organized by St. Joseph Catholic Hospital in the Liberian capital. Doctors here finally diagnosed her condition, but she did not receive surgery.

By the time she arrived, the campaign had ended. She was instead referred to Phebe Hospital in Suacoco, Bong County, where the Liberian government and its partners funded another fistula campaign.

Lorpu estimates that she has spent more than 160,000 Liberian dollars (US$914) searching for treatment.

“I lost all my business money. My farm went down. Even my mother’s red palm oil business went down too,” she said.

Young women afflicted

Women from rural communities in Grand Bassa, Sinoe, Maryland and Grand Gedeh counties interviewed for this story similarly recalled visiting several health facilities before anyone recognized that they had developed a fistula.

According to Tarmay Yekeh-Saa, deputy director of the Family Health Unit at Liberia’s Ministry of Health, about 100 women are affected by obstetric fistula in Liberia each year.

But she stressed that this is only a rough estimate based largely on the number of women who come forward during treatment campaigns.

“There is no clear record of reported fistula cases,” Yekeh-Saa said.

“When we want to take a quick survey and see what is the age range, what kind of women are affected, you often see that they are young people. Close to two-thirds of them are […] not more than 25 years old.”

Surgeon shortage

Ayun Cassell, a urological surgeon and chairman of the Liberia Medical and Dental Council, says while cost of treatment is a problem, shortage of specialists trained to repair obstetric fistula is also a major obstacle.

“We need a system that enhances affordability,” he said. “One of the biggest barriers has been cost. The next thing is that you need trained surgeons on the ground to perform the surgery.”

Yekeh-Saa agrees with this, noting that “for the last five to seven years in Liberia, we really don’t have the surgeons who can be able to correct these injuries”.

According to the UNFPA, obstetric fistula is preventable when women receive timely emergency obstetric care, including Caesarean sections when necessary.

Cassell, who is also a consultant urologist at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center, said the challenge of early detection and managing complications is particularly acute in rural clinics which may struggle to handle complex obstetric emergencies.

“By the time the patient reaches a facility that can intervene, the window for preventing permanent injury may already be gone,” he said. “By that time, they are so physically and mentally tormented that it breaks my heart.”

Lorpu’s case, he said, illustrates the consequences of prolonged labour without timely intervention.

“A woman should not have to remain in labour [unnecessarily] for many hours before someone decides that the delivery is not progressing.”

The WHO Labour Care Guide recommends monitoring of labour progression to identify complications that need quick interventions.

Treatment campaigns

Nowiah Gorpudolo-Dennis, Liberia’s fistula focal person, says the Ministry of Health is trying to move away from periodic treatment campaigns.

In an email, Dennis told the Daily Observer that Liberia is shifting towards “integrating fistula prevention and treatment into the broader maternal health protocol”.

The plans include training specialists, establishing Liberia’s first fistula treatment unit, developing a national fistula strategy, and tracking cases through the country’s Health Management Information System.

She said “patients will not have to wait for yearly or quarterly campaigns,” which are “expensive and organized only when funding and specialist surgeons become available.”

At the same time, Dennis said previous campaigns had helped inform the ministry’s decision to integrate obstetric fistula prevention and treatment into routine maternal healthcare.

For now, however, Liberia remains dependent on periodic outreach to reduce its backlog of untreated cases.

The dependence is further complicated by the shrinking funding landscape. On 31 August, Sweden ended nearly two decades of bilateral aid to Liberia, putting a stop to a partnership that made it the second largest donor and backer of sexual and reproductive health.

The withdrawal comes after the United States shut down USAID, which funded much of Liberia’s health system. Clinics have since reported shortages of essential supplies.

‘Too severe to treat’

In December 2025, the government conducted a nationwide obstetric fistula campaign, the first in nearly eight years.

According to Dennis, the initiative was led by Health Minister Louise Mapleh Kpoto to reduce the number of women waiting for treatment. Two Ethiopian doctors carried out surgeries at Phebe Hospital and Bomi Hospital.

For Lorpu the campaign offered the possibility of finally ending years of isolation. She attended Phebe Hospital in Suacoco, hopeful that her life might change.

Here, she was joined by others, like Jenet*, who had travelled from different parts of Liberia. Some had spent more than two days on the road.

Lorpu and Jenet waited as other women were examined one-by-one, admitted and taken into surgery. Each time a name was called, she hoped theirs would be next.

For Jenet, that call never came. “I thought when they registered me, my problem was going to end,” she said.

“When I saw the other women going for surgery, I believed my own time was coming. But I was told that my injury was too severe and that I should wait for the next surgical outreach.

“That broke me down. After three years of living with this shame, I still could not get treatment.”

More than 100 people were recruited for the December campaign, but only 33 received treatment.

“We have recruited more than 100 persons, and of those, some could not be repaired,” Yekeh-Saa said, speaking at this year’s International Day to End Obstetric Fistula.

“We were able to treat about 33 persons […] we do not have trained surgeons in the country.”

Lorpu also left the hospital without surgery. The Phebe hospital team told her that another surgery would be arranged, but no date was set.

According to Cassell, the length of time a woman lives with the injury can make treatment more complicated.

“The more the injury stays, the more difficult it becomes for surgery,” he said.

While the government’s plans could eventually bring treatment closer to women like Lorpu and Jenet, they remain uncertain promises for women who have already spent years waiting.

Social exclusion

Lorpu, now aged 20, has suffered years of social exclusion, anxiety, and stigma.

Some in her community accused her of being a witch. Others said her condition was punishment for infidelity.

“This sickness is bad […] you can’t go among your friends,” she said through tears, brushing away flies gathering around her.

Cassell said the uncontrolled leakage of urine, feces, or both can push women with fistula into isolation even before they are openly rejected by others. Many begin to see themselves as unclean or inferior and withdraw from social life because they fear humiliation, he explained.

“They become afraid of being embarrassed, so they remove themselves from social life,” Cassell said.

“A woman may stop going to church, stop selling in the market, and stop visiting friends because she does not want anyone to tell her that she smells.”

For Lorpu, the loss of her baby has compounded that struggle. “If my baby were alive today, maybe this pain would be easier,” she said.

“When I see other women holding their children, I think about the child I lost, and the pain comes back again.”

“I lost my baby and, at the same time, I was left to live with this shameful condition. Sometimes I ask myself why both things had to happen to me. Why me?”

Soapmaking but no surgery

When obstetric fistulas are not diagnosed early, not only can it mean that “multiple surgeries” are needed, but also rehabilitation services, which require significant investment, says Cassell. As part of such rehabilitation programs, patients are taught how to sew and embroider and even given a sewing machine upon discharge, he says, “so that they can become participating members of society”.

At Phebe Hospital, Lorpu and Jenet did not receive surgery, but they were able to take part in a rehabilitation programme.

After spending less than a month at the Phebe Fistula Rehabilitation Center, an 11-bedroom dormitory, they joined more than 50 fistula survivors who received training in soap-making and pastry production, according to Liberia’s Ministry of Gender.

The training was backed by US$245,000 in funding from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), which resulted from a 2024 SciDev.Net article that exposed the healthcare gaps for women suffering from fistula in Liberia.

The funding is also supporting two of three Liberian doctors currently undertaking a two-year course in Ethiopia in urogynecology and pelvic floor reconstruction—training that could help reduce the country’s dependence on foreign specialists and periodic surgical campaigns.

Lorpu and Jenet received US$75 each for transportation back to Sinoe and Maryland, along with start-up kits for their soap-making businesses.

Both women now make and sell soap in their communities. They are rebuilding what they can while waiting for the call that has still not come. There is no date yet for their surgeries.

*Real names have been withheld to protect anonymity.

World.title: Dunbar Takes Liberia’s Investment Pitch to the Caribbean
World.content:
ST. THOMAS, U.S. VIRGIN ISLANDS — Liberia is taking its investment and economic opportunities message to the Caribbean, with Ambassador Maisie Dunbar, Special Envoy to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai for Trade and Investment, set to promote Liberia as an emerging destination for investment at the 2026 We Mean Business Summit.

The summit is scheduled for September 16–18 in St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, bringing together women leaders, entrepreneurs, investors and business professionals from the Caribbean, Africa and the wider diaspora.

Dunbar has been invited to participate in a high-level fireside chat expected to focus on investment, economic opportunity and the role of women in shaping markets and communities.

Her participation is being presented as an opportunity to strengthen connections between Liberia, the Caribbean and the African diaspora and explore potential areas of business cooperation.

Pitching Liberia as an Investment Destination

During the engagement, Dunbar is expected to highlight sectors the Liberian government considers to have investment potential, including agriculture, fisheries and the blue economy, tourism, infrastructure, energy and digital transformation.

She is also expected to discuss Liberia’s strategic location on the West African coast, its young population, natural-resource base and opportunities for private-sector partnerships.

“Liberia is not simply a country with resources. Liberia is a country with opportunity,” Dunbar said. “The question is whether we can connect the right investors with the right opportunities and create an environment where capital can come, businesses can grow, and Liberians can benefit.”

The engagement comes as the Boakai administration seeks to attract greater international investment and expand partnerships in support of its development agenda.

However, Dunbar’s participation at the summit is primarily aimed at opening conversations and building relationships with prospective investors rather than announcing specific investment agreements.

Beyond Capital

Dunbar is also expected to emphasize human capital development as an important component of Liberia’s investment strategy.

“Investment in Liberia must also be investment in people,” she said. “Human capital development, workforce readiness, entrepreneurship, education and skills are the foundation upon which sustainable economic growth is built.”

The message is expected to resonate with the summit’s focus on women’s economic empowerment, entrepreneurship, leadership and cross-border business relationships.

Organizers say the National Women’s Collaborative, which is hosting the event, has developed a global network of more than 2,900 women across more than 30 countries.

Seeking Caribbean-Liberian Business Links

Dunbar’s participation is expected to create opportunities for discussions around potential Caribbean-Liberian partnerships in areas including tourism, agriculture, the blue economy, infrastructure, trade, women-led enterprises and diaspora investment.

The Special Envoy said the relationship between Africa and the Caribbean provides a foundation for expanding economic cooperation.

“The Caribbean and Africa share history, culture, resilience and tremendous entrepreneurial spirit,” she said. “This is an opportunity to remind our Caribbean sisters that Liberia is not far away. We are part of the same global African story, and there are opportunities for us to do business together.”

For Liberia, the engagement represents an effort to reach investors and business leaders who may have limited exposure to the country’s investment opportunities.

From St. Thomas to Monrovia

The broader objective, according to the Special Envoy’s office, is to turn international engagements into business connections and eventually investment opportunities.

Dunbar’s participation comes as Liberia seeks to broaden its international economic relationships and attract private capital to sectors identified as priorities for national development.

Whether the St. Thomas engagement results in specific investment commitments will depend on subsequent discussions between Liberian officials, prospective investors and private-sector partners.

For now, the summit provides a platform for Liberia to present its investment case, establish new contacts and encourage Caribbean businesses and members of the African diaspora to explore opportunities in the country.

The 2026 We Mean Business Summit is scheduled to run from September 16–18 in St. Thomas under the leadership of Sharon Jackson, founder of the National Women’s Collaborative.

For the Boakai administration, Dunbar’s participation forms part of its broader effort to position Liberia as a destination for investment while linking economic opportunities with job creation, entrepreneurship and human-capital development.

World.title: Liberia Seeks US$22 Million for First Cancer Treatment Center, Urges IAEA Support
World.content:
VIENNA, Austria Liberia is seeking at least US$22 million to build and operate its first comprehensive cancer diagnosis and treatment center as the West African nation looks to expand access to life-saving healthcare and deepen cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

Addressing the 70th General Conference of the IAEA in Vienna, Vice President Jeremiah Koung said Liberia believes developing countries should have equal access to the benefits of peaceful nuclear science and technology.

He stressed that nuclear technology can play a major role in improving healthcare, food production and climate resilience in countries with limited resources.

“Access to peaceful nuclear technology must not be determined by geography or national income. Its benefits must reach people in countries with the greatest needs,” Vice President Koung said.

Vice President Koung stated that Liberia’s priorities under the government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development are closely linked to the goals of the IAEA.

He explained that the country wants to move beyond individual projects and build a broader partnership that supports national development across several sectors.

“We seek to elevate our cooperation with the IAEA from isolated technical interventions to a coordinated national development partnership that strengthens health systems, enhances food security, builds climate resilience, and establishes a robust radiation safety infrastructure,” he said.

As Liberia expands the use of radioactive materials for peaceful purposes, the government is also working to strengthen its legal and regulatory framework. Koung said a new nuclear law has been drafted to guide the safe and secure use of nuclear science and technology in the country.

“This law will strengthen radiation protection, the security of radioactive and nuclear sources, and compliance with international safety standards,” he intimated.

Vice President Koung highlighted cancer as one of Liberia’s most pressing public health concerns. He noted that thousands of new cases and deaths are recorded every year, while the country lacks the facilities needed to provide specialized treatment for most patients.

“Cancer is one of the most urgent health challenges facing our nation,” Vice President Koung said.
