World.title: Trump claims AI poses no real risk — but even some of his allies disagree
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Fresh warnings that artificial intelligence models could go rogue and wipe out the human race appear to have jolted some U.S. politicians into action, but not President Donald Trump.

In a flurry of posts to his Truth Social platform on Monday, Trump dismissed AI regulation as something that would drive the industry "into oblivion and bankruptcy" and claimed that the economic engine of AI "will not be stopped" while he is president.

"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," Trump declared in one post.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he said in another.

Trump's posts come in response to dire predictions about the technology's potential risks and mounting calls from executives and researchers to rein in the industry.

Last week, engineer Jacob Coxon thrust AI safety into the public spotlight by announcing his resignation from his job with Anthropic in a social media post that warned: " The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

WATCH | Trump rejects calls for regulation: Anthropic CEO calls for AI development to slow down | Duration 2:48 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI development needs to slow down for safety measures to catch up. U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the risk of artificial intelligence when questioned by reporters.

While Trump is the most powerful voice in Washington opposing calls to rein in AI, he is far from the only one.

More than 260 bills have been introduced in Congress containing provisions to address the risks from AI since 2021, yet only two have become law, according to the Brennan Center's AI legislation tracker.

However, experts in AI policy see some encouraging signs in the past few days that the political momentum could now be shifting in favour of regulation.

'Full speed, no brakes'

Chris MacKenzie, vice-president of communications at Americans for Responsible Innovation, a non-profit advocacy group in Washington focused on AI safety, says one of the biggest obstacles to regulation has long been the amount of money stacked against it.

"We have a lot of money on the other side of this issue, a lot of money and lobbyists who do not want to see AI regulations," MacKenzie told CBC News.

"They want innovation at full speed, no brakes."

But as the public outcry grows for Congress to take action and the issue becomes a campaign talking point in the U.S. midterm elections, MacKenzie says he's confident there will be some movement.

Last December, Trump signed an order directing the Department of Justice and the Attorney General to challenge state-level AI regulations in court. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

"At the moment, what we see is a real window of opportunity where lawmakers and the public are mobilized around these issues and there's a clear desire to pass guardrails that will protect people from AI's risks," he said.

One event that helped fuel that desire came in late July, when OpenAI revealed that hundreds of its AI agents had gone rogue by independently breaking out of their secure testing environment and hacking into the servers of Hugging Face, an online platform of AI development tools.

Warnings about the risks have accelerated in the past week, kicked off by Coxon's post stating that AI "could kill us all." They include:

Thursday: Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, said it had banned some accounts linked to foreign governments and military actors for using its AI models to try to develop weapons.

Thursday: Former U.S. president Barack Obama told top Democrats to make AI safety policy a priority. "I f we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous," he said.

Saturday: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay urging a slower pace of AI development to manage the risks. His rivals Elon Musk, chief executive of X, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, supported his call.

Monday: Microsoft published its code of conduct to ensure human control of AI.

While plenty of Democrats lined up on the weekend to call for stricter AI regulation, even a few prominent Republicans expressed openness to tighten oversight. They included Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and the party's candidate for the Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, a former chairman of Intel.

"I believe we must slow down development of AI in order to allow the government and its partners to catch up and put stricter protocols and guardrails in place," Rogers posted on X.

WATCH | The risks of 'superintelligence': Superintelligence is 'an adversary,' says AI researcher | Duration 5:46 Concerns about the risks AI poses to humanity are growing, with some researchers calling for a slowdown in its development. AI researcher Connor Leahy says it's important to distinguish between AI and superintelligence, arguing that superintelligence is not a tool or a weapon, but 'an adversary.'

With major AI companies and an increasing number of Republicans agreeing that something needs to be done, Trump will likely need to compromise, says Nita Farahany, a Duke University professor who studies the legal and social implications of emerging technologies .

"I think it's going to be hard for the president to stay in the camp of 'No, let's go full speed ahead,'" Farahany told CBC News.

"I think you're going to see a shift, probably within the next 72 hours, out of the White House about what their tune is going to be on these issues."

Trump has long resisted AI regulation. Last December, he signed an order aimed at forcing states to drop their efforts at regulating the technology.

The top Republican in the U.S. House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson, says Trump may meet with AI company executives at some point in the next two weeks, but he's making no promises about the outcome.

The meeting would be "a deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play," Johnson told reporters on Capitol Hill on Monday.

One sign that regulating AI appeals across a wide range of the political spectrum is the eclectic list of people slated to attend the launch of the Pro-Human Assembly, a new coalition that says its mission is "charting a better path for AI."

Among the speakers at the event Tuesday in Washington: Steve Bannon, Trump's one-time chief of staff and a prominent MAGA voice, along with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, a darling of the left.

World.title: N.S. families thought they buried their loved ones. Officials are now investigating
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The province and the Nova Scotia regulator of funeral directors are investigating after the new owners of an Annapolis Valley funeral home discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned.

It comes as several Nova Scotia families who used the services of Serenity Funeral Home say they were shocked and horrified to receive calls letting them know that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.

“I kind of started internally freaking out because I buried my mom in 2024,” said Kristina Sweeney.

“I don't even think the shock has worn off yet.… I thought I buried my mom, all of her. I put her in the ground by myself.”

Sweeney wasn't the only one contacted by East Coast Memorial, which recently purchased the buildings from Serenity Funeral Home. Serenity’s head office and crematorium was located in the small community of Coldbrook. The company also had other locations in the Annapolis Valley.

Michelle Carey and her sister Amanda Sabean used Serenity when they buried what they believed were the cremated remains of their father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, in the spring of 2018. On Sept. 8, Carey was informed by East Coast Memorial that her father’s full remains were found in storage.

“Having to, you know, bury him and to do this all over again. It's really hard,” said Carey.

The sisters are also left wondering whose remains they buried.

Hendrik 'Hank' Sabean's family thought they buried his cremated remains next to his family in Weymouth, N.S., in 2018. But recently, they were told by the new owner of the funeral home that handled his arrangements that his full remains were found in storage. (Amanda Sabean)

“There’s a family out there that's missing remains of their family member,” said Sabean.

In an email, Andrew George, the owner of the new business East Coast Memorial, explained that his company discovered “a significant number of cremated remains that had been left in storage, some for many, many years.”

George said he and his staff are carefully reviewing the home’s information to “make every reasonable effort to locate and contact families so that these loved ones could be returned to their families or otherwise laid to rest appropriately.”

‘Dozens’ of other urns found, daughter told

Sweeney said when her mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2024 at the age of 60, her body was cremated. Sweeney chose a green urn, which she received and buried.

This month, the employee of East Coast Memorial who returned what’s believed to be the rest of her mother’s ashes gave her a green urn with a different pattern. It had been identified with a sticky note label as her mother’s. Sweeney said the employee told her that there were “dozens” of other urns found.

Another family told CBC their loved one’s remains were delivered to them in a cardboard box.

When East Coast Memorial recently took possession of Serenity Funeral Home in Coldbrook, N.S., the new staff discovered a 'significant number' of cremated remains. The company has been calling families so they can retrieve them. (Angela MacIvor/CBC)

Sweeney wrote a post on Facebook about her experience and started receiving responses from other families. They recounted similar experiences, believing that they had received and buried their loved ones. Then they were contacted by East Coast Memorial years later suggesting otherwise.

“Every single person I've spoken to was under the impression that they had taken care of all the remains,” Sweeney said. “They were either buried or they took the urn home.”

George said his company is still assessing all the cases and doing its due diligence “as thoroughly as possible for each family,” and so he isn’t able to say exactly how many persons’ remains were found.

Former owner responds

When CBC reached Tony Facey, a former owner of Serenity Funeral Home for 12 years until December 2025, he confirmed there was a “whole stack” of cremated remains dating back as far as 25 years that had never been claimed by families. He said unclaimed remains is a wider issue all funeral homes are dealing with, and this has been an ongoing discussion at the regulatory board. Facey declined an interview.

The president of the Funeral Service Association of Nova Scotia, Kollin Weatherbee, said he’s never heard of a funeral home keeping decades of unclaimed remains.

“It is unusual that a funeral home would hold a portion of someone's ashes without the family knowing,” he said.

Weatherbee added that if a funeral home held ashes for a family, it would only be for a matter of weeks.

And in situations where a next of kin can’t be identified or reached, he said the public trustee usually gets involved within the first 12 days of a death.

Provincial inspectors visit

The province licenses and regulates funeral homes through Service Nova Scotia, while an arm’s-length board licenses and regulates funeral home directors.

The province learned of the stored ashes on Sept. 9 when it was contacted by that board and George, the owner of East Coast Memorial. It assigned two provincial inspectors to visit the crematorium the next day to learn more.

Adam Tipert, the chair of the Nova Scotia Board of Registration of Embalmers and Funeral Directors, told CBC in an email the board is taking the concerns “very seriously” and will collaborate with Service Nova Scotia in its investigation as more information emerges.

The province and the board also conducted an investigation at Serenity Funeral Home in 2018, when the location in Berwick mixed up the bodies of two women. A funeral director had his licence revoked.

That case eventually led to a change in the legislation surrounding funeral homes in 2025.

A provincial spokesperson said Serenity was routinely inspected in 2022, and some non-compliant administrative matters were resolved.

Following the sale to East Coast Memorial, Serenity is no longer licensed to operate funeral homes in Nova Scotia.

George said right now he is keeping focused on doing what is right for the families.

“We do not want to speculate about decisions or practices that occurred before our involvement,” he said, adding that his company will treat the remains with respect and dignity, as they were “received into our care when we acquired Serenity.”

George said his company is making plans for a community burial ceremony for any remains that can’t be reunited with a family, or if the families direct his company to do so.

Hendrik 'Hank' Sabean was 67 when he died in 2018. He had specifics wishes for his funeral arrangements, which included dealing with Serenity Funeral Home for the service and burial of his ashes. (Amanda Sabean)

Hank Sabean’s daughters still have many unanswered questions, especially since their father had been so clear about his own funeral arrangements and being laid to rest with his family.

“He had strong morals and values, and I know that he would think that this is so wrong that this could happen,” said Carey.

Kristina Sweeney said her mother would also be “really, really disgusted.”

“I felt like my mom and I had been violated,” she said. “I expect when someone passes away that, and I'm sure most people do, they're treated with dignity and respect.”

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Zelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There was something extraordinarily refreshing about listening to Volodymyr Zelenskyy say the quiet part out loud.

Asked to comment on the deteriorating relationship between Canada and the United States, the Ukrainian president described it as "strange" and "very dangerous" before drawing — arguably — an imperfect comparison with his country and Russia.

"It's very dangerous that there are some problems between neighbours. We are the example," Zelenskyy told CBC's chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault in an exclusive interview at the end of his visit to Canada last week.

It's well known Zelenskyy has little patience for diplomatic euphemism and he has made something of a habit of dragging the unspoken into the open.

WATCH | Zelenskyy on U.S. 51st state threat: U.S. threats to annex Canada 'dangerous,' Zelenskyy says | Duration 1:34 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says U.S. threats to annex Canada are 'very dangerous' and urges the two neighbours to solve their differences.

But is it a fair and accurate comparison?

Talk to most Canadians and many are inclined to agree with the analogy at least on the surface, especially with the collapse of trade talks where Washington introduced last-minute demands — including a veto over Canada's third-party trade deals and a weakening of domestic cultural protections.

There is an important distinction, of course.

Russia invaded Ukraine.

The United States has not threatened Canada militarily and no American divisions are assembling at the border. There is no Canadian territory that's been annexed.

The Ukrainian president was quick to urge Ottawa and Washington to keep the dialogue going to work out their differences, but three times referred to the ongoing trade war and the associated rhetoric as "dangerous."

You won't find a Canadian political leader or senior official making the same comparison, at least in public.

In some of his language, Prime Minister Mark Carney alludes to it, saying how U.S. President Donald Trump "wants to break us, so he can own us."

But he never completes the thought the way Zelenskyy did.

Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland, who remains an economic adviser to Zelenskyy, has described the Trump administration as an "existential threat" to Canada's future, but never crossed into the territory of comparing the plight of her ancestral homeland with Canada.

Even former prime minister Jean Chrétien, in his fiery, "we bow to know no one" 9/11 speech last Friday, didn't make the link.

One of the prominent Canadian voices to make the comparison is former vice-chief of the defence staff, retired vice-admiral Mark Norman.

Writing in the National Post during the early 2025 annexation controversy, Norman posed the question: "Are we as Canadians any different than Ukraine is to Russia or Taiwan to China?"

In a subsequent interview with CBC's Front Burner, the former commander of the navy used his initial argument as the jumping-off point to examine what Trump's threats meant for Canadian sovereignty.

His message was: While an American invasion is not imminent, the annexation rhetoric and the way the trade war has unfolded should force Canadians to reconsider their assumptions.

What happens when you live beside a vastly more powerful neighbour that starts to treat your sovereignty as conditional?

WATCH | More about the trade war: Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That | Duration 9:14 How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Interestingly, outside Canada, the comparison between Canada and Ukraine has been considerably more explicit.

In a March 2025 analysis story examining Trump's 51st state rhetoric, The Washington Post asked outright: "As Putin sees Ukraine … Trump sees Canada?"

The argument was that Russian President Vladimir Putin's relationship with Ukraine provides a disturbing parallel for Trump's rhetoric toward Canada.

A subsequent Post commentary put it even more directly, and argued that Trump talks about Canada much as Putin talks about Ukraine: as though it were a wayward province rather than a fully separate country.

The comparison resurfaced just recently with an article in The Atlantic, which described Trump's approach to Canada as reflecting a worldview in which sovereign countries can be treated almost as properties to be controlled. The article explicitly drew a parallel between Trump's apparent disregard for Canadian sovereignty and Putin's attitude toward Ukraine.

Trump has threatened to force Canada into the union through economic coercion.

Canada built its postwar prosperity around extraordinary integration with the United States, including supply chains, energy, defence production, intelligence and continental security.

Carney is attempting to untangle that by diversifying trade, especially with Europe.

Dominique Arel, chair of Ukrainian studies at the University of Ottawa, said you can draw some parallels in the sense that Ukraine was extraordinarily dependent on Russia for energy following the collapse of the Soviet Union and has been "with a gun at its head" since the 2014 annexation of Crimea trying to change that.

"Everybody's learning the hard way that basically overdependence is actually a great security risk," said Arel, who noted that the recent collapsed trade talks between Canada and the U.S. looked very Russian-like, but it's tough to know what was in Trump's mind.

"What was demanded by the United States was a direct attack on Canada's sovereignty. But is that just a negotiating tactic to put massive pressure without long-term consequences? It's a bit early to know that. But clearly, it's not much of a negotiation. It's basically an ultimatum, which you could draw parallels with Russia, of course."

Moscow viewed Kyiv's economic overtures toward the European Union as opening the door to security concerns and the possibility that NATO would be parked on its doorstep, Arel said.

For years, Moscow's proposition to Kyiv was essentially: You may technically be sovereign, but your sovereignty cannot be exercised against Russian interests.

Matt Schmidt, an associate professor and national security expert at the University of New Haven in Connecticut and former instructor at the U.S. Army War College, also said there are similarities, but important differences.

WATCH | Security expert weighs in on the comparison: U.S. effort to make Canada a 'vassal state' lacks clear strategy, security expert says | Duration 1:33 Matt Schmidt, an associate professor and national security expert at the University of New Haven in Connecticut and former instructor at the U.S. Army War College, said there are similarities but important differences between the way the U.S. treats Canada and the way Russia behaves toward Ukraine. Russia, Schmidt argues, is more organized and focused about what it wants out of Ukraine.

"What's driving this isn't rational economic thinking. What's driving this is an irrational belief that Canada is not a real nation," said Schmidt.

"Putin knew what he wanted and he was trying different different pathways to get it. I don't think that the president [Trump] knows what he wants. He's really just blurting out a sort of psychological impulse — a pressure in his mind — where he has to act like the big dog in the room.

"And so he pops out with whatever is in there and then the rest of the administration races around and says, can we turn that into real policy?"

He said the idea of dominating Canada doesn't have broad appeal among Americans, whereas in Russia the opposite is true where Ukraine is concerned.

He also said, militarily there's a big difference in that Russia wants to swallow Ukraine whole, while the U.S. is more interested in pulling the strings of its neighbours, including Canada.

Russia, Schmidt argues, is also more organized and focused about what it wants out of Ukraine.

"I don't think there's a clear idea that goes beyond the Oval Office itself that says we have X goal in mind for Canada. We want to make it the 51st state," said Schmidt.

"I think most people in the administration think that's crazy. And so there's no broader strategic plan to say, well, let's do this economically and let's make this threat militarily."

World.title: UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The recovery of hundreds of bodies from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Gaza during the war that began nearly three years ago has raised fresh concerns about possible war crimes, the United Nations human rights chief said Tuesday.

Volker Türk said the remains of what appeared to be entire families were being unearthed from sites destroyed during Israeli attacks, adding that many victims were women and children.

"It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst fears confirmed," he said in a statement.

He said the discoveries revived concerns raised in a 2024 UN report that found Israeli strikes on residential buildings and other civilian sites during the early weeks of the war may have violated international humanitarian law.

The Israeli Prime Minister's Office and Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians and says it acted in accordance with international law while fighting Hamas militants in Gaza.

Israel's assault on Gaza — launched after Hamas's deadly raid into Israel in October 2023 — has generated around 61 million tons of wreckage and debris that could take seven years to clear, according to the United ​Nations.

WATCH | Families wait to bury loved ones in Gaza: These families waited three years to bury loved ones in Gaza | Duration 1:40 In early August, mourners gathered in a Gaza City neighbourhood where it's taken nearly three years to retrieve the remains of 112 people, killed by an Israeli airstrike. Surviving members of the Abu Sharia and Hasayna families said they've long been looking alongside Gaza's Civil Defence crews for their loved ones, but a lack of heavy machinery in the war-torn territory has slowed efforts.

A U.S.-brokered ceasefire brought an end to full-scale fighting in October 2025, but has failed to halt regular Israeli strikes, as both sides accuse each other of violating the truce.

The Palestinian Civil Defence says more than 630 bodies and human remains have been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025.

Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried in the ​wreckage.

Türk said he feared the remains recovered so far could be "only the tip of the iceberg," noting that large parts of Gaza had been flattened by Israeli bombing or later demolition and clearance operations.

He also accused Israel of continuing to level some areas of Gaza where its forces remain deployed, saying bulldozers were operating "with no respect for the dead under the rubble."

Israeli restrictions impeding recovery efforts

Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said that Israeli restrictions on items like DNA kits and excavators were impeding recovery and identification efforts.

"The collective impact of Israel's conduct is making any systematic, large-scale search, recovery, and identification work nearly impossible," he told a Geneva news briefing on Tuesday.

Sometimes, Palestinian teams were having to dig through rubble with their bare hands, he added.

Israeli authorities did not immediately respond to the UN allegations on supply restrictions. Israel's COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, has previously justified long-held restrictions on items it said could be used for a "terrorist buildup."

The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.

More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, ​according to Gaza health authorities.

Israel says it has gone to great lengths to avoid civilian ​casualties and ⁠that Hamas uses Gaza's civilians as human shields in densely populated areas — an accusation Hamas denies.

The UN rights chief called for international investigators to be granted access to all parts of Gaza to help preserve evidence, citing ongoing legal proceedings examining conduct during the war.

Israel has blocked the entry of heavy machinery needed to remove rubble, according to Türk's statement.

Francesca Albanese, the UN expert on the Palestinian territories, has said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified ​before full clearance starts.

This month, the Palestinian Civil Defence said 96 bodies and human remains had been recovered from a single site in the Zeitoun area of Gaza City, including 58 children and 23 women.

World.title: 2026 Emmys: Widow's Bay upsets, The Pitt triumphs at Canada-preoccupied ceremony
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite a raft of surprises that included Canada call-outs, numerous Law & Order gags and Taylor Swift, the biggest surprise of the night was in who took home the gold.

Because even as the Emmys tends to honour the series and stars with more seasons under their belts, it was Apple TV's smash success Widow's Bay that earned top honours. Winning lead actor, supporting actress, supporting actor and director — as well as the night's biggest award, best comedy series — the horror-comedy pulled in a record 14 wins off an impressive 19 nominations.

That beat the single-season record of 13 wins The Studio earned last year, making Widow's Bay the comedy series with the most ever trophies in a single year.

But the star heading into the night was The Pitt, which led the pack with 25 nominations, including for best drama series — which it won — and supporting actress (Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif, Katherine LaNasa and Sepideh Moafi).

Its lead Noah Wylie was awarded with outstanding lead actor in a drama series about midway through the ceremony — his second win in the category after triumphing last year as well. However The Pitt lost best supporting actor to Tasks' Tom Pelphrey: that show's first of the night off of its six nominations.

And despite The Pitt's dominance in the best supporting actress in a comedy category, it was The Diplomat's Allison Janney who took home the award. It is her eighth career Emmy, following her last win in 2021 for Mom. That relatively huge upset set the stage for what would be a night of them — splitting honours between established entertainment juggernauts, and surprise new finds.

Interspersed with all the wins, though, was the comedy. One of the big moments of the night was a scene-specific recreation of Law & Order by host Mariska Hargitay, in which the show's actual stars — including Ice-T — tried to predict whether or not Taylor Swift would show up at the Emmys.

Swift herself appeared in disguise as one of the SVU detectives, theorizing along with the rest of them.

Mariska Hargitay, Taylor Swift and her cat Olivia Benson appear on screen during the 78th Emmy Awards on Monday. (Patrick T. Fallon/Getty Images)

"Maybe she's going to do one of those cool pre-taped sketch things to support the host," Swift said in the pre-taped sketch.

"Do you think she'll sing?" asked one of the other detectives.

"No."

Canadian comments

A speech with a bit more heft came from Sally Field, who won outstanding lead actress in a limited or anthology series or movie for Remarkably Bright Creatures. The actress, who received her first nomination in 17 years for this role, barrelled off the thanks for different people in her life — before arriving at a familiar one.

“And Canada! Blessed Canada!" she said, smiling. Remarkably Bright Creatures was filmed in Deep Cove, B.C. "Our neighbours, our friends!”

Later on was an emotional tribute to the late Catherine O'Hara by Home Alone co-star Macaulay Culkin, and Schitt's Creek co-stars Annie Murphy and Dan Levy.

"The greatest lesson I learned from Catherine, both professionally and personally, was to always say yes. Say yes to her instincts; all of them," Levy said of the comedy legend who died in January. "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness."

Also honoured was Michael J. Fox for the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award. Fox, who retired from acting in 2020 due to the physical toll of Parkinson's disease, was introduced as a "proud son of Canada" and received a standing ovation.

"Eventually I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it," he said in his acceptance speech. "It just meant doing what I could for everyone living with this disease."

Actors Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy speak onstage during an homage to late actress Catherine O'Hara. (Patrick T. Fallon/Getty Images)

Slightly behind The Pitt in nominations was Hacks, another strong performer at the seminal TV awards show. Its nominations for its fifth and final season put it ahead of all comedies with a record-breaking 24.

Lead Jean Smart was, in many bettors' cards, perhaps the biggest lock of the night for best actress in a comedy — an award she won early on, becoming the first woman to win an Emmy for every season of their show.

Hannah Einbinder , who had a breakthrough win last year as best supporting actress in a comedy after four nominations , was up against Kate O'Flynn, who wowed with a breakout performance in the debut season of Widow's Bay — and who ended up taking home the prize.

WATCH | The Pitt, Hacks lead Emmy nominations: The Pitt, Hacks lead 2026 Emmy nominations | Duration 4:19 The nominees for the 2026 Primetime Emmy Awards have been unveiled, with HBO's The Pitt leading all programs with 25 nominations, followed by Hacks with 24. Apple TV's freshman dark comedy Widow's Bay secured 19 nods and its post-apocalyptic Pluribus pulled in 16.

Her win was followed shortly after by a best supporting actor in a comedy award for Widow's Bay star Stephen Root — a category for which Hacks' Paul W. Downs was nominated.

The Emmys' track record had suggested they would shower Hacks in awards for its final, send-off season. But with 19 nominations for a show with a real campaign and surprise upset win for best comedy series, the trajectory of Widow's Bay was far more successful than previously expected.

Fellow newcomer Pluribus, from Breaking Bad phenom Vince Gilligan, was just behind with 18 off the back of its first season. A stunningly bizarre dramedy about an alien invasion and mind control, it was similarly positioned in opposition to The Pitt. With four early wins already, the narrative had long been circling around star Rhea Seehorn.

Rhea Seehorn accepts the Emmy for outstanding lead actress in a drama series for Pluribus. (Patrick T. Fallon/Getty Images)

Given the entire show's focus on her singular performance, voters rewarded the Better Call Saul star with her first Emmy after four nominations.

A laughing, tearful Seehorn briefly thanked her co-nominees, cast and crew, her family and Gilligan. She was eventually played off in the longest speech thus far of the night — where all other winners barely took a minute before rushing off the stage.

Elsewhere, the limited series categories had a diminished role at the main Emmys show after four of them were demoted to the early Emmys weekend.

HBO Max's DTF St. Louis was the big winner of those awards, taking best supporting actor and actress for David Harbour and Linda Cardellini.

Beef brought star power to the lead acting categories, with Carey Mulligan, the consensus favourite for best actress in a limited series, however losing to Field. The show's Oscar Isaac was favoured for best actor, but was similarly upset by Matthew Rhys for The Beast in Me. Rhys also won best lead actor in a comedy series for his role in Widows Bay, making him the first man to win two lead actor awards in the same night.

And after another year of antagonizing U.S. President Donald Trump, the late night shows of Jimmy Kimmel and the now-cancelled Stephen Colbert were both up for outstanding variety series, the latter of whom won.

That show received nine nominations for this Emmys ceremony, following the news that CBS announced its end earlier this year. In his acceptance speech, Colbert joked that if the audience enjoyed the comedy they should thank his old writers — as they wrote it all.

"I got some great news, they are all 'tech avail,'" he said, before speaking earnestly. "We hope you enjoyed the show, we had a great time doing it for you ... we'll catch you all on the flip."

World.title: Trump's latest round of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A new round of U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect just after midnight on Tuesday, adding 50 per cent levies to 110 products ranging from specific cheeses to motorboats, all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and furniture.

The fresh tariffs are part of a series of additions and removals announced by the Trump administration last week. Categories added to the tariff list include aluminum products, paper and wood products, iron or steel beams, electric lamps and mattresses.

The White House said it would simultaneously remove tariffs on 10 items including salt, sugar, cement, switchboards and toilet paper in an effort to "offset the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest."

In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million US worth of toilet paper to the U.S., making it the country's largest international provider.

Canada is also one of the biggest salt providers south of the border, with the U.S. importing roughly $159.2 million US worth of salt from Canada in 2025, according to UN Comtrade and World Bank trade data.

WATCH | How much toilet paper does the U.S. get from Canada?: Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war? | Duration 2:28 U.S. President Donald Trump dropped tariffs on certain Canadian products, including toilet paper, cement and salt. In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million worth of the product, making it the largest international provider of toilet paper to the U.S.

The removals and additions amount to nearly the same economic value, effectively cancelling each other out, experts say.

"In dollar terms they are basically the same," Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway chair in business and trade law at the University of Ottawa, told CBC News.

The categories that had tariffs removed represent roughly $2.41 billion, while the added tariffs cover roughly $2.56 billion of 2025 trade, according to an analysis by Alschner. This amounts to only a slight increase in tariff coverage, representing a fraction of trade between the two countries.

The biggest dollar value is in the category of switchgear assemblies and switchboards — the U.S. imported roughly $750 million US of these from Canada in 2025, which have applications ranging from cars to airplanes, Alschner said.

'You need to salt your roads'

The decision to remove some tariffs shows that the U.S. is paying attention to which costs get passed down to the American consumer, and are willing to recalibrate to ease their own economic pain, Alschner said.

"You need salt to salt your roads in winter. So this is not something that's easily substituted away," he said. "Similarly for cement."

The new measures come after the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a trade agreement in August, ramping up an ongoing trade war.

On Aug. 22, the U.S. followed through with its threat of crushing 50 per cent tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods. Canada retaliated with its own tariffs on nearly 700 categories of U.S. goods, which came into effect on Sept. 8.

WATCH | How will U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians?: How will the new U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians? | Duration 5:22 U.S. President Donald Trump has hit Canada with a new round of trade measures, escalating the trade war. CBC's Peter Armstrong says the scope of the trade war has grown, and as a result, regional disruptions could lead to job losses and the closure of small businesses.

In addition to new tariffs on Sept. 15, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a pending import ban on Canadian booze, motorcycles and a handful of other goods. The import ban doesn't take effect until Sept. 29.

Experts say the scope of the trade war has grown, and as a result, regional disruptions could lead to job losses and the closure of small businesses.

Alschner says the latest tariffs will limit some Canadian companies from pivoting. For instance, an aluminum company might have been able to shift more production to types of aluminum that weren't tariffed before.

But with the addition of more hyper-specific tariffs, "some of these loopholes have been closed."

WATCH | Carney on upcoming import ban: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

Economist Andrew Dicapua told CBC News the muted response from the U.S. to Canada's counter-tariffs, coupled with the longer timeline before the import bans come into effect, could be a sign that we're closer to a deal.

Trump recently commented that a trade deal with Canada could come "fairly soon," while meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin over the weekend, Dicapua noted.

"The fact that those bans were put later than the tariffs themselves should give us an indication that the U.S. is leaving room for negotiation," Dicapua said.

"The bottom line is that we've got to get to an agreement with the United States as quickly as possible. This tit-for-tat strategy, although well-intentioned, is not a sustainable route."

World.title: COVID-19 benefit repayment is hurting low-income Canadians, report says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Over six years after the COVID-19 pandemic started, the federal government is still trying to track down billions of dollars sent to Canadians who were later found to be ineligible for benefits.

According to a report from Maytree, a think-tank and advocacy group that studies poverty, those recollection efforts disproportionately affect low-income Canadians who can't pay, and ultimately cost more than they recover.

It calls for an end to the government's efforts to recover pandemic benefits.

In total, Ottawa distributed about $14 billion in COVID-related benefits to individuals who didn't meet the Canada Revenue Agency's income requirements. Most of that sum was provided under the Canada emergency response benefit (CERB) and later the Canada recovery benefit (CRB).

By the end of last November, the CRA reported that $10 billion was outstanding, over $8 billion of which was owed on CERB and CRB payouts. CBC News reached out to the CRA for updated figures, but the agency was unable to provide them after more than two weeks of requests.

"This is not a story about fraud," the report says. "It is a story about what happens when a government moves fast, makes mistakes and then hands the bill to the people least able to pay it."

John Stapleton, co-author of the Maytree report and a social policy expert, says his group acknowledges some people knowingly applied for benefits they shouldn't have received.

"We're not asking them to absolve those people," he said. "[But] there's some people out there that got caught in this net who are really suffering as a result."

In Budget 2025, Ottawa provided $123 million to support the government's collection of its pandemic response benefits over two years, starting in 2026-27.

According to Stapleton and Tyler Meredith, a senior fellow at the Munk School of Public Policy and a fellow at Maytree, many Canadians who still owe a debt on pandemic benefits are low-income.

"By the time you asked them to repay that benefit, they would have already, frankly, used that money," Meredith said.

Meredith was the head of economic and fiscal policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau and a main architect of the federal government's economic response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

"It was always clear, I would argue, that the intent of the program was to be for people who had lost income," Meredith said.

While he said the government needed to provide certainty to Canadians that support was there if they needed it, the program was misunderstood as a form of universal income.

"Most people don't check the fine print," Meredith said.

CERB was in place from March to October 2020. Applicants had to have earned at least $5,000 in income in the last 12 months, lost income as a result of the pandemic and not been receiving EI in order to be eligible. They received $2,000 every four weeks.

CERB 'didn't have a plan for recovery'

Meredith said the government didn't have a plan to recover ineligible benefit payouts when it was initially launching its pandemic relief programs.

"Our goal, in all of the programs we were designing, was to have something that was like 80 to 85 per cent ready, knowing that we would amend and adjust the program as we went," Meredith said.

"We just didn't have time to wait."

According to Meredith, the government's initial plan was to deliver benefits by traditional means like through the quarterly GST tax credit — now the groceries and essentials benefit — or Canada's employment insurance system. But Meredith said the EI system would have been overwhelmed as millions of Canadians were set to lose work during the pandemic.

Because of this, the government drafted the Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act to create a new system, legislation Meredith said was put together in "a matter of a couple days."

The government allows for interest-free repayment over time.

But CERB's legislation "doesn't have a mechanism inside it to say the government is permitted, or CRA's officials are permitted, to entertain some form of settlement," Meredith said. "From their point of view, their hands are tied."

"The Federal Court has confirmed that the CRA is required to apply the eligibility criteria established by legislation and does not have discretion to depart from those requirements," the CRA told CBC News in a written statement.

The CRA said it is not legally obligated to pursue all ineligible CERB payments. According to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), the CRA can allow payment deferrals if a client is facing financial hardship. If it determines that hardship is permanent, the CRA can recommend a debt for writeoff to ESDC.

Can Ottawa dissolve the debt?

But Meredith says simply writing off the remaining debt owed by those ineligible for benefits is "not a realistic option" and "probably politically unpalatable for any government, at any point in time."

He pointed to the government's use of partial forgiveness on loans from the Canada emergency business account program (CEBA) as a possible guide, and suggested it develop an option to "spread out repayment costs over a much longer period of time."

In its report, Maytree outlined a plan to wind down the collection of pandemic benefits along a suggested timeline. It also recommended the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer examine the cost of the government's collection efforts.

Other recommendations include amending the Income Tax Act to give the CRA discretion to make deals on the remaining debt and for the CRA to resolve over 1,200 outstanding cases by the end of 2026.

"I think it's incumbent upon government to set out a framework," Meredith said.

"Up to now, they've largely avoided making or entertaining any of that, both because there will eventually be some fiscal costs associated with doing so, but also because, I think the reality is people have harsh attitudes towards this.… If you used a program that you shouldn't have, they don't think that you're deserving usually of amnesty."
