The company operates in two segments, Iron Ore Solutions and Vale Base Metals. It extracts, produces, and distributes iron ore, iron ore pellets, briquettes, nickel, copper, other ferrous…

Suing the Regulator

The most consequential feature of the filing is who else is named.

The Agência Nacional de Mineração, Brazil’s federal mining regulator, is a defendant. So is the government of Minas Gerais.

They are being sued alongside Vale, not joining the case against it.

The argument implicit in that structure is about supervision. A prosecutor who names the regulator is saying oversight failed, not only that the operator did.

A Separate Case, a Separate Freeze

A freeze of R$200 million, about US$37.3 million, in Vale assets has circulated in coverage of this filing.

That order belongs to a different action, brought in February.

It is not part of the 9 September case and was not ordered in connection with it.

The two proceedings run in parallel and concern related but distinct questions.

Congonhas sits in the iron quadrangle, about 80 kilometres south of Belo Horizonte.

Why Brazil Reacts This Way

Mariana in 2015 and Brumadinho in 2019 both involved tailings dam failures in Minas Gerais. The second killed 270 people.

Brazilian law and Brazilian prosecutors have been reshaped by those events.

Every containment incident at a Minas Gerais mine is now examined against that history, whatever its scale.

That is why an overflow generates a federal action and a demand for independent audit.

Vale shares fell 3.48% on Tuesday, the heaviest drag on the Ibovespa.

What It Means for Vale

An independent audit, if ordered, produces a document Vale does not control and cannot easily contest.

Vale shares fell 3.48% on Tuesday, the heaviest drag on the Ibovespa, which closed down 0.91% at 185,500.88.

The company faces multiple simultaneous proceedings arising from Minas Gerais operations.

Iron ore production at Viga is not currently suspended.

What to Watch

Whether the court grants the audit request and on what terms.

How the ANM responds to being named as a defendant, which is unusual for a Brazilian regulator.

Whether the February asset freeze is extended, released or folded into a settlement.

And whether the Minas Gerais state government contests the action or negotiates.

Was there a dam rupture?

World.title: Historic honour expected as Belize prepares to name first female National Hero
World.content:
Historic honour expected as Belize prepares to name first female National Hero

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): For the first time in Belize’s history, a woman is expected to be named a National Hero.

The historic announcement is expected during this year’s Tribute to Belizean Patriots, scheduled for later this week as part of the September Celebrations.

The woman’s identity has not yet been officially revealed.

If confirmed, she would join a very small and distinguished group that currently includes only George Cadle Price and Philip Goldson.

The designation would represent a major expansion of Belize’s highest national honour and would place a woman among the country’s most celebrated national figures.

The Tribute to Belizean Patriots recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to Belize through leadership, service, culture, public life and national development.

This year’s programme is also expected to highlight Belizeans who played important roles in the independence movement and helped guide the country from British colonial rule to full Independence in 1981.

The ceremony traditionally forms one of the major national events of September and includes several categories of awards.

The expected naming of Belize’s first woman National Hero is likely to be one of the biggest moments of this year’s celebration.

World.title: Santa Elena stunned after couple found in advanced state of decomposition
World.content:
Santa Elena stunned after couple found in advanced state of decomposition

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The twin towns of San Ignacio and Santa Elena are in shock following the discovery of two young people dead inside their home near Hillview Park.

The victims, 31 year old Michael Williams and 21 year old Delisha Estrada, were found at approximately 10:00 a.m. on Monday.

Officials say there is still no confirmed cause of death.

The bodies were reportedly in an advanced state of decomposition, and investigators spent much of the day processing the residence before removing them at around 5:15 p.m.

The couple’s child was fortunately staying with a relative and was not inside the home when the bodies were discovered.

Family members gathered at the scene and waited for several hours as police and forensic personnel conducted their work.

Mayor Earl Trapp said he knew both Williams and Estrada and remembered them as highly respectful and ambitious individuals who appeared focused on their future.

Trapp acknowledged that residents have growing concerns about safety in San Ignacio and Santa Elena and said he recently requested additional police support from the Commissioner of Police.

Post mortem examinations will be carried out in the Belize District.

Police have not yet said whether foul play is suspected and are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the deaths.

World.title: Belize stays warm and mostly sunny today with only isolated showers
World.content:
Belize stays warm and mostly sunny today with only isolated showers

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize can expect another warm and relatively dry day today, with mostly sunny skies and only isolated showers or thunderstorms.

The National Meteorological Service says conditions across the country will remain generally fair throughout Tuesday, September 15.

The 24 hour forecast calls for mostly sunny skies during the day, becoming partly cloudy tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, although a few more could develop over the Toledo District late tonight.

Temperatures will remain hot, particularly inland, where highs are expected to reach 96 degrees Fahrenheit. Coastal areas will see highs near 90 degrees, while temperatures over the hills will reach around 84 degrees.

Winds over the sea will blow from the east to northeast at 10 to 15 knots, producing choppy conditions and waves between three and five feet.

On Wednesday, skies will become cloudy at times, with a few showers or thunderstorms expected over southern districts during the morning and again at night. Elsewhere, showers should remain isolated.

The National Meteorological Service says no tropical cyclone formation is expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

The forecast was prepared by forecaster Derrick Rudon.

World.title: Collin Francis sentenced to 16 years for manslaughter of Nestor Vasquez, 10 years for attempted murder of nurse
World.content:
Collin Francis sentenced to 16 years for manslaughter of Nestor Vasquez, 10 years for attempted murder of nurse

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Seven years after Nestor Vasquez, 60, was fatally beaten inside a police holding cell, Collin Francis, 33, has been sentenced to 16 years in prison for manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim also sentenced Francis to 10 years for the attempted murder of psychiatric nurse Augustina Elijio. The sentences will run concurrently and take effect from June 6, 2019, meaning the time Francis has already spent in custody will count toward his sentence.

Francis pleaded guilty earlier this year to both offences after psychiatric evidence established that he had been suffering from schizophrenia and was experiencing an acute psychotic episode at the time of the attacks. He had initially faced a murder charge for Vasquez’s death, but the Crown later accepted manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

Elijio was attacked on June 4, 2019, at the Port Loyola Health Centre, where Francis had gone seeking mental-health treatment. Public reports at the time said he returned to the facility in an agitated state and stabbed Elijio multiple times.

Francis was subsequently detained at the Queen Street Police Station. Two days later, Vasquez was placed in the same holding area with him and was brutally beaten. Vasquez suffered massive blunt-force trauma and died at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital on June 8. Police later acknowledged serious failures surrounding the incident, and three officers were placed on interdiction and faced disciplinary proceedings.

Vasquez was the brother of Channel 7 News Director, Jules Vasquez, who attended Monday’s sentencing. Speaking about the case, Jules said he believes police failed his brother by placing him in a cell with Francis despite Francis’s mental condition and the fact that he had attacked Elijio only days earlier.

The case was delayed for years because of questions surrounding Francis’s fitness to stand trial. Justice Pilgrim found Francis unfit to plead in February 2024 and ordered that his condition be medically reviewed every six months. A psychiatrist later assessed Francis as fit to stand trial in 2026.

In his sentencing decision, however, Justice Pilgrim strongly criticized the failure of prison authorities to carry out the court-ordered periodic psychiatric assessments. The judge noted that several reviews should have occurred before Francis was eventually reassessed and said the failure created uncertainty over whether Francis may have regained fitness much earlier.

Justice Pilgrim ruled that it would therefore be unfair to exclude the period during which Francis was deemed unfit from his time served, saying the failure by the authorities to comply with the court’s order should not operate to Francis’s disadvantage.

“There is no excuse for failing to fulfil a court order,” the judge said, while also stressing the State’s constitutional responsibility to provide adequate resources, including psychiatric services, for the proper functioning of the criminal justice system.

Justice Pilgrim also raised the broader issue of how Belize handles accused persons suffering from severe mental illness and recommended that lawmakers examine the need for an appropriate facility to accommodate and treat persons in circumstances such as Francis’s.

World.title: Man detained after wife reports that he burned down their house in Paraiso
World.content:
Man detained after wife reports that he burned down their house in Paraiso

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained Gregorio Espirito as they investigate allegations that he deliberately set fire to his own house, the home he shared with his wife.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero, Head of the National Crime Investigation Branch, said police responded on Saturday to a fire at a residence in Paraiso Village, where an approximately 18-by-20-foot building was engulfed in flames.

According to Romero, Espirito’s wife reported that she was in the area when she saw her husband enter the house. Shortly afterward, the building went up in flames.

Gregorio Espirito was subsequently detained and remains in police custody pending the outcome of the investigation.

Romero confirmed that the couple lived together and that police have received previous reports of domestic violence involving them.

Police are continuing their investigation to determine whether criminal charges will be laid.

World.title: Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry: 30th Expo Belize Market Place draws almost 10,000 visitors
World.content:
Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry: 30th Expo Belize Market Place draws almost 10,000 visitors

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI) is celebrating the success of the 30th Annual Expo Belize Market Place, held September 12–13 at the Marion Jones Sports Complex in Belize City.

This year’s milestone event was held under the theme, “Expo Belize Market Place® – The Original Expo: 30 Years of Connecting Business, Creating Opportunities.”

The BCCI said the weekend attracted close to 10,000 visitors, surpassing last year’s attendance despite early-morning rains and midday heat. The Chamber also reported strong purchasing activity and increased consumer spending throughout the weekend, reflecting continued support for local businesses. The large turnout, however, also highlighted the need for a fully indoor and weather-proof venue as the Expo continues to grow.

The 30th anniversary edition featured several new attractions, including the “30 for 30” Expo Shopping Challenge and hourly giveaways.

Visitors also enjoyed performances throughout the weekend, with the Expo House Band and Super Furia providing entertainment alongside headline performances by Belizean artists Supa G and Vida Magz. The opening ceremony featured remarks from BCCI President Giacomo Sanchez, Belize City Deputy Mayor Elude Miller and Mena Group of Companies Director and Ambassador for Trade in Belize Emile Mena.

Sanchez emphasized the broader role of the Expo in supporting Belizean businesses, stating, “The Expo is more than a trade and consumer show; it is a platform where consumers can discover and support local products and services, entrepreneurs can build relationships, and the wider community can come together to celebrate Belizean enterprise.”

The BCCI also recognized outstanding exhibitors through its Best Booth Awards, with Smart Belize taking Overall Business Excellence and Marketing Excellence, while Taste by Tess won Most Outstanding Micro Entrepreneur, Zesty Squeeze took Most Outstanding Youth Entrepreneur, Pickle La Cochinita Pibil Tacos won Most Outstanding Food Booth, and Digi Belize received Most Innovative Excellence.

To mark three decades of the Expo, the BCCI also honored 13 Legacy Partners whose support has helped anchor the event since its inception in 1996.

World.title: Belize Is Not A Real Place? Croc caught in viral Southside brawl rescued; charges may follow while larger croc remains in neighborhood
World.content:
Belize Is Not A Real Place? Croc caught in viral Southside brawl rescued; charges may follow while larger croc remains in neighborhood

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A crocodile seen tied up as a brawl unfolded in a viral video posted by Breaking Belize News on Belize City’s Southside was safely rescued and relocated Sunday night, but police say charges may follow from the incident, while wildlife responders warn that a second, larger crocodile may still be in the Dolphin Street neighborhood.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero, Head of the National Crime Investigation Branch, confirmed Monday that police have seen the video and that the matter has been referred to the department’s Cybercrime Unit.

Romero said police can investigate potentially criminal acts captured in videos circulating online even without waiting for someone to make a formal complaint.

He said investigators will seek to identify the persons involved and determine whether any offences were committed.

Police are also reviewing the handling of the crocodile, which is a protected animal in Belize, and Romero said persons involved could face charges if investigators determine that an offence was committed.

The Crocodile Research Coalition (CRC) became aware of the incident after the video began circulating online and members of the public contacted and tagged wildlife organizations.

Dr. Marisa Tellez, founder and Executive Director of the CRC, said the footage appeared to show that the crocodile had been captured but was not properly restrained and was being teased or harassed.

Tellez said such treatment of a protected animal could potentially result in charges under Belize’s wildlife laws.

CRC volunteers Erica Holding and Austin Bennett subsequently responded to Dolphin Street on Belize City’s Southside at around 10:15 p.m.

Holding said that by the time they arrived, police were already at the location and the crocodile had been moved into a shed.

Residents had restrained the animal using electrical wire, cable and a cloth.

The volunteers removed those restraints, properly secured the crocodile and transported it from the area with assistance from police.

Despite the chaotic circumstances seen in the viral video, Holding and Bennett said the crocodile did not appear to have suffered injuries during the incident.

Bennett said the animal had minor wounds which appeared to have been caused by previous encounters with other crocodiles.

The crocodile was subsequently released into suitable habitat away from the heavily populated area.

The CRC does not reveal such specific locations where animals are released as doing so could place relocated wildlife at risk.

Holding also revealed that residents reported seeing two crocodiles frequenting the neighborhood.

CRC believes both animals may be males and may have been involved in an ongoing territorial fight.

The crocodile captured Sunday night was reportedly the smaller of the two, while the larger animal left the area after its rival was caught.

That means the second crocodile may still be somewhere in or around the Dolphin Street area.

Holding said she collected contact information from residents and asked them to provide photographs or videos if the larger crocodile reappears.

She and Bennett will then assess whether the animal needs to be captured and relocated or whether removing the smaller male from the area has resolved the problem.

Romero said investigators will meanwhile review both the fight captured in the viral footage and the circumstances surrounding the crocodile’s handling.

No charges had been announced as of Monday.

World.title: World Meteorological Organization warns of very strong El Niño with extreme weather risks into 2027
World.content:
World Meteorological Organization warns of very strong El Niño with extreme weather risks into 2027

By Zoila Palma: El Niño is expected to intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, increasing the risks of extreme weather around the world, according to a new update from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

The climate phenomenon is already firmly established and is expected to have significant effects on rainfall and temperature patterns, with heightened risks of floods, drought and extreme heat.

WMO forecasts indicate an “exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100%” that El Niño will persist through February 2027. The agency said this is the first time one of its El Niño/La Niña updates has been so unequivocal, reflecting strong agreement among forecasting centres and climate experts worldwide.

The phenomenon is being fueled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific.

According to WMO, El Niño is expected to strengthen further during the coming months, reaching a very strong intensity before peaking toward the end of 2026, while its climate impacts are expected to continue into 2027.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned of the growing global risks associated with the event, saying, “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes.”

He added that rising sea surface temperatures and increasing global temperatures are placing the world in a dangerous period of extreme weather, reiterating the need for stronger climate action and preparedness.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said communities and economies could face significant impacts as El Niño intensifies. “El Niño in Spanish means boy child – but it has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” Saulo said, noting that droughts and floods are already causing disruption and devastation and could worsen.

Saulo said the exceptional strength of the event requires increased preparation and response, with national meteorological and hydrological services playing a critical role in protecting lives and livelihoods.

WMO said it is working with United Nations and humanitarian partners to provide climate information to support disaster management and climate-sensitive sectors, including agriculture, health, energy and water resources, emphasizing that “we have no time to lose.”

World.title: JAMAICA gets Disney boost
World.content:
Disney Cruine Line’s Disney Destiny will make its inaugural call on Jamaica next month.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Jamaica’s tourism industry is set to receive a big boost on October 13 when one of Disney Cruise Line’s top modern vessels, Disney Destiny, makes its inaugural call at Falmouth’s historic cruise port bringing just under 2,800 passengers to the island.

The announcement was made by Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose during Monday’s opening of the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) at Moon Palace Jamaica in Ocho Rios.

The arrival of Disney Destiny adds to the growing roster of Disney Cruise Line vessels calling on Jamaica, alongside ships operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Princess Cruises, and Virgin Voyages.

From January to July this year, according to data shared by Rose, Jamaica recorded 234 cruise calls and 736,372 passengers. Montego Bay, Falmouth and Ocho Rios accounted for most visits, while four ships also called at Port Antonio and Kingston.

Rose pointed out that the cruise industry remains an important partner, particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa — which hit sections of Jamaica last October — and reminded that it could provide a pathway to attracting visitors for longer stays.

“It’s often said you can come down, get a little taste of Jamaica on the cruise ship, then we can convert them, or they go back home and say that was too much of a teaser, and they come back,” he said.

The JTB official said cruise visitors are encouraged to venture beyond established resort centres, particularly towards Kingston and Port Antonio, to experience a wider range of the Jamaican product.

Reacting to news of Disney Destiny’s impending visit, Chukka Caribbean Adventures deputy executive chairman and Jamaica Tourist Board member John Byles pointed to the benefit it will bring to local artisans and attractions. According to Byles, Disney passengers tend to leave the ship and spend on Jamaican tourism experiences.

He welcomed the impending Disney Destiny call, describing it as a sign of the company’s growing trust in Jamaica.

“It is always very heartening to see the confidence that a brand like Disney continues to show for the Jamaica product and Jamaica destination,” Byles told buyers and suppliers attending the first day of JAPEX, a staple on the tourism calendar.

The trade show is being held under the theme ’Jamaica Reimagined’. Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brian Heron used his address to stress that Jamaica’s recovery from Hurricane Melissa must lead to a stronger and more adaptable tourism industry.

“Resilience is not simply about recovering, It is truly about what comes next,” he said.

He noted that changing travellers, technology and artificial intelligence were reshaping how people discover and experience destinations, requiring Jamaica to embrace innovation without sacrificing its authenticity.

The JHTA head said Jamaica’s strongest differentiator remains its people, pointing to the warmth of the welcome, culture, creativity, music, spirit, and food.

Officially declaring the trade show open during an address delivered virtually, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett stressed the importance of adapting to shifts in the global tourism marketplace, strengthening competitiveness and building resilience while safeguarding the characteristics that make Jamaica distinctive.

“An event like JAPEX is never just a trade show. Last year, JAPEX facilitated an estimated US$100 million in contracts and business negotiations. Behind that figure are real hotels, real workers, real families, and real communities. That is precisely why, in fact, we do this,” Bartlett said.

World.title: Veteran journalist Balford Henry passes
World.content:
HENRY... his quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter

THE local media fraternity has lost one of its calmest and most easy-going veterans, Balford George Henry, who died on Monday after a brief illness.

He was 74.

Henry’s quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter.

Henry served both national newspapers, The Gleaner and the Jamaica Observer, in several capacities. He also served as consulting editor at the Jamaica Information Service (JIS) and worked at

New York Daily News, WLIB Radio in New York as a correspondent.

Henry was also editor of Reggae Times in the 1990s and reporter for the Overseas Gleaner (North America Edition) in New York during the 90s.

In a 2011 interview with JIS the unflappable Henry said he simply loves to write, and responded to the call to the fourth Estate during the summer of 1971, while a sixth former at Wolmer’s Boys’ School in Kingston.

“At that time, The Gleaner advertised for trainee journalists. I was among scores of young people from across Jamaica who sat the initiative tests, coincidently held at Wolmer’s Boys’ School auditorium. Fortunately, I was among the handful of successful candidates,” he recalled.

At that time, The Gleaner was the only institutionalised daily newspaper in the country and, in the absence of a school of journalism in Jamaica and indeed, the wider region, the North Street facility prided itself as the nursery and training ground for print reporters.

“I was exposed to the veterans of the craft, people like Ken Allen, Calvin Bowen, LK Southerland, and Editor-in-Chief Theodore Sealy. Barbara Gloudon, in particular, discovered very early in my career that I enjoyed writing features, and encouraged and nurtured my efforts,” said Henry in the JIS interview.

He recalled that the training period was tough, with the late Fitzroy Nation “being the only other member of my group to survive that ordeal”.

Henry further honed his skills as a Commonwealth Press Union (CPU) Fellow, London, 1977; earned a journalism diploma as a Thomson Foundation scholar in Cardiff, Wales, 1977; and was one of 12 journalists from around the world chosen by the World Press Institute (WPI) for a fellowship at Macalester College, St Paul, Minnesota, in 1983.

Early in his career Henry reported on sittings of the then Kingston and St Andrew Corporation (KSAC), as well as major social and cultural activities and events.

Later, as a veteran labour relations reporter, he covered industrial relations issues including major strikes and disputes during the volatile 1970s.

The recipient of a number of professional awards, Henry had also been the winner of the Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) Honorary Award for a series on the social and economic problems facing Jamaican youth in Britain’s inner cities, based on his own experience while living in that country in 1977.

He had also won the PAJ Best Story award for his coverage of the funeral of the late reggae icon Bob Marley in 1981; as well as the PAJ’s first Cultural Story Award for the feature entitled: ‘Fall of a Superstar’, on the rise and fall of Jamaican reggae singer Junior Byles.

In 2011 Henry was conferred with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

Reacting to his passing, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness expressed sadness and said he remembers Henry as a committed journalist who understood the responsibility that comes with telling Jamaica’s story.

“His work reflected a deep knowledge of our politics, our people and the issues affecting our country,” Holness said in a post on Instagram.

“His passing is a loss to Jamaica’s media fraternity and to the many people who knew and worked with him over the years. I extend my heartfelt condolence to his family, friends, colleagues and the wider journalism community,” the prime minister said.

Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Minister Olivia Grange also expressed sadness at Henry’s passing, describing him as “a first-rate journalist” who was committed to his craft.

Grange said Henry was an “outstanding writer and questioner whose easy-going demeanour belied the penetrating nature of his questions”.

“I had great respect for Balford. He was always professional in his interactions and in his journalistic pursuits. He was sharp, he was keen, he could be tough, but he was always fair,” Grange said, and offered condolence to his family and colleagues.

Journalist Wilton Dyer, who was already at The Gleaner when a very young Henry arrived in 1971, remembers “a very quiet, contemplative man” who brought a “very dilligent, single-minded approach” to journalism.

“He was very efficient and driven,” Dyer said, recalling that Henry quickly developed a “mastery of labour relations and parliamentary reporting”.

Dyer also recalled that Henry was steeped in Jamaican music and also produced a record of his own called Bits of Paper.

By the mid-1970s Henry was among the leading Jamaican entertainment writers, said Dyer.

Fellow veteran journalist Garfield Myers remembered Henry as a workaholic.

“He was one of those who, when I went to The Gleaner in July 1973, had been there for a couple of years — very young man, a couple of years older than me — and he was one of those who showed me the way,” said Myers, a former Observer sports editor who still writes for the newspaper from St Elizabeth.

He said that Henry became very adept at labour relations and trade union coverage, which was a very important beat back in those days.

“Over time he graduated to Parliament and became one of the better parliamentary reporters, and mastered that beat. He was a very good reporter. Some journalists graduate to become editors but Balford was a reporter par excellence. Trying to make him into something else wouldn’t work,” Myers said.

Observer Executive Editor, Publications Vernon Davidson also commented on Henry’s mastery of parliamentary reporting, noting that he often returned from a long day of covering the legislature with stories missed by some of his colleagues.

“We could always depend on Balford to deliver, regardless of how long the sittings were, as he had an exceptional eye for detail and the type of patience required to cover Parliament,” said Davidson who also worked with Henry at The Gleaner in the early 1980s.

“Bally also provided excellent coverage of politics and would be our point reporter during the annual budget debates,” said Davidson who recalled that Henry joined the Observer in November 2003, left for JIS in 2009, and returned to the newspaper in 2012.

“He was a quiet fountain of knowledge and we are poorer for his passing. We extend our deepest condolence to his family, friends and colleagues,” Davidson said.

Henry is survived by his widow Claudia Stockhausen-Henry and was the father of two sons and two daughters.

World.title: Music in her bones
World.content:
Reggae songstress Sevana strikes a pose during an intimate gathering on Friday evening to celebrate her latest single, Jeans an’ Marina.Karl McLarty

If one were to choose a word to describe Sevana, multi-talented would certainly be in the running.

The Jamaican creative has spent years moving between worlds, so much so that when things appear quiet on one front, chances are something else is unfolding behind the scenes.

And if her recent absence from the musical spotlight left anyone wondering where she had been, Sevana has a simple explanation.

“When we’re quiet one place, we’re working in the next,” she said.

On Friday, the singer welcomed specially invited guests into an intimate, house party-style gathering at Cherry Drive Estates for the release of her newest single, Jeans an’ Marina.

The relaxed setting was fitting for a song inspired not by glamour or exclusivity, but by Sevana’s memories of community, simplicity, and the kind of Jamaican togetherness that requires little more than good company, music, and somewhere to gather.

It also marked Sevana’s re-emergence into a space she insists she never truly left.

“I was working on a lot of acting projects while you weren’t actively hearing from me on the entertainment scene, but I was still making a lot of music,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Sevana has been acting since 2017, but in recent years has deliberately positioned herself “a little deeper into that world”.

Her growing résumé includes an appearance in the Robert Nesta Marley biopic Bob Marley: One Love, while she is also featured in UK series Possession, now streaming on Sky TV, in which she plays an escaped revolutionary woman. She has also landed her first starring role in a feature film, Threads of Us, which she said is currently touring the United States.

“I have different projects that I’m pushing at the moment,” she explained.

But for all the creative lanes she has been exploring, there remains one that feels particularly like home.

“Music is my first love, and it is the thing that has continued to save me time and time again,” Sevana shared. “It’s not something I can let go. It’s in my bones, it’s in my blood and I love it. I will never stop.”

Her return, then, is perhaps less of a comeback and more of a refocusing. Sevana said she resisted the urge to release material simply for the sake of remaining visible, choosing instead to build a catalogue she genuinely believed in.

“Navigating the entertainment industry, it takes a lot out of you, especially if you’re trying to do multiple things at once,” she said. “I was really committed to putting together a body of work that I could be really proud of once I hit the ground running again.”

She wanted, she explained, to feel excitement about everything she eventually shared. “So I wasn’t in a rush to push any singles or anything until now.”

That patience has brought her to Jeans an’ Marina, a record whose roots stretch far beyond the studio and all the way back to Sevana’s childhood in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland.

The inspiration was partly sparked by what she witnessed following last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

Even amid the sombre mood that engulfed sections of the country, Sevana found herself reflecting on the way Jamaicans instinctively pulled together.

“That’s the vibe I was going for on this single. I wanted it to feel like a coming together,” she said.

But the feeling was familiar. Growing up in Savanna-la-Mar, Friday nights offered Sevana an early lesson in what community could look like when stripped of pretence.

“Every Friday night the community would gather in the square under the street light to just hang out,” she recalled. “We’d play dominoes, ludo, listen to music, buss a one beer and just relax.”

There was no dress code. No pressure to manufacture an image for the evening. Nobody needed an elaborate outfit or an exclusive invitation.

“It never felt like pressure to get all dolled up or anything like that. You could wear weh yuh have, and everybody had jeans and merina. You would put it on and just come out and have fun,” she said.

It is that uncomplicated sense of belonging that Sevana has attempted to bottle in the new single.

“The idea back then was for the community to come together and heal each other, and that’s what this song is about — being unified and arite,” she said.

The singer then went on to share that Jeans an’ Marina is not a standalone return to music. It is the opening note of what she hopes will be a sustained new chapter with her next single expected at the end of September. Sevana then plans to release new music every month heading into 2027, tracks that may eventually culminate in something much bigger.

World.title: Inaugural Ultimate a hit with the athletes, says Coe
World.content:
COE... it seems in large part to have worked pretty well Photo: Naphtali Junior

BUDAPEST, Hungary (AFP) — The inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest worked “pretty well”, according to World Athletics President Sebastian Coe, who hailed the “uniquely positive” feedback from athletes.

Coe had dubbed the three-day Ultimate, bringing together 381 athletes from 65 federations in competition for unmatched prize money totalling $10 million, as an “incubator for change”.

An all-black in-field, a long jump pit filled with pink sand, enhanced graphics and quick-fire coverage unashamedly aimed for television, and particularly a younger audience, were all features of the flashy new competition.

“At first inspection, and it’s early, it seems in large part to have worked pretty well,” Coe told journalists in Budapest.

“The athletes have been uniquely positive. At first perusal I think we’re in decent shape.

“We are an innately conservative sport and I just think we’ve moved slightly away from the risk-adverse end of that spectrum — not probably by much, but it’s a start.”

Coe added that there had been a “really good vibe” at three sell-out evenings of action and the competition looked “less last week”.

Jamaican sprint legend Usain Bolt claimed 19 global titles in a storied career, but said he wished the kind of prize money on offer at the Ultimate Championship had been available when he was competing.

“It’s big,” said Bolt. “It’s good for the sport and it incentivises athletes to come out here and do the best, to show up and to be ready.”

The Ultimate pitched 26 Olympic champions from the 2024 Paris Games against 26 World champions from Tokyo last year and 25 Diamond League winners from the 2026 season.

“It’s a good step, a first step to changing track and field for the better,” said Bolt. “I think the athletes are loving it. It’s a different energy, a different vibe.”

With 28 disciplines delivered in a fast-paced, made-for-television format, Coe described the current crop of athletes as one “for the ages”.

“For the last two or three years, I’ve sensed that we’ve now got a far broader bandwidth of talent across all our disciplines.”

The 2028 edition of the Ultimate will follow the July 14-30 Los Angeles Olympics, Coe confirmed.

“Where at all possible, we wanted our world championships and now the Ultimate to be the denouement of the season,” he said.

“That’s important and again the athletes have welcomed that.”

Coe entertained more than 20 International Olympic Committee members in Budapest as well as federation presidents of rowing, table tennis and volleyball.

“We all learn from each other,” he said. “Not everybody that watches the 100m wants all of the 100m. That’s how much it’s changed.”

There were ringing endorsements for the Ultimate from athletes in Budapest.

“They have built a great show and it has a different kind of vibe. I love it,” said Norway’s 400m hurdler Karsten Warholm.

Men’s 100m and 200m champion Kenny Bednarek added that “everything is a little bit more exciting than at the World Championships”.

“This event is awesome and it is cool that World Athletics has $10m to invest into its athletes. I want it to be the prize for every championships!” said American Nikki Hiltz, third in the women’s 1,500m.

There was some concern pre-competition about the field events, with no place for shot put, discus or women’s hammer throw.

“The championship is worse off for not having the other field events,” said Britain’s Jazmin Sawyers, second in the women’s long jump.

Sawyers added, however, that the event had been a “wow moment” for her and she would use her prize money of $75,000 to finance another year in the sport and buy a new sewing machine.

Coe acknowledged that the choice to cut some events had been tough.

“There was some nervousness going in about what it was going to mean for us, inevitable discussions that some disciplines are not there,” he said.

“But that’s not set in tablets of stone; it could look different next time.”

World.title: MOVING ON UP!
World.content:
Lavanya Williams

JAMAICA’S rising sprint sensation Lavanya Williams is crediting her mother for helping fuel her breakout season, and says strengthening her mental conditioning will be a key focus for the 2027 campaign.

Williams, one of the fastest women in the world this year, ended her season over the weekend after competing in the women’s 100m and 200m at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Hungary.

The 20-year-old missed out on a place in the 200m final after finishing seventh in her heat but was able to make the final of the 100m. She finished seventh in a stacked field which featured Olympic and World Champions Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, Julien Alfred and Sha’Carri Richardson.

“This is the experience I always wanted, coming on the big stage, running with the big dogs, as you can see. I came out with a seventh place finish but it has been good,” Williams told World Athletics.

Williams’ performances at the Ultimate Championship earned her US$16,000 ($2.5 million), adding another highlight to an impressive second season as a professional athlete since leaving William Knibb High.

Williams, who is coached by former Jamaica sprint star Michael Frater at the Dynamic Speed Track Club, shattered her personal best in both sprint events.

In the 100m she lowered her personal best from 11.45 seconds set in 2025 to 10.90, which she did at the Felix Sanchez Classic in the Dominican Republic last month. It was the fifth time she had gone under the sub-11-second mark this year, making her the 15th-fastest Jamaican woman of all time in the process.

In the 200m her personal best improved from 24.38 last year to 22.44, earning her a spot at the Commonwealth Games this summer in Scotland where she reached the final and finished just shy of the podium in fifth.

Williams didn’t finish the year empty-handed of silverware, however, as she won relay gold at the Commonwealth Games and the World Athletics Relays, as well as 100m gold and 200m silver at the North American, Central American and Caribbean (NACAC) Under-23 Championships in Mexico.

Williams believes her desire to please her mother made her a better athlete this year.

“This season I told myself that I really need to get on the worldwide radar, and I really wanted to make my mum proud,” she told The Inside Lane UK.

“She did a lot for me. She always talking about, ‘I want my dream house, I want my this, I want my that’, and when I thought about everything [and] not going to college I’m like, ‘Nah, I got to step up and get in the game.’ ”

Williams will be hoping to get her first taste of a major championship when she looks to qualify for next year’s World Athletics Championships in Beijing.

Though happy with her performances so far, Williams says she will have to go a step further to compete with the best in 2027.

“My season has been great. Part of it has been smooth sailing, [other] parts can get a bit demotivating at times because you know how the body works as an athlete. However, it has been good.”

“[My biggest takeaway] is being ready mentally. You can be ready physically but sometimes, mentally, if you’re not there you won’t go far.”

World.title: Fashion Radar: ‘Sākred
World.content:
‘Sākred founder and principal Shelly-Deane Neil makes a statement in the Tie-Side Wrap Set. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Tuesday Style Fashion (TSF) stops by ‘Sākred for this week’s spotlight on retailers. Under the Fashion Radar today is principal Shelly-Deane Neil.

TSF: ‘Sākred is officially open. What inspired you to create the boutique, and what does the name mean to you?

Shelly-Deane Neil (SDN): ‘Sākred was really inspired by my own journey with fashion and faith. As my relationship with God grew, the way I viewed how I dressed began to change, but my love for fashion didn’t. I still wanted to feel feminine, modern, confident and a little edgy. I just wanted what I wore to reflect who I was becoming.

I realised there was space for a brand that spoke to women like me — women who have standards but still genuinely love fashion. I wanted ‘Sākred to show that choosing modesty doesn’t mean losing your personal style.

The name ‘Sākred came from God, and it means “set apart”. For me, it’s not about saying the clothing itself is sacred; it’s about the woman wearing it understanding that she is. That idea really became the foundation of the brand and our approach to modern, modest fashion.

TSF: What gap did you see in the market that made you say,“This needs to exist”?

SDN: The gap became really clear to me here in Jamaica. As my own standards around clothing began to change, I realised how difficult it was to shop locally for pieces that gave me the coverage I wanted while still feeling modern, elevated and fashion-forward. In Jamaica, we have a very vibrant fashion culture, but a lot of what is readily available tends to be more revealing, particularly when it comes to occasion wear and going-out pieces. On the other hand, when you do find more modest options, they don’t always feel as current or aligned with the woman who still wants to make a fashion statement. I felt there was room in the Jamaican market for something in between — a brand where a woman could find pieces that respected her standards without asking her to sacrifice her sense of style.

TSF: Walk us through the process of bringing Sakred from an idea to a physical space.

SDN: Bringing ‘Sakred from an idea to a physical space was probably one of the most hands-on things I’ve ever done. There was so much that I had to learn, research and figure out along the way.

The sourcing process alone was a journey. Before I ever got on a plane, I spent countless hours researching, seeing pieces I liked, trying to get a glimpse of tags, tracing where garments were made, researching manufacturers and following one lead to another trying to figure out where I needed to go and who I needed to meet.

Then came the actual travelling. I travelled for hours, walked for hours, visited different suppliers, went through rack after rack and looked at hundreds of pieces to find the few that actually felt like ‘Sakred. I wanted to touch the fabrics, see the quality for myself, meet suppliers and understand what I was buying. And because our pieces are intentionally limited, I wasn’t trying to buy everything… I was looking for the right things.

At the same time, I was learning the operational side of the business. There were things I could have easily handed over to someone else, but I wanted to understand how my own business worked. Then there was finding the space, overseeing the build-out, developing the brand, hiring, merchandising and all the details that go into actually opening the doors. So when people walk into Sakred now and see this beautiful finished space, I think what they don’t see are all the hours behind it; the research, the travelling, the walking, the mistakes, the learning, the suppliers I had to find, and the things I had to teach myself along the way.

Sakred was very much built hands-on, from the ground up, and I think that’s part of what makes seeing it physically exist now so special.

TSF: How involved were you in the aesthetic and design of the store itself?

SDN: I was involved in absolutely everything. I chose the colour palette, the furniture, the fixtures, the lighting, the mirrors, the racks, the placement of the clothing — down to the smaller details of how everything would work together. I was very particular about creating a space that felt clean, modern and elevated, but still warm and inviting.

TSF: How would you describe your own personal style, and how much of it is reflected in Sakred?



SDN: I would describe my personal style as feminine, chic and a little edgy. I love a clean, polished look, but I also like something unexpected — whether that’s the silhouette, a detail, the way a piece is styled or simply the confidence it gives you when you put it on. And honestly, a lot of that is reflected in Sakred. When I’m sourcing, one of the first things I instinctively ask myself is, “Would I wear this?” I think that’s why the collection feels so cohesive, because there is a very clear point of view behind what makes it onto our racks. At the same time, I’m conscious that Sakred isn’t my personal closet. I’m choosing for different women, different body types, different ages and different lifestyles, so I’ll absolutely select pieces that may not necessarily be something I would wear myself, but still embody the Sakred woman.

TSF: How do you curate the pieces that make it onto Sakred’s racks?

SDN: I’m very selective about what makes it onto Sakred’s racks. I’m not sourcing simply because something is trendy or because I think it will sell. It has to feel like Sakred. I look at the silhouette, especially the quality of the fabric, the fit, the details and, of course, the level of coverage. But modesty for me isn’t necessarily about a specific hemline or neckline, it’s about the overall presentation of the piece and how it can be styled.

And then there’s simply instinct. I know the Sakred aesthetic, so sometimes I’ll see something and immediately know: “That’s Sakred.” Other times, something can be beautiful, but it just doesn’t belong on our racks. The goal is to curate a collection where every piece earns its place.

TSF: Name three ‘Sakred must-haves.

1. A little black dress is timeless. It’s one of those pieces every woman should have because you can dress it up, dress it down and make it completely your own.

2. Statement sets are a big part of Sakred. I love that they give you an effortless, complete look, but you can also separate the pieces and create entirely different outfits.

3. And definitely one of our shorts sets. They’ve become a hot commodity at Sakred. They’re comfortable and easy to wear, but still give you that polished, put-together look. I think those three capture ‘Sakred perfectly: Modern, feminine, versatile and always with a little edge!

TSF: Are there plans to expand beyond the store — perhaps into private styling, and events?

SDN: Absolutely. ‘Sakred is already my label, but I would definitely like to expand into creating original ‘Sakred pieces. I wouldn’t necessarily call myself a designer in the traditional sense — I’m much more visual. I can look at a piece and immediately see how I would change it, whether that’s adjusting the silhouette, changing a detail, adding something or taking something away to make it feel more elevated.

So I see the natural evolution being working alongside designers and manufacturers who can take my creative direction and translate it into original pieces for the brand. Beyond that, I definitely see ‘Sakred growing through events, collaborations and curated experiences. I want women to be able to experience the brand in ways that go beyond simply shopping. We’ve only just opened, so I’m being intentional about allowing the brand to grow organically, but there is definitely a much bigger vision for Sakred. The physical store is really just the beginning.

‘Sakred Boutique

Rogers Commercial Centre

56-58 Lady Musgrave Rd, Floor 2, Unit 309, Kingston 5

Tel: (876)788-7543

E-mail: sakred.certified@gmail.com
