World.title: Balford Henry, award-winning veteran journalist, dies at 74
World.content:
Veteran journalist Balford Henry (right) being conferred by Governor-General Sir Patrick Allen with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

KINGSTON, Jamaica – Award-winning veteran journalist Balford Henry, whose career spanned more than five decades of reporting, has died at the age of 74.

He died on Monday after a short illness.

Henry entered journalism in 1971 as a trainee reporter with the Gleaner while in sixth form at Wolmer’s Boys’ School in Kingston.

Early in his career, he reported on sittings of the Kingston and St Andrew Corporation (KSAC) before making his name as a labour relations reporter and later a parliamentary journalist.

He also covered major social and cultural activities and historical events, including Bob Marley’s funeral in 1981.

Henry also served as a senior reporter with the Jamaica Observer and a consulting editor at the Jamaica Information Service (JIS).

A recipient of a number of professional awards, Henry was the winner of the Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) Honorary Award for a series on the social and economic problems facing Jamaican youths in Britain’s inner cities, based on his own experience while living in the country in 1977, according to the JIS.

He also won the PAJ Best Story award for his coverage of Marley’s funeral as well as the PAJ’s first Cultural Story Award for the feature on reggae singer Junior Byles entitled, ‘Fall of a Superstar’.

In 2011, Henry was conferred with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

He leaves behind two daughters.

World.title: Sigh of relief
World.content:
ARCHIBALD... had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines, remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses

THE Chinese business community is breathing a sigh of relief after the fatal shooting of Dewar Archibald — who police sources say was part of an organised criminal network operating across several parishes — during a reported gun battle with cops in St Andrew early Sunday morning.

According to a highly placed source, Archibald, otherwise called Max, was a thorn in the side of several Chinese individuals as he preyed on their businesses and homes.

“He and his cronies were on their way to hit the home of a Chinese man in the Corporate Area when they were intercepted by the police Sunday,” the Jamaica Observer source said.

Police reported that Archibald, whom they described as a “high-risk criminal target linked to two murders and a series of major robberies and break-ins across Jamaica”, was among three people fatally shot during an operation by members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Specialised Operations Branch along Red Hills Road about 1:45 am.

According to the police, the Specialised Operations team was on patrol in the Red Hills area when information was received that a group of armed men travelling in two vehicles — a red Honda HR-V and a white Toyota Probox — was allegedly preparing to carry out criminal activity in the St Andrew North Police Division.

A preliminary police report said the cops attempted to intercept the vehicles but the drivers did not stop. The Probox eluded the police.

“Police subsequently intercepted the Honda HR-V in the vicinity of Knightsdale Drive. Occupants of the vehicle reportedly opened fire at members of the police team, who then discharged their service weapons,” the police said.

Three people, one of them a woman, were subsequently found with gunshot wounds. The two men were identified as Archibald, 44 years old of Mountain View, Lincoln, Manchester; and Damian Byfield, 39 years old of Fraser’s Content, St Catherine. Police sources said the woman, who was unidentified at press time, was of brown complexion, approximately 5 feet seven inches tall, with braided hair, and was clad in a black dress.

Two firearms along with ammunition were recovered, the police said.

Police said Archibald was a member of the Speculation Gang and had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines (ATMs), remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses.

According to police sources, the woman is critical to the criminals’ modus operandi as “they use her as a lookout or a distraction”.

Archibald has also been implicated in two murders committed within the past nine months — Chevardo Messam at Galleon Beach in Crawford district, St Elizabeth, on December 21, 2025; and Kemar Brown, otherwise called Mars, in Bristol, Alexandria, St Ann, on January 9, 2026.

A woman was shot and injured during the second incident.

Police also reported that Archibald had been linked to a shooting during an attempted theft of an ATM in Drax Hall, St Ann, in April.

Additionally, investigations had further implicated him in a series of robberies and break-ins in Linstead, St Catherine, in February and June; Kingston in April; and Croft’s Hill, Clarendon, in May.

World.title: UN Security Council meets as Houthis tighten grip on Red Sea chokepoint
World.content:
A small fishing boat seen along the Gulf of Aden on Sept. 12, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

The meeting comes after the Iran-backed group seized strategic islands on the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The UN Security Council is scheduled to meet Tuesday afternoon to discuss the situation in the Middle East, as the Houthis’ rapid advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coast raises fresh concerns over global shipping.

The official UN agenda item does not mention Yemen or the Red Sea. But the meeting comes after the Iran-backed Houthis tightened their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait last week by seizing the Red Sea port of Mokha and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim.

Yemeni and Houthi officials say the group has also moved onto the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, although that claim has not been independently verified.

World.title: EU countries to discuss AI rules as Trump calls safety warnings a ‘hoax’
World.content:
A handheld smartphone displays the icons of some of the main artificial intelligence-based apps, in Saint-Mandé, France on July 15, 2026. | Martin Lelievre/AFP via Getty Images

Officials are set to gather in Brussels this week amid growing calls for regulation, including from key figures in the tech industry.

Government officials from across the European Union will gather in Brussels on Thursday to discuss how to set global rules to counter the threat from new AI models, according to two EU diplomats and a draft agenda seen by POLITICO.

The European Commission will give "updates on EU and international AI policy" and give a "technical briefing on recent AI incidents" during a gathering of the Artificial Intelligence Board, which comprises of representatives from every EU member country and regularly convenes to monitor progress on the bloc's Artificial Intelligence Act.

This week's gathering follows a series of calls to slow down AI development by top company leaders such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman. U.S. President Donald Trump immediately rebuffed the calls, calling the AI safety warnings a "hoax" and arguing that slowing down would give China the momentum in AI.

World.title: World Trade Organization reform failure could cost 10% of global GDP, report warns
World.content:
Under enhanced cooperation, global GDP would be 2.9% higher by 2050, while exports would increase by roughly 18%.

Under geopolitical fragmentation, GDP would drop by 5.1% and exports would also fall 19%.

The worst outcome would be a world dominated by bilateral and regional FTAs, where the WTO’s role would be sidelined. Global GDP would drop by 6.9%, and exports would also fall by 27%.

Taken together, the figures represent a gap of roughly 10% of global GDP between the enhanced cooperation and FTA scenarios.

Worst disruption in 80 years

The report states that the current trading system is facing its worst disruption in 80 years.

WTO Chief Economist Robert Staiger said the organization was dealing with an economy that was increasingly different from the one its rules were designed to govern.

World.title: Sabotage suspected as parts of Dutch rail network come to a standstill
World.content:
The perpetrators have not been identified and national police are leading the investigation. ProRail said its priority was to get trains running again, while preserving evidence as far as possible.

Annet Bertram, the secretary of state for infrastructure and water management, called the alleged sabotage “particularly worrying,” adding that “it is now important that this is investigated very carefully.”

The incident happened on Prinsjesdag, the annual day marking the start of the Dutch parliamentary year, when the government presents its budget plans for the year ahead.

Dutch media reports suggest that activist farmers may be responsible. Farmers in the Netherlands have a history of using similar tactics in protests against the government’s nitrogen policy, which they may be linking to Prinsjesdag.

The Farmers Defense Force, a protest and advocacy group, says it is not behind the suspected sabotage, but has not ruled out that farmers are responsible for the disruptions.

This is not the first time the Dutch rail network has been severely disrupted by suspected sabotage on the day of a major event. During last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, trains around Schiphol airport were severely delayed after a fire. No one has been arrested in connection with that incident.

European countries are on high alert amid concerns about an uptick in hybrid attacks on the continent. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last month that Europe faces “an escalating campaign of threats” which were “seeking to divide our Union.”

This story has been updated.

World.title: Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech — live updates
World.content:
European Commission president sets out her vision for the future of the continent.

It’s a big day for Ursula von der Leyen, as she’ll give her State of the Union address, outlining her vision for Europe’s future.

We know she’ll talk about topics such as AI, climate, migration and social media, but in how much detail? And will there be surprises? Plus, what will be the reaction from members of the European Parliament and a watching Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister?

Our top team of reporters in Strasbourg, Brussels and beyond will give you all the latest news and analysis. Scroll down for updates.

World.title: Carney presses 10 EU countries to ratify Canada trade deal
World.content:
Mark Carney speaks at a press conference in Ottawa, Ontario, on Aug. 22, 2026 after trade talks with the U.S. collapsed. | Dave Chan/AFP via Getty Images)

The Canadian prime minister is seeking to deepen ties with Europe amid a trade war with the U.S.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has urged the 10 EU countries that have yet to ratify the bloc’s trade deal with Canada to do so, as he seeks closer ties with Europe after trade talks with Washington collapsed.

Carney made the plea to the 10 countries — Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Poland and Slovenia — in an interview with the Financial Times, arguing that closer ties with Europe were the best approach in an uncertain world. He said the trade deal was a “positive initiative” which is good for Europe and for Canada, adding that it would make both sides “more sovereign, more resilient, more independent” and more prosperous.

The deal is already effectively in operation, Carney said, but ratification by the remaining EU countries could unlock deeper ties: “I would like to use this opportunity to encourage them to do so.”

World.title: Rayner v Streeting, round two
World.content:
As the TUC Congress continues in Brighton, some of Labour’s big beasts have been baring their teeth – with Angela Rayner using an after-dinner speech to land some blows on Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy reveal what was said and whether it was all taken in good fun.

Meanwhile, the economic picture looks bleak as John Healey prepares for his first budget. Sam has a scoop on how one economic forecast could make or break his spending plans.

And Reform remains “100% confident” that two of the biggest donations in British political history were legal. But will that position shift as ministers face growing questions about how a proposed retrospective change in the law would work?

World.title: Alarm in Denmark after Russian ship fires at military helicopter
World.content:
A Danish army helicopter is pictured in Skive, Denmark, on June 29, 2023. | Morten Stricker/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images

“It is part of the pattern we see throughout Europe,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen warned on Tuesday morning.

A Russian ship fired flares at a Danish military helicopter off the southern coast of Denmark on Monday, triggering alarm in Copenhagen as the Kremlin's belligerence against Europe ramps up.

"The Russian frigate fired two flares at the helicopter. One of the flares fired passed within a short distance of the helicopter," the Danish armed forces announced late Monday night.

European nations have accused Moscow of conducting a campaign of so-called hybrid warfare to destabilize the continent while it also persists in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine — but capitals and NATO have hesitated about an escalatory response to Russia.

World.title: 'Is this sport?': Sydney Sweeney faces backlash from female athletes over nude advert
World.content:
It seems that whenever American actress Sydney Sweeney signs on for an ad campaign, the internet ends up losing its mind.

 

Following her hugely controversial American Eagle publicity campaign, which some perceived as promoting White supremacism and eugenics, her latest stunt has sparked fresh backlash. This time, Sweeney has managed to exasperate female athletes and Olympians, who have labelled the  as "infuriating" and "a kick in the face to every woman."

The source of fresh division comes down to Sweeney featuring in a commercial for Novig, the American sports trading app. Read: gambling firm.

In the NSFW advert, the Euphoria actress poses with little-to-no clothing and pieces of sporting equipment. Very little is left to the imagination.

"Novig is just sports," she says, strategically covering her bathykolpian figure with footballs - followed by a baseball bat, a hockey stick, a tennis racket...

"Sports... Sports... Sports..." she repeats, before adding: “No betting on wars or deaths, and no politics. Just you and your takes on sports.”

“The campaign was about embracing a fun idea,” said Sweeney, who is also a Novig strategic partner and equity holder. “The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humour and a playful edge.”

No one bought it, as the focus was less on sports and clearly on appealing to those... titillated by her Sweeneys.

Of course, social media went into overdrive. The ad clearly worked for some and enraged others, who saw it as a shameless way of treating people like idiots.

"Sydney Sweeney is single handedly setting feminism 1000 years back and you can't convince me otherwise," wrote one social media user, while another added: "It's basically soft-core porn."

"Stop sexualizing women's sports," another wrote. "In WHAT world do you need to be butt ass naked for a SPORTS COMMERCIAL?!"

Beyond the usual bile-filled back-and-forths on X, the advert has raised concern among female athletes, who have argued that Sweeney's ad shamefully sexualises women's sports and is "demeaning".

“I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” Ariarne Titmus, a four-time Olympic gold medalist for Australia, wrote on Instagram. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity."

She added: “How do we live in a world where monetising a woman’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?”

Australian World champion boxer Skye Nicolson said it was about making a “mockery” of women in sport. “There’s a big difference between looking ‘sexy’ because you do sport compared to using sex to sell ‘sport’,” she wrote in an Instagram story. “There is nothing wrong with looking good and doing sport and there’s nothing wrong with embracing your femininity while also being a badass athlete.”

As for Canadian skier Cassidy Gray, who competed at the 2026 Winter Olympics, she took to TikTok to respond to Sweeney's ad, noting how female athletes face being sexualised, not being taken seriously and not given the same opportunities as men. Gray went on to describe Sweeney's actions as "idiotic" and "senseless" in a video that now gone viral.

@_cassidy_gray Sydney Sweeney rly out here trying to make sure women never get taken seriously in sports ♬ original sound - Cassidy Gray🇨🇦

Meanwhile, in a post liked by several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, UK athlete Lucy Davis wrote: “I don’t know wtf Sydney Sweeney was doing, but it’s 2026. Stop sexualizing women in sport.”

British sprinter Amy Hunt used a BBC interview to call out the actress. “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like,” she said after racing at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship. “Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening.”

Elsewhere, the Female Athlete Project, which fosters a community for women in sports, posted the following statement: "We're not entirely sure if Novig or Sydney Sweeney and her PR team have ever watched sports. But honestly, wow. It's incredible they could fit so much misogyny in 40 seconds. Sports has long treated women's bodies as commodities, and this objectification does nothing to support real women in sport."

Naturally, this statement also prompted some backlash, featuring a few less than erudite comments and even some support for Sweeney.

"Why don't we blame / name the ad company instead of the actress? I'm sure if she declined the offer someone else would have done it. I don't think it's right to blame her," wrote one user on Instagram. Another commented: "This is so dramatic. It’s a sports betting ad. It doesn’t have anything to do with women in sports. It’s meant to draw in silly men to spend money on sports."

"Sooo guess it’s body positivity if they’re overweight?" queried another, adding: "Pretty sure she never said anything specific about women in sports. Women have been used in sports ads for forever. What if Sydney Sweeney was fat? I’m sure everyone would praise her? What if it was Taylor Swift in the ad? I’m sure everyone would praise her. “Support other women”… unless it’s Sydney Sweeney???"

Sweeney has seemingly responded to the backlash by taking to herInstagram Story to post various covers from ESPN Magazine's The Body Issue from over the years which show nude sports photos featuring athletes including Serena Williams, Ronda Rousey and Megan Rapinoe.

Still, that hasn't stopped more than 200,000 of her followers from smashing the “unfollow” button on her account...

Role play

Screenshot of the Sydney Sweeney ad campaign Novig

The ad has left many wondering what Sweeney is playing at. Provocation for the sake of it? Inviting objectification of her own body and accepting the pornification of whatever big companies want in exchange for a big fat paycheck? Or just doing ads for the love of reminding horny viewers that spherical sports equipment can be reminiscent of breasts?

Whatever it is, sadly, it's working – as her recent stunt has already achieved infamy. But beyond the nose-bleedingly tacky nature of it all – as well as the predictably misogynistic "hot takes" online reminding everyone that X gathers the binjuice of humanity - one aforementioned British athlete raises an important question.

Amy Hunt doubled down on her criticism by warning that the Novig advert risks becoming a "barrier" to young girls wanting to take part in sport.

Speaking on ITV's Good Morning Britain, she said: "I think when we’re trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it’s about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like."

"I think when we see the the stats of 64 per cent of young girls drop out of exercise and sport before they reach the age of 16, we don’t need to place any kind of barrier whatsoever in their way in terms of providing the opportunity and the empowerment for them to still exercise, whatever that looks like, professional or kind of just going to do a ParkRun with your friends. So it’s about empowering young girls and young women and young people to show that you really can just get out there and you don’t have to worry what you look like, you don’t have to worry about what you’re wearing."

She added: "Sport, it’s not pretty, and I think that’s the thing to get to the level that we’re at. It’s shown to people that being aspirational and trying to be elite is something amazing, and you should really want to be the best version of yourself you can be. And that doesn’t always look attractive, and that doesn’t always look nice. Sometimes it looks like throwing up in the corner of the track, or I’ve had sessions this year where I’ve been crying afterwards."

Will Novig and Sweeney take notice or think again in the future? Probably not. They're doubtlessly rubbing their hands at yet another viral Sweeney moment and fooling themselves into thinking they're getting away with the "put the focus entirely on sports" line. Shame, as maybe people would muster more goodwill towards the ad if the makers openly acknowledged that the only thing sex sells is sex itself. Not sport.

World.title: Escalation is 'on the way' but region must keep calm, Syria's al-Sharaa tells Euronews
World.content:
"It looks like escalation is on the way” in the region gripped by the Iran war, and “with all the tensions, nobody can predict” what will happen, but the hope is that the situation “remains stable," Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said on Tuesday.

 

In an answer to a Euronews question at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, al-Sharaa urged the region’s countries to “keep calm” and “work together to alleviate the problems that come” with conflict, which is vital to Syria’s new beginning “after 60 years of destruction and 17 years of war”.

The Arab Media Summit kicked off on Tuesday with a wide array of regional leaders, officials, media executives, analysts, writers and influencers, bringing together eight specialised forums, including Euronews’ Forum on Wednesday, and welcoming some 10,000 participants.

As the headline speaker at the summit opening, Al-Sharaa said, “Syria is being transformed into a story being told across the world,” after overcoming all the obstacles of its past tragic decades and marking “a new beginning” which “could be a big opportunity.”

Syria’s president outlined how his country took the initiative to turn the Iran war-generated crises into opportunities.

“People are talking about Syria as a pathway, as security and supply chains can link the West and the East,” giving the UAE as an example of “targeting the right opportunities” with its moves to bypass the Strait of Hormuz closure.

“Syria has always been a trade pathway as being traders and negotiators has been in our DNA,” al-Sharaa told the summit, adding that with transparency and honesty, “Syria is increasing its credibility,” as “it is not affiliated towards any direction”.

From the podium in Dubai, he said, “We rely on our dear brothers and sisters in the Arab world and learn from them, so we don’t try to reinvent the wheel.

He said Syria is in “a transformational phase” towards a democracy, after being plagued by sanctions that Trump “has been helping to lift,” which led to “breaking the chain” of the past.

“We are expecting some shocks and we need to move into a quieter stage,” and that Damascus “need to give it time” for the reforms and transformations to make their mark.

He further outlined food security and supplies as important targets for the region, where Syria has many opportunities that European investors and neighbouring countries with investments from the Gulf are interested in.

Al-Sharaa told the summit that he hopes the region remains stable and that Syria “tries to find ways to mitigate the damage of war,” and to work together with the Arab world “to spread peace in the region which will help economic growth.”

As a keynote speaker at the Arab Media Summit, Al-Sharaa said, “It is a heavy burden to work in the media, to fact-check and to stay away from politicising.”

“People’s lives are in the hands of the media, as they need to keep up with the Arab societies to be aware of the actual facts of what is happening: authenticate information with channels and people and the messages of media,” the Syrian president concluded.

World.title: Prominent Greek neo-Nazi exits prison and says he will return to politics
World.content:
A former leading member of the Greek neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn, Ilias Kasidiaris, has been released from prison and vowed a return to politics.

 

Kasidiaris was convicted and imprisoned in 2020 as a leading member of the criminal organisation, which for years had been linked to violent attacks on migrants and political opponents, as well as to the murder of anti-fascist musician Pavlos Fyssas in 2013. He served only part of his 13-year sentence.

Leaving prison on Monday, Kasidiaris announced a return to Greek politics, vowing to start a new political movement on Monday.

Dozens of his supporters had gathered outside Domokos prison in central Greece, some were holding Greek flags. The crowd chanted slogans in his favour, including "Ilias, we are with you".

Kasidiaris addressed supporters upon his release: "I had given you my word that as soon as I passed through this gate I would return to the front line of the national struggle. I see that I am not alone, but that alongside me stands a major national party, like those that dominate in Europe.

My aim is for the country to be rid of the most corrupt government of the post-junta era. In these past days I see the politicians whining and conspiring, saying they will not allow me to return to parliament. But in a democracy there is only one judge, the sovereign Greek people."

Political career

Kasidiaris became Golden Dawn’s press spokesman in 2012 and later served as an MP for the party until 2019. Golden Dawn caused a political earthquake in Greece in 2012, when it managed to enter parliament amid intense social and economic upheaval brought on by the financial crisis, the erosion of trust in institutions and the discrediting of traditional political parties.

Golden Dawn spokesman Ilias Kasidiaris shouts slogans during protest in Athens in 2018 AP Photo/Petros Giannakouris

Despite being behind bars, he did not give up political activity. He continued to intervene via social media, mainly through his YouTube channel, which has around 162,000 subscribers.

Before he was imprisoned, in October 2020 Kasidiaris had founded a new political formation, "Greeks", and even from prison tried to take part in the 2023 parliamentary elections. However, the Supreme Court (Areios Pagos) banned his party from standing in the elections.

In 2023, the far-right "Spartans" party won more than 240,000 votes with Kasidiaris’s public backing.

In July this year he found himself in the spotlight after billionaire Elon Musk called the continuation of Kasidiaris's detention was "confusing" or "wrong", triggering fresh reactions to the case. Kasidiaris has described Musk as "the most prominent personality in the world".

Violent past

Kasidiaris has appeared in the headlines over the years after a number of violent incidents. He has been photographed with a swastika tattoo on his left arm and is known for a series of aggressive behaviours.

Kasidiaris at a rally in 2014 AP Photo/Yannis Kolesidis

In 2012, live on television, he slapped Communist Party MP Liana Kanelli and threw a glass of water at an MP from a left-wing party.

He has also been recorded verbally and physically attacking television crews. In a discussion with Golden Dawn supporters in November 2012 he claimed that party members entering parliament were allowed to "carry legally licensed weapons".

Political future

Legal experts say he is still barred from running for office until 2033, although the Supreme Court would rule on his eligibility at election time. Greece’s next elections are due in 2027.

His release comes at a time when the far right is gaining ground in several European countries. In Germany the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made significant progress in the polls, including a recent victory in a regional election contest, for the first time since the Second World War.

World.title: Poké Ball-shaped hotel opens in Japan to mark 30th anniversary of Pokémon
World.content:
A lot of people on the internet point to 2016 as both the moment where Everything Went Wrong, but also the last time the world felt truly united.

 

I won’t get into the former, but the latter is tied to one thing: The release of Pokémon Go. It was a summer of fun, of running around with strangers, of embracing nostalgia.

While it currently feels as though we’ll never reach those highs collectively again, there is still some whimsy in the world – and Pokémon-related whimsy to boot.

That’s because NOT A HOTEL has teamed up with the sleep game app Pokémon Sleep to create a Poké Ball-shaped hotel.

The pod has a curved acrylic window so you can enjoy the views during your stay Pokémon/Nintendo/Creatures/GAME FREAK/NOT A HOTEL/Pokémon Sleep

Located in Tomakomai City, Hokkaido, the hotel pod is three metres across, with a round bed under a curved acrylic window letting you enjoy the lakeside views while relaxing in the Poké Ball.

There are plenty of nods to the beloved anime throughout, including tiles inspired by Snorlax's colors in the bathroom area next to the hotel.

You can even pick your favourite Pokémon on an iPad in the room, which will transform the lighting to match your selection.

The lighting inside will change based on your favourite Pokémon Pokémon/Nintendo/Creatures/GAME FREAK/NOT A HOTEL/Pokémon Sleep

Can you stay there?

Bad news, I’m afraid.

The hotel concept was created to celebrate both the 30th anniversary of Pokémon and the third anniversary of Pokémon Sleep, but only Japanese residents using the latter will be able to enter a competition for a stay.

Users will be able to enter through X, formerly known as Twitter. If you are lucky enough to be eligible to apply, all the details can be found here.

Those chosen will get a free one-night stay between 8 and 18 October.

World.title: ECB invites Europeans to vote on future banknote designs as deadline approaches
World.content:
Birds, rivers and figures from European culture, including composers, are among the design choices the ECB is asking people to consider for future euro banknotes. More than 9 million people have already voted, but the ECB is encouraging more people to share their opinions before the survey closes next Monday.

 

The ECB has previously consulted Europeans about the redesign, but this is the first time it has launched a survey asking them to assess the ten shortlisted designs. The proposed designs also differ markedly from those on existing banknotes.

In an increasingly cashless world, the ECB is sending a message to Europeans: cash is here to stay, and they can help choose what it will look like.

"Cash is not simply a legacy of the past. It is part of daily life for millions of Europeans," ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone said during an event on euro banknotes in Brussels on Monday.

The survey covers ten shortlisted designs under two possible themes: “European culture” and “Rivers and birds”. The results will inform, but not determine, the ECB Governing Council’s final decision, which is expected around the end of 2026. The new banknotes will then take several years to develop and are expected to enter circulation gradually from 2029.

"More than 31 billion euro banknotes, worth over €1.6 trillion, are in circulation, with an annual growth of around 3%. There are also more than 150 billion euro coins in circulation," Cipollone said. He also noted that cash still plays a role when other payment methods are disrupted, for example during power or internet outages.

The role of cash could be further reinforced by proposed EU legislation known as the Single Currency Package. The package, which is under negotiation in Brussels, includes measures intended to strengthen the legal-tender status of cash and its mandatory acceptance.

"Cash provides something that is difficult to replace: a tangible anchor of stability and trust. Cash also fosters financial inclusion. It is simple and intuitive. It protects privacy. And, perhaps most importantly, it safeguards freedom of choice," Cipollone said during his speech.

According to a 2024 ECB survey, a growing majority of Europeans think that retaining cash as a payment option is important.

"Cash is the only form of money that every citizen can hold directly. Once you have cash, you don’t need any intermediaries or devices to use it," Cipollone said.

Digital and physical euro

In its payment strategy, the ECB is investing not only in the redesign of banknotes but also in the creation of the digital euro, an electronic form of central bank money that would complement cash. The ECB says its support for cash is intrinsically linked to this new electronic means of payment, which is intended to enable both offline and online transactions with a high degree of privacy.

The digital euro could be issued for the first time in 2029 if negotiations in Brussels are concluded by the end of 2026.

"We are investing in both euro cash and the digital euro. Together, they will ensure that Europeans have access to central bank money in both physical and digital form for day-to-day transactions," Cipollone said.

Together, the two forms of central bank money could ensure that a "European solution is available for all types of payment, at all times, throughout the euro area," he said.

One reason the ECB has developed a new payments strategy is the need for strategic autonomy amid significant geopolitical uncertainty and the EU's heavy reliance on US payment infrastructure.

Visa and Mastercard, both American, account for 61% of card payments in the eurozone and nearly all cross-border card transactions, according to 2025 ECB data.

World.title: Robot valet parking at Gatwick Airport promises safer, easier long‑stay car storage
World.content:
The robots, developed by French company Stanley Robotics, can park cars with centimetre-level precision. Gatwick says the system can accommodate around 95% of vehicles, although some cars are excluded. Vehicles must weigh no more than 2.6 tonnes, be under 2.3 metres tall, have a wheelbase of less than 3.3 metres and wheels no larger than 21 inches (53,34 centimètres).

 

The parking area is protected by perimeter fencing, floodlighting and 24-hour security patrols, while automatic number plate recognition monitors vehicles entering and leaving the site. Stanley Robotics says the robots are designed to stop if they malfunction, rather than move unpredictably.

Some passengers say the service is quick and easy to book, while others have opted for it because of the added security. The service costs around €6 to €12 more (£5 to £10) than standard long-stay parking.

When it launched, the service required a minimum stay of five days and was mainly available on weekdays between 9 am and 5 pm. Gatwick says these restrictions will be gradually eased.

World.title: How did Greece end up borrowing more cheaply than France?
World.content:
In March 2012 the Greek state had to pay a market yield of close to 40% on its outstanding ten-year bonds, effectively shutting it out of normal market borrowing. Even at that price, it found few takers.

 

That same month, France raised ten-year money at under 3%. Fourteen years later the two have swapped places.

France's 10-year yield, the rate Paris pays to borrow for a decade, is trading near 4.50%. Athens pays about 4.28%.

Investors are now demanding more interest to lend money to Paris than to Athens. The gap is small. What it says is not.

Greece still owes more relative to the size of its economy than almost any country in Europe, while the French economy is more than ten times larger, richer and far more diversified.

On paper the pricing makes no sense. It makes sense once you accept that bond investors have stopped treating the size of a debt pile as the whole story.

What they weigh now is the direction it is moving, how often it has to be refinanced, and whether a government has the political room to stop adding to it.

On all three, Greece and France are pulling apart.

Greece owes more, but the pile is shrinking

At the end of the first quarter, Greek public debt stood at 143.5% of annual output, against 117.6% in France.

Those are the numbers that flatter Paris, and they are the only ones that do.

Over the previous twelve months Greece's debt-to-GDP ratio fell by 9.4 percentage points. France's rose by about four.

The European Commission expects Greece to keep falling, from 146.1% in 2025 to 134.4% by 2027. It expects France to climb above 120% over the same period.

The budget picture is starker still.

Greece closed last year with a surplus worth 1.7% of GDP and is forecast to stay in the black through 2027. France ran a deficit of 5.1%, one of the widest in the European Union, and this year's is getting away from it.

And the French number is getting worse, not better.

On 11 September, Finance Minister Roland Lescure halved the government's 2026 growth forecast to 0.5% and abandoned the 5% deficit target the budget had been built on.

"Five percent is no longer an option," he told reporters, declining to put a new figure in its place.

The statistics office INSEE is gloomier still at 0.4%, and calls France the only large advanced economy expected to slow this year. Greece is growing at close to 2%.

Why Greece’s enormous debt is less dangerous than it looks

Not all debt behaves the same way, and Greece's behaves unusually well.

Most of it was created by the bailouts, which means it is owed to European public institutions rather than to fund managers who can sell at the first bad headline.

The loans run for decades at concessional rates. Greece's Public Debt Management Agency puts the average maturity above 18 years and the annual cost of servicing the stock at 1.94% as of the end of June.

Almost the whole Greek debt is fixed-rate.

Picture a household that fixed a very long mortgage when money was cheap. Rates can climb all they like; the monthly payment does not move.

France does not have anything like that duration of fixed-rate protection.

Bonds sold in the era of near-zero rates keep maturing and keep being replaced at today's cost. Interest payments are on course for €65 billion this year, some €4.5 billion above budget, which makes debt service the single biggest item of state spending.

The Cour des Comptes, the public audit body, has warned the bill could approach €100 billion by 2029.

Economists call the mechanism a snowball.

Once borrowing costs rise faster than the economy grows, debt climbs on its own unless the state runs a surplus before interest, and the OECD has warned that without policy changes French debt could reach about 200% of GDP by 2050.

One country sells €8 billion of bonds. The other sells €310 billion.

Then there is supply. France plans to issue €310 billion of medium and long-term bonds in 2026, net of buybacks.

Greece plans to issue only about €8 billion of bonds this year. It is also repaying roughly €13 billion early, helped by cash reserves of close to €40 billion.

A bigger economy naturally borrows bigger sums, but the market still has to absorb them auction after auction, and a market that has to absorb can name its price.

Political risk has changed address

The ratings capture the reversal.

Greece, which spent much of the previous decade below investment grade, is now investment grade at every major agency. S&P Global and Fitch rate it BBB, while Moody's rates it Baa3. All three have stable outlooks, while several smaller agencies have positive outlooks.

France remains more highly rated. But the direction has changed there as well. S&P and Fitch currently rate France A+. Moody's rating is Aa3, with a negative outlook.

Ratings agencies are not suggesting France is close to default. The concern is more mundane: repeated large deficits, slow growth and limited political agreement over how to reduce spending or raise revenue.

France's fragmented parliament has made that task harder. The presidential election next spring adds another layer of uncertainty.

None of this makes France the new Greece

Nobody is pricing a French default. Paris commands deep markets, a large domestic savings base and a tax capacity Athens could only envy in 2012, and its credit standing remains several notches higher.

What the crossover marks is a change in what investors reward. Falling debt, budget surpluses and a quiet refinancing calendar now buy a discount. Rising deficits, heavy issuance and a deadlocked parliament carry an additional charge on interest rates.

In 2012, investors were pricing in the possibility that Greece would still be using the euro by Christmas. In 2026, the more immediate question is how much further Athens can reduce its debt.

France faces almost the opposite one: how long can debt keep rising before investors demand an even higher price to finance it?

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: US think tank's military plan alarms allies in Asia
World.content:
Analysts warn that a US withdrawal from the western Pacific, as recently suggested by a think tank, would weaken deterrence and strengthen China's position.

A study by a US foreign policy think tank advocates a major military pullback from the western Pacific, prompting concern among long-standing allies of the United States across the Indo-Pacific, analysts say.

The report was authored by Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow and director of military analysis at the right-of-center Defense Priorities Foundation. Kavanagh calls for the US to "narrow its defense commitments in the region" by ending mutual defense alliances with South Korea, Japan, Australia and the Philippines.

The priority for Washington, she states, is to defend the US homeland and safeguard access to key economic markets and trade routes. That would be best served by pulling back from the "first island chain," which runs from Okinawa in southern Japan, through Taiwan and on to the Philippines.

Kavanagh writes that US forces should be pared back and moved to the "second island chain," which runs from eastern Japan to the Northern Marianas Islands in the central Pacific, Guam, Palau and on to Papua New Guinea.

The report states that moving the troops back would make their positions easier to defend and "reduce the risk of a catastrophic war with China."

Taiwan in the crosshairs

Such a withdrawal would arguably be most keenly felt in Taiwan, which Beijing views as a renegade province that must one day be assimilated into greater China.

In her report, Kavanagh notes that the US has no formal commitment to come to the assistance of Taiwan in the event of an attack by China. She warns that any armed clash "would come at an exorbitant cost for the United States, far in excess of any benefits."

"With a cost-benefit calculation this lopsided, a change in the US commitment to Taiwan seems wise," she said. "The United States should shift from strategic ambiguity to a clear non-intervention policy in the event of any military confrontation over Taiwan."

As China threat looms, US pausing arms sales to Taiwan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The countries named in the report have made no formal comments on the think tank's proposals, but its conclusions "will be viewed with shock," William Yang, a Taiwan-based security analyst for the International Crisis Group, told DW.

The concern will be even deeper given that the Defense Priorities Foundation is known for its isolationist foreign and defense policy positions and is reputed to have ties with a number of senior and like-minded decision-makers in the White House, Yang said.

Pullout 'seems to be very accommodating to China'

Yang noted that US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to withdraw troops from allied nations in Europe and Asia if his demands for larger payments or concessions in some other area of the bilateral relationship were not met, Yang said.

"This is a venture into a fully restrained agenda and seems to be very accommodating to China," Yang said.

While there are no indications that the White House is about to adopt the foundation's proposals, they do mesh with many of its isolationist and transactional principles, he said. And if the plans were to find favor with Trump, he said, the consequences would be "earthquake-level."

The Defense Priorities report was published amid broader regional concerns about the durability of US security commitments in Asia, specifically tensions over Taiwan and the South China Sea.

Despite Kavanagh's reassurances, many analysts suggest that a withdrawal of US support in the region would prompt China to quickly seize Taiwan and nuclear-armed North Korea to make greater demands on South Korea. It is also likely to trigger a region-wide spike in defense spending and, ultimately, a rupture in regional nuclear non-proliferation efforts.

Report plays down China fears

Kavanagh's report plays those fears down, concluding that "China's path to regional hegemony would be a difficult one, threats to the US homeland emanating from Asia are few, and challenges to US economic interests are unlikely and to some extent self-deterring."

Why are China and the US so fixated on Taiwan? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Garren Mulloy, a professor of international relations at Daito Bunka University and a specialist in military issues, described the study as "one of the more cogent and informed versions of what Trump and those around him have been arguing inconsistently for years. The idea is that the US has a priority to defend the homeland and all costs incurred in other missions are a waste."

"In my view, this is seeing the cost of everything and the value of nothing," Mulloy said, pointing out a number of "obvious problems": notably that the US leaves a void that China and, to a lesser extent, Russia step in to fill, and Washington has no influence on the region's geopolitics, including "the shaping of norms, standards and laws."

"Is this worth saving money for that Trump would give away in a tax cut or election bribe?" Mulloy asked, in reference to the US president promising thousands of dollars for every American adult if his party wins the midterms.

"This is the ultimate short-term vision that haunts diplomats around the world."

Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, echoes those concerns, describing the plan as "flawed and unrealistic."

"The whole premise of the report is completely different to how collective and cooperative international security has been practiced for decades," he said. "These people have a very different worldview and you wonder if they won't stop at the second island chain and go all the way back to the US mainland."

Fears of a stronger China

US isolationists see NATO and America's other allies "purely as a burden and a cost," Pinkston said, which is "too simplistic."

By withdrawing from security alliances in the Indo-Pacific, the US jeopardizes its trade relationships and largely gives up any influence it presently has over "complex issues" that range from combatting piracy, breaches of international sanctions, efforts to combat cybercrime and espionage, smuggling, climate change, fisheries, cross-border financial crime and a host of other critical matters, he said.

"It's naive to believe that China is going to be benevolent if the US withdraws and will act in anyone else's best interests when it comes to the rule of law, peaceful settlements of territorial disputes or human rights," he said.

World.title: Iran: 'Woman, Life, Freedom' lives on despite war
World.content:
The death of Jina Mahsa Amini triggered a resistance movement in Iran. Four years later, the Iranian regime endures — but so does the legacy of the "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests.

A 22-year-old Kurdish woman, Jina Mahsa Amini, passed away in a Tehran hospital on September 16, 2022. She had left her home in northwestern Iran to visit the capital and was then confronted by Tehran's morality police, who claimed Amini was violating the hijab mandate ordering women to cover their hair. The police arrested her. Three days later, she was declared dead.

For many Iranians, the law enforcement's brutality towards women who allegedly broke the hijab rules is nothing new. And yet, Amini's death triggered an unprecedented outpouring of anger. Protesters all across the country took to the streets under the slogan "Woman, Life, Freedom." They marched for months, but the regime eventually managed to suppress the movement in a violent crackdown.

"From my perspective, the movement 'Woman, Life, Freedom' is the biggest social and cultural change in Iran in decades," said writer, poet and activist Pouran Nazemi.

Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nazemi's work as a women's rights activist has gotten her arrested several times in recent years. Still, she refuses to be intimidated.

She told DW that the movement had clear goals right from the start: Ending the hijab mandate and ending state violence against Iran's population. While those goals were ultimately not met, the protests did trigger an important change — they prompted many people to recognize their own power within the society.

"The institutions still use physical violence and occasional arrests against us," said Nazemi. "But something fundamental has changed."

Hijab law still under debate

Even now, amid the ongoing war with the US, parts of the Iranian regime are still focusing on the hijab mandate. Many politicians are supporting a new bill which would introduce significantly stricter punishments for women violating the hijab order in public places.

One lawmaker described the missing head coverings as a "deep wound in the body of society."

Iranian women unveiled: A shift in hijab enforcement? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The proposed law has been in limbo for years and marked by wrangling between various state institutions.

However, in a virtual parliamentary session on September 6, several lawmakers urged Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf to pass the proposed legislation to the president for signing.

New normal for young Iranians

A 17-year-old female student told DW that she doesn't even think about wearing a hijab in public. Like many other young women, the pupil is posting pictures and videos of herself in colorful skirts and summer clothing on social media. To her, this is the new normal.

"My mother is not wearing a hijab either," the student told DW. "She is still a bit afraid and always carries a scarf so she can cover up in an emergency."

But even this degree of freedom would be hard to imagine just a few years ago. It was only after the 2022 protests that many woman started openly defying the government regulations and deciding for themselves if they wanted to cover up.

Decades of female resistance

The resistance of Iranian women did not start with the "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests. In its decades-long history, another important phase played out some 20 years ago, says women's rights activist and writer Mansoureh Shojaee.

In 2006, together with other Iranian activists and feminists, Shojaee started the "One Million Signatures" campaign. The goal was to gather 1 million signatures to change discriminatory laws targeting women. This campaign became an important role model for feminist activism and societal mobilization in Iran.

Activists went out into the streets, to universities, neighborhoods and private homes. They talked to people about divorce, custody, inheritance, court testimony, and polygamy. They also set up workshops, study groups and other cultural and media events.

Nobel Peace Prize winners among activists facing repression

From the very beginning, the initiative was met with massive state repression. Activists were summoned by the police, arrested and dragged through courts. Nobel Peace Prize winner Shirin Ebadi was among those affected, as was human rights activist Narges Mohammadi, who won the 2023 Nobel Peace Prize. Other activists, including Mansoureh Shojaee, were eventually forced to flee the country.

Fleeing Iran for freedom To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Shojaee left Iran in 2011 and is now living in the Netherlands.

The activists never met their original goal of reaching 1 million signatures. Still, they managed to change the conversation around the legal and social position of women. For this reason, Shojaee does not see the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement as a full-on break with the past, but only as one of the chapters in the much longer story of Iran's resistance.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Bangladesh court sentences 7 Hasina allies to death
World.content:
The latest verdict brings to 22 the number of death sentences handed down in cases stemming from the 2024 uprising that ended Sheikh Hasina's 15-year rule.

A court in Bangladesh on Tuesday sentenced seven senior figures from ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's former ruling party to death in absentia over their role in the deadly crackdown on anti-government protests in 2024.

The seven former officials and Awami League leaders were convicted of crimes against humanity, including inciting and ordering killings during the uprising that ultimately forced Hasina from power.

The United Nations estimates that as many as 1,400 people, most of them civilians, were killed during the unrest in July and August 2024.

Who was sentenced to death?

Those convicted include former Awami League Secretary-General Obaidul Quader and former Information Minister Mohammad Ali Arafat.

The other five all held positions within the Awami League.

All seven remain at large.

Prosecutor Mohammad Aminul Islam welcomed the verdict, saying most of the charges had been proven beyond reasonable doubt.

The court also ordered the seizure of half of the defendants' assets to provide compensation to the families of people killed or injured during the protests.

A court-appointed defense lawyer, M Hasan Imam, argued that the men had not been directly involved in the killings and should have received less severe sentences.

What happened during the 2024 uprising?

The protests began as a student-led movement and developed into a nationwide revolt against Hasina's government.

Hasina fled Bangladesh by helicopter for neighboring India on August 5, 2024, ending more than 15 years in power.

Bangladesh lacks women in politics To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

She was herself convicted of crimes against humanity in November 2025 and sentenced to death in absentia for her role in the crackdown.

Hasina and the Awami League have rejected the proceedings against them as politically biased.

How many people have now been convicted?

Tuesday's verdict brings the number of people convicted in trials connected with the 2024 uprising to 68, according to the AFP news agency. Twenty-two have received death sentences, while only four of those convicted are in custody.

Bangladesh's government, led by Tarique Rahman following elections in February, has requested Hasina's extradition from India.

The 78-year-old former prime minister remains in exile there and has said she intends to return to Bangladesh in December.
