World.title: Berlin election driven by radical ideas
World.content:
The results of the Berlin election are as hard to predict as ever. Three parties are vying for first place, including the socialist Left Party and the far-right AfD. But one issue is most important to Berliners.

Berlin, a city-state of 3.9 million people, is famously diverse, but it's also very atomized — a city of villages, where people often don't stray beyond their district, or Kiez, as Berliners like to call them.

That atomization extends to its political landscape: While the central districts of Berlin have recently voted Green or for the socialist Left Party, the outskirts — where in fact most Berliners live — is dominated by the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and, in certain districts, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). That makes it notoriously difficult to predict Berlin's elections, particularly in the past few years, when more parties have crowded onto the city's lampposts at election time.

Ahead of Berlin's state election on September 20 (when Berliners will elect the state parliament, which decides who is the next mayor) three parties are neck and neck: The Left Party, the CDU and the AfD. In the latest infratest dimap poll, the Left Party has a slim lead: They're at 21%, with the CDU at 20% and the AfD at 18%. Not far behind are the Greens, with 16%, while the center-left Social Democrats, for so long a party of government in Berlin, is currently mustering just 12%.

The AfD's relative weakness in Berlin means the situation is not as dramatic as it was in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, where the scale of the far-right victory likely means it will be impossible to keep them out of government.

Nevertheless, a victory for the Left Party — and yet another defeat for Friedrich Merz's CDU — would both transform the politics of Berlin, where the CDU are currently in government, and increase the pressure on the chancellor.

How to fight for election victory in a polarized city

The capital's disparate political scene makes running an election campaign in Berlin tricky, especially for a conservative party like the CDU.

"Berlin is indeed particularly challenging," Lukas Krieger, the CDU's general secretary in Berlin, told DW.

Krieger is in a perfect position to understand the national implications of regional elections, as he is also a member of the federal parliament, where the CDU is still digesting the result in Saxony-Anhalt.

But, he insists, "Berlin isn't comparable to the country as a whole or to Saxony-Anhalt."

Dressed in a neat suit and about to enter a post-mortem meeting of CDU parliamentarians, Krieger remained bullish about the fight in Berlin, and said it was clear who the main opponent was.

"It's crystallizing more and more as a duel between the CDU and the Left Party," he said. "The AfD in Berlin has no option to negotiate a government. There's no one who wants to work with them. We have a very radical Left Party in Berlin, and that's why we say: Berlin will stay stable, and the CDU is the only party that guarantees that Berlin will stay in the middle of the political spectrum."

Another challenge for the Berlin CDU is dealing with the loss of their incumbent mayor, Kai Wegner, who is still in office but is not running again thanks to his decision to play tennis in the middle of Berlin's biggest power outage since World War II.

Lukas Krieger says Berliners must vote for the CDU if they want to avoid the socialist Left, but his party also has to face the far-right AfD Image: Ben Knight/DW

Instead, the party was forced to hastily present a new candidate, Wegner's Finance Minister Stefan Evers, who now has to navigate a course between two very different political threats: The super-confident AfD and the surging Left Party, both of whom look set to make significant gains on their 2023 election results in the city.

Evers' main opponent is another new face: Elif Eralp, a lawyer born in Munich in 1980 just weeks after her parents fled a military putsch in Turkey. But Berliners are used to mayoral candidates not being natives of the city: Evers was born in North Rhine-Westphalia. In fact, polls show that none of the leading mayoral candidates are particularly well-known: In one recent poll, around half of Berliners said they didn't have any strong opinion on any of them.

Tiny rooms at sky-high prices — Berlin's rental rip-off To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Be credible and make offers

The CDU's problem is that German politics is increasingly radical — as the Saxony-Anhalt election showed — and observers say this is partly because of the perceived failure of the centrist parties of government to present new solutions to the electorate.

"The question is: Do you have your own political offers? Are you trying to unlock new groups?" said Julia Reuschenbach, political scientist at Hamburg University.

She thinks that the Left Party has established itself in Berlin as the most "credible" opposition to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). That's partly, she says, because it's the only one of the left-of-center parties not willing to support the CDU (nor is the CDU willing to collaborate with the Left).

But the Left Party has its own disadvantage: The party has been pursued by accusations of antisemitism after a rapper performing at a campaign event in Neukölln, where many of Berlin's large Palestinian community live, chanted "Death to the IDF," referring to the Israeli military. Eralp condemned the performance and promised an internal investigation, but Gaza has become vital to the Left Party's supporters: In June, the party officially resolved to consider Israel's military action in Gaza a genocide.

Nevertheless, Reuschenbach thinks the Left Party's strength is that it is able to make tangible political offers.

"Of course, they're populist," she said. "They formulate maximalist positions: 'We want to socialize. we want to expropriate.' But it's straight. I'd say that for many people, the Left have more clarity, more of their own proposals."

The pundit was referring specifically to what many consider the Left's most radical demand, an idea that has been at the heart of Berlin's politics for at least half a decade: The Left Party is the only one of the major parties that promises to implement the result of a referendum carried out in 2021, when 59% of Berliners voted to expropriate real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units in the city and transfer their property to public ownership.

Since then, successive Berlin governments, led by center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and then the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), have dragged their feet on the implementation, by setting up commissions on the question.

Kerstin Wolter says one issue dominates Berlin: rents Image: Ben Knight/DW

It's the rents, stupid

Kerstin Wolter, co-leader of the socialist Left Party in Berlin and candidate in the upcoming state election, rejects the idea that expropriating landlords should be considered "populist." After all, she said, the idea was written into the German constitution, or Basic Law, at the founding of West Germany in 1949 — though the expropriation article has never actually been invoked.

As far as Wolter is concerned, there's one reason why the Berlin population became so "radicalized," and made her party so strong.

"All the polls, all the surveys, all the conversations we have with voters ourselves, it's always the same: The rent situation is catastrophic," she told DW. "People can't find an apartment, people are scared of rent increases, people are losing their apartments because the landlords are claiming them for their own use."

Housing, according to a recent Berlin Trend poll , is indeed by far the most important issue in this election: Some 32% of Berliners said it was the city's most important problem — way more than the 10% who said immigration and asylum, or the 9% who said security/crime/terrorism.

Perhaps adding to this taste for revolutionary ideas is that this is the first election in Berlin's history where the voting age has been lowered to 16, and young Germans have become increasingly politicized in the last few years.

"I think a lot of young people — much more than when I was young — are concerned with questions like climate change, will I still get a job," said Wolter. "Even pensions: At an info-stand I had a girl, she seemed about 14, asking me about our pensions policy."

Berlin, which has always been its own mix of conservatism and radicalism, is now also becoming more and more economically diverse, according to Wolter: "We have an increasing number of millionaires in Berlin, as well as an increasing number of people living in poverty."

That contributes to making the city a unique political challenge.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

World.title: Germany news: Police find arms depot near highway
World.content:
Skip next section German coalition split on how to tackle soaring fuel prices

Fuel prices in some places have reached over €3 per liter Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

Divisions are opening up in Germany's government over current surging fuel prices, with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) accusing conservative Economy Minister Katherina Reiche of inaction.

"We've had enough," the SPD's general secretary, Tim Klüssendorf, told the news portal t-online.

"Millions of people in our country are still dealing with completely excessive fuel prices, and the responsible minister, Katherina Reiche, is watching by while oil giants make record profits at the expense of the public," Klüssendorf said. "We urgently need measures against extortionate fuel prices."

What are the SPD's proposals?

The SPD is calling for three measures to bring down the high fuel prices.

They include:

a price cap based on those in place in Belgium and Luxembourg

a tax on excessive profits made by oil companies

transparency on how prices emerge

What have the conservatives suggested?

However, Reiche has rejected the idea of a price cap, instead proposing direct payments to those affected by the fuel prices.

"This would be one way of providing rapid relief, but it would need to be targeted specifically at those income groups that pay little or no tax," she said on Monday.

Economic expert warns on fuel tax cuts

Earlier this year, the conservative-led government put in place a two-month fuel tax cut to relieve motorists.

But the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW) on Tuesday cautioned against repeating such a measure.

IFW economist Klaus-Jürgen Gern told Deutschlandfunk radio that a general fuel tax cut was counterproductive.

"It supports people who don't need it. And in the end, there is a shortfall in public funds, where there are actually more important things to finance. There is then a shortfall for investment, and a shortfall for other important social spending," he said.

Fuel prices soaring

The row comes as gasoline reached a new high of €2.273 ($2.62) per liter ($9.92 per US gallon) on Sunday according to average national figures from the ADAC automobile club.

The ADAC said diesel reached €2.40 per liter on Sunday, just some 4 cents under the record price hit in April as a consequence of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which is the main factor driving the rise in fuel prices throughout the world.

World.title: East German leader styles self as one-woman bulwark to AfD
World.content:
Manuela Schwesig of the center-left SPD has governed the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic Sea coast, since 2017. Ahead of this weekend's election, she is campaigning against the far right.

The late-summer warmth is lingering in the countryside of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Lavender-infused cocktails and savory onion cakes are being served on the spacious terrace of Hasenwinkel Castle, an old country house turned conference hotel not far from the Baltic coast. The largest business association in this northeastern German state has invited members and guests from the political world to a convivial gathering. State Premier Manuela Schwesig, of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), is also in attendance.

It could be a relaxed evening, were it not for the upcoming state election on September 20. "We live in politically turbulent times," says association president Lars Schwarz in his welcoming remarks. But the evening is also meant to serve as an opportunity to "recharge," he says. Days before the election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading in the polls with around 37%. But the SPD is not far behind, with 33%, and has narrowed the gap in recent weeks. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which leads the federal government with the SPD under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is far behind and hoping to remain above the 5% threshold to enter parliament.

The economy needs immigration, the AfD opposes it

The term "remigration" is playing a major role in the AfD's campaign. But as far as the state's business leaders are concerned, sending people of immigrant background out of Germany would be a disaster for the economy.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a significantly older population than most other German states. It's also less densely populated and more severely affected by demographic change. "International skilled workers and laborers have long been an important part of our economic future," said Schwarz. "Openness to the world is not an abstract political formula, but a concrete prerequisite for ensuring that businesses in our state can continue to produce, offer services, train employees, and grow."

In a brief speech at the event, Schwesig recounted encounters she had during the election campaign. She speaks of a conversation with a baker who is concerned not only about high energy prices but also about her employees. "She said, 'Ms. Schwesig, I have employees with immigrant backgrounds working here, and I'm very worried that I'll lose them — because I value them, and because I care about them as people.'"

The head of a planning firm approached the state premier and explained that his Moroccan employee wanted to leave the country. "Because when he goes to the café at the market in Stralsund and waits for his German friends, the people sitting near him either make snide remarks or move to another table." Who, Schwesig asks, would want to live in such a climate?

Fear of social division

Preventing the AfD's victory — that is what the 52-year-old Schwesig has made her stated goal. In the final stretch of the campaign, her posters feature just her face on a red background — no name — above the slogan "The Woman Against Blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.

"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."

Anyone who doesn't want those things must support her, she says. "To do that, you have to go to the polls and vote for the SPD — and that's why I'm the woman against blue."

Perhaps tellingly, the SPD isn't mentioned on most of her campaign posters, however. Only Schwesig herself is visible, dressed in red. The SPD's party color must suffice as a reference. Schwesig is the driving force: She represents the political comeback of the past twelve months. In September 2025, the SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was languishing at just 19% in opinion polls, while the AfD stood at 38%.

Recipe for success: Close to the people and distance from Berlin

Manuela Schwesig managed to close the gap, in part, by trying to stay closely connected to the people of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, seeking direct dialogue with voters as often as possible. She is friendly and approachable, yet also firm. Schwesig listens, answers questions with confidence, marshals the facts, and engages in discussions where she attempts to demonstrate that she is well-informed about everything happening in the state.

Above all, however, she scored points by maintaining maximum distance from the federal government — and thus from her own party too. In Berlin, the SPD governs as the junior partner in a coalition with the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) parties, and the government is more unpopular than any before it. As Schwesig has gained ground, the SPD's support at the federal level has plummeted to 12%.

Imported care giver: Skilled, needed, stalled by bureaucracy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Strong criticism of Friedrich Merz

Schwesig believes much of what is decided in Berlin is wrong — and she says so. "I expect the chancellor and the entire federal government to chart a new political course,” she demanded following the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt in early September.

She has long believed that the reform of the social welfare systems planned by the CDU/CSU and the SPD is heading in the wrong direction. "I expect that the reforms will ensure that those who have worked their entire lives and made contributions are not the ones who bear the heaviest burdens," she says regarding the plans to eliminate the retirement age of 63 for people who have contributed to the pension fund for a particularly long time. "And I'm glad that my criticism is now receiving a lot of support."

Will Manuela Schwesig become SPD leader?

She also receives support from within her own party. Discontent is growing within the federal SPD over the two co-chairs, Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas. There is open speculation about whether Manuela Schwesig should replace them at the party's helm. Amid the SPD's crisis, there are strong arguments for making one of the last Social Democrats who is popular with voters the party leader.

A woman who entered politics relatively late in life. Born in Brandenburg, she was already nearly 30 years old when she joined the SPD in 2003. Prior to that, she had studied public finance and worked as a tax official.

Schwesig served in Merkel's cabinet before returning to Mecklenburg Western-Pomerania Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Schwesig: Underestimated by opponents?

Her political rise was rapid: Local politics in the state capital of Schwerin, Social Affairs Minister in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and finally, in 2013, Federal Family Affairs Minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. By then, she had become well-known nationwide.

Her opponents often underestimated her, especially men. A CDU politician once derisively called her the "coastal Barbie." "Young, blonde, East German" was the headline when she became a federal minister.

Perhaps this was also because Schwesig never came across as a classic power-seeking politician. Her strengths, say her supporters, lie in her calm perseverance, fighting spirit, and pragmatism.

Nord Stream 2

This tenacity nearly proved to be her undoing in the dispute over the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline. In 2017, Schwesig returned to Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania to succeed State Premier Erwin Sellering, who was seriously ill at the time. Sellering had maintained very good relations with Russia, and Schwesig continued his policies.

This included defending the construction of the Baltic Sea pipeline — which was intended to transport even more Russian gas to Germany — in the face of criticism from Eastern Europe, the US, and some in Germany. When the US threatened sanctions in 2021, Schwesig even attempted to secure the completion of Nord Stream 2 by establishing a "climate foundation" funded by Moscow.

Schwesig's support for the Nord Stream pipeline became a political liability Image: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

State premier with a 60% approval rating

After the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, her stance became a political liability. Schwesig made a political about-face and admitted to mistakes. To this day, however, she defends the logic behind her decisions at the time.

This has not caused her any lasting damage. Currently, in a direct election, 60% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania would vote for Schwesig as head of government.

The current state government, made up of the SPD and the socialist Left Party, is also performing well in polls. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to secure another term.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: US confirms it has weapons in space
World.content:
The US Space Force justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. Beijing responded by urging Washington to "stop preparing for war" in outer space.

The United States has weapons deployed in spatial orbit, the US Space Force said, confirming the existence of such capabilities for the first time.

"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a press release. The statement did not provide specifics on the weapons in question.

"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," it said, adding that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes."

US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also confirmed the existence of US weapons in space, while speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday.

The Space Force, the US military's arm dedicated to space, justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. It said both countries pose a threat to American interests in space.

China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," the statement read.

AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What have China and Russia said?

In response, China urged Washington to "stop preparing for war" in outer space.

"We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, warning against an "arms race" in space.

Russia on Tuesday also called for space to be kept free of weapons.

"We believe that space must be free of any weapon," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow, adding: "We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space."

The final frontier

The militarization of space is an issue as old as the race to space itself.

In 1967, the world's biggest superpowers and other nations signed the Outer Space Treaty addressing the single biggest concern — the deployment of nuclear weapons in space.

Since then, Russia, the US, India and China have been exploring ways to fight in space outside of that treaty. That includes targeting each other's satellites critical for military communication, navigation and surveillance.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania
World.content:
The drone, which is believed to have entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, was shot down by an Italian fighter jet in between the cities of Vilnius and Kaunas. There have been no reports of casualties or damage.

A drone which entered Lithuanian airspace in the early hours of Tuesday morning was shot down by NATO fighter jets in between the cities of Vilnius and Kaunas, Lithuanian authorities have confirmed.

Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center (NKVC) said the drone most likely came from neighboring Belarus, an ally of Russia in its ongoing war against Ukraine, and was flying west when it was shot down by an Italian jet.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda thanked the military alliance for its "swift response."

"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region," he wrote on social media. "Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said the NATO response sent "a clear message that NATO stands vigilant, committed, and ready."

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda thanked the NATO military alliance for its 'swift response' Image: Jouni Porsanger/Lehtikuva/REUTERS

What do we know about the latest drone incident?

Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the NKVC, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus and flew along the outskirts of populated areas for about 30 minutes before being intercepted.

The Lithuanian armed forces published video from the ​site of the crash near the village of Pratkunai, close to Lithuania's second-largest city, Kaunas, and about 80 kilometers (50 miles) west of the capital, Vilnius.

The footage showed debris scattered in grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made from wood ⁠and ​some appeared charred.

The commander of the Lithuanian air force, Antanas Matutis, said that the drone had "likely" been carrying explosives.

Lithuania: Was the drone from Russia or Ukraine?

Officials have not indicated whether the drone was Russian or Ukrainian.

While Russia has been launching almost daily drone and missile strikes against Ukraine since the start of its full-scale invasion over four years ago, Ukraine has also been responding with drone strikes of its own.

Ukrainian drones, which often pass close to Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian airspace en route to targets in northwestern Russia, have occasionally been jammed by Russian defenses and steered off course into NATO airspace.

Fighter jets with the NATO ​Baltic Air Defense mission have patrolled the skies over Latvia, Lithuania and ​Estonia since the Baltic ‌countries joined the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray Ukrainian drones over Estonia ​in May, ⁠and over Latvia in June and August.

The Lithuanian military said Tuesday's incident marked the first time that a drone had been shot down in its airspace.

The drone fell around around 80 kilometers (50 miles) west of the Lithuanian capital, Vilnius Image: Lithuanian Army/Handout/REUTERS

How has NATO responded?

Tuesday's incident came less than 24 hours after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said that strikes "close to the alliance's territory" would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Ukraine.

"Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," he said, adding that drone strikes and incursions near NATO territory showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation" and "desire to sow fear and terror."

On Tuesday, Poland, a NATO ally and neighbor of Lithuania, also announced "aviation operations" had commenced in its airspace "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory."

These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions," said authorities in Warsaw.

Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr, are also currently building up a German armored brigade in Lithuania. The combat-ready and independently deployable force, comprising 4,800 troops, is expected to be operational by 2027.

World.title: Uno de los mayores hospitales de Madrid altera la gravedad de los pacientes para maquillar su lista de espera quirúrgica
World.content:
Dos responsables en uno de los grandes hospitales públicos madrileños, el Ramón y Cajal, ordenaron rebajar la gravedad de los pacientes en espera de una cirugía para mejorar artificialmente la situación de sus listas de espera, según documentos internos a los que ha accedido EL PAÍS. Los cambios se hicieron en el sistema informático, sin valorar en persona a esos pacientes y a espaldas de los cirujanos de traumatología que habían determinado la gravedad de esos casos, de acuerdo con cuatro médicos afectados. El motivo era cumplir con los objetivos de productividad que exige la Consejería de Sanidad autonómica, según se deduce de la explicación que dio por correo uno de esos responsables a una doctora indignada. El hospital niega haber cometido alguna irregularidad.

Los hechos ocurrieron entre el 28 de febrero y el 14 de marzo del año pasado, cuando 57 pacientes en lista de espera quirúrgica del servicio de Cirugía Ortopédica y Traumatología del Ramón y Cajal pasaron de la prioridad preferente (quienes deben ser intervenidos antes de 90 días) a la normal (operación antes de 180 días). De ese modo, los responsables ganaban tiempo para lograr el resultado esperado: que los pacientes fueran operados en plazo.

EL PAÍS ha accedido a documentos y correos que muestran que la alteración fue orden de estos dos responsables y ha hablado con cuatro médicos del servicio que aseguran que no se les consultó. El cirujano que ha facilitado estas pruebas, Luis Alberto Martos, denunció lo ocurrido a la gerencia sin lograr una respuesta. Semanas después, el hospital abrió un expediente disciplinario contra él.

La manipulación de las listas de espera es una sospecha generalizada en la sanidad española porque existen incentivos electorales (las administraciones publican esta métrica mensualmente en internet) y también económicos (los médicos con responsabilidades cobran bonos de productividad si cumplen objetivos). En Madrid es conocido el caso que en 2005 llevó a la región a ser expulsada durante 10 años del sistema nacional de cómputo de listas de espera quirúrgicas, cuando se supo que la demora para una operación era contabilizada desde la visita al anestesista, en lugar del momento anterior en que el médico prescribe la operación. Es decir, el cronómetro se activaba después de lo debido para mejorar las cifras.

En aquella ocasión la alteración era puramente cosmética, pero estos cambios del Ramón y Cajal repercutieron negativamente en los pacientes, según los cirujanos, porque se rebajó falsamente su gravedad, aumentando la espera que debían soportar. Esto es así porque la decisión de quién va a quirófano no se toma por orden de llegada, sino por la prioridad (urgencia) del caso.

Martos es un cirujano veterano de 62 años en este hospital del norte de la capital del que dependen 600.128 madrileños. Se indignó cuando descubrió que habían cambiado la prioridad de sus pacientes, tras enterarse por medio de una compañera. Sospecha que estos cambios los habían hecho antes sin que nadie lo notara, pero en este caso la alteración afectó a decenas de pacientes y había huellas. En los documentos internos que ha visto EL PAÍS se pueden leer bajo el apartado “Observaciones” las anotaciones de los cambios con mensajes como “cambio prioridad p.i. (por indicación) Dr. De la Torre” o “cambio prioridad p.o. (por orden) de trah (traumatología) y direcc. médica”. Se trataba del jefe de ese servicio, Basilio José de la Torre Escuredo, y del director médico del hospital, Rafael Martínez Fernández.

La doctora que dio la alarma detectó el 14 de marzo de 2025 el cambio en el caso de una niña de tres años porque era una paciente que le preocupaba. El círculo rojo (prioridad urgente) de su ficha había pasado a verde (normal). Comprobó que nadie había avisado a los padres de la menor.

“Había criterios médicos para intervenirla con prioridad, con mucha prioridad”, comenta la doctora. “No daba crédito. ¿Cómo lo habían hecho sin tener en cuenta mi opinión? Me parece indecente”, añade esta mujer, que, como otros compañeros, ha pedido que se omita su nombre.

Dice que comprobó en los documentos internos que los cambios afectaban a los pacientes de 17 médicos. Habló con la mayoría de ellos y todos le contestaron que no habían sido avisados. También averiguó que las modificaciones habían comenzado 15 días antes, el 28 de febrero. Casi todos los pacientes tenían algo en común. Su demora oscilaba entre los 80 y los 140 días. Esos casos antes “prioritarios” y ahora “normales” dejaban de incumplir el objetivo de ser sometidos a operación antes de 90 días.

Hospital Universitario Ramón y Cajal en Madrid, este lunes. Pablo Monge

Los médicos explican que estas modificaciones pueden pasar desapercibidas debido a la alta carga de trabajo que les hace vivir pendientes del siguiente paciente en espera. A veces, no son ellos quienes programan las operaciones, sino los jefes de unidad, que están en un escalón intermedio, por debajo del jefe de servicio.

La doctora envió un correo al jefe del servicio, Escuredo. “¿Podría explicarme las razones que lo justifican, sin contar con el criterio del cirujano?”, le escribió el 14 de marzo. El jefe admitió esas alteraciones y dio a entender que el motivo era la meta de eficiencia pactada con la Consejería de Sanidad: “Si no son operados en ese plazo, la dirección recibe notificación por parte de la Consejería para que sean operados lo antes posible”, le respondió por escrito. “Tened en cuenta que el compromiso que adquiere el hospital con ellos es ser operados en el plazo de 90 días”.

El jefe añadió que se había reunido con “la dirección y el servicio de admisión” para resolver cómo deben ser tratados los pacientes preferentes y le indicó a la doctora: “Evitad en la medida de lo posible anotarlos como preferentes, y sí quedáis con el paciente en una fecha aproximada para ser operado y el estudio preoperatorio se pide como preferente”. Es decir, podían operarlos cuando quisieran, pero engañando al sistema sobre el tipo de prioridad.

Esta doctora dice que ignoró al jefe e indicó correctamente que la operación de la niña urgía. La operó en cuanto le dieron hueco en quirófano. Era una paciente con un caso tan sensible que había consultado a médicos de Estados Unidos: “Esta niña no podía esperar porque podía perder una pierna”, responde. “Se trató a todos los pacientes como números”.

Otros eran pacientes que “se retorcían de dolor”, dice Martos. Los documentos muestran diagnósticos como anomalías en la columna vertebral, síndrome de túnel carpiano o luxación (dislocación de los dos huesos de una articulación).

Otra doctora cuenta que una paciente suya se enteró del cambio porque los administrativos la llamaron por teléfono para comentarle que su caso no era preferente. “La invité a poner una reclamación, si yo pongo ‘prioritario’ es por algo. Tenía mucho dolor, era cuestión de tiempo que sufriese lesiones irreversibles en la articulación, no podía esperar más”, indica. Consiguió buscarle un hueco en el quirófano gracias a que otro paciente rechazó una cirugía, pero reconoce que no todos los afectados corrieron la misma suerte. Sospecha, como otros compañeros consultados, que muchos no se enteraron del cambio de prioridad. “Lo grave de esto es que no se mantuvo el criterio médico”, expresa.

Otro cirujano también afirma que algunos de sus pacientes sufrieron este cambio sin su autorización. “Me pareció fatal, nadie me preguntó, no sé si quien lo hizo siguió criterios clínicos. Fue la única vez que me pasó algo así”, comenta.

Figurar en la lista como paciente normal puede suponer esperas de hasta nueve meses (270 días). Los afectados podían observar el cambio en su carpeta ciudadana o en la aplicación de móvil, pero según estos doctores, muchos pacientes son mayores con patología degenerativa a causa de la edad y son personas que se manejan mal con la tecnología. Apenas uno o dos llamaron para protestar.

Expedientado

Martos arrastraba conflictos con su jefe, quien años antes le había denunciado, según dice, “con fines difamatorios” con dos acciones penales y sendos expedientes disciplinarios que, asegura, acabaron en nada. Cuando conoció lo sucedido con la lista de espera, montó en cólera. En un correo el 21 de marzo, se dirigió al director médico con tono acusatorio: “Esto se ejecuta por orden de la Dirección Médica (usted) y del jefe de servicio”, le dijo. “Como no hay ningún criterio médico que lo justifique, solo puede responder a criterios políticos y económicos para beneficio de los miembros de esta Dirección Médica (usted) y sus necesarios colaboradores”. Dice que no obtuvo respuesta.

El doctor Luis Alberto Martos, el miércoles en la sede del diario EL PAÍS, en Madrid. Victoria García

El 7 de abril envió una carta al gerente del hospital, Carlos Mingo, denunciando lo que, según le dijo, consideraba una ilegalidad y le advertía de que esperaba que sancionara a esos jefes. “En caso contrario, pensaré que usted también participa de este fraude, por acción o por omisión, y habrá que explorar otras líneas de denuncia”. También la doctora responsable de la paciente de tres años solicitó por correo al gerente una investigación urgente ante una posible ilegalidad.

La norma que regula la gestión de la lista de espera es una orden de la Consejería de Sanidad de 2016 según la cual los cirujanos “son los responsables de la indicación y el establecimiento de la prioridad clínica” de los pacientes. No obstante, el gerente del hospital aseguró en su respuesta a la doctora que la gestión de la lista recae en una diversidad de profesionales y órganos. Además, intentó cerrar el asunto al decir que la incidencia había sido resuelta (porque se le había permitido operar a la niña en la fecha que ella consideró oportuna). Tras destacar esto, el gerente celebró que “el servicio es capaz de ordenarse y reorganizarse para mejor atención a los pacientes incluso en situaciones dificultosas”.

Al cirujano Martos le contestó de forma más escueta, remitiéndole a su jefe de sección y a su jefe de servicio para que aclararan los criterios sobre la lista de espera. Pero en paralelo se había iniciado otro episodio que el médico describe como una ”acusación antinatural” contra él. Los dos jefes señalados solicitaron al gerente la apertura de un expediente por “conflictos internos y acoso” que sigue en curso. El instructor le ha citado para acudir este miércoles a la declaración de su jefe, De la Torre: “Dicen que yo, un subordinado, acoso a mis superiores”, cuenta incrédulo el cirujano, que ha buscado la defensa jurídica del sindicato médico mayoritario en Madrid, Amyts.

La cirujana que operó a la niña denunció en febrero de este año los hechos a la comisión deontológica del Colegio de Médicos, órgano que responde a este periódico que no puede pronunciarse mientras se investiga lo sucedido por un deber de confidencialidad.

Plus salarial

EL PAÍS ha hecho varios intentos de entrevista a los dos responsables señalados. En su lugar, una portavoz del hospital ha contestado por escrito subrayando el compromiso del centro con la correcta gestión de la lista de espera, la atención a los pacientes y el cumplimiento de las normas. Ha añadido que la gestión de la lista corresponde a cada servicio asistencial de acuerdo con criterios clínicos y con la responsabilidad de los médicos que ven a esos pacientes. “Ni la Dirección Médica ni la Gerencia realizan directamente la gestión o modificación de las listas de espera quirúrgicas de los servicios”, asegura. “Por tanto, no cabe atribuir a estos órganos la realización de alteraciones individuales en las historias clínicas de los pacientes”.

La buena gestión de la lista influye en el complemento de productividad de los jefes de servicio y miembros de sus equipos, según el contrato programa del Ramón y Cajal de 2025, el documento por el que el gerente del hospital y sus superiores en el Servicio Madrileño de Salud establecen los objetivos para una gestión eficiente. El indicador 28 (de un total de 63) premia o penaliza en función de si hay pacientes que han superado la fecha límite de intervención (90 o 180 días). El plus de productividad de un jefe de servicio ronda los 3.579 euros.

Aparentemente, estos cambios no alteraron los datos que pueden consultar los ciudadanos en la web de la Comunidad donde se informa del total de pacientes en la lista y de su distribución en cinco tramos de demora (0-30 días, 30-60, 60-90, 90-180 y más de 180), pero no se detalla cuántos han superado la fecha límite de intervención, es decir, si cumplen o incumplen la meta de productividad.

Esa lista muestra que traumatología del Ramón y Cajal era en febrero de 2025 uno de los peores servicios de su tipo en Madrid. Ocupaba el puesto 23 de un total de 28 con una espera media de 77,5 días. Hoy es aún peor: ha crecido hasta los 98,6 días.

La manipulación de las listas por métodos diversos es vista como un mal común de la sanidad pública española. El presidente de atención hospitalaria de Amyts, Javier Ortega, considera que lo que sale a la luz es solo “la punta del iceberg”. “Muchos médicos suelen mirar para otro lado cuando conocen la manipulación”, critica. “Pero con los enfermos no se juega”.

El profesor de la Escuela Nacional de Sanidad-Instituto de Salud Carlos III José Manuel Freire dice que los gerentes de los hospitales no tienen un incentivo para perseguir estos casos y lamenta que para conocerlos haga falta un médico excepcional, “un héroe o un mártir”.

Martos se ha convertido en un paria. Muchos compañeros han dejado de hablarle. Cuando opera, reina el silencio, a pesar de que los quirófanos son ambientes distendidos. Esto llama la atención de los visitantes. “Creen que somos muy diligentes”, dice con una sonrisa. En su WhatsApp ha puesto el siguiente mensaje: “La soledad es el precio de la verdad”.
