World.title: Magyar government plans to hike tobacco taxes, sending cigarette prices sharply higher
World.content:
The Hungarian government is planning a significant increase in excise duties on tobacco products, potentially pushing up cigarette prices by almost HUF 300 per pack from November.

The proposed tax hike was tucked into a bill submitted to Parliament on Monday, which primarily concerns measures linked to financial support for diesel drivers facing higher fuel prices, Telex reports.

The government has requested an expedited procedure for the bill, meaning Parliament could vote on it as early as Tuesday. If approved, the new tobacco tax rates would take effect on 1 November.

Cigarette tax could rise by more than HUF 250 per pack

Under the proposal, the minimum excise duty on cigarettes would increase from HUF 47,140 to HUF 59,800 per 1,000 cigarettes. For a standard pack of 20 cigarettes, this would mean the minimum excise tax would rise from HUF 943 to HUF 1,196 — an increase of HUF 253 per pack. (1 euro = 365 forints)

The actual retail price increase could be even higher. According to calculations cited by Index, a typical pack could become almost HUF 300, or around 10%, more expensive. The proposed changes would affect almost all tobacco and nicotine products.

Product Current excise duty Proposed excise duty Cigarettes HUF 33,690/1,000 + 24% of retail price, but at least HUF 47,140/1,000 HUF 36,720/1,000 + 24% of retail price, but at least HUF 59,800/1,000 Cigars, cigarillos 14% of retail price, but at least HUF 5,450/1,000 14% of retail price, but at least HUF 6,100/1,000 Fine-cut tobacco HUF 29,270/kg + 5% of retail price HUF 32,200/kg + 5% of retail price E-cigarette liquid HUF 38/ml HUF 41/ml Disposable products containing tobacco or used with tobacco HUF 40/item HUF 50/item Liquids in the new tobacco-product categories HUF 79/ml HUF 100/ml Smokeless tobacco products HUF 29,270/kg HUF 32,200/kg Nicotine products replacing smoking HUF 29,270/kg HUF 31,610/kg Heated tobacco products HUF 40/item HUF 50/item

The government says the differentiated increases are intended to address differences in the current tax burden between various tobacco and nicotine products, as well as to secure budget revenues and offset the social and economic costs of smoking.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Why is the tax increase part of a fuel-support bill?

The tax changes appear in a bill whose main purpose is to introduce measures related to rising fuel prices, including a monthly HUF 5,000 subsidy for diesel drivers. The government has not explained why the tobacco tax increase was included in the same legislation.

The bill was submitted to Parliament on Monday morning, and the government has requested an expedited procedure, arguing that the measures are of overriding national interest. The fuel-support provisions would enter into force shortly after the law is promulgated. The tobacco provisions, however, would not take effect until 1 November.

Parliament could decide within days

The proposed changes have already attracted criticism from the Villanypára Association, which represents interests related to vaping products. The organisation said the proposal would fundamentally alter the taxation of tobacco and nicotine products without meaningful professional consultation or sufficient preparation time.

It also highlighted the differing increases between product categories. According to its calculations, for example, the excise duty on heated tobacco products would rise by 25%, while the tax burden on cigarillos would remain essentially unchanged.

The pace of the legislation is also notable. The bill was submitted on Friday evening and was already being considered by Parliament under an expedited procedure on Monday. MPs had only three hours to submit amendments, while the combined debate and final vote were scheduled for Tuesday, 15 September.

If Parliament approves the proposal, the new excise duty rates will come into force on 1 November 2026, leaving smokers less than seven weeks between the parliamentary decision and the planned tax increase.

World.title: Fidesz disputes government’s M6 motorway claims, accuses Tisza of handing strategic assets to foreigners
World.content:
The Fidesz parliamentary group has rejected the government’s statements about the earlier commissioning of the operation of the M6 motorway, accusing the Tisza Party of handing Hungary’s strategic sectors over to foreign economic interests.

The opposition party’s parliamentary group issued a statement to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) in response to comments made by Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy in Parliament on Monday concerning the operation of the section of the M6 motorway between Dunaújváros and Érd-tető.

Fidesz: “Not a single word of this is true”

According to Fidesz, Vitézy claimed that the previous government had unlawfully commissioned the Hungarian Concession Infrastructure Development Company (MKIF Zrt.) to operate the Érd-Dunaújváros section of the M6 motorway between 2026 and 2037.

The opposition party said Vitézy had also claimed that MKIF had agreed to carry out the same task for HUF 149 billion, which Fidesz described as “extremely overpriced”, while the M6 Duna Concession Zrt., which has operated the motorway so far and is supported by Vitézy, offered to do so for HUF 44 billion.

“Not a single word of this is true,” Fidesz wrote.

The parliamentary group added that the previous government had made no decision on the concession-based operation of the affected section of the M6 and had therefore not commissioned MKIF to carry out the work.

Fidesz also disputed the HUF 149 billion figure, saying that MKIF had never offered to perform the work for that amount.

Fidesz questions what the HUF 44 billion offer includes

“It is also not true that MKIF Zrt. agreed to do this for HUF 149 billion; Dávid Vitézy and his colleagues made up this figure,” the statement said. Fidesz also questioned what is included in the HUF 44 billion offer from the foreign consortium behind M6 Duna, which is supported by Vitézy.

The party argued that the company’s current contract, which is now expiring, did not include major renovations of the road surface and pavement structure or the renovation of bridges. By contrast, Fidesz said, MKIF’s concession agreement covering other motorways includes these obligations as well.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Fidesz accuses Tisza government of “handing over” motorways

The Fidesz parliamentary group accused Vitézy of lying and claimed that the Tisza government was preparing to place the operation of Hungarian motorways into foreign hands. It argued that foreign companies are also behind M6 Duna Concession Zrt. and claimed that “Péter Magyar and the Tisza Party will soon seek to hand all concessions over to foreigners”.

In its conclusion, Fidesz accused the Tisza Party of beginning to hand Hungary’s strategic sectors over to foreign economic interests. “Instead of a sovereign, independent country, Péter Magyar and his government are once again putting Hungary on a colonial footing,” the opposition party said.

World.title: Viktor Orbán’s great comeback or a sorry endgame at the Kötcse picnic?
World.content:
After an extended summer break, Viktor Orbán plunged back into the political deep end. But can he still swim?

There was a bit of everything at Kötcse: a great comeback, tough messages, “national resistance”, a fight against the Tisza government and, of course, the unavoidable question: what happens to Fidesz with Viktor Orbán at the helm now that it is in opposition?

The 12 September Kötcse picnic was therefore not simply the traditional opening of the political season. For the first time after sixteen consecutive years in government, the Hungarian right had to gather knowing that it was no longer the one holding the steering wheel.

Viktor Orbán, however, certainly did not arrive looking like a politician preparing to say goodbye.

“I’m back,” he announced before the event, in a video that left little doubt about his intentions. Then, upon arriving in Kötcse, he admitted that sixteen years of continuous government had left him tired and that he had needed a rest. Whether he had actually managed to recharge his batteries, he suggested, would become clear only now.

But perhaps that is not the most important question. The question is not whether Viktor Orbán has recovered. It is whether Fidesz can renew itself with him.

Without Orbán, there is no Fidesz — or is Orbán the reason there is no way back?

There are currently two diametrically opposed arguments on the Hungarian right. According to one, Fidesz would begin to fall apart without Viktor Orbán.

The party has been organised around a single political centre for decades. Orbán is the brand, the strategist, the campaign machine and the politician who led Fidesz to four consecutive general election victories. Even after the defeat of April 2026, he remains the figure most capable of keeping the camp together, identifying the enemy and convincing supporters that the war is not over merely because one battle has been lost.

And there is a powerful argument behind that view. Fidesz–KDNP still received 2,458,337 list votes in the April election. That was enough for 38.61 per cent of the list vote, even though the coalition won only 52 of the 199 parliamentary seats.

To put that figure into perspective, Fidesz–KDNP received fewer list votes in 2014 — 2,264,780 — and nevertheless secured 133 seats, giving it a two-thirds parliamentary majority.

So it would be premature to write off Orbán or the political community he built. But there is another camp on the right that sees precisely the opposite problem. In their view, Viktor Orbán himself has become Fidesz’s greatest obstacle.

How can a party genuinely renew itself if every new face is still associated with the old system? How can it offer a new political direction when the person most closely identified with sixteen years of government remains its central figure?

If the 2026 election was, at least partly, a referendum on sixteen years of Fidesz rule, how can the same man credibly present himself as the face of a new beginning?

This is no longer simply a question of personnel. It is Fidesz’s strategic trap.

Has Orbán become Gyurcsány?

Another comparison is increasingly tempting: Viktor Orbán today could become for Fidesz what Ferenc Gyurcsány became for the Hungarian left after 2006.

The logic is simple. A politician can remain enormously important to his own camp while becoming so strongly rejected outside it that winning a national election with him at the front becomes extremely difficult.

Gyurcsány’s political career after 2006 offers an obvious example. His continued leadership helped keep parts of the left together, but his personal political baggage also became one of the most persistent obstacles facing the opposition.

Could the same thing happen to Orbán? The analogy, however, is far from perfect.

Orbán’s situation is fundamentally different because Fidesz has not collapsed electorally. Quite the opposite. Despite losing government, the party retained a remarkably large electoral base in April. More than 2.4 million voters still backed the Fidesz–KDNP list.

That gives Orbán something Gyurcsány could not rely on indefinitely: a huge, disciplined and still politically relevant organisation behind him. So perhaps the better question is not whether Orbán is becoming Hungary’s next Gyurcsány. Maybe it is whether he can prevent Fidesz from becoming a party permanently trapped in its own past.

Kötcse: a fresh start or the same old record?

The message coming out of Kötcse does not yet suggest a radical reinvention of Fidesz. Instead, Orbán appears to have chosen confrontation.

According to reports from the closed-door meeting, the former prime minister argued that the right’s political mission remained unchanged: defending a sovereign Hungary. He portrayed the Tisza government as a threat to that sovereignty and said the opposition needed to rebuild itself and eventually return to government.

Later that evening, Orbán made the new tone even clearer. The period of patience with what he called the “new communists” was over, he said. Fidesz would “take up the gauntlet” and fight. He also announced the beginning of what he described as a period of “national resistance”.

Politically, this is hardly surprising. Fidesz knows how to fight.

It has spent sixteen years building an exceptionally powerful political organisation, a vast communications network and a loyal electoral base. Opposition politics may therefore be uncomfortable for the party, but it is not unfamiliar territory.

The more interesting question is whether confrontation alone is enough.

Can Fidesz renew itself with Viktor Orbán?

This is where the Kötcse meeting becomes more significant than the speeches themselves. If the same leader, using largely the same political language, focusing on many of the same enemies and defending much of the same legacy, is now expected to rebuild the same party, where exactly is the renewal?

There is certainly room for tactical change. Fidesz can become more active in Parliament. It can mobilise its local organisations. It can attack government decisions. It can build alliances with civil organisations, media outlets and influencers.

But organisational renewal is not necessarily political renewal. A party can change its campaign strategy without changing its political identity. And that may be the real dilemma facing Fidesz.

The April defeat was not simply a bad campaign result. It ended sixteen years of uninterrupted government and created a political landscape in which Tisza controls the government, while Fidesz must work out what kind of opposition it wants to be. That is a very different task from governing.

The real problem may come later

For the moment, Viktor Orbán remains the obvious centre of gravity of the Hungarian right. That may be precisely why replacing him is so difficult.

Who could actually take over? János Lázár? Péter Szijjártó? Gergely Gulyás? Someone else entirely? Or could a new generation of politicians emerge who have never been responsible for the entire sixteen-year Orbán era?

There is no obvious answer. And that is precisely the problem.

A strong leader can hold a political camp together after defeat. But the longer a party depends on one person, the harder it becomes to imagine what comes after that person. Perhaps Fidesz needs Orbán precisely because it has not yet found anyone who could replace him. But perhaps it also needs to find such a person precisely because Orbán remains so dominant.

That contradiction could define the future of the Hungarian right.

And what about Mi Hazánk?

There is another possibility that makes the situation even more complicated. If Fidesz moves further towards “resistance politics” and a harder nationalist message, what happens to Mi Hazánk?

The two parties remain separate political forces, but their political interests increasingly overlap on a number of issues. Mi Hazánk survived the April election and entered Parliament with six seats, while Fidesz is now facing the very different challenge of rebuilding itself from opposition.

Could this eventually lead to closer cooperation? Or even to a broader realignment of the Hungarian right?

A formal Fidesz–Mi Hazánk merger is far from inevitable. A looser alliance would arguably be much more plausible. Yet the more Fidesz struggles to decide what kind of conservative party it wants to become, the more interesting the possibility becomes.

And there is an even more intriguing question. What if the future conflict is not between Fidesz and Mi Hazánk at all? What if it is inside Fidesz itself?

Everything is still possible

Kötcse was therefore neither a simple comeback nor necessarily the beginning of the end. It was something more uncomfortable.

It showed that Viktor Orbán has no intention of disappearing from Hungarian politics. He has returned from his long summer break, reclaimed the political stage and clearly chosen confrontation with the Tisza government.

But it also showed how difficult the next chapter will be. Fidesz has to prove that it can do something it has rarely had to do before: reinvent itself without abandoning the political community that Viktor Orbán built around himself.

That is not an easy task. Orbán may still be the only politician capable of keeping Fidesz together. But if he is also the only politician the party can imagine at its centre, then the problem is much bigger than one election defeat.

Perhaps Kötcse was the great comeback, perhaps it was the beginning of the endgame. Or perhaps, as Hungarian politics has demonstrated so many times before, it was simply the opening move of another political battle whose outcome nobody can yet predict.

One thing, however, is already clear. Viktor Orbán has jumped back into the deep end. Now we will see whether Fidesz can swim with him — or whether, for the first time, it will have to learn how to swim without him.

World.title: Brain Bar 2026: Europe’s biggest festival on the future returns to Budapest this week!
World.content:
Brain Bar, Europe’s largest festival on the future, returns to Budapest on 17–18 September. The event takes place at the House of Music Hungary in City Park. The programme includes more than 100 talks, discussions, music and art shows across five stages, plus workshops in the festival’s Talent Hub.

Host Jenn Zeng on what to expect from two days at the House of Music.

Guest author: Anhao Chen

Gergely Böszörményi-Nagy founded the festival in 2015. It brings scientists, politicians, entrepreneurs, and cultural figures together with a mostly young audience, and every session is built so that visitors can ask questions from the floor. Past speakers include PayPal founder Peter Thiel, astronaut Chris Hadfield, and psychotherapist Esther Perel.

Peter Thiel at Brain Bar. Photo: Brain Bar

From Cory Doctorow to Judit Polgár

This year’s speakers include science fiction writer Cory Doctorow, physicist Carlo Rovelli, and Nataliya Kosmyna, the MIT Media Lab neuroscientist studying what ChatGPT does to the brain. Hungarian names on the bill include Minister of Transport and Investment Dávid Vitézy, Minister of Science and Technology Zoltán Tanács, Sziget Festival founder Károly Gerendai, and football coach Zsolt Szoboszlai, father of Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai.

Judit Polgár, the most successful female chess player of all time, is also speaking. Her foundation is the festival’s goodwill partner this year and receives all ticket revenue, which it uses to develop children’s thinking and creativity through chess.

Sessions run in English and Hungarian. The agenda marks the language of each session.

“How do humans actually connect?”

Among this year’s hosts is Jenn Zeng, the event’s youngest host and first woman president of the LSE Entrepreneurs’ Society, who will take the stage at Brain Bar for the first time.

Jenn Zeng.

Speaking to Daily News Hungary ahead of the festival, Zeng said she is most looking forward to her one-on-one with Jared Henderson, a philosopher and content creator, on the future of friendship in an age of digital isolation.

“This one specifically stands out because right now we are living in a world where everything we talk about is AI,” she said. “There is less and less emphasis on people and how humans actually connect and bond with each other. How do we form truly fulfilling and meaningful friendships in a world of digital isolation?”

Zeng said the festival’s value lies in putting a young audience in front of the people working at the edge of their fields. “I really hope the people feel inspired, make new friends while they are there, and really think about what they could do to contribute to a better world,” she said.

Tickets for the Brain Bar 2026 Festival

Brain Bar 2026 runs 17–18 September at the House of Music Hungary, Olof Palme sétány 3. Students and teachers can attend for free after registering via a form on the festival website, and teachers can sign up entire secondary school classes by email. Anyone without a pass can still use the open outdoor area. A two-day pass costs 39,900 HUF, with a 25% discount for 4 or more passes. Single-day tickets are 26,900 HUF. You can find tickets and the full agenda at brainbar.com.

World.title: Kosovo’s New Govt Challenged in Court as Presidential Pick Withdraws
World.content:
Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s cabinet take their seats in parliament, September 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

The opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, on Tuesday asked the country’s Constitutional Court to assess whether the parliamentary vote that re-elected Albin Kurti as Kosovo’s Prime Minister three days ago was valid.

“We consider that parliament has been inaugurated by violating the constitution. A parliament which is inaugurated unconstitutionally cannot produce constitutional institutions,” Perparim Gruda, a PDK MP, told media on Tuesday.

“Even earlier, we called [on parliament] to not proceed with further decisions before clarifying question marks,” Gruda added.

Tuesday’s filing by the PDK is the second in as many days that it has taken to the top court. On Monday, it complained to the court that Sunday’s inauguration of parliament had violated the rules.

The PDK claims that Kurti’s ruling Vetevendosje party violated the 30-day deadline to inaugurate parliament and that the assembly cannot be considered inaugurated until all five deputy speakers are elected.

On Sunday, the PDK withdrew its candidate for the post of deputy speaker, while four other deputies were elected.

Vetevendosje leader Kurti was re-elected Prime Minister by MPs at a session boycotted by opposition parties. A narrow majority of 62 MPs out of 120 voted in favour of Kurti’s new cabinet. Eight MPs from the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista voted against.

However, on Monday evening, the election of a new state President received another setback when the sole candidate for the post, Bekim Sejdiu, announced his withdrawal following disagreements within his Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, over his candidacy.

Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku had agreed on his name on August 31 – but six LDK MPs then announced they would not support him, leaving the potential vote without the necessary quorum.

Failure to elect a new President within two months of the inauguration of parliament would trigger new elections, the fourth within less than two months.

“Under such circumstances, characterised by the lack of the necessary parliamentary support for my election as President and by the deviation of the entire process into the vortex of internal political dynamics and clashes, I have decided to withdraw from the candidacy for President,” Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, said in a Facebook post.

“I call on the political parties to find a way out of this vicious circle, which, more than anything else, is eroding citizens’ hopes of a prosperous future for them and their families,” he added.

LDK leader Abdixhiku lamented the lack of support for his candidacy. “His withdrawal in the face of political hysteria shows exactly why a person with such a character would be an appropriate pick for President,” Abdixhiku said.

“It’s a pity that we don’t have a President today. Instead of a solution, we have political chaos, a blockade as a means, and new elections, once again, as a goal,” he added.

Vetevendosje also regretted the withdrawal – and accused opposition MPs of trying to provoke new elections.

“When a boycott is used to make a vote impossible, then we don’t have political difference around a candidate but the blockage of a constitutional process and taking the country to repeated elections,” Vetevendosje said.

World.title: Serbian Students Stage ‘Victors’ March’ to Register for Polls
World.content:
Thousands of supporters of Serbia’s opposition Student List gathered on Monday evening in front of the University of Belgrade Rectorate and marched to the Republic Electoral Commission to register their candidate list, “Student List – Students Win”, for the snap parliamentary elections on October 25.

Participants in what the Student List called the “Victors’ March” brought with them a replica of the Victory monument, a prominent Belgrade landmark and symbol of the city.

At the weekend, people queued in cities and towns around Serbia to sign their names in support of the Student List, sometimes waiting in line for a couple of hours.

Student List arose from the long-running student-led protest movement that was established after the Novi Sad railway station disaster in November 2024. It is seen as the main opposition challenger to the long rule of the Serbian Progressive Party of President Aleksandar Vucic.

Vucic plans resign as head of state and campaign for the prime minister’s post in the election. “On September ‌27 ⁠I will resign as president. That evening, I will address the nation and thank people for their support,” Vucic told Pink TV on Sunday.

World.title: Truth and Consequences: Kosovo Special Court to Deliver High-Stakes Verdict
World.content:
The trial panel’s obligation is to carefully evaluate all of the evidence, make findings of fact for each defendant and for each charge, and render a decision for each defendant and each charge, a herculean task given the complexity of the case and the vastness of the evidence.

The presiding judge is Charles Smith III of the US state of Iowa, who is highly experienced and respected, and can be expected to carefully carry out the court’s responsibilities.

The panel has multiple options: it can find all the accused guilty of all charges, guilty of some and not guilty of others, or not guilty of all charges. And the verdicts could vary, defendant to defendant and charge to charge; there are numerous possible combinations.

The court has shown little leniency for the accused. If one reads the panel’s decisions regarding continued detention, numbering 26-28 depending on which defendant, it is not difficult to surmise the lack of trust held for them.

For example, as recently as August 10, Thaci was once again ordered to remain in detention (# 28) because he was still deemed likely to obstruct the proceedings and commit further crimes. Similar decisions have been issued for the other defendants.

Also not to be ignored is Thaci’s concurrent trial for offences against the administration of justice in his war crimes case – leaking confidential information about prosecution witnesses and trying to influence their testimony. Closing statements were delivered just days before the verdict is to be pronounced in the war crimes case.

This is an odd confluence of two related cases that could be seen as influencing each other.

Regardless, the consequences of the various options in the war crimes case can easily be elucidated.

Guilty verdicts

If one or more of the accused are found guilty of the most serious charges, such as command responsibility and joint criminal enterprise, the EU’s monumental investment will be validated; the EU, the prosecution, and the victims and their families can claim that holding war criminals to account is well worth the time and expense. In other words, a spectacular victory.

The defendants would likely receive lengthy prison sentences, perhaps up to 45 years, which would equate to life sentences, given their ages, even with credit for time served.

But to reach guilty verdicts, the panel would have to completely disregard the testimony of the esteemed defence witnesses, which could be viewed as creating a reasonable doubt.

For Kosovo, guilty verdicts will be perceived as rewriting history and undermining the strongly held narrative of the glorious rebellion against Serbia, fought by the revered KLA war heroes who often gave their lives in the cause of freedom. A humiliating defeat, and the verdicts would be reviled, possibly triggering violent protests.

Serbia will be able to characterise Kosovo’s fight, smugly, as nothing more than a joint criminal enterprise, perpetrated by lawless rebels and murderers, with many Serb victims. Relations between the two countries, always highly fraught, could suffer further.

Not guilty verdicts

Not guilty verdicts will be perceived by the EU and others as a horrendous waste of time and money, with no tangible results, including the failure of accountability and the absence of empathy for the victims. A spectacular defeat.

And Kosovo’s fight for freedom, and the ongoing, strong opposition to the Specialist Chambers, will be validated. The defendants could return home just as they left it, as war heroes and liberators.

Either way, the verdicts will not bring about reconciliation between Kosovo and Serbia, which was one of the stated objectives for creating the court; indeed, the opposite result of increased tension and reciprocal provocation and disparagement is more likely.

World.title: Wildfires Burn Thousands of Hectares, Exposing Albania’s Systemic Weaknesses
World.content:
In early September, wildfires engulfed Himara, burning olive groves on the hills around the Albanian coastal city and forcing emergency evacuations. Thick smoke blanketed the city as the flames spread towards inhabited areas.

A preliminary assessment by local authorities said dozens of centuries-old olive trees had been destroyed, while several homes were completely burned down.

Other fires broke out across Albania in early September, mainly affecting pastureland and forests. Official figures show that thousands of hectares of land were affected by wildfires during the summer.

World.title: BIRN Launches ‘Trial Stories’ Page for Hashim Thaci Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Illustration: Tijana Dupanovic/BIRN.

Ahead of the verdict in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against for former senior Kosovo Liberation Army officials at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague on Wednesday, BIRN has launched a special focus page dedicated to the trial and its impact.

The page compiles BIRN’s reporting on the trial since it started in April 2023 – analysis articles as well as news reports from Kosovo and The Hague.

“BIRN is one of the few media outlets that has followed the prosecution of Hashim Thaci and his co-defendants in genuine depth from the beginning, reporting on the latest developments but also examining their potential implications,” said BIRN’s deputy regional director Gentiana Murati.

“The verdict is an event of major significance for Kosovo and the region and BIRN will continue to analyse its consequences as they develop, not only on the day of the judgment,” she added.

Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers are calling for 45-year prison sentences for the four defendants – Kosovo’s ex-President Hashim Thaci and fellow former guerrilla leaders Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi.

They are accused of having command responsibility for a campaign of persecution by KLA fighters during and just after the 1998-99 war, which allegedly included murders, torture, forced disappearances and unlawful detentions.

The defendants have denied the charges and their lawyers are seeking acquittals.

The case has sparked anger in Kosovo, where it is seen as an attempt to vilify the KLA’s war for liberation from Serbian oppression. Supporters of the defendants have staged a series of demonstrations and are expected to rally in The Hague for the verdict.

See the focus page here.

World.title: Turkey Rounds Up 2,447 People in Operation Targeting Crime Gangs
World.content:
Turkish Police and Gendarmerie launched a major operation called “The Streets Are Safe” on Monday, detaining 2,447 people to coincide with the first morning of the new school year in 78 provinces across the country.

“Our streets will not be left to criminal organisations. Our children and young people will not become the human resources of criminal organisations,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said in a statement, defining the detainees as members of “new generation of street gangs”.

The operation targeted criminal groups allegedly involved in offences ranging from drug trafficking, robbery and arms dealing to blackmail, money laundering and illegal betting.

Gurlek said the campaign was intended not only to detain suspects but also to dismantle the criminal groups’ finances, networks, logistical capabilities and ability to recruit new members.

He highlighted the alleged recruitment of young people through social media, accusing criminal groups of seeking to portray involvement in crime as a source of “power and status”.

“We are resolutely continuing our fight against street gangs that threaten the peace of our people, the security of our cities and the future of our children,” the minister added.

In a separate development on Sunday, Turkish police authorities detained members of the LGBTQ+ rights organisation Kaos GL and raided activists’ homes as well as bars and nightclubs in separate operations across 15 provinces, targeting 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses.

Kaos GL said at least 10 of its members were detained. Separately, courts blocked access to websites and social media accounts belonging to a number of LGBTQ+ organisations, activists and rights defenders, including Kaos GL, Lambdaistanbul, Pembe Hayat and UniKuir.

World.title: adidas and HNS Unveil New Croatia National Team Kits
World.content:
adidas has unveiled the long-awaited new official kits for the Croatia national football team, the first set produced under a long-term partnership with the Croatian Football Federation (HNS).

Combining cutting-edge performance innovation with elements founded in Croatian culture and identity, the new kits celebrate the heritage, pride and passion that define Croatian football.

The unveiling marks the start of a new chapter for one of international football’s most recognizable national teams. Having cemented its place among the world’s leading footballing nations, Croatia will step out in an adidas kit for the first time as part of the partnership announced earlier this year.

HNS / adidas

The new home shirt offers a modern take on Croatia’s iconic red-and-white checkerboard pattern, one of the most striking visual symbols in international football. For the first time, letters from the Glagolitic alphabet — the oldest known Slavic script and an important symbol of Croatian cultural heritage — have been woven into the checkerboard design, running throughout the pattern to give one of Croatian football’s most recognizable emblems a fresh, contemporary twist. The back of the collar also features the word “HRVATSKA” written in Glagolitic script, further tying the shirt to Croatia’s cultural history.

The away shirt, meanwhile, draws inspiration from Croatia’s long tradition of lace-making, a craft passed down through generations and another significant part of the country’s cultural heritage. An intricate lace-inspired motif runs across the shirt’s navy base, offering a modern interpretation of that tradition. The design is completed by a collar detail bearing the word “HRVATSKA” in typography inspired by cross-stitch embroidery, linking the traditional craft to contemporary football design.

HNS / adidas

“These shirts are much more than innovative football kits and striking design. Working with adidas, we chose a design that perfectly combines local pride with a global perspective. Those are exactly the values Croatia has always stood for, and now a new generation of fans and players will carry them forward,” said Marijan Kustić, president of the Croatian Football Federation.

Both shirts were developed to meet the demands of football at the highest level and feature the latest adidas CLIMACOOL+ technology. Specially developed stretch fabrics and 3D body-mapping technology improve ventilation and breathability, helping players stay dry through high-intensity matches and in hot conditions. Perforated three-stripe panels and strategically placed mesh zones further boost airflow and comfort.

Croatia’s men’s national team will wear the new kits for the first time during the upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures.

Alongside the new shirts, adidas is also launching a wider Croatia national team collection that includes shorts, socks, training wear and leisurewear, designed for fans who want to show their connection to the national team both on and off the pitch.

A video unveiling the new kits has been posted on the Instagram profiles of @adidasfootball and the Croatian Football Federation.

The new Croatia national team kits, along with the full HNS x adidas collection, are available to buy from today at the official HNS online store. Pick out your kit, step into a new era of Croatian football, and wear it with pride.

World.title: CRANE Forum 2026: Productivity as a European Priority, Judiciary as the Greatest Obstacle to Investment
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – The CRANE Forum 2026 was recently held, which welcomed around 200 guests from the fields of investment to politics, and from economics to financial institution representatives.

As stated, around 200 guests involved with the Croatian economy, entrepreneurs and investors, members of the Government, ambassadors and representatives of international financial institutions, as well as county prefects and mayors, gathered at the Tihočaj estate in the Žumberak – Samobor Hills Nature Park to discuss investment prospects and the frameworks in which they will be implemented.

In Jastrebarsko on the 12th of September 2026, the fourth CRANE Forum, organised by CRANE, the Croatian Association of Investors and Business Angels, was held. The location was the Tihočaj estate in the Žumberak – Samobor Hills Nature Park. Once again this year, the Forum brought together all levels of decision-making on a single investment in one place: 200 guests from the top of the Croatian economy, entrepreneurs and investors, members of the Government, ambassadors and representatives of international financial institutions, as well as county prefects and mayors.

“Since 2008, CRANE has been connecting entrepreneurs and investors and bringing together capital, knowledge and experience with those who make the decisions. For development and new investments, finding an investor is not enough. What is also needed is a state that cooperates and understands the vision, and a local environment that knows how to create the conditions for its implementation. That is why we do not build the Forum as a conference, but as a working meeting at which everyone who decides on a single investment is present,” said Davorin Štetner, President of CRANE.

The key topics of this year’s Forum were the new multiannual financial framework of the European Union after 2027, the tax system as a competitive advantage, the role of local self-government in attracting strategic investments, and investments in healthcare.

Speaking about what Croatia can expect from the EU’s multiannual financial framework after 2027, Nataša Mikuš Žigman, Minister of Regional Development and EU Funds, stressed that the priorities coming from Brussels are focused on security, defence and climate efficiency, but equally on investments in productivity and competitiveness. Croatia, she announced, has already begun preparing a future competitiveness investment programme that will combine public and private funds, with the aim of raising the productivity of the economy. Among the novelties are milder requirements for technical documentation at the application and contracting stage, the possibility for applicants with smaller tax debts not to be excluded from the procedure but to settle them before the decision on the award of support is made, and raising the threshold for the implementation of procurement procedures with simple procurement via the eKohezija platform. In the negotiations on the new multiannual financial framework, Croatia insists that administrative burden relief actually reaches end-users and does not remain only on the Brussels–Member State axis.

On the panel dedicated to the tax system, in which Tomislav Ćorić, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, Davor Baković, President of the Croatian Exporters Association and Chairman of the Management Board of Končar MT d.d., Davor Tremac, Executive Director of Fono, and Domagoj Kamenski, Executive Director of Kamgrad, participated, it was emphasised that the Croatian tax framework in itself is not an obstacle to growth, but in certain segments even represents a competitive advantage, with a corporate income tax rate lower than the average of developed countries and excellent incentives for investment and research and development.

That the tax rate is not decisive is also shown by comparison with the surrounding region: ahead of Croatia on investment attractiveness rankings are the Czech Republic and Slovenia, which have significantly higher corporate income tax rates. The key problem, as Tremac stressed, is distrust in the judiciary, because what is contracted on paper is difficult and slow to enforce before Croatian courts, and this has been pointed out for thirty years without progress. The price of this distrust is measured in capital that does not arrive: when the enforceability of contractual protections is not certain, investors do not abandon the investment, but the jurisdiction, so Croatian companies register their holding companies in Ireland, the Netherlands or Luxembourg, and the tax base moves with them. The conclusion of the panel is therefore that lowering tax rates would not solve a problem that the rates did not create; the greatest contribution to the investment climate would come from judicial reform, i.e. the speed and predictability of resolving commercial disputes.

Speaking about investments in healthcare from the Government’s perspective, Minister of Health Irena Hrstić emphasised that the Government of the Republic of Croatia has invested around €3.4 billion in the healthcare system over the past ten years or so, and that investments continue in line with the policy of balanced regional development – from the new University Hospital Centre Osijek and the project for a new University Hospital Centre for Dalmatia, which the Ministry and the Government have already given the green light, to the hospital in Blato, whose foundation stone will soon be laid and which will be the first “Carbon Zero” hospital in Europe, heated by geothermal energy and financed by European funds. The leading principle is smart investment, with the emphasis that the goal is functional healthcare equally accessible to all parts of Croatia.

A strong diplomatic dimension was given to the Forum by the presentation of new interlocutors of the Croatian business community at the international level: Ronke Amoni Ogunsulire, World Bank Director for Croatia and Slovenia, Her Excellency Anne Toft Sørensen, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Denmark to the Republic of Croatia, and His Excellency Glenn Morrison, Ambassador of Australia to the Republic of Croatia. Their presentation opens new channels of cooperation and a direct link between the domestic business and investment community and partners outside Croatia, which is crucial for attracting investment and strengthening export opportunities. In addition to them, the Forum also gathered other esteemed ambassadors and representatives of international financial institutions, thereby confirming its role as a meeting place of the Croatian economy with international partners.

what is crane?

CRANE – the Croatian Association of Investors and Business Angels is otherwise the oldest Croatian association of investors and business angels, founded in 2008. It connects ambitious entrepreneurs with investors who invest money, knowledge, skills and business contacts in their projects, with the aim that as many innovative companies in the early stage of development as possible grow into successful business stories. CRANE is the national representative of Croatia in the European Business Angels Network (EBAN) and a member of the Global Business Angels Network (GBAN), and in addition to its investment activity systematically advocates a better regulatory and tax framework for entrepreneurs and investors in Croatia and at the level of the European Union. More at www.crane.hr.

World.title: Hybrid Electro-Diesel Train Between Split and Zagreb Now Operational
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – The very first hybrid electro-diesel train between Split and Zagreb is now fully operational. Here are all the details.

As of today (September the 15th, 2026) the very first electro-diesel train will enter service on the Split – Zagreb Main Station route. The train departs (as it has today) from Split station at 07:54. Poslovni reports that the new train is adapted to the specific characteristics of the Zagreb–Split line, which is partly electrified and partly non-electrified. It has 150 seats, and passengers have access to free Wi-Fi, power sockets next to the seats, a modern information system, visual and audio announcements, ramps for people with disabilities, and space for bicycles. The train also features self-service machines for buying coffee and other hot drinks, water, soft drinks, sweets and snacks.

The introduction of the new electro-diesel trains for long-distance transport continues the modernisation of the HŽ Passenger Transport fleet, while at the same time reducing energy consumption, noise and greenhouse gas emissions. Experts from the KONČAR Group, in cooperation with numerous Croatian companies, were involved in the development and production of the trains.

As part of this massive project, six electro-diesel trains are being procured, financed by a loan from the European Investment Bank amounting to 57.3 million euros. All six trains will be put into service by the end of this year. As of December 2026, with the start of the new timetable, Zagreb and Split will be connected by four daily trains, further improving the connectivity of Croatia’s two largest cities and the quality of travel.

Ahead of the first regular journey of the new train, statements for the media will be given by State Secretary for Railways Žarko Tušek from the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure, President of the Management Board of HŽ Passenger Transport Željko Ukić, President of the Management Board of KONČAR Gordan Kolak, Split-Dalmatia County Prefect Blaženko Boban, and Deputy Mayor of Split Matea Dorčić. Also present on the journey will be Zadar County Prefect Josip Bilaver and Šibenik-Knin County Prefect Paško Rakić.

World.title: Brač Fire: Residents Without Electricity Told to Follow TV and Radio
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – Brač residents worried for their properties and indeed their lives in the recent Milna fire were very clumsily advised to follow the TV and radio – despite having no electricity.

The Early Warning and Crisis Management System (SRUUK) was activated on Saturday evening because of a large fire in the wider Milna area on Brač. Lukrecija Zderic reports for Index that residents in that area received a message on their mobile phones with a link to instructions on how to act, along with advice to follow further announcements on television and radio. At the same time, part of Brač had no electricity, which raised the question of how exactly people without power were supposed to obtain new information about the fire.

On Saturday evening, the fire, driven by strong wind, spread rapidly towards Milna as well as the bays of Duboka and Osibova, where Resort Gava with a large number of tourists is located. More than 200 firefighters were on the ground trying to stop the fire from spreading towards the populated area.

false evacuation and sruuk activation

The red sky above Brač and Milna was visible even from Split, while Index readers filmed the firestorm approaching the settlement. As the situation became increasingly serious, various pieces of information about a possible evacuation began to arrive. Shortly before 23:00, a notice about the evacuation of the population was published on the Facebook page of the Milna Volunteer Fire Department. It stated that the situation was critical and called on citizens to make their private boats available for evacuation needs. The post was deleted about half an hour later, and services on the ground reported that there was no official evacuation.

At 23:28 the SRUUK was activated. Citizens in the endangered area received a warning via SMS or Cell Broadcast about the danger, together with a link to additional information. Clicking the link opens a page of the Ministry of the Interior (MUP), i.e. the Civil Protection Directorate, containing “Instructions for Citizens.” These are general instructions on how to behave during a fire, and below them citizens are directed to follow further announcements via television, radio and links of the Civil Protection Directorate. At that moment Milna was already without electricity. The earlier post about evacuation further confused residents. Some did not know whether they should leave the place, so they prepared for evacuation and went out onto the street by the sea.

The SRUUK activated once again that evening at 00:22, when citizens once more received a link with instructions on how to act in the event of a fire. Why residents in the endangered area without electricity were recommended to follow information via TV and radio remains unknown for now. Because of the approaching fire a partial evacuation of the most endangered parts of Milna and the surrounding area was carried out, while the entire settlement was never evacuated at any point.

a fire warning for a fire on an island was received in split… on the mainland

The Civil Protection Directorate was therefore asked for an explanation as to exactly why citizens in an area affected by a power outage were directed to television and radio, who in such a situation is responsible for delivering key information, and how many times the SRUUK was activated during the fire on Brač. We will publish the answer when we receive it. However, the problem was not only in the content of the messages. Residents we spoke to said that some received the warning around 23:00 and then again after midnight, while others received only the first message. According to their accounts, some residents of Supetar received no warning at all.

At the same time, a warning about a significant fire danger was also received by some citizens who were at that moment in Split and on the island of Hvar, even though they were not on the territory of Brač. We have also requested an answer from the Civil Protection Directorate on this issue.

a heavily criticised system

The SRUUK has previously been criticised for not being activated during crisis situations. The last time this happened was during the large fire near Omiš, in which three people died and five more are still fighting for their lives. The fire left enormous consequences — people were left without homes and jobs, thousands of hectares of forest burned, and the safety of the population remains threatened due to possible landslides.

The non-activation of the system at that time was justified by Split-Dalmatia County Prefect Blaženko Boban with the assessment that sending a warning could cause panic. On Brač the opposite question has arisen: did the unclear communication from the services further contribute to confusion and panic among residents? In the fire that has been burning on Brač for several days, around 4,000 hectares of forest, low vegetation and maquis have totally burned, as have private buildings, cars and one resort. Around 700 people were evacuated and two people were injured. There is still some smouldering on the ground, the fire has not been completely extinguished, and firefighters remain on alert.

Over 200 firefighters on the ground have for days been making superhuman efforts to defend houses and protect residents. For the locals they are heroes who risk their own lives to protect people and property. Yet the question remains how much help they receive in crisis situations from a system that the state paid 8.4 million euros for. The SRUUK was conceived as a tool for timely warning of citizens. On Brač, however, it has been shown that simply sending a message is not the end of its job, the key question is whether citizens can, after that message, actually receive clear, timely and useful information when they need it most.

World.title: Coastal and Continental Croatia See Contrasting Rental Markets
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – Coastal and continental Croatia are experiencing drastically contrasting rental markets, with only Zagreb seeing a balance.

Zagreb is the only city among those analysed in which both the supply increased and the asking prices decreased this year. Poslovni reports that the search for student accommodation is an extremely stressful period for students and their families, and resolving the accommodation issue is one of the biggest financial and logistical challenges. There are several causes of the student housing crisis. From tourist rentals, i.e. landlords deciding to rent flats to tourists on a daily basis, which is why they often require students to move in only in November and move out at the beginning of June, to the fact that property prices and interest rates keep rising.

There’s also a seriously chronic shortage of free properties for long-term rental, as well as limited capacity in student dorms, which unfortunately cover only a smaller part of students’ needs. As a result, students are left to the private market, which is often fickle and ruthless, writes Glas Slavonije.

a wide price range

The online classifieds site Njuškalo analysed s published in the first seven months of 2026. The results showed that the long-term rental market is increasingly clearly divided into the continental and coastal parts of Croatia. While Zagreb, Osijek and Varaždin record growth in the number of available flats for rent, Rijeka, Split and Zadar face a decline in supply. Precisely in the cities where the number of s is rising, prices are stagnating or falling, while coastal markets are putting greater pressure on tenants. For students this difference is particularly important, because lower supply means less room for choice, negotiation and finding a flat within an acceptable price range.

Osijek stands out as the most affordable market for students. The average asking rent in the first seven months was around €580, and from January to July it fell from €603 to €559. At the same time, supply increased by 50 percent. Among smaller flats the most favourable districts are Novi grad with an average of €401, Donji grad with €414 and Sjenjak with €417. It’s important to note that Donji grad and Sjenjak also have a relatively solid supply. The range between the cheapest and most expensive Osijek neighbourhood is €143, or 36 percent — the smallest difference among the cities analysed.

Varaždin is also more affordable than the coastal centres, and its special feature is stability. The average asking rent in the first seven months was €650, with growth of only 2.4 percent, while the number of s rose by as much as 65 percent, the highest among all observed cities. For flats up to 55 square metres the July average was €533.

On the coast, the picture is much less favourable, primarily because of the drop in long-term supply. In Rijeka the number of s fell by 29 percent over the seven months, while average asking prices rose by three percent. Still, Rijeka continues to offer students a relatively wide choice of neighbourhoods that combine lower prices with more regular supply. Gornja Vežica, Podmurvice and Krnjevo range from €544 to €558, Zamet is at €571 and Belveder at €602. The cheapest is Pehlin at €498, while Kantrida reaches €829. Rijeka is therefore not cheap in absolute terms, but within the city there are still several price brackets in which students can look for a compromise between price, location and availability.

Split shows the most pronounced seasonality. The average asking price rose during the spring and reached €1,147 in May, but by July it had fallen to €1,055. At the same time total supply dropped by 32 percent, which is linked to the reduced availability of flats for long-term rental during the tourist season.

a shortage of smaller flats

Zadar recorded the largest price increase. The average asking rent rose from €813 in January to €1,055 in June, almost 30 percent, and in July it corrected to €894. The number of s compared with the beginning of the year fell by 26 percent. An additional problem is the very limited supply of smaller flats: in July there were only 109 in the whole city, and only five neighbourhoods had a regular supply throughout all seven months. Višnjik had the largest choice but also the highest average price of €847. The best compromise is Poluotok at €616 with 12 s in July.

Duško Grgur, owner of the Osijek real-estate agency German Nekretnine and president of the professional group at the Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK), says that demand for long-term rental in Osijek is quite high, but the supply lacks smaller flats, studios, one-bedroom and two-bedroom apartments, which students seek the most.

“Just recently I received two flats of 55 square metres for long-term rental, one in Pejačevićeva Street and the other on Vijenac Paje Kolarića. Both flats were rented at the asking price of €550, and to the first tenant who came,” Grgur states, adding that there was no haggling. He emphasises that the Osijek property market has seen an increase in larger flats for long-term rental: those of 60 to 65 square metres rented for €600 per month, those of 70 square metres for €700, and those larger than 100 square metres whose rents range from €900 to €1,000.

Zagreb is, as touched on above, the only city among those analysed in which both supply increased and asking prices decreased this year. The number of active s from January to July rose by 26 percent, while the average asking rent fell from €1,009 to €963. However, the city average hides large differences between neighbourhoods, especially in the segment of flats up to 55 square metres, which is the most relevant for students. Among neighbourhoods with a regular supply, the cheapest was Utrina with an average of €517, while Donje Svetice were at €846. That is a difference of €329 per month, or as much as 64 percent. As a more rational compromise between price and availability, Njuškalo highlights Prečko, Voltino, Gornja Dubrava, Špansko and Knežija.

World.title: Multi-Million Euro Project to Result in New Zagreb Health Centre
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – A multi-million euro project is set to result in a brand new Zagreb health centre with a capacity for 24,000 patients.

The City of Zagreb has launched a public procurement procedure for the construction of the Zagreb West (Zapad) Health Centre, specifically the Špansko clinic at Matije Vlačića Ilirika Street 2, valued at 18 million euros excluding VAT. Hana Ivkovic Simicic/VL reports for Poslovni that the residents of the western part of Zagreb will get a new, modern health centre that will significantly improve the accessibility and quality of primary healthcare services and bring together a wide range of health services in a single location.

“By constructing the new clinic in Špansko, we want to provide residents of this part of the city with more accessible and higher-quality healthcare in modern premises adapted to citizens’ needs. The new clinic will serve around 24,000 residents of the Špansko neighbourhood, as well as other residents of the Stenjevec city district,” Mayor Tomislav Tomašević emphasised. The new clinic will be built with one underground and three above-ground floors, with a total gross floor area of more than 5,800 m². The building is designed so that patients can use health services more simply, quickly and efficiently. The ground floor will house the main entrances and public facilities, while the upper floors will contain consulting rooms, waiting areas and other medical spaces. The underground floor will accommodate the radiology department with X-ray, CT, mammography and dental X-ray, along with technical and auxiliary spaces.

The construction of the health centre will significantly expand the range of health services. In addition to the existing general/family medicine, dental and school medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology and patronage (home-care) services, as well as a pharmacy, the centre will introduce physical medicine and rehabilitation, occupational and sports medicine, radiology, a medical-chemical laboratory, and specialist outpatient clinics. The new health centre in Špansko has been designed to the nZEB (nearly zero-energy building) standard. It will use heat pumps for heating and cooling, and an 85 kW photovoltaic power plant will be installed on the roof. More than 60 percent of the surrounding area will be greened and landscaped, and the new car park will provide 70 parking spaces, the City detailed. Covered porches and landscaped pedestrian approaches will connect the building with the surrounding green areas and footpaths.

“Particular emphasis has been placed on accessibility and functionality. The building will be fully adapted for people with reduced mobility and persons with disabilities, with adapted parking spaces, two lifts and accessible sanitary facilities. In order to ensure continuity of healthcare for citizens, the work of the existing clinic will not be interrupted during construction. After the completion of the public procurement procedure and the selection of the contractor, the start of works is expected at the beginning of 2027.”

World.title: Hajduk Jump Past Dinamo to Top of the SuperSport HNL
World.content:
Hajduk beat Slaven Belupo 1-0 at Poljud in round seven of the SuperSport HNL, with Brazilian forward Dalisson netting the only goal in the 22nd minute. The win was Gonzalo Garcia’s side’s fifth league victory in a row, and it sends them to the top of the table. Hajduk now sit a point clear of Osijek, and three points above both Dinamo and Varaždin, who have a game in hand.

Hajduk set the tempo from the first whistle, with Bamba a constant threat down the right. The hosts thought they’d broken the deadlock in the 15th minute when Hrgović fired home after a quick break and Šego turned the ball into the net, but the effort was ruled out for offside.

The breakthrough eventually came in the 22nd minute, and it came from the same source: Bamba again got to the byline and whipped in a cross from the right, and this time Dalisson rose highest to plant a precise header past Sentić and put Hajduk 1-0 up. It was the Brazilian’s fourth goal in just 15 appearances for the club since arriving on loan from Córdoba in the summer, alongside four assists. It underlined just how well he’s settled in at Poljud.

The tempo dropped considerably after the break. Hajduk were happy to control possession while Slaven struggled to fashion anything in reply. In the 70th minute Dalisson turned provider, squaring for Carlos Martín, who blazed over from a promising position. The game’s defining moment came in the 79th minute, when Filip Mažar was shown a second yellow card for a foul on Dalisson and had to leave the field. With a man advantage for the final stretch, Hajduk saw out the win without any further alarms.

Osijek stunned Dinamo 4-2 in seven-goal thriller

On Saturday, Osijek beat Dinamo 4-2 at Opus Arena in round seven’s other big clash. The hosts were excellent in the first half, racing into a 2-0 lead through Armando León before extending it to 300 with a goal from Luka Vrbančić — only to be made to sweat for the win late on.

Osijek opened the scoring in the 12th minute when Domagoj Bukvić whipped in a cross from the right and León rose highest in the box to head past Dominik Kotarski. The second goal followed in the 34th minute: Dinamo failed to make the most of a chance of their own, and Osijek broke swiftly the other way — after a shot from Ljatifi was saved by Kotarski, León was on hand to bundle the rebound home for 2-0.

Dinamo had a handful of half-chances in the first half without seriously testing Marko Malenica, coming closest through a Miha Zajc free-kick and an Arber Hoxha header from a cross. Mario Kovačević made a triple substitution at the break, but the changes didn’t immediately shift the picture. Osijek kept pushing and made it 3-0 in the 60th minute, when former Dinamo man Luka Vrbančić raced onto a ball in behind after a quick counter and calmly slotted past Kotarski.

Dinamo hit back just a minute later — after a scramble in the box, the ball fell to Zajc, who pulled one back to make it 3-1.

Dinamo pushed hard for a way back into the game in the closing stages. Frane Topić came closest in the 81st minute, heading against a great save from Malenica after a Kačavenda cross. Then, in the 90th minute, Malenica brought down Galešić inside the box, and the referee pointed to the spot. Smail Prevljak converted in the 92nd minute to make it 3-2 and set up a frantic finish.

But Osijek held their nerve, and in the 96th minute they put the result beyond doubt. A major mix-up in the Dinamo defence left Domagoj Bukvić with an empty net to finish into, sealing a 4-2 win. It was a statement victory for Osijek, proof they can go toe-to-toe with the league’s best — and Dinamo’s first league defeat of the season.

World.title: Porsche Made €820 Million on Rimac, €250 Million to go to Pensions
World.content:
September the 14th, 2026 – A consortium led by HOF Capital has officially taken over the stake held by Porsche in the Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac.

The consortium, headed by HOF Capital (with BlueFive Capital as the largest investor), has completed the acquisition of Porsche’s shares in Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac in recent days. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the value of the transaction, fully financed by the consortium’s own funds, is approximately €1 billion. The deal has now been closed, and Rimac Group remains the majority owner of Bugatti Rimac with a 55% stake.

where will this enormous sum go?

Mate Rimac will be supported by a new management team in the new period. Christophe Piochon will step down as President of the Management Board of Bugatti Automobiles and Chief Operating Officer (COO) of Bugatti Rimac. Mate Rimac takes over as President of the Management Board of Bugatti Automobiles, while Marko Brkljačić, former Chief Operating Officer (COO) at Rimac Technology, will join the leadership of Bugatti Rimac as Chief Operating Officer (COO). It is interesting to examine the details of the deal itself, the second-largest M&A transaction in Croatian history, after Barr’s takeover of Pliva back in 2006. From Porsche’s perspective, it was an excellent deal. They once invested €180 million in Rimac and have now realised €1 billion. In other words, Rimac generated €820 million for Porsche. It should be borne in mind that Bugatti had always been unprofitable until last year, when it achieved €200 million in EBITDA.

supervisory boards

To maintain control over its investment, HOF Capital holds three seats on the supervisory boards of both Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac. It is also curious to see how Porsche will use the money it has earned. According to announcements by Dr Jochen Breckner, Member of the Porsche Executive Board responsible for Finance and IT, €250 million will go into the company’s pension fund — specifically for the pensions of Porsche employees. Taking into account the cash inflow and the further funding of pension obligations, the net cash flow margin of Porsche’s automotive segment for the full year 2026 is expected to rise to 5.5–7.5% (previous forecast: 3–5%). Porsche will now focus on its core business.

This is a diplomatic way of saying that the company now has other priorities, including improving profitability and directing resources towards its own product range. Such a move was, in any case, expected after Porsche’s operating profit fell by as much as 93% last year. On the other hand, for Rimac this deal is confirmation of the value he has created, because it is worth remembering that this was Porsche’s first investment in history. They invested the largest amount of capital in Rimac Group, and Rimac was the only one that ultimately integrated components into their cars. Not only that, all of Porsche’s other similar partnerships ended fairly badly. Those projects either no longer exist or are barely surviving, so they are unlikely to bring any tangible benefits. Hisham Elhaddad, co-founder and managing partner of HOF Capital, appeared on Bloomberg News to discuss the completed acquisition of Porsche’s stakes in Bugatti Rimac and Rimac Group by HOF Capital. With this move, HOF has become the largest shareholder in Rimac Group alongside Mate Rimac, and Hisham has joined the supervisory boards of both Bugatti Rimac and Rimac Group.

“We entered Rimac Group back in 2022, but as a small investor with only a one-per-cent stake. So we have been following this story for five years, and especially since Mate Rimac became CEO, when we saw a major positive turnaround. After all, last year was a record year in Bugatti’s 117-year history. We have now completed a transaction worth more than €1 billion and our stake has jumped to 23.5% in Rimac Group and 45% in Bugatti Rimac,” says Elhaddad. 55 percent of the stake in Bugatti Rimac will be held by Rimac, with the remainder by HOF Capital.

a sense of optimism

He added that the investment in Rimac actually fits well with their investment strategy, which over the past ten years has brought a series of investments in the tech sector. “We’ve invested in SpaceX and in Anthropic. We see an explosion of projects in the AI segment on the market. We believe that in the next five to ten years AI will be widely adopted. Value will lie in uniqueness and exclusivity, and there really is no better company than Bugatti where we can see that. Bugatti has survived both world wars, and even this recent crisis. If you want your Bugatti model, you have to wait four or five years. We are excited about the partnership with Mate Rimac and his exceptional team and want to increase the value of this iconic brand. For HOF, this deal is a natural step from our roots in venture capital towards leading complex transactions that cover the entire capital structure,” Elhaddad concluded.

In order to have good control over its investment, HOF Capital now holds three seats on the supervisory boards of Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac. Hisham Elhaddad has joined the supervisory boards of Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac, while Josh Klaczek, a partner at HOF Capital, joins the supervisory board of Rimac Group as the second representative of the firm.
