World.title: Uzbek Fergana, S.Korean SEONGEUN sign MoU to localize concrete production
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Uzbekistan’s Fergana region and South Korean construction materials producer SEONGEUN SPECIAL CONCRETE CO., LTD. have signed a memorandum of cooperation to explore joint projects and the localization of special reinforced concrete production in the region.

This was reflected in the statement by the Fergana regional administration, following a visit of a delegation led by Fergana Region Governor Khayrullo Bozorov to the company’s facilities in Nonsan, South Korea’s South Chungcheong Province, as part of its working visit to the country..

Company head Park Kye-young briefed the Uzbek delegation on production processes, product specifications, quality-control systems and technologies used at the facilities.

Bozorov reviewed the manufacturing processes and finished products, with particular attention to South Korean experience in using durable reinforced concrete structures for engineering and utility infrastructure in urban and rural areas.

The sides discussed establishing cooperation between Fergana region and SEONGEUN SPECIAL CONCRETE, introducing advanced Korean technologies and standards in the region, and setting up local production of specialized reinforced concrete products using locally sourced raw materials.

The meeting concluded with the signing of a memorandum of cooperation and the identification of priority areas for potential joint projects.

The proposed cooperation could support the localization of infrastructure-related construction materials in Fergana while bringing Korean production technologies and quality standards to the region.

Founded in 2013, SEONGEUN SPECIAL CONCRETE specializes in precast reinforced concrete products for urban and rural infrastructure, particularly underground utility networks. The company operates three manufacturing plants. Its product portfolio includes reinforced concrete pipes for sewerage, stormwater drainage and irrigation systems, manhole blocks, open concrete channels and other specialized concrete structures. The company supplies its products to public and private-sector customers and operates in accordance with South Korea’s KS national standards and K-mark quality certification requirements

World.title: Kazakhstan's national crypto reserve reaches $700m
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Kazakhstan's national crypto reserve has reached $700 million, with around $200 million already invested.

This was announced in a statement published by the Kazakh government.

“Under the instructions of the Head of State, the National Crypto Reserve has been established. Its current volume is $700 million. Last year, $350 million was allocated to it, and another $350 million this year. The portfolio is managed by the National Bank's National Investment Corporation. Around $200 million of the $700 million has already been invested, mainly through hedge funds operating with liquidity in crypto markets,” the statement said.

According to the information, the direct investments in Bitcoin have not yet been made. Funds have been allocated, among other instruments, to exchange-traded funds (ETFs), securities backed by digital assets, including Bitcoin and others.

A national crypto custody service has also been established on the basis of the Central Securities Depository, allowing Bitcoin and other digital assets to be held if necessary.

The government said the crypto reserve could be expanded in the future, including through confiscated crypto assets.

Vice Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov said during the government's meeting that tax revenues from digital mining in Kazakhstan reached 22.4 billion tenge (about $50 million) in 2025, up from 9.9 billion tenge (about $22.1 million) in 2024.

Baitursynov noted that the increase in revenues was driven by taxation mechanisms established under the 2023 law on digital assets. In addition to corporate income tax, miners pay a separate fee linked to the amount of electricity they consume. The current rate is 2 tenge per kilowatt-hour.

The vice minister also said the ministry would study the experience of other countries where mining companies operate under preferential tax regimes.

The analysis is expected to be conducted within a month in cooperation with relevant government agencies and market participants. Based on its results, possible amendments to legislation are planned to be submitted during the current Kurultai session.

The conversion was made using the National Bank of Kazakhstan's exchange rate of 447.8 KZT per $1 as of September 15, 2026.

World.title: 12 mosques already restored in liberated territories - President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. I must also state that we began restoration work almost immediately after the Second Garabagh War ended in 2021. The first site to be restored was the Aghdam Mosque, President Ilham Aliyev said at a meeting in Baku with participants of international conferences.

The head of state also stated: "To date, 12 mosques that were either completely or partially destroyed have already been restored and rebuilt, and this process is ongoing."

To note, on September 15, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev received Kubanychbek Omuraliev, Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States, members and observers of the Council of Heads of Muslim Religious Boards of the Organization of Turkic States, as well as a delegation comprising co-organizers of the Yahya Bakuvi International Conference and members of the Supreme Religious Council of Caucasian Peoples.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, Lithuania discuss promising areas of bilateral cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Kyrgyzstan and Lithuania discussed promising areas of bilateral cooperation in various sectors.

According to a statement published by the Kyrgyz Ministry of Economy and Commerce, the issue was discussed on September 15, 2026, during a meeting between Deputy Minister of Economy and Commerce Sultan Akhmatov and Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Lithuania Kristupas Vaitekūnas.

"The meeting discussed promising areas of bilateral cooperation, including port infrastructure, the jewelry industry, agriculture, information technology and the financial sector," the statement said.

Following the meeting, the sides agreed to continue work in the identified areas in order to further expand trade and economic cooperation.

Meanwhile, the areas discussed by Kyrgyzstan and Lithuania cover several sectors with potential for practical business cooperation and investment. Further engagement in agriculture, information technology, finance and industry could create opportunities for stronger ties between businesses and institutions of the two countries.

Cooperation in these areas could also contribute to diversifying bilateral trade and expanding the range of goods and services exchanged between the two sides.

The continued work of the relevant authorities is expected to help translate the identified areas of cooperation into concrete projects and new business opportunities, supporting the gradual expansion of Kyrgyz-Lithuanian economic relations.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, South Korea strengthen trade and investment cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Kyrgyz Minister of Economy and Commerce Bakyt Sydykov held a meeting with South Korean Minister of Trade, Industry and Resources Kim Jung-kwan, during which the sides signed a Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in trade and investment.

According to a statement published by the Kyrgyz Ministry of Economy and Commerce, the signed document is aimed at further strengthening trade, economic and investment cooperation.

"Minister of Economy and Commerce of the Kyrgyz Republic Bakyt Sydykov held a meeting with Minister of Trade, Industry and Resources of the Republic of Korea Kim Jung-kwan. During the meeting, a Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in trade and investment was signed between the Ministry of Economy and Commerce of the Kyrgyz Republic and the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources of the Republic of Korea," the statement said.

As part of the implementation of the memorandum, a Trade and Investment Cooperation Committee will operate under the leadership of the deputy ministers of the two ministries.

The document provides for cooperation in economic and industrial development, trade facilitation and investment promotion.

The sides also intend to expand cooperation in the halal industry, critical minerals, digital transformation, chemical industry and textile production, as well as in developing the business environment, technical regulation and intellectual property protection.

World.title: We have never waged war against civilians as this is contrary to the mentality of our people - President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. During the Second Garabagh War, we targeted only military formations. Unlike Armenia, we have never waged war against unarmed civilians, President Ilham Aliyev said at a meeting in Baku with participants of international conferences.

"This is contrary to both the mentality and traditions of our people. I said back during the war that we must take our revenge on the battlefield, and we did so to the fullest extent. The blood of our martyrs was not spilled in vain," the head of state added.

To note, on September 15, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev received Kubanychbek Omuraliev, Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States, members and observers of the Council of Heads of Muslim Religious Boards of the Organization of Turkic States, as well as a delegation comprising co-organizers of the Yahya Bakuvi International Conference and members of the Supreme Religious Council of Caucasian Peoples.

World.title: South Korea offers advanced tech to modernize Kazakhstan’s industry
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. South Korea is ready to support the modernization of Kazakhstan's industry through advanced industrial and digital technologies, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said during talks with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in Seoul.

This was announced in a statement by the press service of the Kazakh president.

“South Korea and Kazakhstan are expanding the scope of foreign cooperation and pursuing pragmatic diplomacy focused on national interests and concrete results. Kazakhstan is an important partner for us in the field of economic security. The country is not only rich in energy and natural resources, but also has significant potential in promising high-tech industries. We are ready to support the modernization of Kazakhstan's industry through our advanced industrial and digital technologies,” Lee said.

He added that amid an unpredictable international environment, the two countries should strengthen cooperation by combining their respective strengths and potential and actively creating new opportunities for mutually beneficial growth.

Lee also reaffirmed his commitment to further deepening bilateral cooperation and noted the similarity of the two countries' foreign policy priorities.

The South Korean president once again thanked Tokayev for his active assistance in returning to South Korea in 2021 the remains of General Hong Beom-do, regarded as a national hero in Korea, and emphasized that the Korean people remember and highly value the gesture.

Tokayev, in turn, noted South Korea's achievements in the economy, science and technology and described the country as a reliable strategic partner for Kazakhstan.

“Korea is a reliable strategic partner of Kazakhstan,” Tokayev said, noting that a street in Kyzylorda was named after General Hong Beom-do and a memorial complex had been opened there.

Tokayev also said the two countries had agreed to raise bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership focused on the future.

“Last year, we held our first telephone conversation, during which we agreed to continue developing a strategic partnership based on mutual trust and friendship. Today, we have reached an agreement to elevate bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership oriented toward the future,” he said.

The Kazakh president noted that South Korea had invested more than $12 billion in Kazakhstan and that major Korean companies were successfully operating in the Kazakh market.

“We are creating all the conditions for them and will continue to do so in the future,” Tokayev said.

He also highlighted the development of cultural and humanitarian ties, noting that around 51,000 South Korean citizens visited Kazakhstan last year.

Tokayev said the two countries had launched a major joint project to build Alatau City and were signing an agreement to open a branch of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) in Alatau.

“I am confident that this step will give new impetus to deepening our cooperation in education and science,” he said.

The Kazakh president also noted the alignment of Astana and Seoul on the international arena, saying the two countries share common positions on global sustainable development and security.

World.title: 'Complete failure': UK baby killer inquiry findings handed down
World.content:
British nurse Lucy Letby was able to murder seven babies because of a "complete failure" to protect babies at the hospital at which she worked, and some of the deaths could have been avoided, the chair of an inquiry has said.

Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall criticised senior staff for not acting sooner, blaming dysfunctional management at the Countess of Chester Hospital, in northern England, and a basic lack of understanding of safeguarding, when she handed down her findings on Tuesday, local time.

Letby, 36, was convicted in 2023 of murdering seven newborns and attempting to murder six others, making her Britain's most prolific serial child killer of modern times. She was later convicted of another attempted murder charge.

Prosecutors said Letby attacked the newborns by giving them an overdose of insulin, injecting them with air or force-feeding them milk between June 2015 and June 2016, in a case that shocked Britain and drew worldwide attention.

But Letby, who was sentenced to life without parole and maintains she is innocent, has also been the subject of a growing campaign, backed by some medical experts and specialists, which has publicly questioned her convictions.

This public inquiry was set up to examine the events at the hospital and the UK health system's handling of them, not Letby's conviction.

Ms Thirlwall, who previously criticised "noise" around the case, did not address Letby's guilt or innocence in her report, dealing with the Countess of Chester Hospital's response and whether suspicions should have been raised earlier.

She also emphasised the impact on those whose children were harmed, saying: "The families must not be collateral damage in the public argument about whether or not Letby is guilty."

Lady Justice Thirlwall made 17 recommendations on Tuesday. (Pool: Peter Byrne via Reuters)

The contents of her report, though, will be pored over by those who assert Letby's innocence, around two dozen of whom gathered outside Liverpool Town Hall on Tuesday.

It will also be examined by the Criminal Cases Review Commission, an independent body that reviews potential miscarriages of justice and is considering an application from Letby's legal team.

"This inquiry has proceeded on the wrong premise and it follows that this has inevitably affected the report as a whole," Letby's lawyer, Mark McDonald, said in a statement.

"Once there was suspicion that Letby may be causing harm deliberately, safeguarding steps should have been taken," Ms Thirlwall said as she delivered her final report.

" No one seems to have thought that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm," she added. "Suspicion is enough. "

She made a series of recommendations to improve neonatal services in the state-run National Health Service, calling on the government to tackle the "long-standing underfunding of hospital services for babies and children".

Thirlwall also suggested a series of measures to protect patients, including fitting cots and incubators with cameras, stronger insulin storage safeguards and an NHS protocol for when staff are suspected to have deliberately harmed a patient.

Inside the Lucy Letby trial Neonatal nurse Lucy Letby's job was to care for some of Chester's sickest babies. She's now been found guilty of their murder.

Richard Scorer, a lawyer at Slater and Gordon who represents three families, said Thirlwall's recommendations should be implemented without delay. "Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust," he said.

Ms Thirlwall's report was particularly critical of senior executives and nursing leaders at the Countess of Chester Hospital, saying at least two of Letby's murders could have been prevented if action was taken sooner.

Three senior hospital managers were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter and remain under investigation, Cheshire Police said, with one of the three also suspected of perverting the course of justice.

Evidence submitted by the force in support of further charges relating to Letby's time working at the Countess of Chester Hospital and Liverpool Women's Hospital was, however, deemed to be insufficient by prosecutors last year.

Reuters

World.title: Russia accuses Danish military helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships
World.content:
Russia has accused Danish military helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships in the Baltic Sea and handed an official note to Copenhagen complaining about such incidents, according Russia's ambassador to Denmark, Russia's RIA state news agency reports.

Vladimir Barbin, the ambassador, was speaking after the Nordic NATO member's military said that a Russian frigate had fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Denmark on Monday, narrowly missing the aircraft.

Denmark's Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no warning or radio contact was made before a Russian frigate fired the flares.

Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus said Russia gave no warning before firing the flares. (Reuters: Tom Little)

He said the flares passed within "a matter of metres" of the helicopters.

RIA cited Mr Barbin as blaming Denmark for the episode.

"I demanded that the Danish side take the necessary measures to prevent such incidents from recurring in the future, and handed over a note to that effect," it cited Mr Barbin as saying.

Russia's Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin was quoted by RIA as saying he had complained about another similar incident last year. (Reuters: Ritzau Scanpix/Claus Bech)

Asked about the matter, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have details and was not in a position to comment.

Mr Barbin was quoted by RIA as saying he had complained about another similar incident last year.

"In September 2025, during a meeting at the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, I was forced to draw attention to dangerous fly-bys and low-altitude hovering carried out on 27 August by a Danish Air Force helicopter over the large anti-submarine ship 'Vice-Admiral Kulakov'," RIA quoted him as saying.

Such manoeuvres posed a collision risk and could have interfered with the Russian ship's equipment, he added, saying the helicopter had not established radio contact or responded to warnings at the time.

Meanwhile, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Tuesday that the spread of the Ukraine-Russia war to the Black Sea and threatening the safety of Turkish citizens was unacceptable, adding that attacks in vessels in the region were harming navigational safety.

Speaking at a press conference alongside his counterpart in Azerbaijan's Baku, Mr Fidan said Türkiye had intensified its efforts to find a solution to the war through an agreement, without elaborating.

Russian forces hit a cargo ship and a ferry carrying military supplies in Ukraine's port of Chornomorsk, the Russian defence ministry said on Tuesday.

Reuters

World.title: 'Disgusting': Leaders condemn alleged Islamophobic attack on bus
World.content:
The Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia has condemned alleged verbal abuse hurled at a 13-year-old girl, who was called an "immigrant mutt" and a "terrorist" on a Sydney bus last week.

The 50-year-old man, who was charged on Tuesday, appeared in videos of the incident obtained by the ABC allegedly telling another girl, "I can't wait until they kill all of you".

His comments appeared to be directed to Muslim women on the bus last Thursday.

According to the 13-year-old, Janna, the incident began when she stood up for another girl in a hijab who the man was allegedly taking photos of without her knowledge.

NSW Police said he was arrested at a Greenacre home about 2:20pm on Tuesday.

Loading...

He was taken to Bankstown Police Station and charged with stalking and intimidation intending fear or physical harm.

Australia's special envoy, Aftab Malik, said the alleged abuse was not unheard of.

"Unfortunately, the Islamophobia victim pool is getting younger, according to the Islamophobia Register Australia," he said.

"Islamophobia does not require spectacular violence to cause serious harm to people.

"The spread of hateful stereotypes, the normalisation of online abuse, the offline threats, and physical attacks to individuals and institutions, all degrade Muslim Australians."

'Everyone has the right to feel safe when travelling'

Mr Malik said he invited Transport for NSW (TfNSW) to work directly with his office to take active steps to ensure the safety of Muslim school children wearing the hijab.

TfNSW said it was aware of the incident which was reported by the bus driver after the fact.

A spokesperson for the department said it was serious about improving safety across the network.

"We welcome engagement with the Office of the Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia and are willing to meet to discuss any concerns raised," they said.

"Everyone has the right to feel safe when travelling on the public transport network, and Transport for NSW works closely with operators, police and community stakeholders to support customer safety and respond to incidents when they occur."

Premier Chris Minns says Muslim women and children deserve to feel safe while using public transport. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

NSW Premier Chris Minns said he was deeply concerned by the increase in Islamophobia.

"Muslim women and girls have every right to wear a hijab, catch a bus, go to school, or walk down the street without being abused or intimidated," he said.

"What happened to this young girl was disgusting, and she should never have had to defend her right to belong in her own country.

"Everyone, no matter your background or religion, deserves to feel safe and respected in New South Wales."

Shadow Minister for Multiculturalism Mark Coure described the incident as "deeply distressing".

"There is no place for Islamophobia in our community. Racism and religious hatred have no place in our society," he said.

'We have a right'

There has been a 612 per cent jump in reported Islamophobic attacks across Australia in the last three years, according to Islamophobia Register Australia.

The figure is based on an increase of average weekly reported incidents, which has risen from 2.5 reports per week to 18.

The organisation has a backlog of 400 cases like Janna's.

Janna said she was subjected to Islamophobic abuse last week. (ABC News)

Executive director Aishah Ali said government funding had dried up.

"We're going to be relying on community fundraising to actually stay operational," she said.

"We've increased our volunteer team, but it's unsustainable for the breadth and the severity of the work to being encapsulated in a volunteer capacity, and nor should it be, because we have a right to equal safety, protection, remedy and recourse."

The register received some funding from Multicultural NSW for youth education initiatives, which Ms Ali said did not cover their core operational work.

The department has also delivered $15 million to support safety and security at places of worship, including mosques, since February 2023.

'It's their choice'

Janna's mother Roula said some politicians were to blame for the unprecedented levels of Islamophobia.

"I think some of the politicians have … a lot to do with this," she said.

"They have views about Islam, that we're oppressed … us women, but we're not.

"The biggest example is me not being a hijabi, and my daughter is. And it's a choice."

Sydney student Janna with her mother Roula (right). (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

Roula said the government should support what women want to wear.

"It's their choice. You want to walk out naked or want to walk out dressed up, your choice," she said.

The man charged over the incident was refused bail to appear before Bankstown Local Court on Wednesday.

World.title: Impact of colonisation on First Nations people far greater than previous estimates, research finds
World.content:
Australia's Indigenous population was up to seven times larger before colonisation than previously estimated, but was devastated following the arrival of Europeans, new research reveals.

Researchers from across Australia say their findings paint a more accurate picture of the impact of colonisation on First Nations people, updating previous population estimates calculated using anthropological information gathered in the 1930s.

In a research paper published on Tuesday evening, the researchers estimated Australia's median pre-colonial Indigenous population was 2.22 million people — significantly higher than previous estimates of between 250,000 and 1 million people.

Find Deep Time stories of ancient Australia near you Ancient First Nations stories are all around us — if you know where to look.

But according to the new research, an estimated 2.06 million First Nations Australians were likely to have died from diseases, massacres and mortality associated with displacement and other colonial-related disturbances to Indigenous ways of life over the late 18th and 19th centuries.

Just over 70 years after the First Fleet landed in Australia in 1788, only seven per cent of Australia's pre-colonial population was estimated to have survived.

The researchers used computer modelling and reviewed ethnographic observations and archaeological and genetic reconstructions to calculate the revised estimates.

"These research findings challenge us to rethink the scale of what happened after 1788," University of Technology Sydney professor and Eualayai/Gamillaroi woman Larissa Behrendt said.

" We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation, but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story. "

Lethal disease, frontier violence decimated Indigenous population

Report co-author and Flinders University global ecology professor Corey Bradshaw said he found it "unsurprising" that it had taken until now to form a more accurate picture of Australia's pre-colonial Indigenous population, given historical biases and racism towards First Nations people.

He said previous studies underestimated the impact of lethal diseases and frontier and structural violence on the population.

"Aboriginal people were considered fauna under our Wildlife Act as late as the 1970s, the first official census of Aboriginal people in Aboriginal in 1971, so it hasn't been that long that we've woken up to the fact these travesties occurred," he said.

Professor Bradshaw said smallpox alone could have killed up to 220,000 First Nations people along the country's east coast within the first 10 years of colonisation.

Professor Corey Bradshaw said previous research had underestimated the impact of lethal diseases on Indigenous peoples after colonisation. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

He said while some massacres were recorded in databases, the information represented "only the tip of the iceberg".

"Probably most of the frontier violence was done under the cover of night, so to speak," he said.

" We expect that the recorded massacres are probably out by an order of magnitude of what was actually happening. "

Research important to truth-telling and reconciliation

Australia's First Nations population has grown since the 1950s, with latest census data showing in 2021, it was at about 37 per cent of the estimated median pre-colonial size.

Researchers estimate that achieving parity with the 1788 pre-colonial population would not be reached until 2047, if current growth trends continue.

In their paper, the researchers wrote that estimating the size of Australia's Indigenous population before colonisation was "invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation".

"Removing 93 per cent of the (Indigenous) population in 70 years, it can't be interpreted in any other way but disastrous," Professor Bradshaw said.

"On the flip side, these Indigenous cultures survived and these people, despite all that horrendous treatment and dispossession and death, managed to perpetuate their languages, their culture, their managing of country and that is worth celebrating."

World.title: Western Renewables Link passes planning hurdle as cost review ordered
World.content:
Victoria's premier has ordered a cost review of a controversial $1.5 billion transmission line project, the same day the planning minister approved a major planning hurdle.

Ben Carroll ordered the immediate and independent cost assessment of the Western Renewables Link (WRL) today, after Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny announced the approval of the project's environment effects statement (EES) overnight.

Mr Carroll said in a statement the review aimed to reduce building costs, and there would be no compulsory acquisition of property while it was underway.

"I respect the public's money. This project was planned almost 10 years ago and Victorian consumers deserve updated, transparent costings," Mr Carroll said.

The proposed route for the Western Renewables Link. (Supplied: Jeremy Harper)

The proposed 190-kilometre transmission line would run between Bulgana, near Ararat in the state's west, and Sydenham in Melbourne's north-west, to connect renewable energy projects in western Victoria to the energy grid.

In the EES, Ms Kilkenny found the project would likely have a significant impact on the environment, namely on "visual amenity" and "landscape values".

But, overall, she found the possible community benefit meant it could proceed and environmental damage could be managed.

The project has caused significant, enduring unrest for many landholders who live in its corridor.

The premier did not indicate whether Labor was reconsidering its commitment to the project when announcing the cost review.

More approvals required

Mr Carroll said in a statement the EES was not a final approval, and the project still required state and Commonwealth agency approvals and the green light from parliament.

Ben Carroll has ordered an immediate review into the cost of the WRL. (ABC News)

However, AusNet, the company responsible for the WRL, can use the assessment as leverage to gain other approvals.

According to AusNet, those secondary requirements may include a permit to remove protected flora under the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act 1988, a permit to relocate wildlife under the Wildlife Act 1975 and a permit to work within or over waterways under the Water Act 1989.

Mr Carroll said in a statement the EES would be completed by the end of the year and its findings would be made public.

Shadow Energy Minister David Davis condemned the government for approving the EES two and a half months before the November election.

David Davis is critical of the government's energy rollout. (ABC News: Richard Sydenham)

"The opposition wrote to the government and said not to grant or provide approvals at this point under the cover of the pre-election period," Mr Davis said.

"The government has sat on this document, it seems, since July and now released it late in the piece in the lead-up to the state election.

"We say the government should not make steps that bind future governments."

Mr Carroll told ABC he was unavailable for an interview.

The future of the WRL is uncertain if Labor loses the November election.

The Coalition has promised it would pause and reconsider the future of WRL if it was elected.

One Nation has said it would cancel the project entirely.

The latest costing for the project is $1.5 billion, more than three times the initial figure given in 2019.

The project has also suffered timeline blowouts. The latest estimate from AusNet said the project would be completed by 2029.

Project 'does not have social licence'

Ripon's Labor incumbent Martha Haylett, the state member for the local government areas where the WRL and a second proposed transmission line called VNI West are set to be built, said in a statement she was glad Mr Carroll had listened to her objections.

Farmers rally at the Marnoo recreation reserve in support of One Nation and against VNI West. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"It has been 1365 days since I spoke about our community's opposition to the Western Renewables Link in my first speech in Parliament," Ms Haylett said in the statement.

"I have raised my objections to this project with three successive Premiers …

"I've said from day one that this project does not have social licence in our community, and that has not changed."

Fifth-generation beef, sheep and potato farmer Gerald Conroy said the EES identified the same issues he and his neighbours in Ballan had been raising for six years.

He said he disagreed with the government's stance that environmental impacts could be appropriately managed.

Gerald Conroy farms in the project corridor at Ballan. (ABC News: Coco Veldkamp)

Mr Conroy said the project had divided his community, and he would no longer vote for Labor.

"[I'm] very disappointed in the government. They think they can mitigate these issues by giving more money to the community," he said.

Victorian Farmers Federation (VFF) president Ryan Milgate welcomed the cost review and said the government should reconsider the state's transmission rollout more broadly.

Ryan Milgate says the government needs to apply greater scrutiny to all energy projects. (ABC News: Sean Warren)

"Farmers have been saying for years that the WRL needs greater scrutiny. The government has now acknowledged that," Mr Milgate said.

He said the same questions needed to be asked of VNI West and other renewable energy projects.

"What will these projects cost, and are there better alternatives that don't decimate productive farmland and regional communities?" Mr Milgate said.

Generous jobs forecast

An AusNet spokesperson for the WRL said the project was required to support Victoria's transition from coal-fired power stations.

They said WRL would help power 1 million homes and would carry more than 3,000 megawatts of electricity through 500 kilovolt lines.

The WRL spokesperson said it also aimed to deliver lasting benefits to regional communities along the proposed project route.

"If approved, WRL is estimated to generate around 700 full time construction jobs, with more expected at the height of construction," the spokesperson said.

"A further 1,100 jobs are forecast to be created as a result of building the transmission line.

"This includes $15 million in funding made available during the project's development phase in response to community feedback calling for earlier benefits, including a $4 million Local Grants Fund, which recently received almost 200 applications for locally-led projects."

The councils set to host the transmission lines were contacted for comment.

World.title: Aussie fashion brand Cue Clothing falls into receivership
World.content:
Sydney-based fashion business Cue Clothing Co entered receivership on Tuesday afternoon.

In a statement, FTI Consulting, appointed as receivers and managers for Cue, said increased sales and other improvements across the group were not enough to offset the overhead costs.

The company, which was founded in 1968 and operates Cue and its sister brand Veronika Maine, will continue trading while the receivers assess the business and restructuring options.

Cue's store locator map shows 69 stores across Australia, including a retail presence in David Jones, Myer and DFO.

A sale process seeking offers for the business would "commence immediately" to secure the future of the brands, according to FTI Consulting.

Duncan Clubb and Shaun McKinnon of BDO were appointed as voluntary administrators on the same day.

It is unclear at this stage whether there will be any job losses due to the company's receivership.

World.title: Mother's videos of dying toddler may be used to train junior doctors
World.content:
Mobile phone videos of a dying toddler recorded by her mother during her care at two regional NSW hospitals could be used to train junior doctors to avoid other "preventable" deaths, an inquest has found.

Deputy State Coroner Joan Baptie made the recommendation today while delivering her findings from an inquest into the death of two-year-old Pippa Mae White at the Orange hospital in 2022.

Loading...

Judge Baptie said that while the toddler died of "natural causes due to sepsis and bacterial pneumonia", it was due to "delayed diagnosis and treatment" and was "wholly preventable".

Annah White filmed nine short videos of her daughter's deteriorating condition from the time they presented at Cowra hospital on the afternoon of June 12 2022 until Pippa's death 18 hours later at Orange.

Pippa Mae White (right) with mother Annah White in June 2022. (Supplied: Annah White)

Ms White told the ABC she and her husband Brock were "so on board" with the recommendation.

"If it can help prevent the outcome that happened to Pippa [from happening] to other children, we're all for it," she said.

"I think the more junior doctors and nurses that can witness the videos and see that story of Pippa and the outcome, it can help in the future with early detection, earlier implementation of the sepsis pathway and a better outcome.

"That's what we were hoping for."

Pippa White in 2022. (Supplied: Annah White)

The inquest heard Pippa's symptoms should have triggered the "paediatric sepsis pathway" — a protocol that escalates medical oversight and shortens the time between reviews — but this did not happen in a timely manner.

Judge Baptie said the videos "proved to be invaluable" and were described by experts giving evidence as "striking" and showing "a clearly septic child".

"Without that primary source material, it is highly likely this inquest would have come to different conclusions," she said.

The inquest heard that Pippa's family had pushed for a coronial inquest after Orange Hospital determined her death was not reportable because it was not an "unexpected outcome".

Pippa Mae White (left) with uncle John and twin brother Leo in May 2022. (Supplied: Annah White)

Ms White said an experience with Pippa's twin Leo, who suffered a cardiac arrest at a young age, pushed her to write to the coroner asking for an investigation.

"Leo's been in an ICU environment and … I saw how well they worked and how great that outcome was," she said.

"Then I experienced, with Pippa, the opposite … it went so horribly wrong.

"My instincts were saying, 'This is not OK. We need to do something about it.'"

Judge Baptie said the Western NSW Local Health District supported the recommendation.

She said the videos should be provided to the Clinical Excellence Commission to "develop training for junior doctors working in emergency departments or paediatric wards".

Pippa White (front left) with her parents and siblings. (Supplied: Annah White)

For Ms White, the end of the inquest has meant the start of a new chapter advocating for better healthcare.

"We can get into the actual fixing part now and implementing some changes," she said.

"If you ever met Pippa, you would know it was easy to mother her and it's easy to fight for justice and to get some change in her honour.

World.title: Failing to curry favour with the demographic
World.content:
When a 50-year-old actor said in Spectrum that, “I’ve got the knees and the back of a 90-year-old retired librarian”, it didn’t sit well with Nola Tucker of Kiama: “As an almost nonagenarian, retired librarian I take exception to Stephen Curry of The Castle fame comparing his knees and back to such as mine. What did he think we were doing? Tell him he’s dreaming.”

“Geoff Gilligan’s Greek translation tale (C8) gave me a laugh and reminded me of my sad attempt at learning German,” admits Peter Pocock of Hornsby. “The only thing I can remember is ‘the coat hanger is in the wardrobe’. Haven’t used it yet, but you never know.”

“When an AI (C8) breaks into a nuclear-armed country’s military system, hacks the launch codes and uses a few to see if they work, will the world be in an On the Beach situation?” asks Charles Haran of Noosa Heads (Qld). “If so, only a handful of oligarchs will be able to escape to Mars, and I suggest all the rest should band together NOW to stop it from ever happening.” We could always send them to Mars early.

“The article on self-driving cars brought to mind our recent experience in London,” writes Paul Koff of Glenhaven. “As we sped down the motorway, our Uber driver was extolling the virtues of his self-driving Tesla and its foolproof nature. To prove a point, he suddenly grabbed a guitar from the front passenger seat and began strumming it. We were taken aback and vaguely terrified, politely asking if he’d put his hands back on the wheel. He did so, laughingly telling us that many people have that reaction. Gee, how surprising.”

Rob Hosking of Paddington says he doesn’t think the Bee Gees (C8) “had reached the heights of their international fame when I passed Robin standing beside their battered Kombi in Park Street.”

World.title: Labor dangles copyright deal to lure AI giants – but with a catch
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalAI Labor dangles copyright deal to lure AI giants – but with a catch Paul Sakkal September 15, 2026 — 8:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor has offered AI firms open use of Australian content for training if they strike deals with enough Australian companies, in an attempt to break an impasse with tech firms wanting to invest billions. Copyright holders such as authors, musicians or publications could be given the right to opt out, but under the proposal, the AI giants would be free to use any other material. The negotiations over Australia’s copyright laws are a pivotal component of the talks between the Albanese government and firms including Anthropic and OpenAI. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in question time on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen These firms view Australia as arguably the best location to train their models outside the US due to a combination of geography, political stability, renewable energy and space. Labor argues the investment represents Australia’s best chance of creating a new phase of growth like the mining boom.



However, Australia’s existing copyright laws, which are tougher than those in most other countries, including the US, expose AI firms to the risk of being sued by international rights holders in Australia. AI execs also do not want Australia’s laws to create an international precedent. AI firms are chiefly worried they could be sued under Australian law by overseas copyright holders, bucking the common view that the US tech giants are most interested in finding ways to avoid paying for Australian content, which comprises only a tiny fragment of the content used to train models such as ChatGPT and Claude. In his keynote speech on AI on July 15, Albanese signalled that Labor wanted to give local creatives control over whether their work was used. “No company should use Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the artist’s control. That includes the artist’s control of the price and value of their work,” he said. “Anything less is theft.” Attorney-General Michelle Rowland’s department this month began consultations on copyright proposals to settle the deadlock.



One option, according to departmental documents released by Senator David Pocock, gives AI firms legal permission to use unprotected material from owners who have not formally opted out. Related Article Exclusive

AI Australia’s massive data centres to be built away from homes as Trump attacks AI critics It follows plans within the proposed digital duty of care to allow adults to opt out of algorithmic social feeds, as the government seeks to regulate rather than block tech companies in Australia. Firms would need to make payments to an organisation that would then distribute money to rights holders. An alternative model would force tech companies to strike content deals with a minimum quota of Australian companies to receive legal rights to train on Australian content.



The document says a key objective of the proposals was to “uphold the prime minister’s commitment to a strong and vibrant Australian creative and media sector”. On Tuesday, OpenAI said Australia would become the first country to host AI model training if copyright could be resolved. Anthropic has offered similar suggestions and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said in August that the investment window, which rests on the copyright negotiation, would run out in months rather than years because the technology was moving so fast. “We are working at pace here,” Marles said on ABC’s 7.30 Report on Tuesday night, noting that “the opportunity for Australia economically is enormous” if the government can collaborate with the tech giants, but any deal needed “to come on terms which are in our national interest”. Pocock, who has been arguing for a tax on AI firms, said he was deeply concerned by the proposals.



“It would mean putting companies’ interests over everyday Australians, giving AI companies access to all Australians’ content unless they opt out and they somehow put some sort of label on it to say, ‘please don’t use this for training’,” he said. Shadow attorney-general Michaelia Cash described the opt-out proposal as “a text and data mining exception with an opt-out bolted on. It is precisely what the government said it had ruled out,” and demanded the government enforce existing laws and ensure deals were struck with all copyright holders. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘I am the Hoax Buster’: Trump takes on America with seven-post rant promoting AI, data centres The Coalition’s communications spokeswoman, Sarah Henderson, said: “This has all the hallmarks of a dirty deal to hand the intellectual property of Australian creators to global AI giants.” Top AI execs this week called for a global slowdown in AI development due to safety fears. US President Donald Trump pushed back and said China, which is pushing for digital supremacy, would not slow down.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday that Abigail Bradshaw, of the Australian Signals Directorate, had raised the prospect of an “early warning system for advanced AI models” which would involve “companies working together with governments to identify and address AI immediately, rather than before it is too late.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Taller towers in three Brisbane suburbs one step closer
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Taller towers in three Brisbane suburbs one step closer William Davis September 15, 2026 — 8:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Significantly taller residential towers are one step closer in three Brisbane suburbs, with updated plans now set to go from council to the state government for approval. As part of the Schrinner administration’s “tall-not-sprawl” approach to planning, Indooroopilly, Carindale and Nundah were chosen for increased heights due to their proximity to shops and public transport. “These are places we believe could, and can, accommodate more homes,” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner told Brisbane City Council on Tuesday. Nundah Village is one of three Brisbane locations earmarked for taller buildings. William Davis His office said some changes were made after public consultation, with about 200 submissions lodged.



While the original proposal would have allowed 30-storey buildings around Carindale Shopping Centre and the future transport interchange – up from the existing 10-storey cap – this was reduced to 25 storeys following feedback from residents. Up to 10 storeys would also be allowed east of Carindale Street, towards Bulimba Creek. In Indooroopilly, up to 25 storeys would be allowed in some areas around that suburb’s shopping centre and close to the train station and bus interchange. The plan would halve the lot size needed to build to maximum height – from 4000 square metres to 2000 square metres.



In Nundah, up to 15 storeys would be allowed in areas around the major centre east of Sandgate Road, near Nundah Village and the train station. The limit would increase to 10 storeys in other areas. The Labor opposition argued that public transport and other infrastructure in the suburbs would struggle to cope with dramatic population increases, while pointing out the planning system meant taller buildings could still be constructed if developers convinced council they could be justified.



“Given Brisbane’s performance-based planning system, we’ll see developers coming in and saying, ‘you told us it needed to be 25, but we can only stack it up with 30. So can we do it?’ and the LNP will say, ‘sure’,” leader Jared Cassidy said. The opposition abstained from voting on the proposal. A document published on the council website suggested the majority of residents who chose to submit feedback on the plan were opposed to it. Of the 195 submissions, 20 supported the proposed amendments, 57 supported them in part, 119 opposed them, and 22 neither supported nor opposed them but provided general feedback.



The proposed changes will now go to the state government for approval, before returning to council to be included in the City Plan. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Of course I’m frightened’: Australian mother flies to son accused of murder in Syria
World.content:
NationalCourts ‘Of course I’m frightened’: Australian mother flies to son accused of murder in Syria Michael Bachelard September 15, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of a young Gold Coast man accused of murdering another Australian in strife-torn Syria is travelling to her son’s side, against government advice, believing he is innocent. Angela Bell plans to fly out this week with human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan to Idlib province in Syria as her son, Patrick Stevenson – a 20-year-old convert to Islam – waits in a local prison facing charges that, if proven, could result in the death penalty. Patrick Stevenson, a Gold Coast Muslim convert who is now in jail in Syria charged with murdering another Australian convert, Abdullah Glen Burgess. Stevenson has been accused by Syrian authorities of killing another Australian convert, Abdullah Glen Burgess, by shooting him at least eight times with an AK-47 rifle inside the dead man’s home. Burgess’ widow, Amatullah Laurie Duniam, is a witness in the case and another Australian-born convert living in Syria. There is no allegation that Stevenson was allied to Islamic State or any other terror group. After initially being investigated in a prison for Islamic State fighters, Syrian authorities transferred him to a civilian prison and charged him with the pre-meditated murder of his fellow Australian.



Bell and Zaydan say the prosecution’s evidence relies on a confession by Stevenson obtained in unknown circumstances, and Amatullah’s witness statement. Amatullah has so far refused offers of “blood money” payment in return for forgiveness. Stevenson has been diagnosed with serious learning difficulties, ADHD and probable autism. How and why he travelled to Syria are a mystery to his parents. The religious leaders on the Gold Coast who converted the young man have also expressed bemusement, and said that, to their knowledge, he was not radicalised. Angela Bell is going to Syria to help her son. Bell told this masthead she was going to Syria to look after her son, and to help him fight the charges at a court hearing on September 23. “I am frightened, of course I am. But he is my child. I cannot sit safely at home on the Gold Coast knowing Patrick is facing this on the other side of the world and wondering why his mum isn’t there,” she said.



“He’s talking to himself, refuses to eat and shower, doesn’t know where he is – sometimes he laughs and rocks.” Patrick Stevenson as a younger man on the Gold Coast. Stevenson’s father, Clay, visited him in prison in Darkush, a small town near the Turkish border, for a court hearing in July. He told this masthead his son was “like a sheet of glass. He didn’t even know who I was. I tried to give him a hug, and he just looked through me like I wasn’t even there”. Bell said the Australian government has provided her son a Syrian lawyer who speaks no English (Stevenson does not speak Arabic) and has refused to fund Zaydan as his Australian lawyer. She said her son had been in custody since December last year, but that Australian consular officials had not visited him in prison. Australia has no diplomatic presence in Syria and still imposes sanctions on groups from whom the country’s new leaders have emerged.



Human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan, who is going to Syria to advocate for her client. Lawyer Zaydan says her client “has no idea what the hell was being said” against him. In the prosecution file, which she arranged to be translated, there was a handwritten, alleged confession “that’s very hard to read”. Stevenson does not read, write or speak Arabic so it was unclear who wrote it, she said. “There is no way in hell a kid from the Gold Coast would have said those things, or agreed with those things,” Zaydan said. Also on the file is a statement from the widow, Amatullah Duniam, saying she was in the neighbouring room of the apartment when Stevenson killed her husband.



“She never met or spoke with Mr Stevenson, yet she says she is 100 per cent sure she heard his voice while she was in another room at the scene of the shooting,” Zaydan said. She described both key pieces of evidence as “profoundly flawed”. Angela Bell is heading to Syria to advocate for her son who is facing a murder charge. Amatullah declined to comment saying, “we will not be speaking to the media”. Bell said in her communications with her son before his December arrest, he had never mentioned Abdullah Burgess. Zaydan says the prosecution file contains a separate statement from Stevenson that he did not kill Burgess, and an application he made for his phone and laptop, which has not been answered.



“What’s in that file is incredibly concerning, and there’s been no legal scrutiny. I don’t believe from what I’ve read so far that Patrick is responsible,” Zaydan said. Editor's pick Islamic State ‘Rot in jail’: Presumed-dead ISIS doctor may try to return to Australia “Our strategy is that unless we’re there in front of the court ... then Patrick’s legal rights will never be afforded.” Bell said there was no way her son could have organised or paid for a trip to Syria on his own. Bell says Stevenson called out of the blue from Bali, then the next time they heard from him, he was in Syria. “This child couldn’t plan to go to the supermarket with his wallet and his shoes; if he had to buy me coffee, he couldn’t find his keys. He’d show up to weddings without his shoes on,” she said.



“He is intelligent, capable of creative thought, art, but his limitations were chronic dyslexia, executive function, forward-planning and consequences.” His medical file, provided to the Syrian court, says: “Patrick has struggled with inattention, forgetfulness, and organisational abilities throughout his life. He has difficulty completing multi-step tasks and often leaves things unfinished. His ADHD symptoms have impacted his education.” The file said he also had probable autism. “The Australian government are telling us, ‘Don’t travel, it’s not safe’. We know it’s not safe,” Bell said. “But we’re also aware that a potentially innocent child, an Australian held in an incredibly dire position in a foreign country, in prison, and the Australian government can’t even send someone to verify his identity.” As Zaydan puts it: “Their position is you make your bed, you lie in it.”



The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement it was providing consular assistance to an Australian detained in Syria although with no embassy or consulate in the country that help was “extremely limited”. Stevenson’s father, Clay, told this masthead the hearing he attended in July had lasted about 15 minutes in a tiny room in front of three judges. “They asked if I was willing to pay blood money and I said yes. To be fair, I think the judges want the forgiveness,” Clay Stevenson said. “They keep pushing [the widow] to say the best option for her is to forgive and get the money ... I don’t think they want the death penalty.” As for his son, Clay said: “All he did was ask about his younger brother. I was trying to ask him if he did it, and he just didn’t respond.” He hoped Bell would have more luck communicating with him.



Hussin Goss, the chairman of the Arundel mosque on the Gold Coast, who converted Stevenson a number of years ago, said he saw “nothing abnormal – he was not trying to be a jihadist or radicalised”. He also did not know why these three Australians would end up in Idlib province in Syria. “Damascus is the capital of Syria, and obviously, it’s a holy place, but it’s not more holy than Mecca and Medina, so why would he go there?” A representative of Worongary mosque who asked not to be named said the young man had also attended there, and was “probably a little bit odd in some of his social dealings”, but otherwise “very polite, very helpful. If you asked him to do something he’d do it”. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘We dropped the ball’: Former spy boss calls for debate on radical Islam
World.content:
PoliticsFederalNational security ‘We dropped the ball’: Former spy boss calls for debate on radical Islam Matthew Knott September 15, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former ASIO boss Dennis Richardson has called for an open discussion about the role of extremist Islamists in promoting antisemitism as he warns against political correctness shutting down important national security debates. Richardson, who abruptly quit his role as a special adviser to the antisemitism royal commission in March, said the nation had failed to respond with appropriate vigour as attacks on Jewish Australians soared following the October 7 massacre and war in Gaza. Dennis Richardson shocked the Jewish community by resigning from the royal commission. Alex Ellinghausen “I tend to agree with those who argue that, following 7 October, we dropped the ball and failed to draw a line,” Richardson said in a speech to the Lowy Institute on Wednesday night. “I am not implying a straight-line connection to the Bondi terrorist attack, as the ingredients that gave rise to that terrible incident are more complex.



“I do believe, however, that a more forceful and consistent response to the blatant antisemitism we saw in the immediate aftermath of 7 October may well have set a different tone and drawn a clearer line between the acceptable and the unacceptable.” The veteran public servant, who led the Department of Defence and Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, said the sources of antisemitism “must be addressed in a sensible and mature way, including open discussion about extremist Islamists, without Australian Muslims as a whole feeling targeted”. “Mainstream Muslim leaders should have a central role in any such discussion,” he said. “Pretending the issue is not there simply leads to conspiracy theories and plays into the hands of other extremists at the other end of the spectrum.” Liberal frontbencher Julian Leeser has questioned why Bell did not call controversial Muslim clerics such as Wissam Haddad and Sheikh Ibrahim Dadoun to give public evidence at the commission.



Some commentators also accused Bell of failing to sufficiently examine the role of radical Islam in the royal commission’s interim report and expressed concerns the issue would be glossed over in the final report. Former High Court judge Virginia Bell, SC, who presided over the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, and senior counsel assisting the inquiry Richard Lancaster, SC. Janie Barrett Richardson contrasted the saturation media coverage given to prominent footballer Israel Folau when he made homophobic comments on social media to the muted response in 2023 when Haddad posted inflammatory comments about Jewish people. While Folau was “almost run out of town” in 2019, Richardson said Haddad’s comments had “received barely any media attention at all” when they were posted. A Federal Court judge last year found Haddad’s comments to be “fundamentally racist and antisemitic, and devastatingly offensive and insulting”.



Richardson said there would be a “stain on Australia’s social cohesion and multicultural tradition” as long as Jewish Australians needed special security in order to worship, attend school and play sport. Related Article Lunch with My chat with Dennis Richardson was very relaxed. Suddenly, his laid-back tone vanished “The royal commission led by Virginia Bell has already done an enormous public service by putting the spotlight onto the experiences of Jewish Australians because of the antisemitism which has taken root in sections of the community,” he said. “But I still do not understand why it took a royal commission to bring into the public consciousness the fact that some Australian kids have to experience their schooling, sporting and religious life behind the sort of security you would expect to find in a strife-torn country. “This is not something which, as a society, we should be prepared to accept.”



Richardson said media outlets had not provided enough initial coverage of attacks on politicians’ offices over the war in Gaza because of misguided fears it would promote social division. He also said much of “the media focus on the 9 October demonstration at the Opera House was on the precise words used by the mob, instead of on the appalling purpose and nature of the demonstration per se”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese appointed Richardson to conduct an inquiry into potential security failures following the December 14 terror attack in Bondi. His probe was then rolled into the royal commission after Albanese bowed to pressure to hold a wide-ranging inquiry, but Richardson and Bell had insurmountable differences about how the royal commission should work. Richardson said he felt he was being treated as a “highly paid researcher” and expressed concern the royal commission would not include substantive recommendations about intelligence and policing in its interim report.



“I reached a view that, rightly or wrongly, my voice was not going to carry much weight at all,” he told this masthead this year. Bell will hand down her final report on December 18, just four days after the first anniversary of the worst terror attack in the nation’s history.

World.title: Jess gave birth on an opioid treatment program. It inspired her to start a PhD
World.content:
NationalScience Jess gave birth on an opioid treatment program. It inspired her to start a PhD Angus Dalton September 15, 2026 — 7:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday. You’re reading an excerpt – sign up to get the whole newsletter in your inbox. Amid the heroin crisis in the 1990s, Professor Ju Lee Oei was part of a team that established a world-first outpatient clinic in Sydney prescribing methadone to newborns exposed to opioids in the womb. “In the past, if a baby was withdrawing and no one recognised it, they’d likely be sent home and die,” Oei, now a senior neonatologist at The Royal Hospital for Women in Sydney and the Mater Research Institute in Brisbane, says. Associate Professor Kelly Clemens (centre) and Dr Isobel Williams worked with Professor Oei to investigate if a gut supplement could benefit babies exposed to opioids. UNSW “These children often came from poorer parts of the community and were invisible.”



Methadone is a synthetic opioid that can substitute illegal drugs and serve as a treatment for people dependent on heroin or fentanyl. It’s a life-saving intervention for many, including pregnant women and babies, that blocks cravings but doesn’t trigger the “high” of other drugs. Treatment of opioid-exposed newborns has improved since the ’90s. But there are still urgent gaps in knowledge, including ways to address long-lasting effects of opioid exposure in infants, which can lead to difficulties with attention, anxiety, learning and impulse control. Now, a group of researchers including Oei, scientists working in animal models, and people with real-life experience of drug use have come together to find new ways to improve the lives of babies exposed to methadone and other opioids. Results from a new study have raised early hopes of a promising new treatment.



Giving birth on methadone Jess Doumany began a methadone program after becoming dependent on heroin. About six months into the program, she fell pregnant. PhD candidate Jess Doumany, pictured with son Billy, is researching new ways of supporting mothers and babies impacted by perinatal opioid exposure. Jess Doumany “I’d lost my mum about six months prior, and my husband had [died by] suicide about 18 months prior to that. It was a really tumultuous time, but methadone really gave me my life and stability back. And obviously gave my body stability back for the fact I got pregnant,” says Doumany, who was living in the Northern Rivers at the time. “But it quickly became apparent there were no resources or information specifically available for women in this position, in regional areas especially.”



Many of Doumany’s caregivers and midwives admitted they didn’t know much about opioid exposure. “It was only some of the older nurses who were around Lismore and Nimbin in the ’70s and ’80s, who had experience with heroin and knew a bit more.” Related Article Women's health ‘It’s exhausting’: How an inquiry into women’s pain exposed a systemic culture of medical bias After Doumany’s son, Billy, was born, he required morphine-assisted withdrawal due to the methadone exposure. But Doumany says there was little consultation with her about the evaluation of his symptoms, and a lack of information and clear protocols regarding treatment. “Two days before discharge, I had two males from child safety walk into my room while I was breastfeeding. Like, no knocking, no announcement, no nothing. “According to them, the fact that Billy had withdrawals of any nature, even though it was from the methadone, constitutes a notification.



“And I was like, well, if that’s the protocol, then I would appreciate if someone had told me that, you know?” The experience inspired Doumany to pursue a PhD at UNSW focused on improving support for mothers and babies impacted by perinatal opioid exposure, in part by bringing in the stories of people with real-life experience. Part of what’s missing, she says, is a focus on babies’ health once they leave hospital, as well as follow-ups and wrap-around supports for mothers and their children. That’s one of the reasons she’s excited about new research that could one day help mitigate potential downstream effects of prenatal opioid exposure. Jess Doumany working with Billy in tow. Jess Doumany



Gut supplement tested in rats Babies exposed to opioids in the womb go “off a cliff edge” at birth, says Associate Professor Kelly Clemens from UNSW’s School of Psychology. “If you imagine going cold turkey with someone with a heroin dependence, you’re kind of doing the same thing with that infant … they can have seizures in the worst cases. Generally, they end up in the neonatal intensive care unit,” Clemens says. Once weaned off opioids, developmental and behavioural issues may arise years down the track. “What we now know is that their long-term health, especially mental health and cognition, is really impacted.”



The new study, led by Clemens and published in Translational Psychiatry, investigates sodium butyrate as a possible treatment for these effects. It’s produced naturally in the gut upon the breakdown of fibre, helping to nourish a healthy microbiome, and it’s also one of the chemicals produced in the gut that travels to the brain. “It really does span that gut-brain axis in the same way that opioids are involved in both gut and brain functions,” Clemens says. Dr Isobel Williams says they were surprised how broad the benefits were in an animal model. UNSW The researchers tested sodium butyrate on pregnant rats. Some were also given methadone. The methadone-exposed pups proved more fearful and anxious than their counterparts and had some damage to brain tissue.



Those treated with sodium butyrate had less damage, better learning behaviours and were more curious. “We were honestly surprised by how broad the improvements were,” Dr Isobel Williams, who led the experiments, says. “It wasn’t just one area; we saw benefits across memory, attention, and even brain structure.” Real-life experience, real-life impact The study in rats is preliminary and there is much more research needed before human trials. Sodium butyrate led to slightly worse outcomes in rats not exposed to methadone, underscoring the need for greater scrutiny and further study. But the researchers are excited about the prospect of a first-of-its-kind long-term treatment for babies exposed to opioids.



“Treatments like methadone are life-saving, and they make a huge difference,” Clemens says. “We’re just thinking about how we can better support that journey so that the outcomes for everyone are more positive.” Related Article Drugs There’s good news about America’s fentanyl crisis – but it’s not the full story Doumany and the UNSW scientists say insight from people who have real-life experiences with drug dependence and treatment keeps research squarely focused on real-life impact. “What’s really exciting about this research – and it’s early because it is at the stage of animal models – is that it confirms the relationship or axis between gut health and mental health,” Doumany, who didn’t work on the research directly but is working with the UNSW team on other studies, says. Doumany is also the Director of Research at the Australian Injecting and Illicit Drug Users League (AIVL), which co-developed a first-of-its-kind national research strategy for and by people who use drugs.



“It’s about establishing our own ethical standards and protocols,” she says. “It doesn’t make sense that we’ve got people who have never used drugs, who aren’t part of our community, setting research priorities. “Our community needs to be involved every step of the way.” Lifeline 13 11 14 The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence.
