World.title: Failing to curry favour with the demographic
World.content:
When a 50-year-old actor said in Spectrum that, “I’ve got the knees and the back of a 90-year-old retired librarian”, it didn’t sit well with Nola Tucker of Kiama: “As an almost nonagenarian, retired librarian I take exception to Stephen Curry of The Castle fame comparing his knees and back to such as mine. What did he think we were doing? Tell him he’s dreaming.”

“Geoff Gilligan’s Greek translation tale (C8) gave me a laugh and reminded me of my sad attempt at learning German,” admits Peter Pocock of Hornsby. “The only thing I can remember is ‘the coat hanger is in the wardrobe’. Haven’t used it yet, but you never know.”

“When an AI (C8) breaks into a nuclear-armed country’s military system, hacks the launch codes and uses a few to see if they work, will the world be in an On the Beach situation?” asks Charles Haran of Noosa Heads (Qld). “If so, only a handful of oligarchs will be able to escape to Mars, and I suggest all the rest should band together NOW to stop it from ever happening.” We could always send them to Mars early.

“The article on self-driving cars brought to mind our recent experience in London,” writes Paul Koff of Glenhaven. “As we sped down the motorway, our Uber driver was extolling the virtues of his self-driving Tesla and its foolproof nature. To prove a point, he suddenly grabbed a guitar from the front passenger seat and began strumming it. We were taken aback and vaguely terrified, politely asking if he’d put his hands back on the wheel. He did so, laughingly telling us that many people have that reaction. Gee, how surprising.”

Rob Hosking of Paddington says he doesn’t think the Bee Gees (C8) “had reached the heights of their international fame when I passed Robin standing beside their battered Kombi in Park Street.”

World.title: Labor dangles copyright deal to lure AI giants – but with a catch
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalAI Labor dangles copyright deal to lure AI giants – but with a catch Paul Sakkal September 15, 2026 — 8:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor has offered AI firms open use of Australian content for training if they strike deals with enough Australian companies, in an attempt to break an impasse with tech firms wanting to invest billions. Copyright holders such as authors, musicians or publications could be given the right to opt out, but under the proposal, the AI giants would be free to use any other material. The negotiations over Australia’s copyright laws are a pivotal component of the talks between the Albanese government and firms including Anthropic and OpenAI. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in question time on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen These firms view Australia as arguably the best location to train their models outside the US due to a combination of geography, political stability, renewable energy and space. Labor argues the investment represents Australia’s best chance of creating a new phase of growth like the mining boom.



However, Australia’s existing copyright laws, which are tougher than those in most other countries, including the US, expose AI firms to the risk of being sued by international rights holders in Australia. AI execs also do not want Australia’s laws to create an international precedent. AI firms are chiefly worried they could be sued under Australian law by overseas copyright holders, bucking the common view that the US tech giants are most interested in finding ways to avoid paying for Australian content, which comprises only a tiny fragment of the content used to train models such as ChatGPT and Claude. In his keynote speech on AI on July 15, Albanese signalled that Labor wanted to give local creatives control over whether their work was used. “No company should use Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the artist’s control. That includes the artist’s control of the price and value of their work,” he said. “Anything less is theft.” Attorney-General Michelle Rowland’s department this month began consultations on copyright proposals to settle the deadlock.



One option, according to departmental documents released by Senator David Pocock, gives AI firms legal permission to use unprotected material from owners who have not formally opted out. Related Article Exclusive

AI Australia’s massive data centres to be built away from homes as Trump attacks AI critics It follows plans within the proposed digital duty of care to allow adults to opt out of algorithmic social feeds, as the government seeks to regulate rather than block tech companies in Australia. Firms would need to make payments to an organisation that would then distribute money to rights holders. An alternative model would force tech companies to strike content deals with a minimum quota of Australian companies to receive legal rights to train on Australian content.



The document says a key objective of the proposals was to “uphold the prime minister’s commitment to a strong and vibrant Australian creative and media sector”. On Tuesday, OpenAI said Australia would become the first country to host AI model training if copyright could be resolved. Anthropic has offered similar suggestions and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said in August that the investment window, which rests on the copyright negotiation, would run out in months rather than years because the technology was moving so fast. “We are working at pace here,” Marles said on ABC’s 7.30 Report on Tuesday night, noting that “the opportunity for Australia economically is enormous” if the government can collaborate with the tech giants, but any deal needed “to come on terms which are in our national interest”. Pocock, who has been arguing for a tax on AI firms, said he was deeply concerned by the proposals.



“It would mean putting companies’ interests over everyday Australians, giving AI companies access to all Australians’ content unless they opt out and they somehow put some sort of label on it to say, ‘please don’t use this for training’,” he said. Shadow attorney-general Michaelia Cash described the opt-out proposal as “a text and data mining exception with an opt-out bolted on. It is precisely what the government said it had ruled out,” and demanded the government enforce existing laws and ensure deals were struck with all copyright holders. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘I am the Hoax Buster’: Trump takes on America with seven-post rant promoting AI, data centres The Coalition’s communications spokeswoman, Sarah Henderson, said: “This has all the hallmarks of a dirty deal to hand the intellectual property of Australian creators to global AI giants.” Top AI execs this week called for a global slowdown in AI development due to safety fears. US President Donald Trump pushed back and said China, which is pushing for digital supremacy, would not slow down.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday that Abigail Bradshaw, of the Australian Signals Directorate, had raised the prospect of an “early warning system for advanced AI models” which would involve “companies working together with governments to identify and address AI immediately, rather than before it is too late.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Taller towers in three Brisbane suburbs one step closer
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Taller towers in three Brisbane suburbs one step closer William Davis September 15, 2026 — 8:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Significantly taller residential towers are one step closer in three Brisbane suburbs, with updated plans now set to go from council to the state government for approval. As part of the Schrinner administration’s “tall-not-sprawl” approach to planning, Indooroopilly, Carindale and Nundah were chosen for increased heights due to their proximity to shops and public transport. “These are places we believe could, and can, accommodate more homes,” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner told Brisbane City Council on Tuesday. Nundah Village is one of three Brisbane locations earmarked for taller buildings. William Davis His office said some changes were made after public consultation, with about 200 submissions lodged.



While the original proposal would have allowed 30-storey buildings around Carindale Shopping Centre and the future transport interchange – up from the existing 10-storey cap – this was reduced to 25 storeys following feedback from residents. Up to 10 storeys would also be allowed east of Carindale Street, towards Bulimba Creek. In Indooroopilly, up to 25 storeys would be allowed in some areas around that suburb’s shopping centre and close to the train station and bus interchange. The plan would halve the lot size needed to build to maximum height – from 4000 square metres to 2000 square metres.



In Nundah, up to 15 storeys would be allowed in areas around the major centre east of Sandgate Road, near Nundah Village and the train station. The limit would increase to 10 storeys in other areas. The Labor opposition argued that public transport and other infrastructure in the suburbs would struggle to cope with dramatic population increases, while pointing out the planning system meant taller buildings could still be constructed if developers convinced council they could be justified.



“Given Brisbane’s performance-based planning system, we’ll see developers coming in and saying, ‘you told us it needed to be 25, but we can only stack it up with 30. So can we do it?’ and the LNP will say, ‘sure’,” leader Jared Cassidy said. The opposition abstained from voting on the proposal. A document published on the council website suggested the majority of residents who chose to submit feedback on the plan were opposed to it. Of the 195 submissions, 20 supported the proposed amendments, 57 supported them in part, 119 opposed them, and 22 neither supported nor opposed them but provided general feedback.



The proposed changes will now go to the state government for approval, before returning to council to be included in the City Plan. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Diplomacy needed, not aggression and hurt
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Diplomacy needed, not aggression and hurt September 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ONE NATION One Nation keep trying to convince Australians that they are ready to govern this country, yet their words indicate they lack true understanding of what it takes to lead a democratic nation. Australian leaders cannot simply disparage and express hatred for individuals and groups in our society. Leaders must demonstrate that they will serve and represent all people through their words, actions, and policies.

In a democracy, all voices are important, yet One Nation constantly bombard us with aggressive soundbites about who is of value in our society and who is unworthy.

To counteract these messages, we need to remind ourselves and each other that we can win the fight against the global wave of angry voices trying to overwhelm voters with ragebait, because we know that governing a country requires finesse, balance, and diplomacy.

Meagan Noronha, Heidelberg Hanson must apologise for ignorance

Re ″⁣Fury over Hanson’s ‘primitive race’ claim″⁣, 15/9. Pauline Hanson’s denigration of our First Nations people is disgusting and she must apologise. It again suggests racism and ignorance.

Hanson needs to be reminded that this land was occupied by white people who systematically endeavoured to ″⁣breed out″⁣ Aboriginal people in many inhumane ways – disease, stolen land, and massacres – to name just a few.

Our First Nations people have a proud history of their relationship with the land, sea and sky. They carry a spirituality that many of us could learn from.

Judith Morrison, Nunawading



Indigenous Australians didn’t wreck the joint

How many languages can Hanson speak? Is she to be credited with inventing the wheel, or is she just going along for the ride? In the meantime, our Indigenous people can point to their traditional knowledge of their surroundings to show her how they lived on this land without wrecking the joint. If this is “primitive”, Indigenous people should wear this moniker as a badge of honour. We should all be more “primitive” if we want to save the world for our descendants.

Pamela Lloyd, West Brunswick Hanson’s comments feed extremists

Pauline Hanson’s baseless comments about Andrew Hastie, Anthony Albanese’s late mother and Indigenous Australians have brought such a dangerous level of baseness to our politics. Her seeming inability to convert her anger into constructive, accountably evidenced policy for the common good of Australia, will encourage extremist One Nation supporters to follow her example to spread such baseless claims.

Jennifer Gerrand, Carlton North One Nation fracturing an already stressed society

The latest revelations of Pauline Hanson’s hate agenda, while appalling, should come as no surprise (“Fury over Hanson’s ‘primitive race’ claim” 15/9).

Hanson is intent on fuelling rage and anger. In this instance, targeting and belittling our First Nations Peoples displays her complete lack of understanding of their place and contribution to our history.

While the electorate is experiencing economic pain and frustration with the major parties, the answer does not lie in embracing a party hellbent on fracturing our already stressed society.

The upcoming Victorian election will be another test of what we value and who we trust. The Coalition must declare who they will preference on the ballot, so voters can determine who can not only serve their interests but also protect what is fair and just in our society.

Anne Lyon, Camberwell THE FORUM Clueless political class

The recent ABC TV national forum on migration on Monday (14/9) exposed a political class completely out of touch. All sides argue over immigration tweaks and interest rate adjustments, yet completely ignore the structural engine failure ruining the country.

Ever since Covid, everyday Australians have been trapped in survival mode. The real culprit is 40 years of privatisation, corporate outsourcing, and absolute reliance on private developers and global consulting firms. We are paying double for outsourced services while our own public wealth is siphoned into private profits.

We do not need short-term political fixes to win the next election. We need to open a serious national dialogue about returning to the post-war, nation-building model that successfully created our middle class.

That means pausing the corporate ″⁣visa factory″⁣ to upskill our own workforce through proper, hands-on technical schools. It means keeping our own natural resources onshore to guarantee cheap domestic energy and revive manufacturing.

And, it means bypassing private developers so the government builds public housing directly– restoring the historical rule where long-term tenants could buy their home without a bank loan simply by paying their normal rent rate over 19 years.

It is time all sides of government stop serving their corporate donors and fix the country for its actual citizens.

Kylie Bowers, Reservoir



Beware simple solutions

Barnaby Joyce, is now an out and proud populist re slashing migration. He says One Nation is following ″⁣the will of the people″⁣. Perhaps those people want even more critical staff shortages in aged care, nursing and disability sectors? Some aspects of our migration program need tweaking, but surely not in the skilled migrant sector.

Simple solutions are easy to sell politically but don’t solve complex problems. In fact, they just create other challenges.

Sue Peterken, Berwick Driving migrants away

It was sad to learn that articulate and passionate human rights and refugee lawyer Nyadol Nyuon, who professed on the ABC TV’s national forum on migration (14/9) to love her adopted country, feels she needs to leave our shores. She is exactly the kind of person this country needs to attract and keep as part of our multicultural society. We can ill-afford to drive these kinds of people away by the divisive and hurtful comments from One Nation.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Strange patriotism

Since the Vietnam war, Australia’s SAS has been held in high regard amongst global special services units. Then came along Ben Robert-Smith and trashed that reputation, but the law of defamation caught him, and in so doing, helped restore the SAS’s previous reputation.

Unfortunately, two Australian women with a yearning for publicity don’t appear to want that reputation restored. Neither of them has any military experience. They would both claim to be patriots. Go figure.

Barry Toll, Pipers Creek PM, time to step up

Anthony Albanese has long wished for more civility in parliament, and in society more generally. He does his best to model civility in his restrained presence when answering reporters’ questions, but he is more at home in the rough and tumble of question time in parliament where the Coalition opposition behave like a zoo at feeding time.

Then there’s Pauline Hanson, modelling the nastiness and ignorance which has been her trademark for decades and which appeals to her followers. Albanese needs to step up, take the limelight off Hanson, and offer a greater vision of what his Labor government stands for.

There is time, but he can’t wait for the economy to become more productive, inflation to fall and real wages to rise. Be civil, but take the initiative. And by initiative, I don’t mean attacking the aged care sector and those depending on the NDIS for a manageable life. Can’t he find any big issues to reignite the light on the hill?

John Whelen, Box Hill Sth No cuts to aged care

The ceasing of the rebate to pensioners for health insurance to fund aged care is counter productive. The aged cannot linger on public health lists for essentials such as hip surgery, cardiac procedures and cataracts. Many pensioners who can’t afford increases in health insurance and will exit the system. This will result in more demand for aged care and hospital waiting lists.

Maria McKinnon, Northcote



So who volunteers for cuts?

A survey recently asked how governments should reduce debt. The majority of participants opted for decreased services. Not the services they individually use or rely on, I assume. Infrastructure improvements, like rail crossing removals, are quickly taken for granted, as are the dozens of new schools that government must provide. When governments, state or federal, attempt to curtail expenditure in any area, there are hordes of objectors. Where are the corresponding hordes of people offering to pay more tax, or forgo a subsidy?

Yes, there are many areas that require more, often urgent, funding, but despite what many seem to imagine, governments do not have vast orchards of money trees.

Gaye Boswell, Burwood East Alternative facts

What reasoning is used by a politician in admitting to being a conspiracy theorist? As the term implies, conspiracy theorists don’t rely on reality to create their falsehoods; that is, all they need is an audience of fools. Which, it seems is what One Nation’s Warren Pickering thinks of people who would vote for him.

Henry Herzog, St Kilda East BYO solar panels

Re ‴⁣⁣Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia″⁣, 15/9. What more evidence do we need to confirm the pathetic standard of planning we have in this state and country, when renters and even apartment owners are expected to celebrate being able to bring their own solar panels with them?

Talk about a patch-up job to compensate for dumb design. Too bad for those with overshadowed balconies or just facing south. So much for the promise of urban consolidation. No wonder most of us prefer a detached house, rooftop solar of course, and room enough for children to play and oldies to top up their vitamin D, in a happily, sustainably decentralised Victoria.

Bernadette George, Mildura Power costs plummet

It’s great to see renters and apartment dwellers will soon be able to take advantage of cheaper power through plug-in solar and batteries (15/9). The safety and affordability of accredited panels and batteries are assured through their established use in countries across the globe.

Since installing rooftop solar and a home battery, our power bills have plummeted in parallel to our reduced reliance on gas. It is only fair that all Australians can take advantage of our continent’s abundant renewable energy.

Julia Croatto, Kew Time on duck season

More of the same under new Premier Ben Carroll is unlikely to return the Labor state government in November.

Changes in direction such as a royal commission into Big Build indicates a difference, but more is needed.

The annual assault on our native waterbirds called duck shooting season is an opportunity for change rather than continuing pandering to the gun shooters lobby as his predecessors Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan did.

The latter ignored the report commissioned by her own government to end this hopelessly outdated activity and now is the opportunity for this to occur under the new leadership.

Tony Delaney, Warrnambool



Player behaviour

As an avid watcher of many sporting codes, I am ashamed at the on-field disrespect that some AFL players display towards opponents.

It seems to be acceptable for some players to rub their opponent’s face into the ground, point out their obvious mistake via a tirade of abuse, and generally bring the game into disrepute with a win-at-all-cost attitude.

Coaches at junior level would be frustrated by this approach knowing that the youngsters mimic the behaviour of their AFL heroes.

I would hope that senior coaches are not encouraging this nasty, demeaning approach but, unfortunately, it appears that winning at the expense of your opponent’s dignity is what supporters are prepared to accept.

Peter Cooke, Gisborne High speed Dutch

Your correspondent (Letters, ″⁣Ride as Dutch do″⁣, 15/9) writes of the nirvana of the Netherlands and its cycling paths of gold.

My first experience with the paths was trying to cross a street in Amsterdam in 2014 and nearly being run down by blinkered, high-speed Dutch giants, on said paths, not giving any heed to the pedestrians in their midst.

Rather frightening to experience!

Shaun Dunford, Mount Gambier, SA Joy of Jack Russells

Re Letters and biting dogs (14/9). We had a Jack Russell terrier for 16 years, during which time she never bit anyone, not even strangers.

She was a rescue dog – someone dumped her, as a puppy, on Flemington racecourse. She was intelligent and loving and quick to understand what she was asked to do. She only had to be told once. I can’t understand why anyone would say “Don’t get a Jack Russell”.

Sue Bursztynski, Elwood AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding



One Nation

Indigenous people lived for 65,000 years in places where a white person would die in a day.

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick Barnaby Joyce says to follow the “will of the people” and ignore the advice of economists. He’s become quite the expert in telling us to ignore experts, so I think I’ll take his advice and ignore him.

Barry Miller, Kyneton I am annoyed by the huge publicity One Nation and Pauline Hanson are getting. However, the more exposure she gets, the more we know about her hateful “policies”.

Maureen Goldie, Blackwood, SA Pauline is right, our Indigenous people didn’t invent the wheel. But their culture has existed for more than tens of thousands of years. Our society, however, might not survive much longer!

Martin Siegrist, Moriac Pauline has just trumped Trump.

Bernie O’Brien, Fairfield



Furthermore

When I play 500, my friend’s favourite call is No Trumps.

Alan Rainer, Carlton North According to Trump ″⁣The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a strong and smart and (high IQ) president″⁣. Pity they don’t have one.

Russ Davis, Camperdown How long before we start calling AI, AE? Artificial Extinction.

Ron Mather, Melbourne Who wants more of their life misappropriated by tech?

Bill Burns, Bendigo The Victorian government has spent billions digging holes under Melbourne while in the regions we’ve dug our own at risk to lives. Follow a swerving driver on the Mornington Peninsula, you know it’s a local dodging familiar potholes. Fix them properly, please.

Fran Henke, Hastings



Re ″⁣Hands up for self driving cars″⁣ 15/9. There’s some irony in having your car insurance reduced if you choose to keep your hands off the steering wheel.

Robin Jensen Castlemaine The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Of course I’m frightened’: Australian mother flies to son accused of murder in Syria
World.content:
NationalCourts ‘Of course I’m frightened’: Australian mother flies to son accused of murder in Syria Michael Bachelard September 15, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of a young Gold Coast man accused of murdering another Australian in strife-torn Syria is travelling to her son’s side, against government advice, believing he is innocent. Angela Bell plans to fly out this week with human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan to Idlib province in Syria as her son, Patrick Stevenson – a 20-year-old convert to Islam – waits in a local prison facing charges that, if proven, could result in the death penalty. Patrick Stevenson, a Gold Coast Muslim convert who is now in jail in Syria charged with murdering another Australian convert, Abdullah Glen Burgess. Stevenson has been accused by Syrian authorities of killing another Australian convert, Abdullah Glen Burgess, by shooting him at least eight times with an AK-47 rifle inside the dead man’s home. Burgess’ widow, Amatullah Laurie Duniam, is a witness in the case and another Australian-born convert living in Syria. There is no allegation that Stevenson was allied to Islamic State or any other terror group. After initially being investigated in a prison for Islamic State fighters, Syrian authorities transferred him to a civilian prison and charged him with the pre-meditated murder of his fellow Australian.



Bell and Zaydan say the prosecution’s evidence relies on a confession by Stevenson obtained in unknown circumstances, and Amatullah’s witness statement. Amatullah has so far refused offers of “blood money” payment in return for forgiveness. Stevenson has been diagnosed with serious learning difficulties, ADHD and probable autism. How and why he travelled to Syria are a mystery to his parents. The religious leaders on the Gold Coast who converted the young man have also expressed bemusement, and said that, to their knowledge, he was not radicalised. Angela Bell is going to Syria to help her son. Bell told this masthead she was going to Syria to look after her son, and to help him fight the charges at a court hearing on September 23. “I am frightened, of course I am. But he is my child. I cannot sit safely at home on the Gold Coast knowing Patrick is facing this on the other side of the world and wondering why his mum isn’t there,” she said.



“He’s talking to himself, refuses to eat and shower, doesn’t know where he is – sometimes he laughs and rocks.” Patrick Stevenson as a younger man on the Gold Coast. Stevenson’s father, Clay, visited him in prison in Darkush, a small town near the Turkish border, for a court hearing in July. He told this masthead his son was “like a sheet of glass. He didn’t even know who I was. I tried to give him a hug, and he just looked through me like I wasn’t even there”. Bell said the Australian government has provided her son a Syrian lawyer who speaks no English (Stevenson does not speak Arabic) and has refused to fund Zaydan as his Australian lawyer. She said her son had been in custody since December last year, but that Australian consular officials had not visited him in prison. Australia has no diplomatic presence in Syria and still imposes sanctions on groups from whom the country’s new leaders have emerged.



Human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan, who is going to Syria to advocate for her client. Lawyer Zaydan says her client “has no idea what the hell was being said” against him. In the prosecution file, which she arranged to be translated, there was a handwritten, alleged confession “that’s very hard to read”. Stevenson does not read, write or speak Arabic so it was unclear who wrote it, she said. “There is no way in hell a kid from the Gold Coast would have said those things, or agreed with those things,” Zaydan said. Also on the file is a statement from the widow, Amatullah Duniam, saying she was in the neighbouring room of the apartment when Stevenson killed her husband.



“She never met or spoke with Mr Stevenson, yet she says she is 100 per cent sure she heard his voice while she was in another room at the scene of the shooting,” Zaydan said. She described both key pieces of evidence as “profoundly flawed”. Angela Bell is heading to Syria to advocate for her son who is facing a murder charge. Amatullah declined to comment saying, “we will not be speaking to the media”. Bell said in her communications with her son before his December arrest, he had never mentioned Abdullah Burgess. Zaydan says the prosecution file contains a separate statement from Stevenson that he did not kill Burgess, and an application he made for his phone and laptop, which has not been answered.



“What’s in that file is incredibly concerning, and there’s been no legal scrutiny. I don’t believe from what I’ve read so far that Patrick is responsible,” Zaydan said. Editor's pick Islamic State ‘Rot in jail’: Presumed-dead ISIS doctor may try to return to Australia “Our strategy is that unless we’re there in front of the court ... then Patrick’s legal rights will never be afforded.” Bell said there was no way her son could have organised or paid for a trip to Syria on his own. Bell says Stevenson called out of the blue from Bali, then the next time they heard from him, he was in Syria. “This child couldn’t plan to go to the supermarket with his wallet and his shoes; if he had to buy me coffee, he couldn’t find his keys. He’d show up to weddings without his shoes on,” she said.



“He is intelligent, capable of creative thought, art, but his limitations were chronic dyslexia, executive function, forward-planning and consequences.” His medical file, provided to the Syrian court, says: “Patrick has struggled with inattention, forgetfulness, and organisational abilities throughout his life. He has difficulty completing multi-step tasks and often leaves things unfinished. His ADHD symptoms have impacted his education.” The file said he also had probable autism. “The Australian government are telling us, ‘Don’t travel, it’s not safe’. We know it’s not safe,” Bell said. “But we’re also aware that a potentially innocent child, an Australian held in an incredibly dire position in a foreign country, in prison, and the Australian government can’t even send someone to verify his identity.” As Zaydan puts it: “Their position is you make your bed, you lie in it.”



The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement it was providing consular assistance to an Australian detained in Syria although with no embassy or consulate in the country that help was “extremely limited”. Stevenson’s father, Clay, told this masthead the hearing he attended in July had lasted about 15 minutes in a tiny room in front of three judges. “They asked if I was willing to pay blood money and I said yes. To be fair, I think the judges want the forgiveness,” Clay Stevenson said. “They keep pushing [the widow] to say the best option for her is to forgive and get the money ... I don’t think they want the death penalty.” As for his son, Clay said: “All he did was ask about his younger brother. I was trying to ask him if he did it, and he just didn’t respond.” He hoped Bell would have more luck communicating with him.



Hussin Goss, the chairman of the Arundel mosque on the Gold Coast, who converted Stevenson a number of years ago, said he saw “nothing abnormal – he was not trying to be a jihadist or radicalised”. He also did not know why these three Australians would end up in Idlib province in Syria. “Damascus is the capital of Syria, and obviously, it’s a holy place, but it’s not more holy than Mecca and Medina, so why would he go there?” A representative of Worongary mosque who asked not to be named said the young man had also attended there, and was “probably a little bit odd in some of his social dealings”, but otherwise “very polite, very helpful. If you asked him to do something he’d do it”. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘We dropped the ball’: Former spy boss calls for debate on radical Islam
World.content:
PoliticsFederalNational security ‘We dropped the ball’: Former spy boss calls for debate on radical Islam Matthew Knott September 15, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former ASIO boss Dennis Richardson has called for an open discussion about the role of extremist Islamists in promoting antisemitism as he warns against political correctness shutting down important national security debates. Richardson, who abruptly quit his role as a special adviser to the antisemitism royal commission in March, said the nation had failed to respond with appropriate vigour as attacks on Jewish Australians soared following the October 7 massacre and war in Gaza. Dennis Richardson shocked the Jewish community by resigning from the royal commission. Alex Ellinghausen “I tend to agree with those who argue that, following 7 October, we dropped the ball and failed to draw a line,” Richardson said in a speech to the Lowy Institute on Wednesday night. “I am not implying a straight-line connection to the Bondi terrorist attack, as the ingredients that gave rise to that terrible incident are more complex.



“I do believe, however, that a more forceful and consistent response to the blatant antisemitism we saw in the immediate aftermath of 7 October may well have set a different tone and drawn a clearer line between the acceptable and the unacceptable.” The veteran public servant, who led the Department of Defence and Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, said the sources of antisemitism “must be addressed in a sensible and mature way, including open discussion about extremist Islamists, without Australian Muslims as a whole feeling targeted”. “Mainstream Muslim leaders should have a central role in any such discussion,” he said. “Pretending the issue is not there simply leads to conspiracy theories and plays into the hands of other extremists at the other end of the spectrum.” Liberal frontbencher Julian Leeser has questioned why Bell did not call controversial Muslim clerics such as Wissam Haddad and Sheikh Ibrahim Dadoun to give public evidence at the commission.



Some commentators also accused Bell of failing to sufficiently examine the role of radical Islam in the royal commission’s interim report and expressed concerns the issue would be glossed over in the final report. Former High Court judge Virginia Bell, SC, who presided over the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, and senior counsel assisting the inquiry Richard Lancaster, SC. Janie Barrett Richardson contrasted the saturation media coverage given to prominent footballer Israel Folau when he made homophobic comments on social media to the muted response in 2023 when Haddad posted inflammatory comments about Jewish people. While Folau was “almost run out of town” in 2019, Richardson said Haddad’s comments had “received barely any media attention at all” when they were posted. A Federal Court judge last year found Haddad’s comments to be “fundamentally racist and antisemitic, and devastatingly offensive and insulting”.



Richardson said there would be a “stain on Australia’s social cohesion and multicultural tradition” as long as Jewish Australians needed special security in order to worship, attend school and play sport. Related Article Lunch with My chat with Dennis Richardson was very relaxed. Suddenly, his laid-back tone vanished “The royal commission led by Virginia Bell has already done an enormous public service by putting the spotlight onto the experiences of Jewish Australians because of the antisemitism which has taken root in sections of the community,” he said. “But I still do not understand why it took a royal commission to bring into the public consciousness the fact that some Australian kids have to experience their schooling, sporting and religious life behind the sort of security you would expect to find in a strife-torn country. “This is not something which, as a society, we should be prepared to accept.”



Richardson said media outlets had not provided enough initial coverage of attacks on politicians’ offices over the war in Gaza because of misguided fears it would promote social division. He also said much of “the media focus on the 9 October demonstration at the Opera House was on the precise words used by the mob, instead of on the appalling purpose and nature of the demonstration per se”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese appointed Richardson to conduct an inquiry into potential security failures following the December 14 terror attack in Bondi. His probe was then rolled into the royal commission after Albanese bowed to pressure to hold a wide-ranging inquiry, but Richardson and Bell had insurmountable differences about how the royal commission should work. Richardson said he felt he was being treated as a “highly paid researcher” and expressed concern the royal commission would not include substantive recommendations about intelligence and policing in its interim report.



“I reached a view that, rightly or wrongly, my voice was not going to carry much weight at all,” he told this masthead this year. Bell will hand down her final report on December 18, just four days after the first anniversary of the worst terror attack in the nation’s history.

World.title: Christchurch police close to arresting psychiatric patient before murder - inquest
World.content:
Christchurch police were close to arresting a psychiatric patient for attacking a nurse shortly before he murdered a woman while on community leave from Hillmorton Hospital, an inquest has heard.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home on 25 June 2022.

Hussein was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 13 years in November that year.

He had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

At the time of Waka Tunidau's death, Hussein was allowed to leave Hillmorton on unescorted community leave but failed to return when required.

On Tuesday, the inquest heard a nurse had complained that Hussein had tried to stab her in the neck with a shank in December 2021 but she was able to fend him off.

Before the attack Hussein was said to have been brooding over being declined leave.

Waka Tunidau family lawyer Nikki Pender put to another nurse giving evidence that it had been a serious attack.

"It was potentially a very, very serious assault wasn't it? If she had been taken unawares and he had stabbed her in the neck, it could have been fatal couldn't it? It was that level of severity," Pender said.

The nurse agreed, saying she was aware of the incident and a complaint being made to police.

The inquest heard that police emailed Hillmorton Hospital staff in February 2022 to say they were intending to arrest and charge Hussein and were seeking assistance to ensure it was not too disruptive.

Police then took a further statement from a staff member on 14 June and told them that police were about to arrest Hussein.

Pender said the process took some time, partly because police were under the impression that Hussein was in a secure unit and would not be released into the community.

The nurse who reported the attack said one of the reasons she laid the complaint was because she was concerned that Hussein might be released, Pender said.

The inquest heard that Hussein made a hot cup of coffee and threw it at nurse in 2018.

He was still serving the sentence for his 2012 crimes, so was transferred back to prison.

On the day of Waka Tunidau's murder Hussein was irritable and unhappy about staples being removed from a magazine, telling the nurse who took them out that they were "cruel, not kind".

Another nurse who was working in the unit on 25 June said that it was important to recognise that forensic health care staff were working with patients not prisoners.

"So people being able to go into the community as safely as possible was always something that in pyschiatric nursing was really important because when people aren't in their community it impacts their mental health further," the nurse said.

"For Mr Hussein at that time was there was a significant recognition that being institutionalised and contained within the environment negatively impacted his mental state."

When Hussein was feeling upset or not at a "complete calm baseline", giving him leave to go for a walk or to McDonald's was useful, the nurse said.

The nurse agreed that leave was used therapeutically at times when Hussein was agitated and upset.

Another nurse told the inquest that the unit was under "super stress" at the time of Waka Tunidau's murder.

He said there had been a lot change in systems and staff at the unit, the team was "ragged" and many people had not worked there for long.

Less experienced staff sometimes took on special patients, which was a particularly hard job and a "bit of a nightmare", and was the case at the time of Waka Tunidau's death, the nurse said.

"You've got stressed nurses, some burnt out, some of the time I am too, and everybody is trying to do their best but there are holes in the system," he said.

On Monday, the inquest heard Hussein had left the hospital on 35 occasions and returned without incident between being granted leave in late April 2022 and the day of Waka Tunidau's murder.

Her family has questioned how he was ever assessed as safe enough to leave the hospital on his own.

World.title: 'I understand how that sounds': Police push back on Tom Phillips finding
World.content:
Inquiry into handling of the Tom Phillips says harm overlooked by agencies Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

While Oranga Tamariki is admitting fault and failure in the Tom Phillips case, police are pushing back on the finding that it could have been prevented or ended earlier.

Police Deputy Commissioner Jill Rogers told Checkpoint host Lisa Owen she remains proud of what police investigators did to recover the children.

Phillips died in a shootout with police a year ago, nearly four years after disappearing from Marokopa with his children.

Government ministers apologised after the release of the damning report into the handling of the case on Tuesday afternoon.

Multiple instances of missed opportunities were found, including police failing to begin a search after the disappearance and again after the discovery of Phillips' ute, failing to pass on details about Phillips' alcohol use and concerns about his safety with firearms, and Oranga Tamariki dismissing concerns raised by the children's mother and failing to inform the Family Court of those or the police investigation.

Agencies working together, the inquiry found, could have prevented the children's disappearance and brought them back sooner.

Rogers said the report highlighted "occasions when we didn't get things right, but I will point out that it also highlighted just how complex this investigation was".

She acknowledged that did not excuse police failings in the case, calling the report a "learning document and a lessons identifying document", but pushed back on the idea the children's disappearance could have been prevented or ended early as the report claimed.

"We don't know that there would have been different outcomes. We had an extremely determined father there. He had nothing to lose, and so every activity that we did was couched in the full awareness of the risk that he posed," she said.

"We've publicly said that we accept the recommendations. But we are also aware the report acknowledges the effort and the diligence of those investigators and what they did over those four years.

"The outcomes, we just don't know what, and when it would have ended."

She said police regretted not following up a sighting of Phillips in May 2023, saying that had been a "golden opportunity" to narrow down the area he was in, but "it was never as simple as just going into the bush to get him out".

"It was picked up at a later stage by another officer ... it was too late but we don't know that that changed the outcome or the timing of when we recovered the children."

Authorities could have prevented Tom Phillips disappearing with kids Checkpoint Download MP3 14m

The discovery of Phillips' abandoned ute had been "assumed that that was another staged effort by Tom Phillips to divert us away from his activities".

Owen: "There's a few assumptions going on here, Jill."

Rogers: "There are, and I understand how that sounds when you add them all together. But what I would say is the report also highlights over the four years the extensive work that shows that despite some delays, the activities that the investigative team did do didn't bring up any of the results that people thought or assumed would come from a normal investigation."

Rogers acknowledged it was "stark reading" to see the magnitude of failings but said "this was a complex, unique, and never-anticipated event".

She said that did not justify the mistakes made, and there was "such a degree of sadness amongst those investigators".

Rogers: "Did we get some things wrong? Yes. Did we miss some opportunities? Yes. Were we slow to react to some things? Yes. But would it have changed the outcome? No.

Owen: "How do you know it wouldn't have changed the outcome ... you can't know that."

Rogers: "Yeah, our mission was always to recover the children. That was always our priority, and you know I remain proud of what those investigators did in recovering the children."

Amanda Malu. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Oranga Tamariki chief executive Amanda Malu told RNZ they had "failed the children and the mother and older sisters".

"We did not listen and pay anywhere near as much attention as we should have to what the mother and sisters were telling us, and we didn't speak with our police colleagues anywhere in anywhere near enough detail," she said.

"This is one instance, and it had awful consequences for these children, and I'm deeply sorry about that. I do know that we have made a number of changes since ... that really addresses any concerns around implicit bias and ensures that we are taking the views of all family members into account."

Malu, who was appointed to head Oranga Tamariki in December, said there was still work to do there, "and that's why I am here".

"I understand the concerns, and it simply isn't good enough ... I am seeking some further answers."

She said she had not been chief executive when an affidavit from an older sister of the children was ignored by the social worker who received it.

"I can't speak to why they were ignored. I can tell you though that you know I I am absolutely blown away by their perseverance and the courage that they showed.

"It's not acceptable. We've been down this road before, and I'm not prepared to go down it again. I think we need to step up our game as government departments."

World.title: Missing Hoon Hay woman found
World.content:
A woman reported missing in Christchurch has been found, safe and well.

Stacey left her Hoon Hay home between 8am and 9am on Monday for a routine walk. She did not return and family were unable to locate her, despite making enquiries with friends and associates.

Earlier, her family said her disappearance was out of character and they were becoming increasingly concerned for her welfare.

World.title: Possible hung parliament as Labour and National slump in latest poll
World.content:
Both major parties are below the 30 percent mark with less than two months until the election, according to a new poll.

The latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, funded by Infrastructure New Zealand, shows neither the current coalition bloc nor the opposition bloc would have the numbers to form a government, with both blocs on 60 seats.

Since the last of this poll in June, Labour has slumped by 7 points. It remains in the lead, but only just.

National has also fallen, by 2 points, while the Greens, New Zealand First, and ACT have all gone up.

For the first time in this poll, the Opportunity Party is above the 5 percent threshold, but its numbers are still not enough to help the left bloc into government.

Labour: 28 percent (down 7)

National: 27 percent (down 2)

Greens: 14 percent (up 4)

NZ First: 13 percent (up 1)

ACT: 9 percent (up 1)

Opportunity: 6 percent (previously included with 'other')

Te Pāti Māori: 2 percent (no change)

Other: 2 percent (down 1)

According to The Post's calculations, which assume that parties win electorate seats broadly in line with their share of the party vote, and retain at least one electorate seat each, the coalition bloc would have 60 seats, while the parliamentary opposition would have 53. Add in Opportunity's 7 and that leads to a hung Parliament.

Those numbers could change if there is an overhang, as Te Pāti Māori has been campaigning on.

In the preferred prime minister stakes, Chris Hipkins is on 45 percent, up 1 point from June's poll. Christopher Luxon is down 2 points to 35 percent. A further 16 percent of people chose neither, while 4 percent were unsure.

A majority of voters also still believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, with 56 percent saying so. Those feeling the country is heading in the right direction numbered 27 percent.

National Party campaign manager Simeon Brown is dismissing the poll, saying the the only poll that matters is election day, and National remains focused on winning.

Luxon was reluctant to discuss the poll with reporters at Parliament on Tuesday, saying he remained focused on "the only poll that matters" - the election.

"I don't comment on polls," he said.

"You may think that's important to you. It's not important to me."

Luxon insisted he was getting a "great reaction" from New Zealanders on the ground and felt "really positive" about the road ahead.

"I'm enjoying this campaign, loving getting out and about and seeing people and finding out how actually how we help them."

Hipkins was more reflective, acknowledging Labour needed to lift its performance in the poll.

"It's not where we need it to be. We're going to be fighting hard to get our numbers up," he said. "Look, I'm happy that we're ahead of National, but I want us to do significantly better than that."

Hipkins said Labour would be fighting hard to earn every vote. He believed New Zealanders were upset with the "whole political establishment" right now.

"They are working hard, they are playing by the rules, they're doing everything right, and they feel like they're going backwards.

"That means that they're really frustrated and annoyed at the moment. I hear that and I feel that. I am determined to change that."

World.title: Former NZ First MP and party leader's brother Jim Peters dies
World.content:
Former MP Jim Peters has died, with Parliament holding a moment of silence to honour him on Tuesday.

James Leonard Peters, the brother of New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, was himself a NZ First MP between 2002 and 2005.

He was also appointed a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2008 for services to local body affairs, education and the community

Speaker Gerry Brownlee informed the House of his passing on Tuesday, and requested MPs stand to observe a period of silence to mark his memory in respect.

NZ First paid tribute to Jim Peters in a post on Facebook on Tuesday evening.

"It is with deep sadness that we mark the passing of New Zealand First life member and former Member of Parliament, Jim Peters MNZM," the post said.

"Jim dedicated his life to public service, education, and regional development. A widely respected educator, he shaped countless young minds throughout his career - serving as head of department at Mount Albert Grammar School in Auckland, as principal of Northland College in Kaikohe, and later leading tertiary education as pro vice-chancellor Māori at the University of Auckland.

"His commitment to service in politics saw him elected as chairperson of the Northland Regional Council and in 2002, Jim entered Parliament as a list MP for New Zealand First.

"Within New Zealand First, Jim was a foundational figure. A stalwart life member and long-serving electorate chairperson, he was revered across the party for his quiet wisdom, integrity, and principled guidance.
