World.title: Police appeal after woman assaulted while putting rubbish out in Wellington
World.content:
Police are appealing for witnesses and footage after a woman was assaulted by two men in Wellington's Mount Victoria.

Police were called to Austin Street about 11.40pm last Wednesday after the woman was randomly approached while putting rubbish out for collection.

Detective Senior Sergeant Tim Leitch said the two men were standing on the footpath a short distance south of Derby Street before speaking briefly to the woman and producing weapons.

The offenders fled after neighbours heard the struggle and came to her assistance.

The woman suffered wounds to her arm.

The two men then ran south along Austin Street. A police dog handler tracked them to Porritt Avenue, where the trail was lost near the intersection with Ellice Street.

"We suspect they had a vehicle parked there and fled in it," Leitch said.

Both men were described as muscular and wearing dark hoodies. One was about six feet tall, with the other slightly taller.

One was wearing a face covering, while the other had dark hair and a dark complexion.

World.title: Conservationists call on bird-watchers to help save one of NZ's most endangered birds
World.content:
Amateur bird-watchers are being called on to help with the great bittern bird count.

The bittern Matuku-hūrepo lives in wetlands around the motu and is one of New Zealand's most endangered birds.

There are concerns that some of its wetland habitat is being destroyed and poor water quality is affecting the birds' food supplies, with fewer than a thousand of the species left.

Every year there is a head count to see how the bittern population is tracking.

The Love Bittern project co-ordinates the great Matuku-hūrepo muster to avoid the birds being double-counted.

Project founder Wendy Ambury told Checkpoint the bittern's reclusive nature made them hard to count.

However, spring time means breeding time for the normally shy birds, and the "mighty boom" of the male makes them much easier to track.

"Their mighty boom at this time of the year, especially going into spring, their breeding season, is heard across those wetlands up to 5 kilometres away."

Ambury said the booming was a similar sound to that made by blowing over the top of a glass bottle.

"We can hear that from quite a distance away, which puts us in the unique spot where we can have listeners listening at wetlands around the country to record the boom of the male bittern as an indication of their presence."

She said humans were currently their only resource for tracking the bittern.

Bird-watchers called on to help with Bittern bird count Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

"We can actually record the direction that boom is coming from and estimate the distance to the boom as well, which means that we can triangulate the position of each booming and determine how many individuals we've got."

That helped create a population estimate.

Ambury said typically around 400 to 500 people volunteer to help with the count each year, but she is hoping to boost that number to at least 1200.

The task involves finding your nearest wetland and sitting at the edge of it, keeping an ear out for any booming bird calls.

"Record the time and try and estimate the distance and the direction to that boom [and] how many booms he's boomed before he's stopped for another break."

DOC researchers also work to put GPS trackers on the birds, which Ambury said gave them vital information about how the birds are travelling from region to region.

With over 90 percent of Aotearoa's wetlands already lost, the bittern are also being lost at great rates.

"As long as we continue to lose wetlands, we're losing that vital habitat that they need to thrive."

World.title: SA school charged after student hurt in hammer-throw incident
World.content:
Criminal proceedings have been lodged against an Adelaide school after a student was seriously injured during an athletics training incident.

A Christian Brothers College student was struck in the head with a hammer-throw ball at St Albans Reserve at Clearview on September 5, 2024.

In a statement, SafeWork SA said a worker was also allegedly "exposed to the risk of being struck".

It said it had lodged the proceedings against Edmund Rice Education Australia Colleges Ltd, trading as Christian Brothers College (CBC), in South Australia's Employment Court earlier this month.

The safety watchdog said it had charged the school with a category two offence under the Work Health and Safety Act.

"It is alleged that workers and students participating in athletics training at St Albans Reserve, Clearview, were exposed to risks to their health and safety while undertaking javelin and hammer throw activities, in close proximity to each other, on 5 September 2024," SafeWork SA said in the statement.

"SafeWork SA alleges the school failed to provide adequate instruction or training to workers responsible for organising and supervising the athletics training and failed to ensure its safety policies and procedures were followed."

SafeWork SA says it lodged the proceedings against Christian Brothers College earlier this month. (YouTube: SafeWork SA)

The safety watchdog said it would be further alleged that the school "failed to perform an adequate hazard identification and risk assessment for the athletics training".

According to the statement, the school allegedly "failed to maintain a safe work environment" by failing to ensure the hammer throwing was not carried out in close proximity to students participating in javelin and by not using a safety cage that complied with the relevant industry safety standards.

"SafeWork SA alleges these failures exposed workers and students to a risk of death or serious injury from being struck by a hammer throw ball," SafeWork SA said.

The matter is expected to appear in the SA Employment Court at a later date.

World.title: Cowan warns BBL privatisation could 'spiral out of control'
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes that the Big Bash League doesn't need to rush privatisation to compete with other T20 leagues around the world.

A Cricket NSW board member, Cowan told the ABC Cricket Podcast fears of a player exodus to rival leagues was premature, and a move toward privatisation could "spiral out of control".

Cricket Australia (CA) confirmed earlier this month that they would go ahead with an opt-in model that allows states to take their BBL teams to market with the option of selling stakes or entire franchises to private investors.

"[In previous seasons] they've been able to reshape scheduling, to reshape international stars and the salary cap around that. We've seen already there's no friction to attracting some of the world's best players," Cowan said.

Former England captain Ben Stokes will join the Adelaide Strikers for BBL16. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde-ICC)

"Ben Stokes is going to Adelaide, Finn Allen has just signed a mega deal. So the argument that is put forward is we're gonna lose players to the South African League. We haven't lost one yet.

"There's a view that the business could be run more effectively, which would enable some time to work out whether you actually do need to sell your star assets or not.

"Because when you start burning the furniture to warm the house, it can spiral quickly out of control from there."

The BBL has, in recent seasons, reshaped the fixture of the competition to make it shorter and in turn has increased viewership and attracted some of the games biggest names.

In the 2025/26 BBL season fans were treated to the likes of Colin Munro, Chris Jordan, Muhammed Rizwan and Sam Billings tearing up the competition. Coupled with Australian Test stars like Steve Smith, Alex Carey and Mitchell Starc who joined the tournament after their international duties finished.

Steve Smith has played 40 matches for the Sydney Sixers, including 6 in BBL15. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Compare that with recent seasons of The Hundred where Mitchell Marsh, Adam Zampa, Jos Buttler and Trent Boult were some of the biggest name players in that competition, all of whom have played in the tournament or are set to play in the upcoming BBL16 season.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

Cricket Australia believes that privatisation would allow the BBL to keep up with other T20 leagues around the world, like The Hundred in the UK and the SA20 in South Africa.

"There are opportunities now for our best Australian players to play in other leagues at the same time potentially with bigger salary caps. So when we talk about should we wait for two years or four years? No, we can't wait," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"Those challenges are on our doorstep today. So we've got to make some decisions about how we compete.

"We're a relatively small country in a big global sport. So it's incumbent on us to make decisions that we can compete with elsewhere and that's exactly what we're doing."

Cricket NSW has been the most vocally opposed to the current model, while Queensland Cricket has also said it will likely have further questions but intends to hold on to its BBL franchise for the time being.

Mitch March playing for the Leeds Sunrisers in The Hundred in the UK. (Getty Images: Annabel Lee-Ellis)

"We will closely monitor the sales process and at this stage, intend to retain 100 percent ownership of the Brisbane Heat, but of course remain open to private investment at the appropriate time," Qld Cricket Chair Kirsten Pike and CEO Terry Svenson said in a statement.

Meanwhile, Cricket Victoria is in support of the move, and will be the first to sell a license with the Melbourne Renegades set to be put to market to be sold in full.

"Private investment will unlock value for reinvestment across Victorian cricket, from the grassroots through to the elite game," Cricket Victoria Director Shaun Richardson said in a statement.

CA and the state's cricketing associations will continue negotiations ahead of the BBL16 and WBBL12 seasons starting, which are likely to be the last seasons involving the original eight franchises.

World.title: Dockers will not be 'ambushed' by 'galvanised' Swans, Longmuir vows
World.content:
Many see it as a golden opportunity for Fremantle to reach just their second AFL grand final, but Justin Longmuir insists there is no chance the Dockers will underestimate a Sydney side missing a host of star players in Friday night's preliminary final at the SCG.

Fremantle is set to enter the game as warm favourite, despite being away from home against a team which thrashed reigning premier Brisbane by 53 points in their qualifying final, with the Swans hard hit by suspension and injury.

When Sydney stood down Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice in the wake of the off-field scandal at a Melbourne hotel, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said they had "effectively torpedoed" their season.

Remarkably since then, they have defied expectations, beating North Melbourne just days later before the stunning upset of the Lions.

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

That was despite losing Callum Mills during the game, with the captain joining the long list of absentees, ruled out for the season with a knee injury.

Longmuir has urged his side to put its full focus on the Sydney players who are taking the field, rather than those ruled out.

"Already done that. They dropped 141 points on Brisbane who were the flag favourites, it's a wake-up call," he said.

Errol Gulden and the Swans are undermanned but coming off a dominant qualifying final win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They didn't seem to miss those guys, so we just play what's in front of us.

"Clearly they haven't lost any of their scoring power, and all I can go on is what I see from the last two games, and playing like a really galvanised team, playing with great spirit, great physicality.

"It looks like whatever has happened has galvanised them, and they're playing a really tough brand of footy.

"We're definitely not going up there and getting ambushed by what they're trying to do. We've seen [it] in the last couple of weeks and we've seen it work really well.

"We've got to make sure that we don't just think it's going to happen for us, we've got to make sure we impose our footy."

Longmuir calls for no fear

The Dockers rebounded from their qualifying final loss to Hawthorn with a 14-point semifinal victory over Geelong, with Longmuir pleased with how his players took the contest on against the Cats.

Luke Jackson was instrumental in Fremantle's semifinal win and shapes as a big factor against Sydney. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

He urged his side to not to be afraid of making mistakes on the big stage, and to always be prepared to move on to the next contest.

"If we're going to make mistakes, let's make sure we make mistakes playing our way and playing with the right mindset, because usually those mistakes you can move on from a little bit quicker," he said.

Dockers show they have the steel to be AFL's best Fremantle booked a spot in the AFL preliminary finals with a stirring win over Geelong, breathing life into the club's premiership dream.

"At times we didn't make those mistakes the right way against Hawthorn and we stood still after, because we didn't move on from them.

"It's been a message for a long time because we play such an imperfect game, players who have played their best games would've been full of mistakes. It's just the nature and the scrappiness of our game, so let's make them with the right mindset."

The Dockers are set to fly to Sydney on Wednesday, with the two clubs naming their teams on Thursday ahead of the clash.

World.title: The moment this Knights finals rookie will hold on to forever
World.content:
Last Friday's semifinal win over South Sydney was one of the great nights in Newcastle's recent history, and nobody enjoyed it more than Jermaine McEwen.

In his first finals match, the 21-year-old had the game of his young life, inspiring the 20-10 upset victory that has the whole Hunter dreaming big ahead of Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.

McEwen scored the first double of his NRL career and ran for 187 metres, the best mark of his 37 first-grade matches, and set the tone for the Knights' right-edge defence with a physical brutality that would make a mafia kingpin proud.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

On a night of many highlights, McEwen's personal favourite was his second try that helped Newcastle kick clear in the second half, as he backed up winger Dom Young to score right in front of the Knights faithful.

McEwen crawled the last few metres before slamming the ball down so hard it's a wonder they could dig it out of the turf.

"The only reason I slammed it was because my parents and my family were right in front of me. I just looked at them, and I was like, 'hell yeah,'" said McEwen.

"That was the best moment I have ever had in my footy career. That moment right there, that's something I will hold forever. So I am just super grateful and so happy."

McEwen's first try of the evening helped get things started as he again trailed Young after the Englishman claimed a bomb inside the first five minutes.

It brought Newcastle into the match and gave the team the start they needed en route to their first away finals win since 2013 and just their third since their last premiership 25 years ago.

Repeating the dose in Auckland is a tall order, but even before the win over Souths, McEwen and his teammates did not lack for belief.

"The Knights have given me everything, and I believe in the coach, Justin (Holbrook). He's allowed me to be the greatest version of myself on that field," said McEwen.

"But when I put the ball down and looked up and saw all the fans, I was (thinking) how happy I am to be a Knight. I'm just so grateful.

"We just wanted to go out there and play with energy and lift each other up."

Newcastle's right edge did a fine job shutting down South Sydney's attack. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

McEwen spent much of the week thinking about how the Knights would shut down South Sydney's left edge, which is just about the most dangerous attacking weapon in the NRL.

Between them, Alex Johnston, Latrell Mitchell, Tallis Duncan and Cody Walker scored 63 tries in 2026, two more than Newcastle managed as an entire club last season.

But McEwen, Sandon Smith and Dane Gagai rose to the occasion magnificently, locking onto the superstars and refusing to let go, moving and defending as one.

Souths did end up scoring down the left through Jye Grey, but only after McEwen had left the field late on.

"When you have challenges, you get more prepared for it. You think about it more. When you're at home or training, you get flashbacks of what you have to do," said McEwen.

"When I have Cody Walker and their left edge — they do it the best in the whole comp. Cody Walker, he is just so good at that stuff.

"Us in D, we had a big job to do, and we just went out there and did it."

Jermaine McEwen and the Knights will look to pull off another finals ambush this Sunday against the Warriors. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The journey through this year to Sunday's knockout final has not always been smooth for McEwen.

He was suspended for one match in June after being charged with low-range drink driving, an incident for which he apologised unreservedly and left him "deeply ashamed".

At the time, McEwen said he let his community down, and he's been trying to make amends ever since.

"Bro, at the end of the day we're all human and just because I play footy doesn't mean I'm special," said McEwen.

"In those circumstances, with the rollercoaster (of this year), that has taught me a lot in life.

"I feel like people can either shy away from it or own up to it. I wanted to show up for the fans and show them what I could do, and repay them in that way."

"Because I know how much the town speaks to this club and the hold this club has on the town. I wanted to repay them with good footy."

A sellout crowd is expected at Eden Park on Sunday, and a win would send Newcastle to just its second preliminary final in the last 25 years.

They'll again be underdogs against a Warriors side that beat them just three weeks ago, and the match marks the biggest game of McEwen's career, as it is for several of his teammates.

But the same was true last Friday, and by leaning on the experience of men like Gagai and prop Tyson Frizell, McEwen was inspired to make a difference, and all he wants is to do it all over again.

"These are experienced boys who have been in the game for a lot of years, and when you have them talk to you, it makes you more comfortable," said McEwen.

"You're not nervous. You're going out there to do a good job."

World.title: HYROX apologises after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
World.content:
A founder of HYROX has apologised after an athlete who suffered sudden faecal incontinence mid-competition was allowed to continue, with the incident sparking rule changes after backlash online.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk experienced the medical episode during the competition that she went on to win in Beijing at the weekend.

The incident went viral on Chinese social media, with videos of her competing while visibly soiled shared widely.

HYROX sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) holds the HYROX Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

Following the incident, many online criticised HYROX's health and safety standards, while some also questioned athlete responsibility.

"Blast HYROX. Blast the race director," Chris Hersh posted on a HYROX community Facebook page.

"But please leave the athlete alone or have a tiny bit of empathy for someone that really just was in a horrible situation and got zero assistance from anyone in a high pressure, make a decision on the fly scenario."

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste took to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," Fürste said in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

He said that new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

Following the event in Beijing, HYROX World issued a statement saying that "protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".

HYROX China said the competition area was cleaned after the competition finished and relevant equipment was removed.

It also said it would replace the floor at the venue to protect future athletes.

The incident went viral in China, with many taking aim at HYROX organisers and rules. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

Wietrzyk, an elite HYROX athlete, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

The ABC has also contacted HYROX for comment.

Event's growing popularity

HYROX is held in indoor venues, with a consistent race format that lets athletes compete against each other worldwide.

Organisers say it suits both elite athletes and people trying to improve their general fitness.

Chinese netizens have described HYROX as "paying to do farm work", with an individual entry fee of 799 yuan (about $170), on top of the cost of training and equipment.

The sport has attracted Chinese celebrities, including elite athletes, singers, and actors, helping it reach beyond the traditional fitness crowd.

Hybrid training is a healthy social media trend Thousands of social media followers are trying out the hybrid training model, but it's not something to dive straight into.

Some Chinese media have even dubbed HYROX "the new identity card of the middle class".

HYROX held its first event in mainland China in November 2024, attracting fewer than 1,700 contestants.

By 2025, average registrations had surged to 5,079 per event — more than three times the previous year's figure, according to Grace Yu, research director at Daxue Consulting.

"China's HYROX scene is heavily community-oriented, with doubles and relay formats accounting for roughly 66-72 per cent of Beijing participants across 2024-2026," Ms Yu said.

By April 2026, the #hyrox hashtag on Xiaohongshu, known as RedNote outside China, had surpassed 130 million views and generated more than 780,000 discussions.

World.title: Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris re-signs with reigning premiers
World.content:
Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris has signed a two-year contract extension, tying him to the club until the end of 2029.

The 21-year-old, who earned his first All-Australian blazer this year, was set to be one of the biggest names on the market at the end of next season.

The signing comes as the Lions prepare to take on the Hawks in a preliminary final on Saturday at the MCG.

"There’s no point dragging [contract negotiations] out if I know what I want to do, and I wanted to stay at Brisbane," Morris said.

"I wanted to just get it done and now I can focus on this week, and hopefully the next few years will be exciting."

Morris kicked 67 goals in the 2026 home-and-away season, finishing second in the Coleman Medal behind Sydney's Charlie Curnow.

It marks the third huge signing coup for the Lions in a week, after Zac Bailey and Dayne Zorko also extended their careers with the club.

When asked about interest from other clubs that may have made higher offers, Morris said he had not given much thought to the money.

"I just thought … more about what I'm happy with and the team that I'm at; I don't want to leave a team where I'm happy where I am mentally and I've got a good group of mates," he said.

"I think playing within a good team that’s got good values and playing with all my mates is more valuable to me than a bit more money, so that's what it ultimately came down to."

World.title: Ella Heads cops big ban for bump that broke star Demon's jaw
World.content:
Port Adelaide defender Ella Heads has been handed a three-match AFLW ban for her bump that fractured the jaw of Melbourne's Eliza McNamara.

McNamara had just fired off a handball in Sunday's 51-point win when Heads ran in and collected the midfielder front-on with her shoulder.

A dazed McNamara had blood coming out from her face as she was assisted from the ground.

The 24-year-old was taken to hospital, with the Demons confirming on Monday she had undergone surgery, with no timeline set for her return.

The incident was classified as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, drawing a three-match ban.

"That was a really poor challenge," former AFLW star Kate McCarthy said.

"It was probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen on the AFLW field in regards to being late, being high and just being really careless and not eliciting that duty of care that we now know is placed on you as an AFLW player when you elect to bump."

That equates to a quarter of the 12-round home-and-away season, and Heads will miss games against Sydney, the Western Bulldogs and Adelaide unless Port can downgrade the charge.

In other tribunal news, West Coast's Abbygail Bushby was handed a one-match ban for her clumsy collision with the Brisbane Lions' Sophie Peters.

Peters had her head over the ball when Bushby ran in and tumbled over her opponent.

Richmond's Montana McKinnon was handed a one-match rough conduct ban for her run-in with St Kilda's Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw.

World.title: India refuses to accept Asia Cup cricket trophy from Pakistani minister
World.content:
Political tensions between India and Pakistan have spilled onto the cricket field again, with India's women refusing to accept the Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) chairman Mohsin Naqvi.

India dominated from the start to win the tournament for a record eighth time, beating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final in Dubai.

After winning the toss, India scored 5-183 before dismissing Sri Lanka for 111 in 20 overs.

The presentation ceremony was delayed nearly an hour, during which the Indian team conducted its own medal presentation, with Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia presenting the best fielder medal to Nandani Sharma.

Naqvi — chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board and the ACC, as well as Pakistan's interior minister — stood on the dais with several ACC officials, but the Indian team did not appear to receive medals or the trophy, with social media footage showing them leaving the field as the officials waited on stage.

The ceremony ended abruptly after medals were presented to the Sri Lankan team and match officials, and Naqvi presented the runners-up cheque to Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu.

"This is BCCI's stand [to not take trophy from Naqvi]. We can't say anything on this," India coach Amol Muzumdar said.

"India are officially the champions. Trophy or no trophy doesn't matter to us.

"For us, this tournament is over, we are the champions. That's good enough. It was on the big board that India are the champions of Asia Cup 2026."

Cross-border tensions between India and Pakistan brought the two countries to the brink of war last year, with the acrimony also spilling onto the cricket field. Indian cricketers have avoided handshakes with Pakistan players and refused to accept the trophy and medals from a Pakistani official at several tournaments.

The Indian men's team beat Pakistan three times in the Asia Cup, including the final, but Suryakumar Yadav's team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi and did not shake hands with Pakistan players in any of the three games.

The Indian women's team did not shake hands with the Pakistan team in its match earlier in the tournament, after which Muzumdar also said: "That stand has been taken by BCCI and we stand by it."

Tech.title: GM updates its trucks’ native software to coexist with CarPlay
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

General Motors is polishing up the software experience in its bestselling trucks in an effort to reduce the amount of dangerous tapping and swiping that’s required to access the most-used controls. It’s also giving Apple CarPlay and Android Auto spiffy new picture-in-picture displays — which is notable given GM’s previously stated hostility to phone mirroring in its electric vehicles.

When the next-generation interface makes its debut on the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 later this year, vehicle owners will see a number of changes, including slick new graphics for its advanced driver-assist system, animated transitions between displays, and simplified layouts for heavy-duty truck stuff like trailering and off-roading. And they’ll be seeing it all on 60-plus inches of screen real estate — the combined size of instrument cluster, central display, and passenger screen in some of its trucks — that’s designed to enhance but not overwhelm the driving experience.

For GM, larger displays do not necessarily mean more distractions. Instead, the automaker views the additional space as an opportunity to be smarter about how information is presented and to make interactive elements larger, said Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Larger buttons and bigger tap zones can make the system easier to operate, particularly under difficult driving conditions, he said.

“The buttons can be larger and make it easier to do,” McCormick said. “Living in Michigan, the roads are terrible, so I’m trying to tap on a very small tap zone while hitting a bunch of potholes. These larger displays give you better functionality in that standpoint.”

Previous Next





1 / 4

There are still plenty of physical buttons for key functions like HVAC. But when you want to control the direction of the airflow, a new menu appears as a flyout. Customers have repeatedly professed their love for physical controls, so GM understands that moving key functions onto the screen just because there’s more real estate doesn’t necessarily earn them any goodwill. There are some formerly tangible tools that are now becoming digital only. The oil dipstick, for example, is now a virtual measurement that exists on the truck’s status screen. But the majority of the physical touchpoints remain physical.

Borrowing from the world of smartphone design, GM’s designers added a swipe-down notification interface for quick access to functions such as switching connected devices, entering settings, and privacy controls. Truck owners can disable the vehicle’s microphone directly from this interface, for example. The new interface also distinguishes between settings, which vehicle owners will likely visit once and then rarely ever again, and controls, which they may want to tweak more frequently.

GM wanted to address the complaint that its existing interface can feel disjointed because various functions abruptly take over the entire display, McCormick said. So rather than constantly replacing the entire screen, displays such as the media player can remain visible while an additional queue panel slides in from the side. By using animated transitions, the automaker is hoping to create a more contextual experience when moving between functions.

Lots of truck owners love to haul trailers, so GM put a particular focus on that experience with its new software designs. Trailering information now appears both in the driver information display and in the smaller homescreen card. The trucks include built-in trailer-aware navigation, so once a trailer is connected, the vehicle identifies it, and Google Maps can provide a route that accommodates the trailer. Customers enter the trailer’s dimensions, and those measurements can be carried from one vehicle to another through the customer’s GM account.

Previous Next

1 / 2 GM is using picture-in-picture for Apple CarPlay…

But it’s when using Apple CarPlay or Android Auto that Chevy and GMC truck owners may see the most noticeable differences. Again, engineers were hoping to use the added screen real estate “intelligently,” McCormick said. And they didn’t want phone projection to completely take over the truck’s native infotainment, nor did they want to force customers to choose between them.

The solution: picture-in-picture phone mirroring, in which CarPlay and Android Auto occupy a large contextual card rather than taking over the entire screen. When a phone is connected through CarPlay, the phone icon changes into a CarPlay icon; selecting it brings up CarPlay within that large card. Pressing the native home button returns the driver to the split-screen home view. This allows customers to use Apple’s apps while retaining access to native GM functions, like trailering info.

The new layout is even more interesting when you consider GM’s seismic decision in 2023 to drop Apple CarPlay and Android from its EVs. Despite pushback from customers, GM has stood by its decision, arguing that it can deliver a better software experience to its customers without phone mirroring. GM CEO Mary Barra even suggested (in an interview on Decoder) the ban would eventually extend to the automaker’s gas-powered trucks and SUVs — only to walk it back days later.

That’s left GM to tweak CarPlay and Android Auto’s appearance in its Chevy and GMC trucks to enable the native GM-branded software experience to peek through. Phone projection will no longer occupy the entire screen, which McCormick argues was forcing drivers to switch back and forth when they needed to access their truck’s native controls. In this way, truck owners can choose to project their phone while also accessing key information, like trailering or off-roading details, McCormick said.

“I think we’re landing in a spot where… we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection, or, oh, I want to use the native system,’” he said. “That’s our sweet spot.”

The new UI will roll out to new Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks later this year, but only to new customers. Existing owners will be stuck with the previous-generation experience. The goal was to put the new interface on GM’s “bread-and-butter” trucks rather than first introducing it on lower-volume vehicles, which is more typical for a new experience, McCormick said. GM is so confident in the system that it’s launching it on its bestselling trucks so it can get in front of as many customers as possible.

GM sells close to 900,000 of these trucks a year, meaning the company expects to receive a substantial amount of feedback once the new interface is live and being used by customers. Some aspects of the first version may work extremely well, while others may need to be changed.

”We’ll take that experience, and the OTAs will allow us to get there,” McCormick said.

Tech.title: Microsoft issues emergency Windows 11 update to fix its record-breaking patch
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft has started rolling out an emergency out-of-band update to fix problems with its record-breaking September patch Tuesday update. The software giant patched nearly 1,000 flaws in its biggest update ever this month, but it also introduced some bugs that have affected businesses, developers, and gamers.

The September patch Tuesday affected folder shares on Hyper-V-based Linux virtual machines, Remote Desktop Services sessions, and some USB audio devices. Microsoft’s out-of-band update, released yesterday, addresses these issues across Windows 11 versions 26h1, 25H2, and 24H2. Microsoft has also released updates for Windows Server 2025 and 2022, the LTSC versions of Windows 10, and Windows Server 2012 and Windows Server 2012 R2.

In the past it was unusual for Microsoft to issue out-of-band updates to Windows, but it has become far more common this year. In January, the company was forced to issue four out-of-band updates after a buggy Windows 11 patch. In March, the company then had to issue two emergency updates because of installation failures and Microsoft account sign-in problems. Microsoft also released an out-of-band update in July to address an Intel driver issue that was causing performance issues and battery drain.

Tech.title: Volvo’s plug-in hybrid XC60 and XC90 can really go the distance
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Most plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEV) today get an average of around 30–50 miles of battery-only range: decent, but not mind-blowing. With hybrid sales dominating the market today, Volvo is out to prove that its PHEVs can push the limits of what’s possible.

Today, the Swedish automaker revealed the updated PHEV versions of its popular XC60 and XC90 SUVs are its first “long range plug-in hybrids,” delivering class-leading ranges of 78 miles and 73 miles, respectively. That’s more than double the electric range of previous PHEV variants. The numbers are still preliminary and based on EPA testing standards. But if confirmed, they would make Volvo’s PHEVs “the longest electric range of any plug-in hybrids available in the American market,” the automaker claims.

Volvo took a page from its all-electric vehicle design by integrating the battery directly in the floor of both vehicles for improved efficiency. The batteries are also higher capacity — 41.2 kWh (37.9 kWh usable) for both — and able to send more energy to the motors, which are also more powerful.

Previous Next



1 / 3

Of course, those batteries are just dead weight if owners forget to charge them — which tends to happen with a lot of plug-in hybrids. Hybrid owners often neglect to charge, thanks to the gas tank that continues to power their vehicle even with a dead battery. Still, the higher capacity batteries in the XC60 and XC90 are sure to appeal to a lot of car shoppers who may still like the sound of increased range even if they don’t exactly plan on taking full advantage of it.

The XC60 is getting new styling to bring it inline with Volvo’s new design language. That includes an upgraded grille, redesigned front bumper, hood, front wings, rear bumper, tailgate, new wheel designs, and a refined “Thor’s Hammer” LED headlight light signature. Like the redesigned XC40, the XC60 also has a more expansive driver assist that includes Automatic Emergency Steering and Braking, collision prevention, and a door-opening cyclist alert.

The addition of Google’s Gemini chatbot as the new voice assistant rounds everything out. Volvo was one of the first automakers to adopt Google’s software for its infotainment systems, so naturally that now includes Gemini.

Production on the XC60 and XC90 begins late Fall 2026, with customer deliveries scheduled to begin in early 2027. Volvo is hoping that a boost in hybrid sales can help fund its future pure EV models, like the EX50, EX60, and new affordable model that will replace the EX30.

Tech.title: Valve is still figuring out ‘how and when’ to do Steam Deck 2
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Now that Valve has finally launched its entire 2026 hardware lineup — the Steam Controller, the Steam Machine, and today’s Steam Frame — are we any closer to a next-gen Steam Deck handheld? Valve isn’t saying so yet. The company is figuring out “how and when we can deliver something like that,” Valve designer Pierre-Loup Griffais now tells IGN.

Valve has been clear for years that 1) a Steam Deck 2 will indeed happen, and 2) it’s not coming until Valve finds the right chip. The original Steam Deck worked because it delivered the right combination of price, performance, and battery life, and Valve has repeatedly said it won’t sacrifice efficiency in the sequel.

“We also don’t want more performance to come at a significant cost to power efficiency and battery life,” Griffais told me in 2023, saying he wanted to see a “leap” instead — but suggesting that leap might not be physically possible for another couple of years.

Earlier this year, Valve got my hopes up that the wait for a chip was over — when Griffais revealed the team was “hard at work” on the next Steam Deck gaming handheld in an interview with IGN. He wouldn’t say when it might happen. I assumed that was caution, because RAMageddon had already pushed the company to delay and reprice the Steam Machine and Steam Frame headset by then.

Today, IGN’s new question was: “Has the current hardware shortage impacted the way Valve is thinking about actually putting a Steam Deck 2 into development?” Griffais’ immediate answer was “Not really.”

That could be good news for impatient gamers — or it could mean that the company will wait out RAMageddon before it dares intercept the silicon supply chain again. Valve originally wanted to build a “far more affordable” headset, for instance, but instead it faced brutal RAM negotiations to eventually arrive at a $1,059 price tag.

The real question is: Has Valve yet identified the future chip that will appear in the Steam Deck 2? Because the company will work backwards from that chip’s availability to create the hardware it lives within.

Intel’s Panther Lake handheld chip in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus is the first I’ve tried that comes close to the kind of “generational leap” that Griffais has been talking about, but Panther Lake handhelds are incredibly expensive, and the Intel chip wasn’t a silver bullet in my tests. But I bet Valve has seen the future of Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm chips, and maybe a future one will do the trick.

I hope a Steam Deck 2 will kick-start a new golden age of handheld gaming; I fear it may cost too much for that.

Tech.title: Is Big Tech’s AI slowdown a safety pact or a cartel?
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotted an ulterior motive immediately. The AI titans had declared that their aim was to “pace the frontier,” signing on at least partially to a proposal for embedding third-party auditors, regulating domestic labs, and reaching a global slowdown agreement. Their critics, however, argued they simply wanted to stop would-be competitors, kneecap the open-source movement, and avoid real legal safeguards — some dubbed it an outright “cartel.”

The truth is more complicated, according to sources across the industry. The three-step proposal, laid out in an essay by Amodei, is calling for changes long espoused by AI safety advocates. While it could become a substitute for regulation, under Trump, substantial regulation is unlikely anyway. But experts say that on an issue that’s only likely to grow in importance, AI leaders aren’t the best people to lead the charge.

“The industry as a whole needs new champions,” said Nick Reese, an adjunct professor at New York University and the Department of Homeland Security’s former director of emerging tech policy. “We’ve looked at people like Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk as these people who are closest to the problem and working on it every day, and they’re the ones who know best. But the truth is there’s never been a realistic vision for what we’re building toward.”

“The industry as a whole needs new champions.”

Concerns about AI advancement have been escalating for months, sparked largely by revelations that swarms of agents were behind rogue hacks going on right under the noses of leading frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. Reports from both companies fueled the fire, as did the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who posted a public letter explaining his choice. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote, adding that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is “acting responsibly” and rather “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Dire warnings about AI aren’t anything new inside the industry, but Coxon’s letter seemed to break containment. It’s been viewed more than 170 million times on X alone, while Coxon and his story have made the rounds in newspapers and on TV.

To a significant chunk of AI safety researchers and AI nonprofit workers, however, this is simply drawing more attention to an already widely discussed issue. “A lot of people are thinking of this as Dario’s idea, or it’s coming from the CEOs, but that’s false,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, an ex-OpenAI employee who now leads the AI Futures Project, an AI research nonprofit. “People outside the companies have been calling for this for years … There’s been this growing chorus of voices saying, ‘Please don’t build superintelligence soon. We are not ready. You need to slow down.’”

Kokotajlo said that after years of people “yelling at them to do this” — including more than 1,000 AI lab employees signing a public letter from July, which called for a slowdown in AI development after the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — the CEOs are “now bowing to that pressure and also claiming credit for it, [although] not rightfully.”

Overall, a handful of sources told The Verge they believe that the verbal agreement made by the AI leaders is a step in the right direction. NYU’s Reese said he “do[es] not think it’s all hot air.” Apollo Research CEO Marius Hobbhahn called it “a good idea,” saying “it’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.” The Midas Project’s Tyler Johnston said it was a “good sign.” Redwood Research CEO Buck Shlegeris said it was “some great news — obviously it’s hard to know whether this is going to convert into anything real, but I’m feeling cautiously optimistic.” All agreed, though, that there was still a lot of work to do to make this verbal commitment a reality, particularly when it comes to making it an ironclad agreement.

“It’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.”

Many still question the motivations of AI’s leaders. The larger tech industry has spent years getting ahead of regulation by lobbying for its own preferred rules or promising self-regulation. Big platforms have proposed policies that could hit smaller competitors harder, using altruistic language to justify self-serving goals. They’ve been accused of safety-washing, or making meaningless changes that give the false impression of actual safeguards. It’s no surprise people are concerned this will happen in the AI industry as well, particularly since AI labs’ voluntary safety frameworks have been criticized for years.

Several sources believe that concerns of safety-washing are valid. “There’s a serious concern that they’re not actually going to slow down,” Kokotajlo says, adding that the fear is that “they’ll just bring in some external auditors, do a bunch of safety paperwork — some of which will be genuinely good — but at the end of the day, it actually won’t slow them down very much at all.”

NYU’s Reese compared this gambit to the social media platforms’ playbook a decade ago, when companies began calling for regulatory action to get ahead of impending, less favorable laws. For the AI industry, Reese said, “the hammer may not come in this administration, but I think if there were a Democratic administration after the next election, there would be a really good possibility.”

That kind of regulation would be vital, said Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. She said any voluntary framework is essentially regulatory capture and that “we should not be letting the foxes run the henhouse. This is not an opportunity for Congress to once again outsource responsibility to industry.” Daniel Lobo-Lewis, co-founder of the Political Integrity Project, said that voluntary regulation will likely go the way of Meta’s largely toothless Oversight Board.

Most people also, however, believe companies are in no imminent danger of regulation, besides the model pre-release review periods AI labs have agreed to under the Trump administration. President Trump posted on Monday that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He also called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at a conference — Trump told the crowd on speakerphone that recent concerns about AI were a “hoax” and that “the robots will not be taking over.”

As for concerns that regulation could hold back other companies or open source developers, calls for slowdowns have been almost exclusively aimed at big frontier AI labs defined by exact size metrics, many industry experts told The Verge.

With no government AI regulation incoming, the best option may be to push companies into an immediate, measurable, and enforceable agreement. Kokotajlo’s AI Futures Project, for instance, proposed AI labs giving auditors access to their compute budget — and pledging to decrease their compute budget for research significantly, which would then slow down AI advancement and allow other AI labs to catch up. (Amodei’s essay already called for AI labs to allow external third-party auditors — like METR, Apollo, and Redwood Research — to embed within their organizations to some extent and potentially be able to flag, and blow the whistle on, problematic findings.)

“If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”

Arguably the single biggest challenge to an AI slowdown can be summarized in one word: China.

AI leaders and politicians alike have long positioned China as the reason why US AI progress can’t slow down — because no matter how dangerous the technology may become, they’d rather it be in US hands than Chinese ones, and China won’t pump the brakes. Lobo-Lewis compared China fears to the Cold War missile gap. One X user wrote, “If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”

Redwood Research’s Shlegeris said it wasn’t in the best interest of neither the US nor the Chinese government to pursue AI development in a “reckless” way, adding that “it would not be unprecedented levels of international coordination.”

“[People are] taking for granted that China won’t cooperate,” Johnston said, adding, “This is an issue so serious and so widespread that it seems like it’s in everyone’s interest to coordinate on it, in the same way it was in both the US and Russia’s interest to coordinate on nuclear de-proliferation.”

On Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did push back on the calls for a slowdown, calling it “fearmongering.”

The Midas Project’s Johnston and Redwood Research’s Shlegeris both said that even in the absence of Chinese cooperation, it’s still vital to encourage US coordination. And for the Tech Oversight Project’s Haworth, the slowdown presents an opportunity to “position ourselves as the compass for how AI technology can be developed and used.” She sees arguments to the contrary as part of a familiar playbook. “China gets brought up as a bogeyman every time that an industry wants to escape oversight.”

Kokotajlo simply compared the situation to a cartoon he’d seen, with people in a car driving off a cliff. He recalled the speech bubble saying something like, “Hooray, we’re ahead of China.”

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

The issue underlying all the recent panic is a milestone known as recursive self-improvement, and based on the industry’s current trajectory, we’re only hearing the beginning of the alarm bells.

RSI refers to a potential industry milestone at which point AI models can train, advance, and create new versions of themselves — all without human involvement. Anthropic has said this point could come as soon as early 2027, and OpenAI’s chief scientist wrote earlier this month that OpenAI is directing a lot of resources towards reaching this goal. Increasingly, engineers and researchers in the AI industry worry that RSI precedes a whole host of new and more serious AI concerns, including more severe cybersecurity incidents that more deeply impact society at large.

Amodei cited RSI as a major factor in his decision to call for a slowdown: “since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster.” He wrote in his recent essay that RSI is “starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic … Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.” Amodei proposed implementing “some kind of ‘speed limit’” on the rate of RSI and compared it to caps on missile numbers.

In Jacob Coxon’s resignation post from Anthropic, he warned of “superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.” Many other researchers at leading AI labs echoed his concerns. It’s “hard to overstate how dangerous” it is to speed towards RSI, wrote Jasmine Wang, an OpenAI researcher. Vishal Maini, an ex-Google DeepMind employee, said RSI is “now so imminent that no other option makes sense.”

Fears about RSI can easily turn apocalyptic. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” Samuel Marks, an Anthropic researcher, wrote on X “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” Another Anthropic researcher and team lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote on X that “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” (He put the chance at greater than 10 percent over the next decade.) Alex Turner, a former Google DeepMind employee, wrote that “many researchers believe they are building something that could kill everyone on the planet. It was literally my day job to think about how to stop that.”

Micah Carroll, an OpenAI researcher, wrote that Coxon’s belief is a “cross-partisan position” with research teams across “all frontier AI companies,” and that they all believe that “business-as-usual AI development poses unacceptable catastrophic risk.”

“But,” Carroll added, “we should also not hyperstition catastrophic risks into existence – they can be greatly reduced via safety requirements with teeth, international coordination, and a consensus to not build [artificial superintelligence] unless there are sufficient safety advances to make us collectively confident to do so.”

That kind of “international coordination” is exactly what AI leaders, and the public at large, are now calling for.

“We have never been in a situation where we actually understood what we were driving towards with regard to AI,” NYU’s Reese said. “We’ve always had this amorphous undefined end state that we don’t really understand but we have to beat China to get to. It’s really hard to race when we don’t even understand the path or even understand what the finish line is — or even if there is one.”

Tech.title: Apple Home’s new security camera features cost as much as $60 a month
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

With the public release of iOS 27 and tvOS 27, Apple Home is getting an injection of Apple Intelligence — but you’ll have to pay more for it.

Apple Intelligence for Home brings AI-powered video summaries to HomeKit Secure Video, so you can get short text descriptions of who and what compatible security cameras saw, along with the clip. It also adds a new video search feature and the ability to stitch footage from multiple cameras into one clip, making it easier to keep an eye on what’s happening around your home without scrolling through footage.

AI-generated video summaries provide text descriptions of what a camera sees.

But to get these features, you’ll need to pay $9.99 a month for the 2TB iCloud Plus plan (or $39.95 a month for an Apple One Premier subscription) — and that’s just for one camera. According to an Apple support page, to add Apple Intelligence to a second camera, you’ll have to pay $29.99 a month for the 6TB plan. For up to five cameras, it’s a whopping $59.99 a month for the 12TB plan. No word on whether you can add more than five cameras. (Recordings from HomeKit-connected cameras don’t count toward your storage quota.)

That’s way too expensive. While the improved video features are useful — I’ve been testing them in beta and have been impressed — they’re not good enough to justify that big a price jump.

HomeKit Secure Video has always been behind a paywall, but it started at a very reasonable $1 a month. That’s for the 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which includes recorded footage from one camera, plus smart alerts and facial recognition. For more cameras, you bump up to 2TB / $9.99 a month (up to five), and 6TB / $29.99 a month or higher for unlimited cameras. But the cost for the Apple Intelligence features is a huge increase.

Previous Next





1 / 4 Apple Intelligence requires the 2TB $9.99 a month plan, for more cameras you need to upgrade to 6TB or 12TB.

I currently pay $40 a month for Apple One Premier, which includes 2TB of iCloud storage and gets me HomeKit Secure Video support for five cameras. With the new pricing tier, I keep those benefits and now get Apple Intelligence on one camera. But to get it on all five cameras, I’d need to pay an additional $60 a month. That’s $720 a year, for a total of $1,200.

Amazon’s Ring and Google Nest charge around $20 a month for subscription tiers that include similar AI-powered features for their cameras, and both companies offer more features than Apple currently does. An iCloud Plus plan does include storage for photos, files, and device backups, and higher plans may get you higher limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features, but Apple hasn’t released any details about that.

The good news is that none of this changes what you get with the standard HomeKit Secure Video today, and the new software releases have added under-the-hood upgrades that improve speed and reliability, plus the service now supports 4K video resolution. The change only applies if you want the new Apple Intelligence video features. But while Apple Intelligence feels like a significant improvement for Apple Home, at these prices, the value just isn’t there.

Screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Tech.title: What execs and politicians are saying about slowing down AI development
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Dario Amodei kicked off a flood of statements over the past few days about AI safety by publishing a long essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” detailing why AI development should be slowed down. Other AI leaders and politicians are speaking out in favor of or opposing his points, and we’ve compiled some of them here.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

Amodei’s Saturday morning essay outlined three steps for pacing AI development: embedded third-party evaluators that can verify if a company is adhering to safety practices and commitments and report incidents, coordination between frontier AI companies in democratic countries on standards and limits, and global coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments on pacing AI development “to the extent this is possible.” Amodei said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing to the first of these steps.”

However, Amodei noted that pacing “does not mean halting model training or technical progress, ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman said shortly after Amodei posted about his essay on X. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” Altman also committed to having independent evaluators at the company, calling it a “great idea.”

On Sunday, Altman said OpenAI welcomes “a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI.” He added that OpenAI hopes other companies “learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes.” Like Amodei, Altman also said that “When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”, noting that progress should be “slower than it otherwise could be.”

Altman also noted two ways that he thinks AI progress “could go very badly”: losing “control of the future to AI” and ending up “in a world with too much concentration of power,” which he said can be avoided by “walking a narrow middle path.”

Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis

“Dario’s essay points towards the right path forward,” Hassabis said in reply to Amodei’s essay. “The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.” Hassabis also pointed to a framework for an AI standards body he published in July.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk

“Dario is right,” Musk said, reposting Amodei’s essay.

US President Donald Trump

In a rambling Monday morning Truth Social post, Trump pushed back on the idea of an AI slowdown:

The only control or “guardrails” that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! The Trump Administration has stopped AI “people” from doing bad, or potentially bad, “things,“ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a “perfect little angel” - and we will continue to do so! We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE! Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

While taking a call from Trump onstage at an event and putting the president on speakerphone, where he said that “the robots will not be taking over,” Huang said that “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.”

US Vice President JD Vance

Vance said that he feels it’s a “little bit weird” that frontier AI tech companies are “kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them” and added that it “feels a little bit to me like a bit of a trojan horse.” He also pointed to the President saying that “we know the Chinese are engaged in this long term AI race against the United States.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson

As part of a Sunday interview with Jake Tapper on CNN, Johnson said that “I think the leaders and the providers of all these platforms… They need to come together in a meeting with us and sit down and figure out what the right balance is. We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us. And that’s the challenge. It’s national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.” It’s unclear if or when this meeting might actually happen, but Johnson said he would do it “tomorrow.”

Senator Bernie Sanders

Sanders said he agrees with Wall Street Journal columnist and former Ronald Reagan speechwriter Peggy Noonan, who published an article titled “Pause AI for Humanity’s Sake.”

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg

“For Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real, is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and to the world,” Buttigieg said in an NBC News interview. “There need to be safeguards, there need to be rules, there need to be limits, there needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI.”

Former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks

”Dario has written that we need to ‘pace the frontier,’ and Sam has agreed,” Sacks said in a long post on X. “People may be surprised by my response: go ahead.” Sacks also told them to “stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission” and “stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.”

Former FTC Chair Lina Khan

”Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products,” Khan said to kick off a long post on X. “We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.”

Former Vice President Kamala Harris

“We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development,” Harris said as part of a thread, adding that “A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest.“

Former Meta Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun

“Dario was already claiming that GPT2 was too dangerous to open source back in 2019,” LeCun said in a reply on X. “I made fun of them then. Everyone should make fun of them now.”

Update, September 14th: Added more statements.

Tech.title: Trump throws out power plant climate pollution rules
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Environmental Protection Agency announced its plans today to kill any remaining standards on how much greenhouse gas pollution power plants are allowed to emit in the US. The move will only make electricity dirtier as AI, electric vehicles, and a revival of domestic manufacturing drive up power demand.

The EPA’s proposal today is a major escalation of President Donald Trump’s efforts to promote fossil fuels while making it easier to build out energy-hungry data centers. Environmental and consumer advocates, meanwhile, are fighting back — arguing that Trump’s deregulation spree comes with higher costs for the environment, public health, and Americans’ pocketbooks.

A major escalation of President Donald Trump’s efforts to promote fossil fuels while making it easier to build out energy-hungry data centers

“Failure to limit climate pollution means more children ending up in the emergency room with asthma attacks and heatstroke, more families struggling to rebuild homes after harrowing storms,” Moms Clean Air Force director and cofounder Dominique Browning said in an emailed statement. “It means higher health care bills, higher insurance costs, and more economic struggle at a time when Americans cannot afford it.”

There is scientific consensus that greenhouse gas pollution from fossil fuels causes climate change. But in its press release today, the EPA argues that greenhouse gas pollution is “out of its scope to regulate” because its impacts are “global in nature, and any potential public health harms are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the U.S. power sector.” The US has produced more greenhouse gas pollution than any other country in history and is still a leading carbon emitter after China.

The agency today is finalizing its repeal of Biden-era greenhouse gas requirements for power plants, as well as proposing the elimination of any remaining limits to that climate pollution for the power sector. The EPA claims the finalized rule would save $310 billion while the additional proposed actions would shave off $370 million “in direct compliance costs.”

Related Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute

The EPA’s proposed changes will be open for public comment for 45 days, and are likely to face a raft of legal challenges. “The Sierra Club will fight back against this reckless and dangerous proposal with everything we have in the courts, in Congress, and in communities across the country,” Sierra Club chief program officer Holly Bender said in an emailed press statement. “While wildfires rage, floods devastate communities, and families struggle to afford skyrocketing electricity bills and insurance premiums, the Trump administration is handing the fossil fuel industry a license to keep polluting.”

Tech.title: New Italian unicorn Exein rides the physical AI wave
Tech.content:
Europe has a new unicorn: Italian startup Exein has just raised a $270 million funding round led by Headline at a $1.7 billion valuation on the promise of providing a cybersecurity layer for physical AI — an evolution of its initial focus on IoT.

“The concept of Exein is that every device should be able to defend itself, regardless if they are connected to a secure network or not,” CEO Gianni Cuozzo told TechCrunch. The Rome-based company has been doubling down on this approach; its latest product, Photon, is a runtime security solution to prevent attacks at the kernel level of a device.

This approach requires working in close partnership with manufacturers, and Exein says it has been doing so since its inception in 2018. According to Cuozzo, the choice to work directly with OEMs and silicon vendors was driven by the conviction that connected devices were on the rise.

This created significant tailwinds for Exein, which claims to have secured more than 2 billion connected devices in sectors where cyberattacks could be paralyzing, including aerospace, industrial automation, automotive manufacturing, energy, healthcare, and semiconductors.

The startup expects its growth to be sustained by the rise of physical AI, which uses the same supply chain. Cuozzo noted that his product can cover AI-powered robots, drones, self-driving cars, sensors, smart appliances and other connected devices running models on the edge.

Investors seem to agree: Exein says that its latest round was significantly oversubscribed. Its valuation has increased thirty-fold since its Series B some two years ago, and more than doubled since it secured equity and debt in December 2025 following its Series C earlier last year.

Besides valuations, AI has also boosted attackers’ capabilities. According to Cuozzo, this is being facilitated by open-source models that can run without guardrails, and make it much easier and cheaper to target physical devices in novel ways.

Exein has already seen an increase in what Cuozzo calls “machine-speed attacks,” and intends to respond with a foundational model for Physical AI security. The company is currently training the model on machine data and telemetrics, and plans to have it ready in the first quarter of 2027.

In the meantime, Exein intends to use the fresh funding for M&As to complete its portfolio of products, and hire staff to accelerate its expansion in the U.S. and in the Asia Pacific, which currently drives half of its revenue.

Cuozzo said being spread across three continents has been Exein’s main challenge so far. The breadth of its presence took some adjusting to, but it has borne fruit, he said, noting that the company is “growing 400% year on year.”

While such growth numbers are often hard to maintain, Exein could get a hand from the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act, whose reporting obligations kicked off last week. The Act will come into full force in December 2027, and requires manufacturers to “make sure all digital products are safe from cyber threats.”

Pictured from left to right: Gerardo Gagliardo, CFO & co-founder; Gianni Cuozzo, CEO & founder; Giovanni Alberto Falcione, CTO & co-founder.

Tech.title: Salesforce and Nvidia’s new reasoning model is everything the AI labs should fear
Tech.content:
A new AI model called Koa is one of the biggest announcements from Salesforce this week at its giant Dreamforce tech conference. Koa is the company’s first reasoning model, built on Nvidia’s open-weight Nemotron model. The two companies worked together to post-train Koa to excel at sales, marketing, and customer-support-related tasks.

Koa is a shining example of how the enterprise world’s needs for AI are diverging from what the frontier labs are offering. Proprietary AI labs would rather have enterprises uploading files, code, prompts, and feedback directly into their models and agents, and spending millions to do so.

But with the model, Salesforce is offering its enterprise customers:

an open-weight alternative to closed frontier models

a model trained to do specific work tasks (rather than to solve impossible math problems)

one that has not ingested any actual customer data and therefore cannot leak it to others

a model that helps reduce AI spending, since it uses fewer tokens to do the same work

one that can be automatically routed through an AI “gateway,” depending on the need

and a model that follows all of a customer’s data requirements and security embedded within Salesforce.

Koa will be provided as an alternative to the other models Salesforce offers in its Agentforce platform, where its customers build agents to handle rote tasks like answering customer service questions or scheduling appointments.

“We’ve built many small task-specific language models, which are part of Agentforce’s portfolio,” Jayesh Govindarajan, EVP of Salesforce AI, told TechCrunch. “But reasoning has always been something that we’ve relied on the frontier model providers for. Until now.”

Before Koa, if an agent needed to reason through a long-running or multi-step task, those prompts would be routed to a frontier model like Claude or ChatGPT through Agentforce’s AI gateway (the system that decides which model handles which request).

“One of the reasons we hadn’t done this before, train our own enterprise-grade frontier model — we always wanted to — but the challenge has always been the lack of a pre-trained base model to start with. Until Nemotron came along, there was no sovereign American pre-trained model that was available, one, and two, that was state of the art, and, three, that had clear data provenance. We have no idea what Qwen trains on,” Govindarajan said, referring to the popular Chinese open-weight model produced by Alibaba.

Post-training a model like this means taking it from a general-purpose system to one well-versed in sales and customer support knowledge, and to do that, Salesforce and Nvidia did not use any actual data from Salesforce’s customers. Instead, they crafted synthetic data that mimicked customers’ patterns.

“We actually simulated a customer service environment with a persona customer service professional, including irate customers that call into the customer service center, all the way to a sales professional who’s trying to close a deal,” Govindarajan described.

Koa is meant to be better at the work tasks Salesforce customers want an agent to do — and cheaper, in terms of tokens burned — than sending those same tasks to Claude or ChatGPT.

With Nemotron, “we have a unique architecture for inference to be token efficient,” Kari Ann Briski, Nvidia’s VP of Generative AI Software for Enterprise, told TechCrunch. “It’s kind of the trifecta of things that you need to have: sovereign AI, time to first token, efficient reasoning, for the tokenomics of it all.”

However, Salesforce isn’t exactly abandoning Anthropic or OpenAI. It just announced a partnership with Anthropic called ClaudeForce that allows companies to use Claude as their AI interface, while their data remains in Salesforce’s system of records, secured by its infrastructure.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang took a call from Trump, and showed off something else, too
Tech.content:
In Brief

Correction: An earlier version of this piece identified the phone Jensen Huang used to take President Trump’s call as Apple’s iPhone Duo. That was incorrect — the device appears to be a different foldable. The piece has been updated to remove references to the iPhone Duo and the conclusions that were based on that error.

Jensen Huang made headlines Monday at the All-In conference in L.A. when President Trump called him, live, on stage. But there was something else worth noting about his appearance. Huang, dressed in his now-signature alligator leather jacket, was handed a foldable phone to answer it.

Once he got Trump on speaker, the conversation turned to AI safety, and the two seemed to agree that mounting fears about AI equate to what Trump called a “hoax.” Trump argued that the real winners of the AI panic are China and “political people,” and that the technology is too big — “bigger than the internet,” he said — to slow down over. (“Did you hear that? Thousands of people are clapping,” said Huang to Trump during this same exchange.)

Whether Huang truly shares that same view or isn’t in a position to say otherwise, we’ll never know. Nvidia’s business model depends largely on AI labs buying more chips, so downplaying existential risk is the only move if he cares about his company’s share price. (It’s still up 33% for the past year but fell a few percentage points today.)

Tech.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang tells Trump ‘we’re not going to let [an AI slowdown] happen’
Tech.content:
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was onstage at the All-In Summit on Monday morning in Los Angeles, he got a phone call that he couldn’t send to voicemail — it was from President Donald Trump.

“I’m onstage with the besties,” Huang told Trump, referring to the venture capitalists who host the podcast All-In, including tech investors Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and White House advisers David Friedberg and David Sacks.

In a move that will spark night terrors for public relations professionals everywhere, Huang flaunted his comfort with the president by putting Trump on speaker for conference attendees to hear.

Holy crap POTUS just phoned in @JensenHuang live on stage at All In Summit



We will not lose the ai race! And whatever Dario said this weekend won’t stop our progress
